exp.0:11:
It says that each of these living creatures moved straight ahead, in the direction its face pointed. They went wherever the Spirit wanted them to go, and as they moved they did not turn or change direction. The phrase about moving straight toward the front of the face simply means "straight forward." "Spirit" can be understood as the Spirit of God or as the will that moved them; scholars interpret it both ways.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon beside the river Chebar. He recounts a vision God gave him: living beings with four faces beside a throne of glory. This vision showed him that God was still governing, even far from the temple in Jerusalem.

For today: we can learn to follow God's guidance with determination, without looking back or being led off course. Before deciding, pray and seek his direction in the Bible. Then move forward with firmness and confidence in what he shows you.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that the living beings Ezekiel now sees in the temple have the same appearance as the ones he saw beside the river Chebar at the beginning of his calling. "Their appearances" means their outward look, and "their appearances and themselves" means they were identical. "They went every one straight forward" means each one moved straight ahead, without turning aside.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet and priest who was exiled in Babylon. In this vision, the glory of God is about to leave the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's idolatry. Ezekiel recognizes that these are cherubim, and that it is the same God who spoke to him in exile. God's presence was not tied to one place.

For today: God remains the same in every place and circumstance. If you feel far from home or are going through a hard time, remember that he is with you, and move forward with purpose, without turning aside. Walk with confidence and with a clear direction.
exp.3:0:
God tells Ezekiel to take a tile, that is, a brick of clay still soft, set it in front of him, and draw the city of Jerusalem on it. "Draw" here means to carve or sketch. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, reminding him that he is an ordinary human being.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, together with other Jews. God asks him for a symbolic action, like a play with a message, to announce that Jerusalem would be besieged because of its sins. The verses that follow explain the siege in detail. Many of the exiles believed the city would not fall, and this gesture challenged that false hope.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity, even though at times we find it hard to accept. We can ask him to give us humility to hear his correction in time, instead of clinging to what comforts us but is not true.
exp.6:2:
It says the final moment has now arrived for Israel. God says he will pour out his anger on the people and will judge them according to the way they have lived. "Fury" is an extremely intense anger, and "abominations" are the detestable practices, especially idolatry and injustice, that the people had committed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." The message is for the land of Israel, shortly before Jerusalem fell to Babylon. After much patience, the people had again and again rejected God's call to turn back to him.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and God takes them seriously. Today you can ask him to show you what you should leave behind and return to him with sincerity, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.7:9:
He says that Ezekiel went in through the door he found in the wall and saw, painted all around, images of creeping things, of disgusting animals, and of all the idols of Israel. "Abomination" means something that God hates. "Serpents" here translates a word that refers to animals that crawl.

God speaks to Ezekiel in a vision, around 592 B.C., while the prophet was in Babylon. He shows him what was happening in secret inside the temple in Jerusalem. Seventy elders were worshiping in hiding, thinking that God did not see them. God was showing them their sin to explain why judgment would come.

For today: God sees what we do in private. We can ask him to examine our heart, confess what is hidden, and let him cleanse us, instead of living with a faith that is only for show.
exp.6:17:
They will dress themselves in mourning clothes, made of rough cloth called sackcloth. Trembling will cover them like a blanket, and their faces will show shame and confusion. They will also shave their heads, which was a sign of deep grief.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and injustice. The people had trusted in their riches and idols, and now they would see that none of that could save them.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to return to God. We can examine what we truly trust in, whether money, success, or security, and give that place to Him today, for He is the one who can truly sustain us.
exp.7:16:
God asks Ezekiel, "Have you seen this?" Then he says that what Judah was doing in the temple was no small matter, for besides filling the land with wickedness, they kept returning again and again to provoke his anger. "They put the branch to their nose" is a difficult phrase; it is understood as something that offends God. Some scholars believe it alludes to an offensive gesture, but there is no certainty.

God speaks in a vision that shows the prophet what was happening in Jerusalem. Shortly before, twenty-five men, with their backs to the temple, were worshiping the sun, something God had forbidden. Judah joined social injustice with idolatry, and God sees them together.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith in the temple or the church is sustained by a just life at home and at work. God is not pleased with a worship that coexists with injustice and with the routines that dishonor him.
exp.5:8:
God says that some who survive the judgment will be taken captive to other nations. There they will remember Him. They will understand that God suffered because of their unfaithful heart, which turned away from Him, and because of their eyes that went whoring after their idols, that is, they were unfaithful to Him like a betrayal in love. Then they will feel shame for their wickedness. The phrase "I am broken" can be understood to mean that God was deeply grieved.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Israel had abandoned God for idolatry. Even in punishment, God leaves a remnant, and his goal is that the people recognize Him and return to Him.

Today we can remember that our sin does not only break rules; it also grieves the heart of God. If anything has taken his place in our lives, let us thank him for correcting us, and return to him with humility and sincerity.
exp.2:13:
The verse tells how the Spirit of God lifted Ezekiel up and carried him away. The phrase "I went in bitterness" refers to going with a heavy heart, and "in the heat of my spirit" speaks of inner anger or turmoil. Even so, "the hand of the Lord was strong upon me" means that God held him firmly and did not let him go.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here. He lived in exile in Babylon with other deported people. He had just seen the glory of God and received the call to bring a hard message to a rebellious people. That is why it is understood that he went with a heavy heart. The text does not explain in detail the cause of his bitterness, and it can be interpreted in several ways. He then spent seven days stunned and silent among the exiles.

We can obey God even when we feel sadness or anger. He does not pull away from us because of our emotions; his hand remains firm over us. Bring to him honestly what you feel.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that the wheels moved together with the living creatures. When they walked, the wheels walked beside them; when they rose up from the earth, the wheels also rose up.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, speaks here. He describes a vision of God's glory that he received by the river Chebar. The verses that follow explain that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels, so everything moved in perfect unity. Interpreters explain the meaning of the wheels in various ways, but many see in them that God is not limited to one place.

For today: even if you feel far from everything, as Ezekiel did in exile, God remains present and in motion. Trust that He accompanies you and directs your path.
exp.5:4:
He says that God will leave the corpses of the people of Israel lying in front of the idols they worshiped, and that their bones will be scattered around their altars. The phrase "around" in this sentence is the word "round" from the verse, meaning "all around." It is a harsh image: the idols they trusted could not save them, and the places of their false worship will be filled with death.

The passage is spoken by God through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God addresses the mountains of Israel, where the people had set up altars to other gods. He announces judgment by the sword, and the final purpose is that they will know that he is the Lord.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we place our trust in instead of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. None of these can save us. Let us return to God with humility, for he wants us to know him and live.
exp.7:1:
Ezekiel sees a figure that looks like a man, made of fire. From the waist down it is fire, and from the waist up it shines like amber, a gleaming metal.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, speaks from exile in Babylon. He is in his house with the elders of Judah when he feels the hand of the Lord, a phrase that indicates God has taken hold of him to give him a vision. Soon he will be carried in vision to Jerusalem to see the people's idolatry.

Many think this figure is connected with the glory of God he saw earlier, although the text only says it has the appearance of a figure.

For today: God is holy and shows himself as he is, not as is convenient for us. Ask him to show you honestly what is in your heart, and listen to him with humility.
exp.2:9:
God tells Ezekiel to first fill himself with what He is going to say to him. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a fragile human being. "Receive in thine heart" means to keep and ponder the words deep within, and "hear with thine ears" means to listen carefully.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. Just before, God promises to strengthen him so that he would not fear a people who resisted listening. Then He commands him to go to the exiles and speak to them, regardless of whether they listen or not. First he had to receive the message himself.

For today: before speaking of God to others, set aside time to read the Bible and meditate on it calmly, letting it first transform your own heart.
exp.6:5:
It says that the end is coming without fail. The phrase is repeated for emphasis: "the end is come." The words "it is awake against you," which are not in the verse, are not needed here; the point is that the end has risen up and is coming straight against the people, like something that wakes and moves toward them. "Behold, it is come" is a warning: it is already on its way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. He addresses the land of Israel, which had fallen into idolatry and into practices that God calls "abominations." Many understand that he announces the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. God warns that the judgment is just, since it answers to the people's ways, and that it will not be a surprise without explanation.

Today we can take God's warnings seriously and not mistake his patience for indifference. If there is something in your life that you know does not please him, do not put it off. Return to him sincerely, because his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.9:2:
This verse describes a scene in Ezekiel's vision. The cherubim, heavenly beings who serve God, stood on the right side of the temple when the man clothed in linen went in. A cloud filled the inner court, that is, the inner courtyard.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet, from exile in Babylon. God is about to judge Jerusalem for its sin, and the man clothed in linen is commanded to take burning coals and scatter them over the city. The cloud points to the holy presence of God. Scholars see it as a sign of his glory and also of his judgment.

For today: God is holy and deserves our reverence. Live with a sincere heart, and when you fail, return to Him in humility. His presence corrects us, but it also invites us to come back to Him.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that God wants to give his people a new heart so that they will live according to what he commands. "Statutes" and "ordinances" are his commands and his just decisions. "Keep" means that they put them into practice. At the end appears the central promise of the covenant: "they shall be my people, and I will be their God," a relationship of belonging and closeness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Many in Jerusalem had filled themselves with idolatry. Even so, God promises to gather the scattered, to cleanse them, and to give them a soft heart, not one of stone. Obedience is the fruit of that inner change, not the starting point.

For today: instead of obeying only by your own effort, ask God to transform your heart. Pray sincerely and let his Word shape you from within.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that fear and weakness will overcome everyone. "All hands shall be feeble" means the hands will go limp and lose their strength, as if they had been knocked out of place. And "all knees shall be weak as water" describes knees that tremble and give way, like water that spills and cannot hold its shape.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. He announces judgment for their idolatry and their wickedness. Before that judgment, neither strength nor wealth will be able to save them, as the verses that follow show.

For today: let us not place our security in money or in our own strength, because they fail. It is better to turn back to God now with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.1:7:
God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," meaning simply a human being. He tells him to listen closely and not to be rebellious like the people. Then he orders him to open his mouth and eat what God gives him.

God speaks, calling Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles of Israel, a stubborn people who may not listen to him. Before Ezekiel speaks, God wants him first to receive the message. What follows is a scroll written with laments and woes, and in the next verse it becomes clear that this scroll is what Ezekiel must "eat," an image of receiving the message completely.

For today: before speaking about God to others, let his Word fill you first. Read the Bible with a heart willing to obey, not just to offer opinions.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that the visible presence of God, called "the glory of the Lord," left the entrance of the temple and came to rest over the cherubim, which are heavenly beings with wings. The "threshold" is the entrance of the house, and "stood" means it stopped in place.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon, speaks here. He describes a vision in which he sees God gradually leaving the temple in Jerusalem. This happens because the people had fallen into idolatry and sin. Some scholars see here a judgment, and also a warning that God is not bound to a building.

For today: let us not take God's nearness for granted. Let us care for our lives with humility and obedience, and remember that he remains faithful and can be with us in any place.
exp.3:1:
It says Ezekiel should portray a siege against Jerusalem. The "siege" is the blockade of the city; the "fort" is a tower or wall used for attack; the "mount" is a ramp of earth for climbing up to the walls; the "camp" refers to the soldiers' encampments; and the "battering rams" are heavy beams for breaking down gates and walls.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. He asks him to draw Jerusalem on a clay tablet (a brick of mud) and act out a siege. It was a sign for Israel, which thought the city was safe. God was warning that his judgment for the people's sin was real and would come.

For today: God speaks to us clearly before the consequences arrive. We can ask him to show us any sin we are ignoring, listen to him with humility, and return to him in time, trusting in his mercy.
exp.5:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of reminding him that he is simply a human being. He tells him to set his face toward the mountains of Israel, that is, to look at them with a firm gaze, and to prophesy against them, that is, to announce a message of judgment.

The LORD speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The mountains were places where the people had built altars and idols. By addressing the mountains, God is in fact confronting the people who worshiped there. The message is harsh, but its purpose is to make them recognize who the Lord is (v. 7).

For today: ask yourself what things in your heart are occupying the place that belongs only to God. He speaks to us with truth because he wants to bring us back to himself. Listen to him with humility.
exp.1:0:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of saying "human being" or "mortal." He tells him to stand up because he is going to speak with him. The phrase "stand upon thy feet" is old-fashioned language for "stand up" or "stand firm."

The one speaking is God. Ezekiel has just seen an impressive vision of the glory of the Lord and fell face down on the ground. God does not leave him prostrate, but raises him up to give him his mission: to speak to a rebellious people. According to the text that follows, the Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet.

For today: God treats us with respect and equips us to hear and obey him. When you feel weak or overwhelmed, ask him to lift you up by his Spirit, and pay attention to his voice, because he speaks to give you strength and direction.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that the wheels moved in exact step with the living creatures. When they walked, the wheels walked; when they stopped, the wheels stopped; and when they rose from the ground, the wheels rose with them. The reason given is that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. Here the word "creatures" refers to living beings, not ordinary animals. And "spirit" can be understood as their drive or inner force that guided them.

The passage is spoken by the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of God that he received by the river Chebar while he lived in exile in Babylon. Many understand that the vision showed God's glory present even far from the temple in Jerusalem. The exact meaning of each detail is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God is not confined to one place. If you feel far from home or in a difficult season, you can trust that he moves with you, and you can ask him to guide your steps.
exp.11:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "The word of the Lord also came unto me, saying," means the same as "the word of the Lord came to me." The word "saying" announces that the message follows right away. It is a common way in this book to mark that God takes the initiative to speak.

Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon along with the people of Judah, speaks here. God gives him a new message. According to what follows, the people heard and saw, but did not want to respond. For that reason God asks Ezekiel to represent it with a visible action, so that perhaps they would react.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Before asking him for anything, take a moment to listen. Read the Bible carefully and with a willingness to obey what you understand.
exp.7:11:
God asks Ezekiel whether he has seen what the leaders of Israel do in secret. Each one has his own room with painted figures on the walls, that is, idols. They think, "The Lord does not see us; he has forsaken the earth." The word "chambers" refers to private rooms, and "dark" speaks of what is hidden.

God speaks in a vision shown to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, about what was happening in the temple in Jerusalem. Seventy elders were worshiping images in hiding. God shows them their sin and explains why judgment is coming. They believed that God was far away or was not paying attention.

For today: God also sees what we do when we are alone. Instead of hiding something that pulls us away from him, we can confess it honestly, ask for his forgiveness, and ask for his help to change.
exp.8:9:
God says that he will show no pity and will not let the sin of the people pass. "My eye will not spare" means that he will not look on them with indulgence. "I will bring their way upon their own head" means that he will repay them with the consequences of their own path, that is, of their actions.

God speaks in a vision received by the prophet Ezekiel. Jerusalem was full of violence and injustice, and the people thought that God saw nothing. Ezekiel intercedes and asks whether God will destroy all the remnant of Israel. God answers that the wickedness is very great. Then the man clothed in linen reports that he has carried out the command, which in this chapter includes marking those who grieved over the sin.

Today we can remember that God does see, even though at times he may seem silent. This invites us to live with honesty, to reject injustice, and to seek his forgiveness with humility, without taking his patience for granted.
exp.0:4:
It says that within that cloud of fire, Ezekiel saw four living creatures. Here "living creatures" is the sense of the word, not common beasts. They had a form resembling that of a man, though, as the text goes on, with very different features: four faces and four wings.

Ezekiel was a priest and writes from exile in the land of the Chaldeans, beside the river Chebar. There, far from the temple, God reveals Himself to him in an impressive vision. The one speaking is Ezekiel, telling what he saw. Many understand that this vision shows the glory and throne of God, and that He was not limited to Jerusalem. The details of these beings are interpreted in various ways.

For today: even when you feel far from everything familiar, God is not far away. He can meet you in your own "Babylon," in a difficult season, and show you that He still reigns. Seek Him in prayer, even where you feel like an exile.
exp.7:0:
Ezekiel tells us that one day, on the fifth day of the sixth month of the sixth year, he was sitting in his house. The elders of Judah were with him. Suddenly, the hand of the Lord fell upon him. This expression means that the power of God seized him and gave him a vision.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon with other Jews. The elders had probably come to seek a word from God. According to the calendar of the exile, this happened around 592 B.C., although the exact date is calculated in different ways. Here a vision begins in which God shows him what was happening in Jerusalem.

God can speak in the midst of everyday life, even in a house and an ordinary conversation. It is good to be alert and willing to listen to him, even when we think we are only sitting and waiting.
exp.2:2:
God tells Ezekiel to eat the scroll he hands him, to fill his stomach with it. Ezekiel does so, and it tastes sweet like honey. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a simple human being. "Cause your belly to eat" means "feed yourself," and "bowels" refers to his inner being.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who will be a prophet to the exiles of Israel. Before speaking, he must receive the message completely. The scroll contains God's words, though according to the passage it also includes laments and mourning (2:10). The sweetness shows that God's word is good, even when the message is hard.

For today: before sharing the Bible with others, let it first enter your own heart. Read it calmly, meditate on it, and obey it, trusting that it is sweet and good even when it corrects.
exp.10:24:
This verse says that Ezekiel told the exiles, the people who had been carried away and were living in Babylon, all the things that God had shown him in the vision. The name of God is the LORD, and the exiles are the Jews who had been taken away into captivity.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet and priest who was himself in exile. In the vision he saw the glory of God leave Jerusalem because of the people's sin. When the vision ended, he returned to his fellow exiles and faithfully passed on the message, even though it was hard to hear. Some believe this also pointed ahead to the hope that God would remain with the exiles.

For today: when God teaches us something in his Word, we should share it honestly and with love, adding nothing and taking nothing away. Let us speak faithfully, even when the message is not easy.
exp.11:2:
God tells Ezekiel to prepare baggage, like someone going into exile, and to leave his house in broad daylight, so that everyone can see him. "Packing gear for the road" refers to the things a person takes along on a long journey. The phrase "in their sight" means "in front of their eyes." The phrase "perhaps they will pay attention" means that they might react and take notice.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. The people did not want to listen or believe that Jerusalem would be taken into captivity. That is why God uses a visible action, a prophetic sign, as a message that can be seen and not only heard. Even so, the hope that they might "perhaps pay attention" shows his patience.

For today: God still wants us to listen to him. Ask him for an attentive and teachable heart, and let your life, not only your words, speak with honesty and clarity.
exp.1:2:
God says to Ezekiel: "Son of man," meaning simply a human being, and sends him to the people of Israel. He calls them "a rebellious nation," because they had turned away from God. That rebelliousness came down from their ancestors and continued "even unto this very day."

God speaks, and Ezekiel listens after the Spirit has set him on his feet. Ezekiel was a priest and was among the exiles in Babylon. God calls him as a prophet and warns him from the start that the people may not pay attention to him. His task is to speak faithfully.

For today: God asks us to be faithful in speaking his truth with love, even when others do not receive it. Our calling does not depend on the results. We can also ask ourselves whether, in some area of our lives, we are resisting God, and return to him with humility.
exp.5:12:
God says that when the bodies of the people lie among their idols, beside their altars, on the hills, the mountaintops, and under the leafy trees, then they will know that He is the Lord. The phrase "sweet savour" refers to the incense they offered to the idols. "Thick oak" is a large tree that gives a lot of shade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The people of Israel had filled the land with false altars on the high places, and God announces a judgment by sword, famine, and plague. Most likely these words were meant to wake the people up and bring them back to God, even though it was late.

For today: everything we put in God's place, such as money, success, or prestige, ends up failing us. Today you can ask yourself what thing is receiving your best time and your trust, and give it back to the Lord.
exp.6:14:
It says there will be no way to escape. Outside the city waits the enemy's sword, and inside, plague and famine. Whoever is in the field will die by the sword; whoever is in the city will be consumed by famine and plague. The sentence that explains one of the phrases is rewritten as follows: the word translated "sword" here means the sword itself, that is, war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and its injustice. The people kept trusting that nothing serious would happen, but God says that his wrath is already determined and that no one will be able to save themselves by their own means.

For today: do not take lightly the patience of God. If He shows you something you need to correct, do not put it off. Return to Him with humility, remembering that in Christ there is forgiveness and refuge for whoever repents.
exp.9:9:
This verse describes how the four wheels beside the cherubim looked. All four had the same form, and each one seemed to be set crosswise in the middle of another, like a wheel within a wheel. Many understand that this is how they could move in any direction without having to turn.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting what he saw in a vision from God. He was exiled in Babylon with his people. In this scene, the glory of God is getting ready to leave the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The exact meaning of the wheels is understood in several ways.

For today: even when it sometimes feels like everything is moving without direction, God is not limited or bound to one place. He sees everything, moves with perfect order, and continues to govern. Trust Him and seek His presence wherever you are.
exp.3:15:
God says to Ezekiel that he will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. This means he will take away the supply of food. The people will eat their bread rationed, by weight, with anxiety, and they will drink the water measured out, with dread, that is, with great fear that it will run out.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who acts as a sign for the people. Through symbolic actions, he announces the siege of Jerusalem. Earlier, Ezekiel asked not to eat something unclean, and God allowed him to change the fuel. The cause is the people's wickedness, as the following verse says.

For today: God invites us not to take for granted what we have. We can thank him each day for bread and water, share with someone who lacks them, and humbly examine whether there is anything in our lives we should repent of.
exp.6:18:
It says that when God's judgment comes, people will throw their silver and gold into the streets as if it were worthless. That money will not be able to save them or satisfy their hunger. The phrase "fill their bowels" means filling their stomachs. Also, the gold became a "stumbling block of their iniquity," that is, what made them fall into sin.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. He announces the day of the Lord's fury against a people who had become filled with pride and idolatry. According to the following verse, they even used their jewels and precious metals to make images of their idols.

For today: money cannot give us lasting security or fill the soul. We can ask ourselves whether our riches help us do good or whether they have become a stumbling block. Let us trust God first and use what we have with generosity and humility.
exp.3:13:
Ezekiel protests before God. He says that he has never been defiled: he has not eaten an animal that died on its own (a carcass), nor an animal torn apart by beasts, nor any impure meat. He has kept himself pure from his youth until now, and no impure flesh has ever entered his mouth.

The prophet Ezekiel was a priest. God had commanded him to perform a symbolic act: to cook his bread with human waste, to show that Israel would eat defiled food among the nations. Ezekiel is distressed because he had guarded ritual purity his whole life. God answers with compassion and allows him to use cow dung instead, though the message of scarcity and anguish still stands.

For today: you can be honest with God about what it costs you to obey. He listens with patience, and sometimes He answers with mercy in the midst of a hard task.
exp.4:16:
God says he will send famine and wild animals to destroy Jerusalem. He also speaks of plague (sicknesses that spread quickly), of bloodshed (violent deaths), and of the sword, that is, the sword of war. He ends with the words "I the Lord have spoken it," which means this word is serious and will be fulfilled.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The message is for Jerusalem, whose people had turned away from God and followed other religious practices. These punishments had already been warned about earlier in the law of Moses. The tone is harsh, but it aims to help the people recognize their sin.

For today: God is in earnest, but his warnings are an opportunity to return to him. Today we can ask ourselves with humility whether there is something in our lives we need to correct, and draw near to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.3:8:
God tells Ezekiel to mix six kinds of grain and legumes (wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, or another grain), to store them in a single pot, and to make bread from them. That will be his food during the 390 days he lies on his side.

God himself speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He is commanded to portray the siege of Jerusalem with his own body. This scarce, rationed bread shows the shortage the people would suffer during the siege. Scholars debate how the 390 days should be understood, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: God speaks with seriousness, but he does not leave his people without warning. If today we feel that God is correcting us, we can listen to him with humility and return to him without delay, trusting that his purpose is to restore us.
exp.10:1:
It says that God speaks to Ezekiel and shows him some men. The phrase "plotting wickedness" means planning evil with cunning. The second phrase, "giving bad counsel," means leading others down a mistaken path. God points to these men as responsible for what is happening in Jerusalem.

God is speaking, and Ezekiel is in a vision, carried by the Spirit to the east gate of the temple. There he sees twenty-five men, among them two leaders of the people. According to the context that follows, they were saying that it was not a time to worry and that houses should be built, as if Jerusalem were a safe pot. God confronts them about their false sense of security.

For today: those who advise others, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace, should ask God for wisdom. Advice that soothes the conscience but ignores the truth ends up doing harm.
exp.6:21:
God says he will turn his gaze of protection away from them. "Turning away the face" means withdrawing his favor and his care. Then violent people will enter his secret place, which many understand to be the holiest sanctuary of the temple, and they will defile it, that is, treat it as common and unclean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had made images of idols, had filled the land with violence, and took pride even in the jewels of the temple. Because of this, God allows foreign nations to plunder it. Some debate whether the secret place is the Most Holy Place or the treasury of the temple.

For today: let us not take God's favor for granted while we live in pride or with hidden idols. Let us examine humbly what things hold his place in our hearts, and return to him soon.
exp.2:14:
Ezekiel arrives at a place called Tel-abib, beside the river Chebar, where the Jewish exiles were living. He sits down where they were sitting, and he stays there seven days, stunned, overwhelmed, and speechless.

Ezekiel is both a priest and a prophet, and he writes in the first person. He has just seen an overwhelming vision of God's glory and has received the call to speak to his people. He goes with bitterness and anger in his spirit, but with God's firm hand upon him. Those seven days of silence prepare him before he receives his mission as a watchman.

Before speaking, it is often wise to sit beside those who are suffering. Listen, accompany them, and keep patient silence. In this way God prepares your heart to offer words that are true and compassionate.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that God himself sets himself against Jerusalem. The repeated "I" adds emphasis: it will not be just any enemy, but God himself who acts.

The word "judgments" refers to punishments or just sentences. The phrase "in the sight of the nations" means that all the surrounding peoples will see what happens.

Speaking through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon, God says that Jerusalem had received God's law and lived in the midst of the nations, but rejected it, and according to the text, did not even keep the standards of the neighboring peoples. For this reason God announces a public and serious punishment.

For today: God takes seriously the way we live, especially if we claim to belong to him. We can humbly ask ourselves where we have ignored his word, and return to him without excuses, trusting in his mercy.
exp.10:10:
God says that the city will not be a pot that protects its leaders, as if they were the meat kept safe inside. The explanation of the two quoted words is not needed here, since the reader's verse already uses "caldron" and "border," so those sentences are rewritten in terms of the verse's own words: a caldron is a large cooking pot, and a border is the edge of a territory. God will judge them at the borders of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. Some leaders of Jerusalem were saying that the city's walls would protect them (v. 3). God answers that this is not so, because they followed the customs of the neighboring nations and not his commands. Many scholars connect this judgment with the execution of leaders at Riblah, but that is understood in different ways.

For today: let us not trust in places, positions, or appearances to feel secure. Our true protection is found in obeying God and in trusting his mercy.
exp.8:3:
The Lord tells the man dressed in linen to go through Jerusalem and put a mark on the foreheads of those who grieve and cry out over the evil done in the city. Those words speak of deep pain, and the abominations are practices that God detests, such as idolatry.

The prophet Ezekiel receives this vision from the Lord while the people are living in rebellion, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. God is going to judge the city, but first he sets apart, with a sign, those who are still faithful to him and who feel sorrow over sin. The judgment begins at his own sanctuary.

Today we can ask ourselves whether the evil around us still hurts us or whether we have grown used to it. God sees those who are grieved by sin and cares for them. We can pray for our family, our church, and our community with a sensitive heart.
exp.4:4:
Here God says that Jerusalem is the city he himself placed at the center, surrounded by other nations and lands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Earlier, Ezekiel had performed a symbolic act with his hair, which represented the judgment on Jerusalem. Many understand that its central location shows that God wanted the people to be a visible witness to the others. But they rejected his commands, and that is why punishment comes.

God gives us places, gifts, and opportunities so that others may see his goodness in us. Today we can ask ourselves: does the way I live in my family, my work, and my neighborhood reflect God, or does it contradict him? Let us ask him for help to obey him sincerely.
exp.3:4:
God tells Ezekiel that each day he lies on his side represents one year of Israel's sin. There would be three hundred and ninety days, and so Ezekiel would bear the guilt of the people. "Guilt" here means blame or sin, and "bear" means to carry its consequences, in a symbolic way.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Before the final attack against Jerusalem, God commands him to act out this message as a visible drama, together with the drawing of the siege. Many think the 390 days stand for years of sin of the northern kingdom or of the whole people, but scholars do not agree on the exact calculation.

Today we can learn that God does not hide the reality of sin or its consequences, and He speaks to us with clarity to lead us to repentance. If anything in our life pulls us away from Him, it is wise to acknowledge it honestly and return to God while there is still time.
exp.3:6:
Here God tells Ezekiel to fix his gaze on Jerusalem, which is pictured as a city under siege, and to have his arm bare, that is, without a sleeve, ready to act. In this way he is to prophesy against the city. The phrase "set your face" means keeping a steady and determined gaze.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. He commands him to act out, lying down and bound with cords, the siege of Jerusalem and the weight of its sin. It was a way of teaching that judgment was coming because of the people's rebellion. Some understand that the days stand for years of punishment, but scholars interpret this in several ways.

For today: God asks us to be faithful and steadfast when we speak the truth, even when it costs us. Let us speak with love and humility, without cowardice, and with our eyes fixed on Him.
exp.2:21:
The explanation says that God laid his hand upon Ezekiel, that is, he took hold of him with his power and presence. He told him to get up and go out into the field, that is, into the plain, because there he was going to speak with him.

The explanation notes that the verb "came" in this verse is the same as the word "came" in modern English, and that "told me" is the same as "said to me" in the verse above.

Here the Lord speaks with Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. God had just appointed him as a watchman, someone who warns of danger, and explained how heavy that task is. Now he calls him aside to speak with him in private. Afterward, Ezekiel sees the glory of God, falls face down on the ground, and the Spirit lifts him up.

For today: if God entrusts us with something important, first we need to set ourselves apart to listen to him. Finding a moment of quiet, without noise or hurry, prepares us to speak to others with humility, truth, and love.
exp.6:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel, called "son of man," that is, a simple human being. He commands him to announce to the land of Israel that the end is coming. The word "the end" is repeated to stress that it is certain and urgent. The "four corners" are the edges or extremes of the land; here it refers to the whole territory of Israel, leaving no place free.

Ezekiel was a prophet and priest among the exiles in Babylon. God speaks through him because the people had fallen into idolatry and wickedness, and judgment was already near. The verses that follow explain that God would act according to his ways, so that they would know that he is the Lord. Some scholars see here the fall of Jerusalem, and there is no doubt that this is a historical judgment.

Today we can take God's warnings seriously and not postpone repentance. If something in your life does not please him, bring it to him today with sincerity; his patience is an invitation to return, not an excuse to stay the same.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel.

The one speaking is the Lord, the God of Israel, and the one receiving the message is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The verses that follow show that God asks him to speak against the mountains of Israel, where the people had set up places of worship to other gods. God wants to warn them about the consequences of their idolatry.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Before asking him for anything, take a moment to listen. Read the Bible calmly and ask yourself: "Lord, what do you want to say to me today?"
exp.0:0:
This verse tells us that in the thirtieth year, on the fifth day of the fourth month, Ezekiel was among the exiles by the river Chebar. There the heavens were opened, and he saw visions of God. The word "carried away" describes people taken far from their land, that is, the exiles. The phrase "in the thirtieth year" is not fully explained in the text; some think it refers to Ezekiel's own age, others think it refers to a different way of counting time.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in Babylon with the Jewish people who had been deported. The following verse places him in the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin. God calls him to be a prophet in the middle of a wounded people, far from the temple and from their land.

For today: God is not limited to a beautiful or comfortable place. Even in exile, in sorrow or uncertainty, he can reveal himself and speak to you. Today you can pray with confidence, even when you feel far from home or without direction.
exp.1:1:
When God spoke to Ezekiel, a spirit entered into him and set him on his feet. The verse says the spirit entered him as God spoke, and that Ezekiel was lifted to his feet so that he could hear the one speaking to him. After he stood up, Ezekiel was attentive to hear what God was telling him.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He has just seen the glory of God and had fallen face down on the ground. God addresses him as a human being and lifts him up to give him his mission: to speak to a rebellious people. Some understand the spirit to be the Spirit of God; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when God calls us to something difficult, He himself gives us strength to rise. First let us listen to His voice with humility, and trust that He sustains those whom He sends.
exp.2:23:
The verse tells us that the Spirit of God entered Ezekiel, set him on his feet, and spoke to him. He was commanded to go into his house and shut himself inside. Where the explanation comments on the wording, the phrase "set me upon my feet" is the verse's own wording, and the sentence explaining the old word is removed.

God is the speaker. Ezekiel had fallen on his face when he saw the glory of the Lord in the plain. Now God raises him up and sends him to his house. The verses that follow explain that the people were rebellious, and that Ezekiel would be mute and restricted, speaking only when God gave him a message. Interpreters debate whether all of this was literal or symbolic, but the sense is clear: his silence was part of the message.

When God shows us something great, He sometimes asks us for stillness before we speak. Learn to wait for His voice, and let Him sustain you when you feel without strength.
exp.4:8:
God says he will punish Jerusalem in a way he has never done before and will never do again. The reason is "all your abominations," that is, its detestable practices, above all idolatry.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God accuses Jerusalem of being worse than the nations around it: it had received his law and his temple, yet it despised them. The verses that follow describe a terrible siege, and interpreters connect it with the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: the more we have received from God, the more responsible we are to live faithfully. Instead of excusing ourselves by what others do, we can ask him to show us where we need to return to him sincerely.
exp.7:14:
God asks Ezekiel whether he is seeing what is happening, and tells him to turn again, because he will see things that are even more serious and offensive. "Abominations" are practices that God detests, above all idolatry.

God speaks with Ezekiel in a vision, around 592 B.C., while Judah was living in sin. He takes him through the temple in Jerusalem to show him how the people mixed the worship of God with false cults. In the nearby passage, women are seen weeping for Tammuz, a pagan god. God shows this to explain why judgment is coming.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something in our hearts that competes with God, even though we keep going to church. Ask him to show you it, and open that area to him with sincerity.
exp.10:12:
It says that while Ezekiel was prophesying, a man named Pelatiah, son of Benaiah, suddenly died. Ezekiel fell face down to the ground and cried out loudly. His question is: "Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?" The word "consumption" here means total destruction, and "the remnant" refers to those who were still surviving.

Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon, and in a vision he saw the leaders of Jerusalem giving deceitful counsel. Pelatiah was one of them (Ezek 11:1). His death seemed to be a sign of God's judgment. Ezekiel feared that the punishment would leave no one behind. We do not know for certain how he died; the text presents it only as part of the vision.

For today: when you see sin and its consequences, do not remain cold. Pray with humility and intercede for others, trusting that God is just and also merciful.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that if the prophet warns the wicked person, and that person does not turn from his wickedness or from his evil way, the wicked person will die because of his own sin. But the prophet will be free of guilt. To "warn" means to give a clear caution. A "wicked" person is someone who lives without respect for God. To "deliver your soul" means to be saved from responsibility.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. God calls him a watchman, that is, a lookout who sounds the alarm when danger comes. His task was not to make people change, but to faithfully announce what God said. The decision to respond belonged to each person.

For today: if God puts it on your heart to warn someone you love, do it with love, truth, and humility. You cannot control how they will respond, but you can be faithful in speaking and leave the result in God's hands.
exp.0:25:
The explanation says that Ezekiel saw, above something like a vault spread over the living beings, something resembling a throne. Its appearance was like sapphire, a bright blue stone. Upon the throne he saw a figure with the appearance of a man seated. A "firmament" means a solid expanse, like a sky or a vault. Note that he uses words like "appeared" and "likeness": he is trying to describe something that goes beyond words.

Ezekiel speaks in the first person. He was a priest who was among the exiles in Babylon. There, far from the temple, God revealed himself to him. Verse 28 calls this vision "the likeness of the glory of the LORD." God was not limited to Jerusalem; he also reigned in exile.

For today: when you feel that your life is disordered or far from what is familiar, remember that God is still on his throne. Before asking him to fix everything, you can pause, worship him, and trust that he governs.
exp.6:26:
The explanation says that sorrow will reach everyone: the king will mourn, the prince will be covered with desolation, and the people of the land will tremble with fear, their hands left without strength. It says the people will be dismayed, filled with terror. God will act "according to their way," that is, in keeping with their conduct, and will judge them by the same measure they used to judge others. In the end, they will acknowledge that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and injustice. The preceding verses show that no one will find help: neither prophet, nor priest, nor elders. Here the blow falls on the leaders and on the common people alike.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to seek God. Listen to his Word now, correct your course, and live with honesty, because God takes seriously what we do.
exp.9:5:
God gave a command to the man dressed in linen: take fire from between the wheels, that is, from between the cherubim. The man obeyed, went in, and stood beside the wheels. The phrase "man clothed with linen" refers to a man dressed in linen.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he had during the exile. God speaks from his throne, surrounded by cherubim, and is about to judge Jerusalem. The fire this man takes is later used as a sign of that judgment. Some believe the fire represents purification and others destruction; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God acts with holiness and order, and his servants obey his word calmly. We can ask him for a heart willing to obey, even when we do not understand everything he does.
exp.2:24:
God tells Ezekiel that they will put ropes on him and bind him, and he will not be able to go out among the people. "Ropes" are cords or bindings, and "bind" means to tie up. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, emphasizing that he is a mere human being.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lives among the exiles in Babylon. God commands him to shut himself up in his house and be unable to speak, because the people are a rebellious house. Scholars debate whether the ropes were physical bonds or an image of the restrictions the people would place on him; the text does not make this clear. His silence would be a sign to them.

For today: sometimes God leads us into times of limitation or silence that we do not understand. We can trust that he keeps speaking in his own time and obey him even when we cannot see the purpose, knowing that he will open our mouths when the time is right.
exp.2:3:
God tells Ezekiel to go to the house of Israel, that is, to the people of Israel, and to speak to them with God's words, not his own. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a simple human being.

God is speaking. Shortly before, Ezekiel had eaten a scroll containing the divine message, and it tasted as sweet as honey. This shows that he first had to receive God's word and make it his own, and only then pass it on. God sends him to his own people, who spoke the same language as he did, though later it is said that they would not listen to him easily.

For today: before speaking about God to others, let yourself be fed by his Word. Read it calmly, pray with it, and let it transform you. In this way you will be able to speak with sincerity, without adding your own ideas to what God says.
exp.0:14:
As Ezekiel kept looking at the living creatures, he saw a wheel on the earth beside each of them. The text calls them living creatures; the King James Version word here is simply "living creatures," so no further comment is needed. Each wheel stood beside one of the four beings, and each of them had four faces.

Ezekiel was a priest who had been taken into exile in Babylon along with the people of Judah. He describes the vision he received near the river Chebar, when God revealed himself to him. The wheels appear as part of that chariot of glory. Scholars interpret their meaning in various ways, and the text does not fully explain it. Many see in them the presence of God in motion.

For today: even when you are far from home or going through a hard time, God is not bound to one place. He moves and is present with you. Pray today trusting that he sees you and walks with you.
exp.8:7:
Ezekiel reports that, while the executioners were doing their work, he was left alone. He fell face down on the ground and cried out to God. With grief he asks whether God is going to destroy all the remnant of Israel by pouring out his fury on Jerusalem.

God has shown Ezekiel a judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and violence. Those who had the mark were protected. Ezekiel, who was both a prophet and a priest, speaks here as an intercessor for his people. God answers that the wickedness is great, since the people were saying that he did not see, but that he would not overlook their sin.

For today: when you see injustice or sin around you, do not stop at criticizing. Pray with grief and humility for your family, your church, and your country, trusting that God is just and that he also sees.
exp.1:3:
God tells Ezekiel that he is sending him to a people of "hard faces" and "hardened hearts." That is, stubborn, brazen people whose hearts are set against change and who do not want to turn back. Ezekiel is to say to them: "Thus says the Lord GOD," meaning that his message is not his own but comes from God.

The one speaking is God himself, after his Spirit lifted Ezekiel up, since Ezekiel had fallen face down before his glory. Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile, and God calls him as a prophet to a people who had rebelled against him for generations. From the start, God warns him that the people may not listen.

For today: God asks us for faithfulness, not results. We can share his Word with humility and love, without changing it, and leave each person's response in his hands.
exp.9:20:
It says that each of the cherubim had four faces, four wings, and something resembling human hands under the wings. The cherubim are heavenly beings who serve God and accompany his presence.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision. He sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem, because the people had fallen into idolatry. Ezekiel recognizes that these are the same beings he had seen earlier by the river Chebar. The exact meaning of the four faces is interpreted in several ways, and the Bible does not fully explain it here.

For today: God is holy and above all things, but he is also present and attentive. Today we can take his presence seriously, live with reverence, and not give anything else the place that belongs to him alone.
exp.2:20:
It says that if Ezekiel warns a righteous person not to sin, and that person heeds the warning, he will live because he was warned. And Ezekiel will be free of guilt. The quoted words that the source explains as old or unusual are handled by rewriting: the warning word is simply "warn," and the word "indeed" stands in for the sense of certainty.

God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he set as a watchman, that is, a lookout for the people of Israel, who were living in exile in Babylon. His task was to warn them of the danger of sin. The previous verses show that if he did not warn them, he would bear responsibility. Here the positive side is shown: if he warns and the person listens, all turns out well.

For today: if, with love and humility, you see someone moving away from the good path, do not stay silent. Speak with respect and without judging, and let God do his work in that person. Your faithfulness counts, even though you do not control the response.
exp.6:15:
It says that some will survive the disaster and flee to the mountains. There they will be like doves of the valleys, which tend to coo with a sad sound. Each one will weep and mourn over their own wickedness. The verse says "escape," which means to get away, and the wording about sin refers to wickedness or sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their idolatry and their injustice. Even the few who are saved will not remain indifferent: they will recognize their guilt. Some scholars see in the doves an image of sorrow rather than of peace.

For today: it is not enough to escape the consequences; God seeks a heart that acknowledges its sin. Today you can confess to Him, sincerely, what you have done wrong, trusting that He forgives those who repent (1 John 1:9).
exp.10:20:
This verse says that there are people whose heart goes after what their unclean desires want and their detestable practices. God says that He will bring their way down on their own heads, meaning they will receive the consequences of what they have chosen.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the people of Jerusalem shortly before the city fell. Just before this, He promises one group a new and tender heart. Here He contrasts them with those who remain attached to idolatry. Right after this, the glory of God leaves the city.

For today: ask God to heal your heart and do not let yourself be carried away by what only pleases you. What we sow with our decisions, sooner or later we reap.
exp.1:6:
God tells Ezekiel that he must faithfully deliver his words to the people, whether or not they listen. The reason is that they are "most rebellious," that is, stubborn and unyielding.

God speaks, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. He warns that the people will be hard, like briers, thorns, and scorpions. Even so, the prophet must not be afraid. His task is not to get them to heed him, but to be faithful. Then God asks him not to be rebellious like them, and to receive his message.

For today: when you share God's truth with love, do not measure your faithfulness by other people's reaction. You be faithful and entrust the result to God. Before you speak, first listen to what He tells you.
exp.6:23:
He says that God will bring the most cruel peoples to take the houses of Israel. He will also take away the pride of the powerful, and the places they regarded as holy will be defiled. "Defiled" means treated without respect, as if they were not holy.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The people were full of violence and injustice, and they also trusted in the temple as if it would protect them. God shows that judgment is serious, and that religion without obedience does not save.

For today: let us not trust in our reputation, our religious customs, or our possessions. Let us examine the heart, put aside pride, and seek God with humility and sincere obedience.
exp.4:5:
God says that Jerusalem changed his laws and commands into wickedness, and that she did so worse than the neighboring peoples. "Changed" means turned; "ungodliness" means living without reverence for God; "rejected" means refused. In other words, they not only drifted away from God, but despised what he had taught them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, God had placed Jerusalem at the center of the nations, probably so that his people would be an example of a faithful life. Because they rejected his Word, God announces judgment on the city.

For today: the more we have received from God, the greater our responsibility to obey him. It is worth asking ourselves whether we only hear the Word or whether we truly put it into practice in our daily lives.
exp.5:13:
God says he will stretch out his hand, that is, he will act in judgment against the people. Their land will be left desolate, meaning ruined, and empty of people, more than the wilderness toward Diblath. This will happen in all the places where they lived. In the end, they will know that the Lord is God. As for Diblath, it is not known with certainty which place it was; some believe it is a variant of Riblah, but this is uncertain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The people of Israel had filled the land with idols and altars on the hills and under the trees. God announces the consequences of that idolatry, so that they may recognize who the only true God is.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart. God calls you to return to him before those things leave you empty.
exp.3:16:
It says that in Jerusalem the people will go hungry and thirsty. With bread and water rationed, they will look at one another in horror and dread, because all of them will suffer. The words "astonied" and "consume away" in the verse are explained as follows: to be astonied means to be stunned and terrified, and to consume away means to slowly grow weaker and waste away. The cause the text gives is their iniquity, that is, their sin.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. He commands him to act out a warning: to ration his own food as a sign of the siege that would come upon Jerusalem. The people had been unfaithful to God for a long time. The consequences He announces are harsh, but He had already given warning before, giving them the chance to turn back to Him.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly. If something in my life pulls me away from Him, it is wise to recognize it and return to Him soon, for His correction seeks to restore us.
exp.6:4:
God announces through Ezekiel that a calamity is coming upon his people. The phrase "an evil, an only evil, behold, is come" repeats the word to stress that the disaster is certain and very near. "Evil" here means misfortune or calamity, not only something morally wrong.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. His message is for Israel, which had practiced idolatry and violence. God says he will judge them according to their ways. Many understand this as the announcement of the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC.

For today: God warns us clearly because he wants us to return to him. If you sense that something in your life does not please God, do not put it off. Confess it today, and ask him for forgiveness and for his help to change.
exp.7:4:
God says to Ezekiel that he should look toward the north ("north" is the word used in the verse). There, beside the gate of the altar, the prophet sees an "image of jealousy," that is, an idol that provoked God's jealousy or anger. It was right at the entrance of the temple.

God speaks, showing Ezekiel in a vision what was happening inside Jerusalem. Although the prophet was in Babylon, the vision takes him to the temple. There he sees that the people were practicing idolatry in the most sacred place. God shows him this to explain why judgment would come. It is not known for certain exactly which idol it was.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something we have placed in the place that belongs only to God. These can be good things, like work or money, that become too important. Let us ask him to show us those areas with sincerity and give him first place again.
exp.2:4:
God tells Ezekiel that he is not being sent to a foreign people with a strange speech and a hard language, but to his own people, the house of Israel. The words "deep speech" and "difficult language" refer to a strange tongue, with sounds that are hard for the listener to understand.

God is speaking to Ezekiel, who has just been given a scroll to eat, a sign of receiving God's word deep within himself. Ezekiel was a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. God warns him that the difficulty will not be the language, but the hardness of Israel's heart. Foreigners, he says, would have listened better.

For today: sometimes we think the obstacle to sharing our faith is not knowing what to say. But often the real challenge is the disposition of the heart. Speak clearly and with love to your own people, and leave the results in God's hands.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying," means that a message from the Lord came to him. It is the way Ezekiel introduces a new message that he did not make up himself, but received from God. Here only the arrival of a word is announced; what God says begins in the following verse.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He tells that God gave him a message for the people of Israel. What follows is a strong warning: God's judgment was drawing near because of the people's wickedness and crooked ways. God does not speak on a whim, but to call them back to Himself.

For today: God still speaks through His Word. Before reading the Bible, we can pray with humility and readiness, prepared to listen, even when what God says confronts us or invites us to change.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel, who was a priest and the son of Buzi. This happened in Babylon, here called "the land of the Chaldeans," beside the river Chebar. The phrase "the hand of the Lord" speaks of God's power that took hold of him and prepared him to receive the message.

Ezekiel writes this as an exile. He had been carried away captive along with King Jehoiachin, far from the temple in Jerusalem where he would have served as a priest. God reveals himself to him right there, in a foreign land. This is how his calling as a prophet begins. Scholars debate exactly what "the thirty years" in verse 1 refers to, and it is best to acknowledge that uncertainty.

For today: God is not limited by the places where we feel far away or out of place. Even in times of loss or exile, he can speak to you and give you purpose. Stay attentive to his voice.
exp.3:10:
God tells Ezekiel to drink water that is rationed, only a sixth part of a hin, and to take it at fixed intervals during the day. A hin was a Hebrew measure of liquids; a sixth part comes to a little over half a liter, although exact calculations vary.

The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet exiled in Babylon. Through this symbolic act, God announces what will come upon Jerusalem during the siege: a shortage of bread and of water, as a consequence of the people's rebellion. Ezekiel lives out the message in his own body so that everyone can see it.

For today: learn to value what God gives you, like the daily bread and water, and to live with gratitude and moderation. Also remember that God warns in love before correcting; listening to him in time spares us much pain.
exp.10:7:
God says to the leaders of Jerusalem: "You have feared the sword, and I myself will bring the sword upon you." The word for the weapon here means the sword, that is, war. The phrase about fearing is simply "you have feared."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The city's leaders believed they were safe, like meat inside a pot, but they had filled the streets with the dead because of their injustice and violence. God answers that he will not protect them in their sin, but will judge them. Some scholars see here the siege of Jerusalem by Babylon; the text gives no further details.

Today we can learn that there is no true security in our own plans or in our own power. If we live with injustice, our fears can become reality. It is better to turn back to God with humility, seek his justice, and trust in his care.
exp.11:1:
God tells Ezekiel that he lives in the middle of a rebellious people. They have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear. It is not that they are blind or deaf in body, but that they refuse to understand and to obey.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel is his prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God prepares him for a sign: he will act out a departure in front of everyone, so that they may see with their own eyes what is coming. God holds on to the hope that they might take notice, although he knows how hard their hearts are.

For today: we can hear the Bible many times and still not change. Ask God for a willing heart, and when you understand something of his Word, obey it today in a concrete action.
exp.2:1:
It says that Ezekiel opened his mouth and God gave him a scroll to eat, that is, a rolled-up scroll with messages written on it. The sentence that explains the old wording, "é hízome," meaning "and he made me," has to be rewritten here for a word that appears in the verse above, so I have rewritten it: the phrase "he caused me to eat" in the verse means that God was the one who gave the scroll. Ezekiel did not swallow it by force; he opened his mouth in obedience.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. God calls him to be a prophet to a rebellious people. Before speaking, he must receive the message within himself. Eating the scroll is an image: just as food enters the body, God's words must enter the heart. Scholars agree that it is symbolic.

For today: before sharing the Bible with others, let it first nourish you. Read it calmly, obey it, and let it transform your life.
exp.11:4:
God tells Ezekiel that, while the people watch him, he is to dig a hole through the wall of his house and go out through it. The word "dig through" means to break open or make a hole. It is an instruction for Ezekiel to act like someone who leaves his house secretly.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God asks for these actions as a visible sign, since the people were a rebellious house and did not want to listen. Through them he announced that the inhabitants of Jerusalem would be taken into exile. Many understand that Ezekiel represented the people fleeing from the city.

For today: God takes seriously reaching our hearts, even through unusual methods. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his voice with humility, or whether we are hardening ourselves against what he shows us through his Word.
exp.9:18:
The explanation says that the cherubim lifted their wings and rose from the ground while Ezekiel watched. The wheels moved along with them. They stopped at the entrance of the east gate of the temple, and the glory of God was over them.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon, speaks here. He is seeing in a vision how the presence of God is leaving the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. This departure is a judgment, but it also shows that God is not bound to a building. Later, the glory stops at the east gate, and other passages speak of its return.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he does not abandon his own forever. We can examine our hearts, turn back to him with sincerity, and remember that his presence goes with us wherever we are.
exp.0:21:
Over the heads of each living creature there was what looks like a vast expanse, a kind of sky or arched dome stretched out, gleaming like an astonishing crystal. Here the word for the creatures refers to living beings in general, not to ordinary animals. The description of what was seen is about how it looked to the observer.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon along with other Jews. He describes a vision of God. Beneath that dome are the living creatures and their wings, and higher up, in the verses that follow, the throne of God appears. Interpreters differ on the exact meaning of each detail, but all of them see the greatness and holiness of God.

For today: even in times of exile, pain, or uncertainty, God continues to reign above all things. We can draw near to Him with reverence and confidence, remembering that no circumstance is beyond His reach.
exp.2:16:
God tells Ezekiel that he has made him a watchman, someone who stands guard from a high place and gives warning when danger approaches. His task is to listen to what God says and to warn the people of Israel clearly on God's behalf.

The LORD speaks. Ezekiel was living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, beside the river Chebar. After seven days of being overwhelmed and silent, he receives this call. God reminds him that he will be responsible for delivering the message faithfully, no matter how the people respond.

For today: if God gives us the opportunity to speak of Him to someone, let us do it with love, truth, and humility. First let us listen to His Word, and then share it with respect, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.2:10:
God tells Ezekiel to go to the captives, that is, the Jews carried off as prisoners to Babylon, who were his own people. He must tell them what the Lord God has said, whether they listen or refuse to hear. The phrase "whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear" in the King James Version means "whether they will hear or whether they will forbear."

God is speaking, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles. He had already warned him that the people were rebellious, so he strengthened him with a forehead as hard as diamond. His task did not depend on the results, but on being faithful to the message.

For today: when you share God's truth with love, your responsibility is to be faithful and clear, not to control other people's response. Trust that God works in hearts.
exp.7:3:
It says that Ezekiel saw there the glory of God, that is, his radiant and majestic presence. It was the same kind of vision he had had before "in the plain," probably by the river Chebar (chapters 1 to 3). Some older words: "locks" are strands of hair; "north" is the direction; "jealousy" here refers to an idol that provoked God's anger.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, tells what God showed him in a vision: he was carried to Jerusalem. There the glory of God was still present, yet the people practiced idolatry in the very temple. God shows him these abominations to explain why judgment would come.

For today: God is holy and near, even when we have turned away. We can sincerely ask him whether there is something in our lives that we have put in his place, and return to him with humility.
exp.0:8:
This verse describes the living beings that Ezekiel saw in his vision. Their wings touched one another, forming a joining between them. As they advanced they did not turn their bodies, but each one went straight forward, in the direction it faced.

Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived exiled in Babylon. He tells of the vision of God's glory that he received beside the river Chebar. These beings bear up the throne of God. Many understand that they show God's power and his perfect order. The exact details of their symbolism are interpreted in various ways.

For today: we can learn to serve God with unity and with focus. The living beings went together and without being distracted. Today we can ask God to help us walk alongside other believers, moving forward with firmness toward what he has entrusted to us, without going off course.
exp.9:19:
Here Ezekiel says that the beings he now sees are the same ones he saw years earlier by the river Chebar. Earlier he called them "living creatures." Now he understands that they are cherubim, beings who serve God and surround his throne. The phrase about the God of Israel means that they were holding up his glory.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. In this vision he sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem, a sign of judgment for the people's idolatry. Recognizing the cherubim confirms to him that it is the same God who called him at the beginning.

For today: even when we feel far from home or confused, God does not change. He is the same in every place, and we can trust that he is still present and in control.
exp.4:1:
God tells Ezekiel to use his own hair, cut off, as a sign. A third part he is to burn with fire in the middle of a drawing of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled. Another third he is to strike with the sword all around the city. The last third he is to scatter into the wind. God says that he will draw out a sword after those who are scattered.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, and asks him for a visible action. The text indicates that it represents Jerusalem and the judgment for its rebellion. Many understand it as death by fire, by the sword, and by dispersion.

For today: God is in earnest when he warns, but he does so so that we will return to him. Today we can ask him what things we should leave behind, and answer him with humility before the harm grows.
exp.9:1:
He spoke to the man clothed in linen, and told him to go in between the wheels, under the cherub, and fill his hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city. He went in while Ezekiel watched.
