Here God is the one speaking, in a vision Ezekiel receives among the exiles in Babylon. His glory is preparing to leave the temple, and the burning coals are an image of judgment on Jerusalem for its persistent sin. Scholars discuss exactly what the fire symbolizes, but the general message is clear: God acts with justice.

For today: God is holy and takes sin seriously, but he also warns us before he acts. Today we can respond to him with humility, acknowledge what we need to correct, and return to him without delay.
exp.2:26:
God tells Ezekiel that there will be times when he will leave him unable to speak, but when He gives him a message, He will open his mouth. Then Ezekiel is to say, "Thus says the Lord GOD." The phrase "he that heareth, let him hear" means that whoever is willing to listen should listen. "He that forbeareth, let him forbear" means that whoever decides to ignore the message may leave it that way. The reason is that the people are a "rebellious house," that is, a stubborn nation.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, the Lord had announced that he would be bound and would remain silent. Thus, Ezekiel would speak only when God gave him words. His message did not depend on his own opinion. Some understand this as a sign for the people, and others as a real but limited silence.

Today we can speak of God faithfully and simply, without forcing anyone. Our task is to share his truth with love; the response of each person is up to God.
exp.2:7:
It says that God himself made Ezekiel firm and unyielding to face those who would oppose him. "Face" and "forehead" speak of a person's attitude and determination. Just as the people had hard foreheads, God gives his prophet a forehead just as strong, so that he will not bend.

God speaks here, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He warns that Israel will not listen to him, not because the message is difficult, but because they do not want to hear God. For this reason he prepares him with a special firmness, so that he can carry out his mission without fear.

For today: if God asks you to speak or live with truth in an environment that resists it, do not depend on your own character. Ask God for the strength that he gives, and stand firm with kindness, without letting fear or rejection silence you.
exp.0:23:
Ezekiel tells us that he heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they moved. It sounded like great waters, like the voice of the Almighty (God, the all-powerful one), like the noise of a crowd or an army. When they stopped, they let their wings down, that is, they lowered them and let them rest.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He is describing a vision of the glory of God that he received beside the river Chebar. The living creatures carry God's throne, and the loud noise shows his greatness. Some think the phrase "the voice of the Almighty" is only a comparison; others see in it an echo of divine majesty. Either way, the text gives no further detail.

Even in the midst of difficulties, God remains great and reigns. When everything seems noisy or confused, pause for a moment to listen to him and to worship him.
exp.5:10:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to make strong gestures: strike with the hand, stamp with the foot, and lament over the wickedness of Israel. "Stamp with your foot" means "stamp hard." The "abominations" are the detestable acts of worshiping idols. The message is that the people will fall to three blows: war, hunger, and disease.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had turned away from God to follow idols, and He describes this as unfaithfulness, like a broken marriage. The punishment is not whim: God says that heart which has drifted away grieves Him, and He wants them to know that He is the Lord.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously because He loves us. It is worth asking ourselves what things occupy the place that belongs to Him, and turning back to Him with sincerity.
exp.2:8:
God tells Ezekiel that he has made him firm, like a diamond, harder than flint (a very hard stone). He asks him not to be afraid of the people, because Israel is a "rebellious house," that is, a people who resist obeying.

God is speaking, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He warns that the people will not listen to him, because in truth they do not want to listen to God. For this reason he strengthens him so that he will remain faithful, even though they reject him.

For today: when God asks you to speak or live the truth with love and people resist, do not depend on their approval. Ask God for firmness, and remember that being faithful to him matters more than being accepted.
exp.0:9:
It says that each living creature had four faces: the face of a man in front, the face of a lion on the right, the face of an ox on the left, and the face of an eagle (probably at the back).

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, a priest exiled in Babylon. He describes a vision of God's glory among the exiles. The four faces are often understood as symbols of the noblest parts of creation: intelligence, strength, service, and speed. Their exact meaning is not explained here, and there are several interpretations.

For today: even when you feel far from home or from God, He remains on His throne and is not limited to any place. You can worship Him with confidence, even in difficult times, because His glory reaches you wherever you are.
exp.1:8:
It says that Ezekiel looked up and saw a hand stretched out toward him, holding a roll of a book. In that time books were rolls of leather or papyrus, rolled up for storage. The hand holds the message that God wants to give him.

God, who has just called Ezekiel as a prophet to the people of Israel, whom he calls rebellious, is speaking. Before showing him the roll, he asks him not to be rebellious like them and to open his mouth to receive what he gives him. It will be seen afterward that the roll contains laments and painful warnings.

For today: before speaking of God to others, we need to receive his Word with humility and obedience. We can begin the day by reading the Bible with an open heart, ready to listen even to what costs us.
exp.2:25:
God says he will make Ezekiel's tongue stick to the roof of his mouth, meaning he will be unable to speak. He will be silent and unable to rebuke or correct the people, because they are a rebellious house, that is, a stubborn people who resist God. A reprover is someone who warns or corrects.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier he told Ezekiel to shut himself up in his house, and it was said that he would be bound with cords. His silence was a sign to a people who would not listen. Scholars debate whether all of this was literal or symbolic. God would only open his mouth again when he had a message from God to deliver.

For today: we do not always need to speak much; sometimes it is wise to stay silent until God shows us what to say. Before correcting someone, let us ask God to give us his words and not only our own.
exp.3:2:
God tells Ezekiel to take an iron plate, a kind of pan or sheet of metal, and set it up as a wall between himself and the city drawn on the clay tablet. Then he must turn his face toward it, as one who lays siege to it. A siege means a blockade of a city, and a sign is a warning that can be seen with the eyes.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, and sends him to act out this message before the people. Jerusalem had not yet fallen, and the people believed they were safe. Many understand the plate to represent a barrier between God and the city, though some see it as the force of the siege.

For today: God speaks to us with seriousness because He loves us. When something in your life pulls you away from Him, do not ignore it; listen to it and return to Him with humility.
exp.7:17:
He says God will respond in anger to what he has seen. He will show no pity and will not spare with his gaze. Even if the people cry out loudly asking for help, God will not listen to them.

God speaks in a vision that he shows to Ezekiel. Inside the temple, about twenty-five men, with their backs to the sanctuary, were bowing down toward the rising sun, that is, they were worshiping creation and not the Lord. In addition, the land was full of violence and injustice. God announces here the judgment on Judah, which had rejected his covenant.

For today: God takes sincere worship and justice seriously. It is not enough to be in a religious place if the heart turns toward other things. Today we can examine what holds first place in our lives and return quickly to God with humility, knowing that he offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.10:3:
God commands Ezekiel to speak on his behalf against certain men. The repetition, "prophesy, prophesy," stresses that the command is serious and urgent. "Son of man" is the title by which God addresses Ezekiel throughout the book, and it reminds him that he is an ordinary human being carrying a divine message.

God speaks in a vision. Ezekiel sees leaders of Jerusalem who plan evil and give bad advice. They say, "It is not near; let us build houses," meaning that judgment is not close at hand. They feel safe, like the meat inside the pot. God confronts them because he knows what they think and what they have done.

Today, God sees beyond our words and knows our thoughts. It is wise to examine whether we live with false security, putting off repentance for later, and to listen humbly when God corrects us.
exp.10:18:
God promises to change his people from the inside. The "inner parts" are the deepest part of a person. A "heart of stone" is a hard heart that neither listens nor obeys; a "heart of flesh" is a tender heart that responds to God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had fallen into idolatry, and God promises to gather them and return the land to them. But returning to the place is not enough; they need an inner change to walk in his statutes and truly be his people.

For today: we cannot fix our hearts on our own. Ask God sincerely to soften the areas where you have become hard, such as forgiveness or obedience, and open yourself to whatever he shows you in his Word.
exp.4:2:
God tells Ezekiel that from the hair he has cut and divided, he is to set aside a few strands, counting them, and keep them tied up in the hem of his cloak. "A few in number" means a small number, counted out. "Hem of your robe" is the edge or the end of the garment.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. With this symbolic act he announces judgment on Jerusalem: some would be burned, others would fall by the sword, and others would be scattered. These few strands kept aside show that some would survive. However, the next verse indicates that even among them some would be thrown into the fire, so God's care does not lessen the seriousness of the judgment.

For today: God sees and cares for his people one by one, even in difficult times. This invites us to take his correction seriously and to trust that his faithfulness sustains us.
exp.0:5:
It says that each of the four living beings Ezekiel saw had four faces and four wings. The word "faces" refers to the faces, and the word "living beings" in the earlier context refers to living creatures, not ordinary beasts. They had a form similar to that of a man, but with extraordinary features.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon with his people. He recounts a vision of God's glory that he received by the river Chebar. Scholars interpret the meaning of the four faces and the wings in various ways, so it is wise to be cautious. What is clear is that the vision showed God as majestic, present, and active, even far from the temple in Jerusalem.

For today: even if you feel far from your home, your church, or what you once knew, God is not limited to one place. Today you can worship him and pray to him with confidence wherever you are.
exp.2:0:
God tells Ezekiel that he is called "son of man," that is, simply a human being. He orders him to eat what he finds, a scroll, and then go and speak to the people of Israel.

The one speaking is God, who has just shown Ezekiel his glory and called him as a prophet. The people of Israel were living in rebellion, and Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. Eating the scroll is a picture: the prophet must receive and take in God's message before announcing it. Scholars agree on this general sense, though not all of them agree on every detail of the symbol.

For today: before speaking about God to others, let yourself be fed by his Word. Read it calmly, meditate on it, and obey it, so that what you share comes from a heart that has already received it.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that, under the wings of the cherubim, something resembling a man's hand could be seen. "Form" means shape or appearance. Ezekiel does not say it was a real hand, but that it had that form, and he uses it to describe what he saw in his vision.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision of the glory of God. God is about to display his judgment against Jerusalem, and that is why a man clothed in linen takes fire from among the cherubim. Many understand the hand as a sign that the heavenly beings act in obedience to God, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: God acts with order and purpose, even when we do not understand everything. Trust that he knows what he is doing, and offer him your hands to serve him in obedience.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that God explains to Ezekiel the meaning of his symbolic action: just as the prophet will eat bread that is unclean, the people of Israel will eat food that is impure when they are scattered among the nations. The nations are foreign peoples, and unclean means ceremonially impure, not fit according to the law of Moses.

The Lord speaks to Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. God had commanded him to portray before the people the siege of Jerusalem and the scarcity that would come because of their disobedience. Bread baked with dung was a sign of humiliation. Ezekiel protests because he had always kept himself pure, and God allows him to use cow dung instead.

For today: sin has real consequences, but God still speaks with mercy. If you feel today that you are living far from what God wants, listen to his voice and return to him with humility, knowing that he hears our complaints.
exp.0:17:
It says the wheels of the vision had rims or edges that were very high, so tall that they caused fear. Moreover, those edges were full of eyes all around, on all four wheels. The word for the "rims" of the wheels is rendered as the rings, and "dreadful" means that they gave great fear or astonishment.

It is Ezekiel speaking, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon with his people. He recounts a vision of the glory of God, with living beings and wheels that moved alongside them, guided by the Spirit. The eyes are usually understood as a sign that God sees everything, though not all interpreters explain it the same way. The message was that God was not bound to Jerusalem.

For today: even if you feel far from everything or in a difficult place, God sees you and continues to work. Trust that his watchful eye and his guidance accompany you wherever you are.
exp.1:4:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Israel, whether they listen or not. The word "whether" here means "perhaps" or "maybe," so the sense is that the people may or may not listen. The important point is that, whether they listen or refuse, they will know that God has sent them a prophet.

God speaks, calling Ezekiel "son of man," that is, simply a human being. He is sent to a people who have rebelled again and again, with parents and children alike stubborn. Ezekiel lives among the exiles in Babylon. His task is not to make them believe him, but to be faithful in saying, "Thus says the Lord GOD."

For today: our duty is to be faithful in sharing God's truth with love, even when others do not respond. The results do not depend on us but on God. Let us speak with sincerity and trust Him.
exp.1:5:
God tells Ezekiel not to be afraid of the people he will be sent to. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a human being. The "briers and thorns" and the "scorpions" are images of a hurtful and dangerous setting. A "rebellious house" means a people who refuse to obey God.

God speaks at the moment he calls Ezekiel as a prophet. The people of Israel were in exile in Babylon. God warns him in advance that many will not want to listen to him, but that his task is to speak faithfully. According to the text, even if they do not heed him, they will know that a prophet had been among them.

Today, when you want to speak with truth and love but fear rejection or criticism, remember that God asks you for faithfulness, not for everyone's approval. Pray, speak with respect, and leave the results in his hands.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that the living creatures (the translation used by the source calls them "animals") moved back and forth with a speed like that of lightning. Your verse says "ran and returned," so the comment about the word "returned" will be rewritten to match it: "returned" means they went and came back again. The image conveys speed, energy, and a light that flashes.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, a priest who was exiled in Babylon beside the river Chebar. He describes a vision of God that he received there. The living creatures, the fire, and the wheels show the glory and power of God, who is not confined to the temple in Jerusalem but is with his people in exile. Scholars interpret the details in different ways.

For today: when you feel far from home or feel that everything has come to a standstill, remember that God moves and works with power even where you cannot see it. Pray today with confidence, knowing that he is present with you.
exp.6:9:
It says that the day of God's judgment has already arrived. "The morning has gone forth" suggests that dawn has broken, that is, that the moment is already here. "The rod" may be the rod of punishment or the power that punishes, and "has blossomed" indicates that it is now ready. "Pride has budded" means that the people's arrogance grew and bore fruit. Scholars do not fully agree on what the rod is: some think of Babylon, others of the wickedness of the people themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces that Jerusalem will be judged for its idolatry, its violence, and its pride, after a long time of refusing to change.

For today: pride seems harmless while it grows, but in the end it bears bad fruit. Today you can ask God to show you where you find it hard to recognize your mistakes, and to decide to humble yourself and return to Him in time.
exp.4:11:
God's judgment on Jerusalem will have three parts: a third of the people would die of disease and hunger inside the city, another third would fall by the sword all around it, and the last third would be scattered in every direction, and even there the sword would pursue them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Earlier, Ezekiel had acted out a sign with his hair, divided into three parts. God explains that Jerusalem had defiled his temple with idolatry and detestable practices. It is a harsh message, announcing what would happen when the city was conquered.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also warns before he acts. Today we can hear his call to turn back to him without delay, instead of growing used to what we know displeases him.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that the wheels moved together with the cherubim. When they walked, the wheels went beside them. When they lifted their wings to rise from the earth, the wheels did not turn away from them. Everything moved in perfect harmony.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision. He is among the exiles in Babylon, and he sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. Ezekiel recognizes that these beings are the same ones he saw by the river Chebar. The next verse explains that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

For today: God is not bound to one place, and his direction is perfect and coordinated. We can trust that he continues to work even when everything seems lost. Seek to move in step with his guidance.
exp.5:11:
Ezekiel 6:12 says that no one in Israel would escape God's judgment. Whoever was far off would die of disease; whoever was near would fall by the sword; and whoever survived in a besieged city would die of hunger. Here "wrath" means God's righteous anger, and "accomplish" means He would carry it through to the end.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had filled the land with idols and with altars on the mountains. God warns that the punishment would come so that they would recognize that He is the LORD. Even in judgment, His aim was that they would know Him.

For today: let us not take sin or God's warnings lightly. If there is something in your life that takes the place that only He deserves, do not wait for the consequences to show you it; return to Him today with humility, knowing that He forgives those who repent.
exp.0:27:
Ezekiel compares the brightness around the throne to the rainbow, which appears in the clouds when it rains. He says that this was the appearance of "the likeness of the glory of the Lord", that is, something resembling God's glory, not the glory itself. When he saw it, he fell on his face to the ground, and he heard a voice speaking.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a priest who was living in exile in Babylon with other Jews. Beside the river Chebar he saw this vision of God above a throne, before receiving his call as a prophet. God revealed himself to him even far from the temple in Jerusalem. The bow evokes beauty and, for many readers, the faithfulness of God, although the text does not explain this.

For today: before we speak, God deserves our reverence and attention. Today you can begin your prayer in silence, acknowledging who God is, and then listen to his voice in the Bible with humility.
exp.7:2:
It says that a figure with the appearance of a man, made of fire and brightness, stretched out his hand and took Ezekiel by the hair. The Spirit lifted him up between heaven and earth and brought him, in visions of God, to Jerusalem. There, at the north gate of the inner court, stood the image of jealousy, an idol that provoked God to jealousy.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, lived in exile in Babylon. While the elders of Judah listened to him, God showed him in a vision what was happening in the temple. He wanted Ezekiel to understand why judgment was coming. It is not known for certain what that image was, but it was clearly idolatry within the holy place.

For today: God sees what happens in the hidden places of our hearts. We can ask Him to show us what things occupy the place that belongs to Him alone, and turn back to Him with sincerity.
exp.3:9:
God tells Ezekiel that his daily food will be small and measured: about twenty shekels by weight, which comes to roughly 230 grams, and he is to eat it at set times. The phrase "from time to time" means at fixed hours.

God speaks to Ezekiel, his prophet, so that he will represent the siege of Jerusalem with his own body. This rationing showed the scarcity that would come upon the people because of their rebellion. Scholars debate some details of this symbolic action, but the central message is clear: there would be hunger and distress.

For today: learn to receive what God gives you with humility and to live with moderation. If you go through scarcity today, remember that God sees you and that obeying him is always better than ignoring his voice.
exp.5:9:
They will come to know that I am the true God, the Lord. The verse also affirms that his warnings were not empty words: "not in vain" means "not without purpose" or "not for nothing." The "evil" here is the punishment that was announced, not any wrongdoing on God's part.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Israel had turned away from God and worshiped idols, which God calls an unfaithful heart, meaning disloyal, like a broken marriage. Even so, he promises that some will escape and, in exile, will remember God and feel shame for their sin.

For today: when God corrects us, it is not to destroy us but to wake us up. If we notice that something has taken God's place in our heart, we can return to him with humility, without waiting for the consequences to teach us by force.
exp.6:13:
It says the people will blow the trumpet to call for war and will have everything made ready, but no one will go out to fight. The reason is that God himself has poured out his wrath on the whole multitude.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their idolatry and injustice. The trumpet was the usual sign of alarm, but this time it will not help, because the people will have neither courage nor strength. It is a judgment already decided.

For today: let us not trust in our preparations, plans or resources as if they were enough without God. It is wise to examine the heart in time, to turn back to him with humility, and to seek his mercy before the consequences arrive.
exp.3:3:
He says that God commands Ezekiel to lie on his left side and to lay upon it the wickedness, that is, the sin, of Israel. He would bear that guilt for a certain number of days. Here the verb "lie" means to lie down, not so much to sleep at night.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. With this action, which was a sign for the people, God showed that Jerusalem would be besieged because of its rebellion. The verses that follow explain that each day represents a year of sin. Scholars discuss how to understand those 390 years, and not all of them interpret it the same way.

God takes sin seriously, but he also communicates clearly and patiently before he acts. Today we can listen to his warnings in time, recognize our faults, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.0:7:
It says that under the wings of these living beings, on their four sides, there were hands like a man's. Also, each one had faces and wings toward the four sides. The comment about the old spelling of "a" is removed, since it refers to a word not in the verse. Human hands suggest service and action.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon with the people of Judah, speaks here. He describes a vision of God that he received beside the river Chebar. These beings surround the divine throne. Scholars interpret them in various ways: as angels, or as an image of God's glory and power. God revealed himself to his people even in exile.

For today: God is not far away when we feel exiled or without a way out. Just as those beings had hands ready to act, we can ask God how we might serve today with our hands, even in difficult times.
exp.0:24:
When the living creatures stood still, they let their wings down, and then a voice was heard from above them, from the firmament, which is a kind of firm, shining vault or platform over their heads. "Let down" means that they lowered or relaxed their wings. "Was heard" is what the verse says.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He recounts a vision of the glory of God. First there is a loud noise of wings; then silence and a voice. After that a throne appears. Many understand that God shows himself close to his people, even in exile, and is about to speak to them. The details of the vision are interpreted in various ways.

For today: before hearing God, it is good to pause. Find a moment of stillness, without hurry or noise, to listen for his voice in the Bible and in prayer.
exp.0:1:
This verse gives the date of the vision: the fifth day of the month, in the fifth year since King Jehoiachin was taken captive to Babylon. The word "captivity" in the verse is the key term here, and the explanation refers to the forced removal of the people from their land. Jehoiachin was carried away into exile in Babylon along with many Jews, and among them was Ezekiel.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who had been carried into exile, living beside the river Chebar in Babylon. He records the date carefully because his message comes from a real and painful moment: the people are far from their land and from the temple. There is some uncertainty about what the "thirty years" in verse 1 refers to; some think it is his age, and others think it is a different way of counting the years.

For today: God does not stay far from us when we go through a time of loss or exile. He can find us and speak to us even in places we did not choose. Today you can open your heart to him, no matter where you are.
exp.2:22:
Ezekiel obeys God's command: he gets up and goes out into the field. There he finds the glory of the LORD, that is, the bright and powerful presence of God, just like the one he saw by the river Chebar. When he sees it, he falls face down on the ground.

The word "arose" in the verse means "got up," and "behold" means "look" or "suddenly I saw."

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. God had just called him as a watchman to warn his people. Before sending him out, God summons him to the field to speak with him. The vision of the glory reminds him who is sending him. The "river Chebar" is a canal near Babylon, where he had already seen that glory (chapter 1).

For today: before speaking on God's behalf or taking on a difficult task, first seek to be alone with Him. Obey His call and spend time in His presence, with humility and reverence, to receive strength and direction.
exp.8:0:
He spoke with a loud voice in my ears, saying that "the ones appointed over the city" had already arrived. Here, the word "visitors" does not mean friendly visits, but those assigned to come and carry out a punishment. Each one had a destroying weapon in his hand.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel hears him in a vision. This takes place while the prophet is living in exile in Babylon. God shows him that Jerusalem will be judged for its idolatry and injustice, described in the previous chapter. The verses that follow speak of six men and of another dressed in linen, who marks the faithful. Scholars interpret these figures in various ways, and the text does not explain them fully.

God is patient, but he is also just and takes sin seriously. Today we can take advantage of his patience to turn back to him with humility and sincerity, without putting off what he asks us to change.
exp.10:15:
God tells Ezekiel to announce to the exiles: although He Himself sent them far away, among the nations and through many lands, He will be with them as a little sanctuary in the places where they arrive. A sanctuary is a place where one is near to God. Some understand that God Himself would be their refuge; others, that He would be a place of worship in place of the temple. The verse allows both ideas.

Ezekiel is among the exiles in Babylon. Those who stayed in Jerusalem looked down on them and said that the land belonged to them alone. God answers with comfort: the exiles have not been abandoned, and later He promises to gather them and bring them back to their land.

For today: even if you feel far from your home, your church, or your safe place, God does not depend on a location to be with you. Seek Him in prayer right where you are.
exp.8:8:
God answers Ezekiel's complaint. He says that the sin of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of bloodshed, that is, of violence and unjust killing, and the city is full of injustice, meaning the twisting of what is right. The people justified themselves by saying: "The Lord has forsaken the earth, and the Lord does not see."

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision where Jerusalem is judged. Ezekiel had just fallen face down, distressed, asking whether God would destroy all that remained of the people. God explains that the judgment is not arbitrary: the violence was widespread, and the people had abandoned faith in a God who sees and judges.

For today: it is dangerous to live as if God were not watching. When we think no one sees our choices, we can excuse wrongdoing. Remembering that God sees, and that he is also just and compassionate, invites us to live with honesty and to seek his forgiveness.
exp.9:3:
Ezekiel 10:4 says that the glory of God, which had been above the cherub (a heavenly being that supports God's throne), moved toward the threshold of the temple. Then the house was filled with a cloud, and the court was full of the brightness of that glory.

Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile in Babylon, recounts a vision. God is preparing judgment against Jerusalem for its idolatry and sin. That his glory moves toward the threshold seems to indicate that God is beginning to withdraw from the temple, though some understand it as a preparation for judgment.

God is holy and deserves to be taken seriously. We cannot give him a place of decoration while we live in sin. Today we can ask him to cleanse our hearts so that his presence may remain with us.
exp.10:0:
The Spirit of God lifted Ezekiel up and brought him to the east gate of the temple, the gate that faces the place where the sun rises. There, at the entrance, he saw twenty-five men. He recognized two of them: Jaazaniah, son of Azur, and Pelatiah, son of Benaiah. The text calls them "leaders of the people," that is, leaders.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who was exiled in Babylon. This scene is a vision: his body did not move, but God showed him what was happening in Jerusalem. In the verses that follow, God says that these leaders were giving bad advice and making wicked plans. They felt secure, although God was warning them of judgment. The twenty-five men may be the same as those in Ezekiel 8:16 or a different group; the text does not make this clear.

For today: those who have influence should ask themselves whether their advice comes from God or from their own comfort. Let us ask for wisdom before we guide others.
exp.6:12:
The explanation says that whoever sells a property will not be able to get it back again, even while still alive. It also says that the vision of judgment over the whole multitude will not be overturned, and that no one can save their life through their wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. He announces that violence and ungodliness have reached their limit. According to the law, land that had been sold could return to its owner in the year of jubilee, but now the judgment will be so complete that this hope will be lost. Many understand this as a sign that the exile would be harsh and long.

For today: do not place your security in possessions, businesses, or plans, because all of that can be lost. Seek God with humility and correct today what you know is wrong.
exp.7:15:
He brought me into the inner court of the Lord's house, and there, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord, between the porch and the altar, I saw about twenty-five men. They had their backs to the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they were bowing down to the sun as it rose.

God speaks, showing Ezekiel in a vision what is happening in Jerusalem, while the prophet is among the exiles in Babylon. This is the third abomination in a series. These men were in the most sacred place and yet they were worshipping something created instead of the Creator. God explains in this way why judgment is coming. Some think the twenty-five were priests, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today we can ask ourselves what good thing has taken the place of God in our hearts. A person can be in church and yet, inwardly, have their back turned toward Him. Let us look to Him again with sincerity.
exp.7:6:
It says that the Spirit of God brought Ezekiel to the entrance of the court, the courtyard of the temple in Jerusalem. There he looked and saw a hole in the wall.

Ezekiel was a prophet who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, God took him to Jerusalem to show him the hidden sins of the people, above all their idolatry. God speaks with him step by step, and each scene is worse than the one before. The hole in the wall is the beginning of a discovery: what was being done in secret would come to light. Scholars do not offer a single explanation for the detail of the hole, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: what we hide is not hidden from God. Let us ask him to show us, in love, what is in our hearts, so that we may confess it and be healed.
exp.9:10:
It says that the creatures with wheels moved in any of the four directions, forward, backward, or to the sides, without needing to turn. Wherever the head went, the one at the front, the others followed it.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was in exile in Babylon, speaks here. He tells again the vision of God's throne, which he had already described in chapter 1. Here he sees it in the temple, when God's glory is about to leave Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The image shows order, unity, and free movement. Interpreters understand it in several ways, but almost all see in it the power and presence of God.

God is not bound to a place or to our plans. You can trust that He goes with you and guides you, even when the direction changes suddenly.
exp.0:16:
The explanation says that the wheels Ezekiel saw beside the living creatures (called "beasts" in this older version) could move toward any of their four sides without needing to turn around. The word "sides" here means the four directions. In other words, they moved in any direction without losing their course.

Ezekiel was a priest living in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision of God's glory that he received by the river Chebar. The wheels, with eyes all around them, accompany the living creatures. Interpreters understand them in several ways, but many see in them the presence and power of God, who is not limited to a single place.

For today: God is not bound to one place or one circumstance. Even when your life takes unexpected turns, He remains with you and knows where it is going. You can trust that He is with you in every direction.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that the living creatures and the wheels moved together, as one thing. Wherever the spirit wanted to go, they went, and the wheels were lifted up along with them. Here the source's word for the creatures is explained as "living creatures," and to walk means to move. The reason is that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

Ezekiel speaks here, a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. He recounts the vision he had of the glory of God beside the river Chebar. The wheels full of eyes speak of movement and of complete sight. Many believe they show that God is not bound to one place and rules over everything. Some think "the spirit" is the Spirit of God; others, a force that guided them. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: even when your life seems far from home or out of control, God keeps guiding. Ask Him to direct you and walk in step with what He shows you.
exp.9:8:
Ezekiel says he saw four wheels beside the cherubim, one next to each of them. Their appearance shone like a precious stone, a term from older usage that many understand as a gem of golden or sea-green color, though it is not known for certain which stone was meant. The word "beryl" in the verse above refers to this same kind of stone.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, speaks from exile in Babylon. He is seeing a vision in which the glory of God is preparing to leave the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The wheels and the cherubim recall the vision of chapter 1, where God appears in motion and with complete freedom.

For today: God is not confined to one place or to our circumstances. Even when everything seems lost or distant, he still rules and is present. Today you can trust that he is with you, and live with reverence, never taking his presence for granted.
exp.10:6:
The explanation says that the dead whom Jerusalem's leaders caused through their violence and injustice are like the flesh inside a pot (a large cooking vessel). God tells them that they believe they are safe in the city, but He will bring them out of it. "Your slain whom you have laid in the midst of it" means the people you killed. "I will bring you forth" speaks of judgment, not rescue.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who is in exile in Babylon, and sees in vision the leaders of Jerusalem. They had said the city was a pot that would protect them (v. 3). God answers that what really fills the city is the fruit of their injustice. Interpreters see here a judgment upon them.

For today: let us not trust in our position or our security, but in living with justice and compassion, because God sees what we think and do.
exp.9:16:
The explanation says that the wheels moved exactly like the cherubim: when they stood still, the wheels stood still too; when they rose up, the wheels rose with them. The reason is that the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels. Here "living creatures" means the same beings described in chapter 1. The phrase "lifted up" means they rose.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, is in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision in which the glory of God leaves the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The detail of the wheels shows that everything moves in perfect unity under God's direction. Scholars interpret the exact symbolism of the wheels in several different ways.

For today: God is not confined to one place, and his work moves with order and purpose. We can ask him that his Spirit guide us, to move forward or to stop when he indicates.
exp.4:9:
God says that the city will suffer a famine so terrible that fathers will eat their sons and sons will eat their fathers. Furthermore, God will bring punishments upon it and will scatter the few who are left in every direction, to all the winds, that is, in all directions.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing Jerusalem. She had sinned with idols and abominations, even inside the temple. This warning announces the siege by the Babylonians. Moses had already warned of something similar if the people broke the covenant (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53).

For today: God speaks seriously about sin, but his warnings are a call to return to him. Let us not ignore his voice; if anything in our lives has taken his place, let us repent today and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.0:6:
It says their feet were straight, with no bends or bent joints, and that the soles of their feet were like the sole of a calf (a young bull). Also, they shone like very polished bronze. The word "sparkled" means flashing or glinting, and "burnished" means polished until it gleams.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision of God that he had by the river Chebar. These beings support the divine throne. Interpreters explain the details in several ways: some see strength and firmness; others see service. The text does not explain them, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: God shows himself powerful and steady even when everything seems to be falling apart. If your life feels unstable, remember that God is still on his throne, and you can walk with confidence, moving straight toward what he asks of you.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the time of God's judgment is already coming. The phrase "those who live in the land" refers to the people who lived in the land of Israel. The word "morning" is hard: some understand it as the turn to be judged, others as a cycle or fate that is fulfilled. The word "tumult" means confusion and terror, not the festival of the mountains, where celebrations were held and also false worship took place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. God announces that Jerusalem and Judah will fall because of their idolatry and injustices. The people had ignored many warnings. God warns clearly, so that they will know that He is the Lord.

Today we can take God's patience seriously and not mistake it for indifference. If He shows us something we must correct, let us do it today, with humility and repentance, without waiting for the consequences to arrive.
exp.10:8:
It says that God will bring the leaders of Jerusalem out of the city, deliver them into the hands of foreigners, and punish them. "Strangers" means people from other nations. "I will execute judgments among you" means that God will apply his justice to them.

It speaks God through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. The leaders of Jerusalem felt secure, like the meat inside a pot that protected them, but they had filled the city with injustice and violence. God tells them that this false security will not save them. The exact historical details of how this was fulfilled are explained in several ways, but the central message is clear.

Today we can learn that neither power, nor position, nor walls protect us from God. It is wise to examine our hearts, correct what is wrong, and trust in God's mercy, not in our own security.
exp.8:5:
God commands certain executioners to punish Jerusalem without exception: old men, young men, virgins, children, and women. Only those who have the mark on their forehead are spared. The judgment begins "at my sanctuary," that is, at the temple, and the first to fall are the elders who were standing in front of it. The "young men" are the youths.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision, a few years before Jerusalem fell to Babylon. The people, even their religious leaders, had filled the temple with idolatry and the city with violence. The mark protects those who grieved over these wrongs. Ezekiel, seeing this, pleads for the rest of Israel.

God takes sin seriously, especially among those who claim to serve him. We can ask him to give us a heart that feels pain over evil, and not one that grows used to it.
exp.0:12:
The living creatures Ezekiel saw looked like burning coals of fire, like torches blazing. The fire moved back and forth among them, shone brightly, and lightning came out of it.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon with the people of Judah, tells of the vision God gave him by the river Chebar. The living creatures are beneath God's throne, and the fire shows his holiness and his power. God revealed himself to a people who felt far from their land and their temple.

For today: God remains holy and present, even when we feel far away or in the midst of trials. We can draw near to him with reverence and confidence, and pray today: "Lord, help me to remember that you reign."
exp.2:12:
Ezekiel reports that he heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and all of it together made a great rushing noise. The "animals" mentioned here are the living creatures he saw in his vision of God's glory.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God had just sent him to speak to them, whether or not they would listen. Then the Spirit lifted him up, and those sounds accompanied the movement of God's glory. Ezekiel was deeply moved, and the verses that follow say that he felt bitter and astonished.

For today: God is great and cannot be contained by our small ideas. Before speaking or serving, take a moment to stop, listen, and acknowledge who He is. His calling is fulfilled with reverence and obedience, even when we do not know how others will respond.
exp.0:10:
This verse describes the living beings that Ezekiel saw in his vision. Each one had four wings: two were stretched upward and joined the wings of the being beside it, and with the other two they covered their bodies.

"Such were their faces" refers to the faces he has just mentioned: man, lion, ox, and eagle.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who lived in exile in Babylon by the river Chebar. He tells of the vision God gave him when God called him to be a prophet. Many understand that the covered wings express reverence, and that the vision shows the glory and majesty of God, although the details of the faces are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God deserves our respect and awe. Before asking him for anything, we can pause for a moment to worship him with humility, knowing that he is present even when we feel far from home or in difficult times.
exp.10:14:
God tells Ezekiel that his brothers, those who are exiled with him, and the whole house of Israel, are the people to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem said, "Get far away from the Lord; this land has been given to us as a possession." "Kindred" refers to his family and his people; "the Lord" is the name of God.

Ezekiel is among the exiles in Babylon. He has just seen Pelatiah die while he was prophesying, and he cries out in distress, fearing that God will finish off the rest of Israel. God answers him. Those who remained in Jerusalem looked down on the exiles, thinking they were far from God and that the land now belonged only to them. God corrects that idea with a promise of care.

We may think that God is far from someone who suffers or has failed, but He promises to be present in the midst of pain. Today, instead of judging others by their trials, let us remember that God remains near to those who seek Him.
exp.7:12:
He tells that God speaks to Ezekiel after showing him a terrible vision. "Turn thee yet again" means "turn around once more" or "look again." God warns him that there are still worse things, called "greater abominations," that is, acts that God detests, and that the leaders and people of Jerusalem were committing them.

God speaks, addressing the prophet Ezekiel in a vision. Before this, he saw seventy elders of Israel burning incense in secret before images, thinking, "The LORD does not see us." God shows him that nothing is hidden and that his people had turned away from Him. This explains the judgment that comes afterward.

For today: God sees what we do in secret, and He does so with the intention of healing, not humiliating. Today we can ask Him to show us honestly what is in our heart, confess it, and return to Him without fear.
exp.10:21:
The cherubim, heavenly beings who support God's throne, lifted up their wings. The wheels beside them moved as well. Above everything was the glory of God, that is, his visible and majestic presence.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, recounting a vision he received among the exiles in Babylon. God shows him that his presence is departing from Jerusalem because of the people's idolatry. Even so, God first promises a renewed people who will walk in his commands. Scholars agree that the departure is a judgment, but they also see that God is not bound to a temple.

For today: God is not limited to one place, but he invites us to live close to him with an obedient heart. Ask him today to remove whatever pulls you away from him.
exp.5:6:
It says that, when God's judgment comes, there will be dead people in the midst of the people of Israel. "Fall" means that they will die, above all in war. And the final result is that they will know, by experience, that the Lord is God.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had filled the land with idols and false altars. God announces that those idols will not be able to save them. But the passage does not end in destruction: God promises that some will escape and, while far away, will remember him with repentance.

For today: what we put in the place of God, such as money, success or pride, cannot sustain us when a crisis comes. Examine what gives you security and turn your heart back to God before a difficulty forces you to do so.
exp.8:2:
The explanation says that the glory of God, which had been over the cherub in the temple, rose up and moved to the doorway of the house. From there, the LORD called the man dressed in linen, who carried at his side a case for a scribe, that is, a container with ink and a pen for writing.

Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile in Babylon, sees in a vision how God judges Jerusalem for its idolatry. Here the glory of God begins to withdraw from the temple. Before sending the punishment, God orders those who grieve over the city's sin to be marked. Some understand that the scribe represents God's care for his own people.

God sees who laments the evil and does not forget them. Today we can ask him to give us a heart that is sensitive to sin, without growing used to what grieves him, and to trust that he cares for those who are faithful to him.
exp.0:22:
Under the expanse (the shining platform or firmament that was above the heads of the living creatures), their wings were stretched out straight, "straight, the one toward the other," meaning touching or lined up with one another. Each creature had four wings: with two it flew, and with the other two it covered its body. Here "living creatures" is the sense of the word rendered as "beasts" in some translations.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, describes a vision of God's glory beside the river Chebar. God revealed himself to him in the middle of the exile, when the people felt that he was far away. Some see in the covered wings a sign of reverence, though the text does not explain it.

For today: God deserves our respect and awe. Before we ask or act, we can pause to worship him with humility, remembering that he is present even in difficult times.
exp.9:11:
This verse describes the cherubim and their wheels. Their whole body, that is, the flesh, the backs (here "ribs"), the hands and the wings, as well as the four wheels, were full of eyes all around. "Flesh" refers to the entire body of these beings.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest exiled in Babylon. He recounts a vision in which he sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. Eyes can speak of a complete sight; many think they point to the total knowledge of God, although the text does not explain this clearly.

For today: nothing is hidden from God, and that is a comfort. He sees our struggles, our injustices and our pain. He also invites us to live with sincerity before Him, trusting that His gaze is that of a holy and faithful God.
exp.10:11:
It says that Israel will come to know who God is through judgment, because it did not live according to God's statutes and judgments, but copied the customs of the nations around it. "Statutes" are his commands, and "judgments" are his righteous rules. "Nations" are the peoples around them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He had shown the leaders of Jerusalem that they were giving bad counsel and filling the city with violence. They said they were secure, like meat in a pot. God answers that it will not be so: they will be judged. Then Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel cries out in concern for the rest of the people.

For today: examine whom you imitate. It is easy to copy what the majority does. Ask God that his Word, and not fashion or social pressure, guide your daily decisions.
exp.10:17:
This verse says that the Israelites would return to their land and there remove all their detestable things and all their abominations. These are old words for speaking of the idols and the impure practices that had defiled their worship of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people live in exile in Babylon. Earlier, in Jerusalem, the city had become filled with idolatry. Even so, God promises to gather them, give them back the land, and be with them as a little sanctuary in the place of exile. The next verse shows that the cleansing would not be only outward, for God would give them a new heart.

For today: God does not only want us to leave behind what separates us from Him, but also wants to change us from within. You can ask Him to show you what things have taken His place in your life, and trust that He helps you let them go and gives you a heart that is sensitive to Him.
exp.8:6:
He says that God orders the executioners of judgment to "defile the house," that is, to make it unclean by filling the courts of the temple with corpses. The word translated "fill" means to fill up, and the courts are the open yards of the temple. Then they go out and begin to strike down the people of the city.

God speaks in a vision that the prophet Ezekiel receives. The people had filled Jerusalem with violence, injustice, and idolatry, even inside the temple, and they said that God did not see. Judgment begins at the sanctuary, and those who bore the mark were protected. Ezekiel responds with grief and intercedes.

For today: God is not indifferent to sin, and his judgment begins with his own house. Today we can examine our hearts with humility, seek his forgiveness, and, like Ezekiel, pray with compassion for others.
exp.4:13:
God tells Jerusalem that he will leave her in ruins and in shame. A "desert" is an empty, destroyed place. "Disgrace" means dishonor or mockery. A "passerby" is anyone who goes along the road. Everyone who passes by will see her fall.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem had fallen into idolatry and disobedience, and had despised the covenant with God. For this reason he announces a severe judgment: famine, sword, and scattering. The text says that God speaks "in his zeal," meaning that it grieves him that his people abandon him. His purpose is that they will know that he is the Lord.

For today: let us not take God's correction lightly. If he shows us something crooked in our lives, it is better to repent quickly and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.9:14:
The cherubim were lifted up. Ezekiel recognizes them as the same living creatures he had seen earlier by the river Chebar.

The word "creature" here means "living being," not a common beast. "Were lifted up" means they rose up.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. In his vision, the glory of God leaves the temple in Jerusalem, a sign of judgment for the sin of the people. When he says "this is the one I saw," Ezekiel connects this scene with his first vision in chapter 1: it is the same God who called him.

For today: God is not bound to a place or to our circumstances. Even if you feel far from home or from what you once knew, the Lord remains present and in control. Seek him where you are, with reverence and confidence.
exp.11:3:
It says that Ezekiel must bring out his bags, or "aparejos," which are his things for a journey. First he brings them out by day, so that everyone can see them. Then, in the evening, he himself goes out in plain view of the people, like someone going into exile.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. The people did not want to listen or believe, so God asks him for a message that can be seen, like a sign. Many understand that it announced that Jerusalem would also go into exile. How exactly he did it, the text does not detail further.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us and we pretend not to hear, because his message makes us uncomfortable. Today you might pray: "Señor, dame oídos dispuestos," and obey that simple word you already know.
exp.2:6:
God tells Ezekiel that the people of Israel will not listen to him. The reason is that, deep down, they do not want to listen to God himself. "Impudent" means shameless, foolish, unashamed of anything, and "hardhearted" speaks of a stubborn will that resists changing.

God speaks to Ezekiel when he calls him as a prophet, during the exile in Babylon. He explains that he is not sending him to foreigners whose language is hard to understand, who, God says, would have listened. He is sending him to his own people, who understand the message but reject it. Right away God promises to make him strong enough to endure that opposition.

For today: sometimes the problem is not understanding God's Word, but being unwilling to obey it. We can ask God for a soft and willing heart. And if we share his message and others do not respond, we remain faithful without losing heart.
exp.5:5:
In all the places where the people live, the cities will be left empty and in ruins. The "high places" were raised sites where false gods were worshiped. Those altars will be destroyed, the idols broken, and the sun pillars (probably columns or altars used to worship the sun) will be cut down. Everything they made with their hands will disappear.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Israel because his people turned away from him to worship idols. But the next passage shows that not everything ends in destruction: some will escape, and so they will know that the LORD is God.

For today: examine which things in your heart have taken the place that belongs to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Hand them over to him before they collapse on their own.
exp.4:14:
God tells Jerusalem that it will become a public disgrace, a source of mockery, a warning example to others, and a cause of horror to the nations around it. This will happen when He carries out His judgments in fury, in indignation, and in severe punishments of anger. He ends by declaring, "I the Lord have spoken it," as a seal that what He has said is certain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had rejected God's laws and practiced idolatry, so God announces a harsh judgment. What made it serious was that the chosen people were meant to show the nations who God is, and instead they had failed in that.

For today: God takes seriously the faithfulness of those who bear His name. We can humbly examine whether our lives reflect what we say we believe, and turn back to Him without delay, trusting in His mercy.
exp.3:5:
God tells Ezekiel that, when he has finished lying on his left side, he is to lie on his right side for forty days. There he will "bear the iniquity" of the house of Judah, that is, the sin and its consequences. Each day stands for a year.

God speaks, and the prophet Ezekiel is living in exile in Babylon. Through this strange action, God announces the judgment that is coming upon Jerusalem. Ezekiel acts as a sign that everyone can see. Interpreters do not agree on which exact years the forty days represent, and it is better not to claim a certain figure.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also speaks to us clearly before the consequences arrive. If you sense his call to change today, do not put it off; answer him with humility and trust in his mercy.
exp.5:3:
God says that he will destroy the places where the people worshiped idols. The altars were places for offering sacrifices, and the sun-images were figures or pillars used in pagan worship (the exact meaning of the Hebrew term is debated). Desolate means ruined or destroyed. Moreover, the bodies of the dead would lie scattered in front of those same idols, which could not save them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Israel because his people had stopped worshiping him and were practicing idolatry on the mountains. The judgment would come by the sword, that is, by war.

For today: examine what things occupy in your heart the place that belongs to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. None of that can save you, but God can. Return to him with sincerity.
exp.5:7:
God says that, in the midst of the punishment, he will not destroy everyone. Some of the people will escape the sword and will live among the nations, when they are scattered through various lands. Here "sword" means war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who had fallen into idolatry. He announces judgment on their altars and idols, but leaves a promise: a remnant will survive. The verses that follow explain that these survivors will remember God and will repent.

For today: even when we face the consequences of our mistakes, God remains merciful. His discipline seeks to bring us back to Him, not to destroy us. If today you feel far away, you can remember Him and return with sincerity.
exp.6:19:
God says that the people used their beautiful jewelry, the gold and silver that He had given them, to feed their pride. With that material they made idols and detestable statues. Therefore God turned those riches into something repugnant to them. The word that the explanation discusses here suggests something unclean that one turns away from. Some think that "its ornament" also refers to the temple, but the text does not make that entirely clear.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry. Its riches could not save it, because they had become its stumbling block.

For today: examine which of God's blessings might be feeding your pride or taking His place in your heart. Use your possessions with gratitude and generosity, and not as a source of security or of self-glory.
exp.4:0:
God tells Ezekiel to take a sharp knife, like a barber's razor, and run it over his head and his beard. Then he must weigh the hair on a scale and divide it into parts. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel throughout the book.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who lived in exile in Babylon. This is a symbolic action, a kind of acted-out message: the hair represents the people of Jerusalem, and what follows announces judgment for their disobedience. Shaving the head was also a sign of mourning and shame, and for a priest it was a very strong thing to do.

For today: God takes our disobedience seriously, but he also warns before he acts. Today we can listen to his voice with humility and correct our course in time.
exp.6:25:
It says that disasters will come one after another, and that alarming news will not stop. In their anguish, the people will seek a word from God through the prophet, but they will not find it. The priest will no longer have teaching from the law, and the elders will have no counsel. "Ruin" means destruction or disaster; "news" is information, almost always bad.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for the people's idolatry and violence. They had ignored God for a long time, and now, in the crisis, their leaders could not guide them. Interpreters understand this silence as part of the judgment itself.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to seek God. If we read his Word and obey it now, we will have direction and peace when difficult times arrive.
exp.10:16:
God promises his scattered people that he will gather them. "Gather" and "bring back" mean to bring together and return those who had been scattered among other nations. He will also give them back the land of Israel.

Ezekiel speaks on God's behalf while many Israelites are exiled in Babylon. Those who remained in Jerusalem looked down on them and said that they were far from the LORD and that the land now belonged to those who had stayed behind. God answers that he has not forgotten them: even in exile he would be with them as a small sanctuary. The following verses show that the promise includes an inner change, a new heart.

For today: If you feel far away, rejected, or lost, remember that God does not abandon his own. He can sustain you wherever you are and make your heart new. Draw near to him with confidence.
exp.0:15:
The explanation says that the wheels Ezekiel saw beside the living creatures shone with a color like beryl, a precious stone with a golden or greenish tone (it is not known with certainty which exact color was meant). The four wheels were all alike. Each appeared to have one wheel inside another, crossing through it, which may explain why they could move in any direction without turning.

The one who speaks is Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, who describes a vision of the glory of God. God prepares him this way to call him as a prophet to a people in exile. Interpreters differ about the meaning of the wheels, but many see that they show God present and active everywhere.

For today: even when you feel far from home or without direction, God is not limited by your place. He moves with you and continues to rule. Trust in Him today.
exp.7:7:
God tells Ezekiel to dig a hole in the wall. As he does, he discovers a hidden door.

God calls the prophet "Son of man," and the verse says that God spoke to him. Where the explanation explains the old phrases, I am leaving them out, since they do not appear in the verse you are reading.

God speaks, and Ezekiel tells what he saw in a vision. He is in the temple in Jerusalem, and God shows him, step by step, the idolatry the people were practicing in secret. The hidden door leads to a place where they worshiped images. God wants Ezekiel to understand why judgment is coming upon Jerusalem.

For today: nothing hidden is hidden from God. We can ask Him to show us what we have kept silent about or hidden in our hearts, and confess it with confidence, knowing that He forgives those who turn back to Him.
exp.9:13:
Every living being that Ezekiel saw had four faces: the first was the face of a cherub, the second the face of a man, the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. A cherub is a heavenly being who serves God and guards his holiness.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision of the glory of God, which leaves the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. In Ezekiel 1:10 the first face is the face of an ox, not of a cherub. Scholars explain that difference in several ways, and there is no certain answer.

For today: God is not confined to one place. His glory moved with his people, even in exile. If you feel far from everything, remember that God can find you wherever you are. Seek him with humility and reverence.
exp.2:11:
This verse tells that the Spirit of God lifted Ezekiel up, and that behind him he heard a very loud voice, like a great rushing sound. The voice said: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place." The sentence about the word "lifted" is removed here, since the verse above already reads "took me up." The word "rushing" in the verse above is the same idea as the great sound described here, a very large and strong noise.

Ezekiel speaks here, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He had just seen the glory of God and received the task of speaking to his people, though perhaps they would not want to listen. Before sending him, God shows him his greatness. It is not known with certainty who speaks these words; some think they are the living creatures or angels, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: before doing what God asks of you, stop to praise him. Remembering who God is gives you strength and encouragement to obey, even when the task is difficult.
exp.10:23:
Afterwards the Spirit lifted Ezekiel up and brought him back, in a vision given by the Spirit of God, to the exiles in Chaldea. The phrase about those carried away refers to people taken into exile. The phrase meaning he was brought back again is rendered in the verse as "brought me in a vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea." When it ended, the vision left him.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he lived as an exile in Babylon. In the vision, God took him to Jerusalem and showed him the sins of the people and the judgment that was coming. Then he saw the glory of God leave the city and stop on the mountain to the east. Now the vision ends, and Ezekiel returns to his fellow countrymen. According to the next verse, he told them everything God had shown him.

For today: what God shows us in his Word is not only to be kept to ourselves, but to be shared with humility and faithfulness, even when the message is difficult to say or to hear.
exp.6:8:
God says that this time he will show no compassion and will not hold back. He will repay them according to their conduct, and their detestable practices (the things God loathes, such as idolatry and injustice) will fall back on themselves. The word "smiteth" in the verse means striking down, that is, punishment. The purpose is that they will recognize that the Lord is the one who acts.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. After a long time of warnings, they kept on in idolatry and violence. The judgment is not an outburst without reason, but the consequence of having rejected God again and again.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with indifference. If there is something we know displeases him, today is a good day to acknowledge it and turn back to him, who continues to offer forgiveness to whoever repents.
exp.6:24:
This verse says that destruction is coming. People will seek peace, but they will not find it. The word "destruction" here can also be understood as "distress" or "calamity," depending on how the Hebrew is translated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The city was full of violence, injustice, and pride. God announces judgment as the consequence of those ways. The verses that follow show that neither the prophet, nor the priest, nor the elders would be able to offer a way out. The ultimate purpose was that they would know that the LORD is God.

For today: true peace is not achieved in a hurry once the crisis has already arrived. It is wise to seek God now, with humility, correcting injustice and pride in our lives, before distress comes.
exp.0:3:
Ezekiel sees a strong storm coming from the north. It is a great cloud with a fire that folds in upon itself, surrounded by a brilliance. At the center of the fire something shines like amber, a bright metal, though some scholars think it refers to an alloy such as electrum.

Ezekiel was a priest and was exiled in Babylon, beside the river Chebar, with other Israelites taken captive. He himself tells what he saw. God appears to him in a vision, and it is notable that this happens far from the temple in Jerusalem. This prepares his calling as a prophet to speak to a wounded and rebellious people.

For today: God is not limited to one place or to our circumstances. Even when you feel far from home, without strength, or in a time of crisis, He can make Himself present. Seek Him with reverence and listen to His voice, for His glory is greater than any situation you face.
exp.5:2:
God commands Ezekiel to speak to the mountains, the hills, the streams, and the valleys of Israel, as if they could hear him. He announces that God himself will bring a sword, that is, war, and that he will destroy the high places, the elevated sites where the people worshiped idols.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The mountains represent the land and its people, who had filled those high places with idolatry. God warns of judgment because his people had abandoned him.

For today: God does not overlook what takes the place that belongs to him alone. We can honestly ask ourselves what things we love or trust more than God, and ask him to help us return to him before those things harm us.
exp.4:15:
It says that God will send famine like harmful arrows, which bring destruction. When the famine increases, He will take away "the support of the bread," that is, the sustenance, the thing the people leaned on to live, as if He were breaking the staff of bread. "Harmful" means damaging and deadly. The arrows are the famine itself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. The people had rejected His laws and practiced idolatry, and for this reason God announces judgment. This happens before the city falls to Babylon. He had already warned of these consequences in the law of Moses, and here He confirms His word: "I, the LORD, have spoken."

For today: let us not place our final trust in provision, work, or money, but in God, who gives us everything. If He corrects us, let us listen and return to Him with humility.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that Ezekiel heard someone calling out to the wheels: "Wheel!" The word "wheel" here is understood as a call or a command. Some translations render it as "whirlwind" or "vortex," so the exact sense is uncertain and is interpreted in several ways.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, recounts a vision of God while in exile. The cherubim and the wheels full of eyes accompany the glory of God. Shortly afterward, that glory leaves the temple in Jerusalem, as a sign of judgment for the sin of the people. The detail that the wheels receive a command suggests that they move under God's authority.

For today: even when life seems to spin out of control, nothing moves outside of God's authority. You can rest in the fact that He sees everything, and entrust to Him today what you do not understand.
exp.6:22:
God tells Ezekiel to make a chain. That chain symbolizes the captivity that is coming upon the people. The reason is that the land is full of "bloody crimes," that is, of sentences and crimes that poured out innocent blood, and the city is full of violence.

God speaks in the middle of the announcement of Jerusalem's end, shortly before its fall to Babylon. The people had filled the city with injustice and idolatry. That is why God allows outsiders to plunder and defile it. Some understand the chain as a sign of captivity; the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God takes injustice and violence seriously. We can ask ourselves where we mistreat others, and ask Him to make us just and peaceful people who defend the weak.
exp.7:13:
It says that the prophet Ezekiel, guided by God in a vision, came to the north gate of the temple in Jerusalem. There he saw women sitting and weeping and wailing for Tammuz. "North" is what the word for the direction means. Tammuz was a god of the religions of Mesopotamia; many scholars connect him with rites of mourning over his death, although the details are debated.

God speaks to Ezekiel while the people are living in sin, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The leaders were saying that God did not see them, but He shows them that He sees everything. This is the third of several "abominations": worship of idols inside His own house.

For today: honestly examine what things occupy in your heart the place that belongs to God. God sees what is hidden, and His gaze is an invitation to return to Him with confidence.
exp.7:10:
It says that seventy men, leaders of the people of Israel, were standing before the painted images of idols on the wall. Each one held a censer, that is, a vessel in which incense is burned. Among them was Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan. The smoke of the incense is fragrant, and from it rose a thick cloud.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who in a vision is brought to the temple in Jerusalem. God shows him that the leaders were worshiping images in secret, while saying that God did not see them.
