That is why the judgment coming upon Jerusalem has a clear reason. Some think that this Jaazaniah is different from the Jaazaniah of Jeremiah 35, but this is not certain.

We can ask ourselves whether there is something we do in the dark, in secret, that we would not do in front of others. God sees the heart. Having one public life of faith and another hidden one does not please him. Today we can honestly confess to him what is hidden and ask him to be the only Lord of our worship.
exp.6:3:
God says that he will not look on his people with pity or treat them with compassion. He will make them bear the consequences of their evil way, and their detestable practices will be left out in the open in the midst of them. In the end they will acknowledge that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces judgment on Israel for years of idolatry and injustice. This is not a whim of anger: the people had repeatedly rejected his warnings. Some understand the phrase "without mercy" as the limit of patience after a long time of calls to repentance.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and God calls us to turn back to him before it is too late. Today you can honestly examine a habit you know does not please him, and ask him for forgiveness and help to change.
exp.3:11:
God tells Ezekiel to prepare bread of barley and bake it over hot ashes, using human excrement as fuel. He must do all of this in plain view of the people, that is, right in front of them. "Dung" refers to waste matter, and "baked under the ashes" means baked among the embers.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Through this symbolic act, together with the scanty rations of the previous verse, he announces the siege of Jerusalem and the unclean food Israel would have to eat among the nations. Ezekiel protests, and afterward the text tells that God allowed him to use cow dung instead (v. 15).

For today: God takes sin seriously, and sometimes his message is uncomfortable. Let us ask for humility to hear his correction in time, knowing that his aim is to bring us back to himself.
exp.9:0:
Ezekiel tells us that he looked again and saw, in the firmament or vault above the heads of the cherubims, something like a sapphire stone. It had the appearance of a throne. The firmament is that stretched-out vault, and the cherubims are heavenly beings who serve God and surround his presence.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, exiled in Babylon. He is seeing a vision of the glory of God, similar to the one in chapter 1. Here the throne appears just before God orders that burning coals be scattered over Jerusalem, as a sign of judgment for the sin of the people.

For today: God still sits on his throne, even when everything seems confused or unjust. This invites us to take him seriously, to live with reverence, and to trust that he governs with justice. Today you can pray, acknowledging his authority over your life.
exp.2:5:
God tells Ezekiel that he is not being sent to foreign peoples, whose speech is strange or hard to understand, and whose words he could not comprehend. And He adds something surprising: if He had sent him to them, they would have listened to him.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel when He calls him to carry His message to Israel, His own people. Ezekiel shared a language and culture with them, so there would be no excuse of misunderstanding. God points out that the problem would not be communication, but Israel's hardness of heart, since they were already rejecting Him.

For today: sometimes we believe people do not respond to God because of a lack of clarity or of arguments. This verse reminds us that the heart also has an influence. We can speak with love and simplicity, and trust that God is the one who opens ears.
exp.2:17:
God tells Ezekiel that if He announces that a wicked man will die for his evil way and Ezekiel does not warn him, that man will die for his sin, but God will hold Ezekiel accountable.

Scripture here speaks of Jehovah speaking to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. God appoints him as a watchman, one who gives warning of danger. His task was to pass on faithfully what God said, and the purpose of the warning was that the people would turn and live.

For today: if you know someone who is turning away from God, do not stay silent out of fear or comfort. Speak to him with love, humility and truth, and leave the results in God's hands. Many believers understand that this calling applies in different ways to each person.
exp.6:20:
It says that God will hand Jerusalem over to foreigners to be plundered. The "wicked of the earth" are pagan peoples, and they will defile the city, that is, they will profane it. "Spoil" means war booty. The "strangers" are people from another nation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The people had filled the temple with idols and trusted in their wealth. That is why God announces judgment. Many understand "my secret place" to refer to the temple or its holiest part, though there are different opinions.

For today: silver and gold cannot save us when we fail before God. Today we can ask ourselves what we are placing in the place of God, and return to trusting him with humility.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that violence has grown until it has become a "rod" of wickedness, that is, a stick used to punish. The phrase is hard, and some think the rod is the violent people themselves, while others think it is the punishment itself. It announces that none of that crowd will remain, and that no one will mourn for them. The word translated as "wailing" in the verse is the same as the one behind the phrase here: to mourn their loss.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah, which were full of violence, injustice, and idolatry. God had already warned them many times, and now he says that the time has run out.

For today: God sees injustice and does not take it lightly. We can ask ourselves whether there is harshness or abuse in our words, our business dealings, or the way we treat others. While there is still time, we can repent, seek justice, and turn to God, who is merciful to those who come to Him.
exp.3:7:
God says to Ezekiel that he has placed cords on him, that is, bonds, so that he cannot turn from one side to the other. He was to remain this way until the days of the siege were complete, the siege of Jerusalem that he was representing.

God is speaking, and Ezekiel is his prophet among the exiles in Babylon. Through this symbolic action, God announces the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem and shows that the people would bear the consequences of their sin. Scholars debate whether the cords were literal or an image of his restriction; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God speaks in earnest, but he also draws near. Ask him to show you if there is something you have minimized, and respond to him with sincere repentance, trusting in his mercy.
exp.1:9:
God shows Ezekiel a scroll spread out before him, written on both sides. On it were dirges (sad songs sung over a dead person), lamentation (weeping) and woes (cries of pain and anguish). In other words, the message contained judgment and sorrow.

Ezekiel is a priest living in exile in Babylon. God calls him to speak to Israel, a rebellious people who do not want to listen. Before sending him, God asks him not to be rebellious like them, but to listen and receive the word. The scroll written on both sides suggests a complete message, although some interpret it in other ways.

Today, God invites us to receive his whole word, even when it is uncomfortable. We can ask him for a heart willing to hear his truth with humility, not choosing only what comforts us, trusting that his correction seeks our good.
exp.9:6:
It says that one of the cherubim reached out his hand toward the fire that was between them, took coals, and put them into the hands of the man clothed in linen. That man received them and went out.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he had among the exiles in Babylon. God had commanded the man clothed in linen to take fire to scatter over Jerusalem (10:2). This represents judgment for the sin of the people. Some scholars see here a symbol of purification, others of punishment; the text itself speaks of judgment upon the city.

For today: God is holy and acts with justice, but also with order and purpose. We can trust that none of his judgments is arbitrary. This invites us to live with reverence, to examine our hearts, and to turn to Him with sincerity.
exp.7:5:
God asks Ezekiel whether he sees what the people are doing: great abominations, that is, things God detests, committed in the temple. These actions drove God away from his sanctuary, his house. And he warns him that he will see things even worse.

He speaks, in a vision that shows the prophet Ezekiel what was happening inside the temple in Jerusalem. Near the gate there was an idol that provoked the anger of God. Scholars do not agree on exactly what the figure was. God shows the cause of his judgment: his people had abandoned true worship.

For today: ask God to show you which things in your life are occupying the place that belongs to him. With humility, set them aside, and return to worshiping him sincerely, for he desires to dwell near his people.
exp.10:22:
It says that the visible presence of God, his "glory," left Jerusalem. It stopped on the mountain east of the city, which is usually identified with the Mount of Olives. The word "stood" means it came to rest there.

Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, sees this scene in a vision. Earlier he saw that Jerusalem had idolatry and wickedness, even in the temple. That is why God withdraws gradually. It is a very serious judgment, but also a sign that God is not bound to a building and would remain with the exiles.

For today: God desires a faithful heart, not merely outward religion. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something we are putting in God's place, and return to him sincerely, trusting that he remains near those who repent.
exp.2:15:
It says that seven days passed, and then God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" means that God broke the silence and gave him a message. In other words, God broke the silence and gave him a message.

Ezekiel was a priest exiled in Babylon. He had seen a vision of the glory of God and received his call as a prophet. Then he came to Tel-abib, by the river Chebar, where other exiles lived, and he stayed there seven days, stunned and silent. Afterward God told him that He had made him a watchman, one who warns of danger, to warn Israel.

God does not always answer right away, and sometimes He asks us to wait and take in what we have lived through. If you feel confused or overwhelmed, do not be troubled by the silence. Stay close to God, pray, and keep watching for His guidance, because He speaks in His own time.
exp.3:14:
God tells Ezekiel that, instead of using human dung to bake his bread, he may use cow dung. The explanation of the word for dung and the phrase about preparing the bread is set aside here, since the reader's verse uses the plain words "dung" and "prepare," which need no explanation.

God speaks with Ezekiel, who represents through his actions the siege of Jerusalem. Earlier, God had commanded him to bake the bread over human dung to show that the people would eat unclean bread in exile. Ezekiel protested because he had always guarded his purity. God accepts his plea and grants a change, though the message of judgment still stands.

For today: God listens patiently to our sincere objections and can show mercy even when he asks us to do difficult things. We can speak to him honestly in prayer.
exp.10:4:
The explanation says that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Ezekiel with force and commanded him to speak on God's behalf. God tells the people that he knows what they have said and even what they think in secret. The phrase "the things that come into your mind" refers to the thoughts that arise in their minds.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles. The leaders of Jerusalem felt secure; they thought the punishment would not come soon, and they talked about building houses. They saw themselves as the meat protected inside the pot. God answers that he heard everything and that his judgment is real.

For today: God knows both my words and my hidden thoughts. I can be honest with him, ask him to correct my false sense of security, and live with humility, without assuming that my decisions have no consequences.
exp.9:4:
The explanation says that the sound of the cherubim's wings was so loud that it could be heard as far as the outer court of the temple. It is compared to the voice of the Almighty God when he speaks. A "roar" means a very loud noise, like thunder.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, describes a vision. The glory of God, shown as a cloud and a great brightness, moves within the temple in Jerusalem. This happens as God prepares to judge the city for its idolatry. The man clothed in linen will carry fire over Jerusalem. Many interpreters see here a sign that God is withdrawing from his temple, although the text does not explain every detail.

God is not small or manageable. His presence deserves respect and awe. Today we can draw near to Him with confidence, but also with reverence, taking seriously his voice and his Word, without treating Him lightly.
exp.8:4:
God speaks to six other men, and Ezekiel hears it with his own ears. He orders them to go through Jerusalem behind the man who marks the faithful, and to strike without pity. "Strike" means to hit or kill; the phrase about the eye means that they must not feel any sorrow.

The LORD speaks in a vision that Ezekiel receives while in exile. Jerusalem had filled up with idolatry and violence, and God decides to judge it. But first he commands that those who grieved over those evils be marked, to protect them. The judgment begins at the sanctuary, where the guilt was greater. Scholars understand this as a real judgment, though not all of them interpret its details the same way.

For today: God sees both the wickedness and the pain of those who suffer because of it. We can ask him for a sensitive heart, one that does not grow used to sin, and trust that he cares for his own.
exp.10:5:
God tells the leaders of Jerusalem that they have caused a great many deaths in the city. The word "filled" in the verse is a more old-fashioned term, but the sense is that the streets were full of the dead because of them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision where he sees the leaders of the people giving bad counsel in Jerusalem. Many understand that these dead were victims of the violence and injustice of the rulers, although the text does not give all the details. God confronts them because he knows what they think and say, and announces that judgment will come.

For today: God sees how we use the authority or influence we have. Let us ask him to help us care for people, not to take advantage of them, and to defend justice.
exp.0:26:
He says Ezekiel sees someone seated on the throne, and his body looks like glowing amber, like metal at red heat. From the waist up he seems surrounded by fire, and from the waist down it also looks like fire, with a brightness all around.

The word "loins" here means the waist or the middle part of the body. "Amber" here probably refers to a bright metal, though some understand it another way.

Ezekiel was a priest exiled in Babylon, by the river Chebar. He tells what he saw himself. God appears to him in an overwhelming vision, and Ezekiel makes clear that he saw only an appearance of the glory of the LORD, not God himself as he truly is. This prepares him to be a prophet among a people in exile.

For today: God is still glorious, even when we live through difficult times. Before we ask him for things, we can pause to worship him with reverence and humility, as Ezekiel fell on his face.
exp.10:2:
Some leaders of Jerusalem spoke with false confidence. The phrase "It is not near" means that the punishment was not close at hand, so people should keep building houses. They said the city was like a caldron (a large iron pot) and they were the flesh, meaning that inside the city they were protected.

God himself shows Ezekiel, in a vision, twenty-five men at the east gate of the temple. They were leaders of the people who gave bad counsel. God commands the prophet to speak against them, because He knows what they say and what they think. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the phrase, but the idea of false confidence is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security. If we think that nothing will happen to us, or that God will not call us to account, we deceive ourselves. It is better to listen to his voice with humility and seek his correction in time.
exp.4:6:
God asks Jerusalem with sorrow and firmness: how is it possible that, being a numerous and blessed people, you have not obeyed his commands? The phrase "because ye multiplied more than the nations" can be understood as "you have been more rebellious than the nations" or "you have had more abundance." They did not even keep the standards of the pagan peoples around them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem was placed at the center of the nations to be a witness, but it despised God's laws. That is why the judgment announced in the following verses is coming.

For today: blessings are no excuse for drifting away from God, but one more reason to obey him. Today we can ask ourselves whether what God has given us draws us closer to him or makes us forget him.
exp.7:8:
God tells Ezekiel to go in through the opening he has found in the wall and see for himself what the people are doing there. The phrase that would be rendered "he told me" is simply the speech of God to the prophet, and the wicked practices described are deeply offensive to God, especially idolatry. God wants the prophet to see these things with his own eyes.

God speaks in a vision that Ezekiel has while he is in Babylon, where he is carried in spirit to the temple in Jerusalem. The Lord shows him that the people and their leaders practice false worship in secret while appearing to be faithful. Many understand this as the reason for the judgment that would come upon the city.

For today: God sees what we do in hidden places. We can ask ourselves what things we keep out of sight, and what we give the place that belongs only to God. Instead of pretending, we can confess it honestly and ask him to cleanse us and guide us.
exp.4:12:
It says that God will carry his judgment through to the end. Where the source speaks of his fury being fulfilled, that means his anger will be brought to completion. Where it speaks of his wrath coming to rest on them, that means his anger will be satisfied once the punishment is finished. The word about his zeal refers to his demanding love, which will not tolerate his people betraying him. In the end, they will know that God meant what he said.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had defiled the temple with idols and sinful practices. God had warned them, and now he announces the consequences: famine, war, and scattering. Scholars understand this zeal as the pain of a faithful God in the face of betrayal.

For today: we should not take God's warning lightly. If anything in our lives competes with him, it must be corrected soon. His discipline seeks to bring us to recognize him and return to him.
exp.8:1:
This verse describes a vision that Ezekiel receives: six men come from the gate facing north, and each one carries a weapon for destruction. With them comes a seventh man dressed in linen, with a writing case with ink and pen at his waist. They all stop beside the bronze altar, in the temple.

God shows Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon, the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem because of its idolatry and its detestable practices. The men who come are carrying out God's judgment. Some think they are angels; the text does not say so with certainty. The man in linen will mark those who grieve over the sin of the city.

God is just and judges evil, but he also sees and cares for those who suffer because of the sin around them. Today we can ask him for a sensitive heart, one that does not grow used to injustice, but that prays and trusts in his mercy.
exp.10:9:
It says that the leaders of Jerusalem will die by the sword. God will judge them "in the border of Israel," that is, at the frontier or limit of the land. "Sword" means the blade itself, or war. "Ye shall know that I am the Lord" means that through the punishment they will recognize that God is real and that he means what he says.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. He addresses the leaders of Jerusalem who gave unjust counsel and felt secure, like meat inside a protected pot. God reminds them that they feared war, yet they lived far from his laws and copied the customs of the neighboring peoples. Some scholars see a fulfillment here in what happened near Riblah, although this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: do not settle into false security. Examine whether your life follows the Word of God or only what most people do.
exp.6:11:
It says the time of judgment has already come. The phrase "the day draws near" means that the day is very close. "Let not ... rejoice" means that no one should be glad, and "multitude" refers to all the people of the nation. Neither the buyer nor the seller should carry on as usual, because God's wrath falls on everyone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Judah and Jerusalem for their violence, their pride, and their idolatry. Many understand this to refer to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. Buying and selling will no longer matter, because everything will be lost.

For today: let us not set our hearts on material things, which pass away. Let us live with humility and return to God in time, without assuming that there will always be another opportunity tomorrow.
exp.4:3:
He tells that Ezekiel must again take a few hairs from those he had tied up in his garment, and throw them into the fire until they are burned. From that fire another fire would come out that would reach the whole house of Israel.

God speaks, giving a command to his prophet Ezekiel. He uses Ezekiel's hair as a sign to show what would happen to Jerusalem: siege, death, and scattering. The following verse gives the reason: the people despised God's laws and lived worse than the surrounding nations. Even the few who were spared were tested again by fire.

God takes our disobedience seriously, but he also cares for his own. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his Word or setting it aside, and return to him with humility.
exp.6:7:
God says he is about to punish his people, and that it will happen soon. The words that were rendered "soon" and "at once" in the source mean "quickly" or "right away." The phrases "pour out my anger" and "carry out my fury" are strong ways of saying that his wrath will reach its full extent. "I will judge you according to your ways" means the punishment will match the people's conduct. The "abominations" are detestable practices, above all idolatry.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He addresses Israel, the land of Judah, which had turned away from him. The text presents this as a judgment already announced: the end is coming. Interpreters connect it with the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC.

Today we can take seriously that God sees our lives and is not indifferent to evil. It is wise to examine our ways with humility and turn back to him while there is still time, trusting that he welcomes those who repent.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again. The phrase "Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying," means that a message from the Lord came to him. It is the way the prophet announces that God is going to answer him.

Ezekiel has just watched Pelatiah, one of the leaders, die while he was prophesying. Frightened, he fell face down to the ground and asked God whether He would destroy all the rest of Israel. Now God speaks, and He does not answer in anger, but with a word about the exiles, whom He has not abandoned.

When we are distressed and full of questions, we can bring our fear before God with honesty, as Ezekiel did. God listens, and in His time He answers us, often through His Word.
exp.4:10:
God swears by his own life that he is going to punish Jerusalem. The reason is that the people defiled his sanctuary, the temple, with their abominations, that is, with idols and practices that God hates. That is why he says he will break the people, that his eye will not spare them and that he will have no pity. Here "spare" means more or less "have pity" or "let pass."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Before the fall of Jerusalem, the people had mixed the worship of the LORD with idolatry. The punishment was not sudden: God had warned them many times. The verses that follow describe the siege of the city, with famine, war and scattering.

For today: God takes the purity of our worship seriously. We can ask ourselves what things occupy in our hearts the place that belongs to him, and return to him soon, while there is still time to repent.
exp.8:10:
The explanation says the man clothed in linen, with the writer's case at his waist, went back to report. His reply is brief: "I have done as you commanded me." The "writer's case" was the case holding ink and pen that scribes used, and the "linen garments" are the linen clothing he wore.

In Ezekiel's vision, God ordered this man to mark the foreheads of those who grieved over the wickedness of Jerusalem, so they would be spared from judgment. Afterward, others carried out the punishment. Now the man reports that he has completed his task. God had said the city was full of violence and that the people thought He did not see. The scene shows that He did see, and that He knew who belonged to Him.

For today: God sees both injustice and those who suffer because of it. We can live with sensitivity toward evil, pray with sincerity, and trust that He takes care of His own.
exp.2:19:
Ezekiel 3:20 says that if a person who had been living righteously turns away from what is good and does evil, and God places an obstacle in his path, that person will die in his sin. His past good deeds will not be remembered. And if the watchman did not warn him, God will hold the watchman accountable for that person's blood.

God is speaking to Ezekiel, whom he appointed as a watchman for Israel during the exile in Babylon. His task was to warn faithfully, both the wicked and the righteous. If he gave the warning, he fulfilled his responsibility, even if the people did not listen. Scholars debate how to understand "he shall die," whether it refers to physical death or spiritual death.

For today: if you see someone close to you turning away from God, do not stay silent out of fear or comfort. Speak to them with love, humility, and truth, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.45:20:
Here the guide, who in Ezekiel's vision is a man with an appearance like bronze, leads the prophet into the outer court of the temple. He makes him walk to the four corners, and in each one he sees a small court. The outer court is an open space that surrounds the temple, and the corners are the places where the courts stand.

Ezekiel receives this vision of a new temple, with very exact measurements. Just before, the guide showed where the priests would cook the offerings, so that the holy things would not be carried out into the court where the people were. These courts, according to the text that follows, are places prepared for cooking the people's offerings. How this vision is fulfilled, interpreters understand in several ways.

For today: God cares about the details of worship, with order and respect. We can draw near to Him with reverence, also in everyday life, knowing that even simple things, like preparing a meal, can be done for Him.
exp.34:7:
It says that God will fill the mountains of Seir, that is, of Edom, with the dead. The words "fill" and "will fill" are the same idea here. "Hills" are low rises of land, and "valleys" are the low ground between them. The phrase "shall fall by the sword" means they will die in battle. The picture is of total defeat across the whole territory.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, had long shown hatred toward Israel, and according to this chapter it rejoiced when Israel fell and wanted to take its land for itself. That is why God announces a judgment that matches that violence: "blood shall pursue you."

For today: resentment that is held onto can grow until it destroys us. Ask God to heal any bitterness you carry, and when someone falls, do not rejoice; help them. God sees injustice, and he is the one who judges with justice.
exp.41:1:
This verse gives the measurements of the chamber building that stood on the north side of the temple. Along the side of the north door, it measured one hundred cubits in length and fifty in width. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters. So the building was large.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, a man sent by God guides him and measures the temple in detail. These chambers were for the priests (Ezekiel 42:13). Scholars debate whether this vision describes a literal future temple or teaches, in symbolic form, the holiness and order of God.

For today: God cares about details, and he wants his presence to be approached with reverence. We can ask ourselves what order and respect we give to our time of prayer and worship.
exp.15:46:
It says that Jerusalem did not merely follow the wickedness of her neighbors Samaria and Sodom. She went far beyond them. Walking in their ways means living the way they lived, and the practices God detests are the things He calls abominations. The sentence about it being a very little thing is ironic: copying their sin was already serious, but Jerusalem outdid them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter He compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman whom He cared for and loved. She responded with idolatry and alliances with other nations. By comparing her to Sodom, known for its wickedness, God wants to show the seriousness of her sin and call her to acknowledge it.

For today: the more we have received from God, the more responsible we are. Let us avoid comparing ourselves with others to feel better; rather, let us examine our own hearts with humility and return to God, who is merciful.
exp.36:23:
God promises that his servant David will be king over the people and will be a shepherd to all of them. In this way, the people will live according to God's commands: they will walk in his just judgments, keep his instructions, and actually put them into practice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people of Israel who are in exile, divided, and wounded. He promised to gather them, cleanse them, and restore them. Here "David" is not the ancient king, who had already died, but a future king from his line. Christians see in this Jesus, the good shepherd; others interpret it in other ways.

For today: Jesus not only guides us, he also cares for us. Following him is not only listening to his words but practicing them. Today, choose one of his teachings that you know well and put it into practice in your home or at work.
exp.16:9:
It says the vine was planted in good soil, yet God asks whether it will prosper. The answer is no: the east wind, a hot, dry wind from the desert, will dry it up completely. Even in the furrows where it had grown green, it will wither.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Israel, who was in exile. This is a parable: the vine represents Judah and its king Zedekiah, who rebelled against Babylon. As the following verses say, the king of Babylon had already taken the earlier king and his officials captive. God shows that trusting in human alliances and breaking the covenant would not bring success.

Being in a good place does not guarantee a fruitful life if we turn away from God. Today we can ask ourselves what we trust more: our circumstances or the Lord.
exp.47:18:
This verse says that the people who will work in the city will come from all the tribes of Israel. "Serve" means they will be dedicated to tending to and sustaining the city. "Common land" is the shared ground around it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision near the end of the book. There he divides the land among the tribes and describes a city with its sanctuary. That the workers come from every tribe shows that the city does not belong to just one group, but to the whole people. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: as literal, as symbolic, or as referring to the future.

For today: In the church and in the community, all of us have a place to serve. We can ask ourselves what part of the shared work falls to us and do it gladly, no matter where we come from.
exp.47:31:
This verse describes the east side of the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It measures four thousand five hundred reeds, and it has three gates named for Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan. The reed was a measuring rod. Here "Joseph" stands for the tribes of his sons, Ephraim and Manasseh.

God shows Ezekiel this vision at the end of the book. The people were in exile, and God promises them restoration and his presence among them. The city ends up being called "The LORD is there." Scholars interpret it in several ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic.

For today: in this city there is room for all the tribes, each with its own gate. God does not leave anyone outside of his people. We can welcome other believers with love, even when they are different from us.
exp.27:18:
This verse says that all who knew the king of Tyre among the nations will be amazed at his downfall. His end will be one of "terror," that is, of dread and horror. "Thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt thou be any more" announces that his power and glory will disappear completely.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is judging the king of Tyre, a rich trading city. The king took pride in his beauty and wisdom, and used them badly through injustice and corrupt dealings. Some see here only a human king; others think the language also alludes to Satan. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: success, talent, and wealth are gifts from God, not reasons to think ourselves superior. Let us ask him for a humble heart, one that uses what it has to serve honestly and not to exalt itself.
exp.47:22:
This verse says that, after the holy portion, the one for the Levites, the city, and the prince, the rest of the land would be divided among the other tribes. Benjamin would receive a strip that runs from east to west. The sea mentioned in the original is the Mediterranean Sea, and the word for "portion" means share or inheritance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a final vision about the restored people. By showing an orderly division of the land, God gave hope to an exiled people. Interpreters differ on the meaning: some read it literally, others as a symbol of God's future kingdom. Benjamin is placed beside the holy territory, near Judah.

For today: God makes sure that each person has their place and their share. You can rest in the knowledge that he does not forget you, and serve with gratitude where he has placed you.
exp.42:3:
What it says: Ezekiel sees the bright presence of God, called "the glory of the Lord," enter the temple through the gate that faces east. "Way" means path, and "faced toward the east" means that gate looked toward where the sun rises.

Context: Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile in Babylon, speaks. Earlier, in another vision, he had seen the glory of God depart from the temple because of the people's sin. Now, in this vision of hope, God returns by the same side from which he had left. Interpreters differ on whether this temple describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of restoration.

For today: God desires to dwell again with his people when there is repentance. We can ask ourselves what we should open or correct in our lives to receive him, and pray with confidence, knowing that he is faithful to restore.
exp.38:22:
This verse says that the nations will understand why Israel was taken away as prisoners: not because God was weak, but because of the people's sin. They rebelled against God, and he "hid his face" from them, that is, he withdrew his protection and his closeness. He gave them into the hand of their enemies, and many fell by the sword, that is, by the sword. "Went into captivity" means they were carried off into exile.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Before promising Israel's restoration, he makes clear the reason for the punishment. In this way the nations will see that God is holy and just. The following verse announces that he will have mercy and bring his people back.

For today: God corrects with justice, but not in order to destroy us; he does it to bring us back to himself. If you recognize a sin, do not hide; return to God with sincerity, trusting in his mercy.
exp.33:7:
God speaks with a very serious oath: "As I live," meaning "by my own life." He says his flock was left exposed to being robbed and devoured by the wild beasts, because it had no true shepherd. The shepherds did not go out to look for the sheep; they took care only of themselves.

Here the Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile of the people in Babylon. The "shepherds" were the leaders of Israel, above all the kings, and also other officials. God accuses them because they used their position for their own benefit and neglected the people.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the church, in the family, or at work, ask yourself whether you are serving or only serving yourself. Look carefully after those whom God has placed in your charge.
exp.35:35:
The explanation says that the neighboring nations that survive will see Israel's restoration and will acknowledge that it was God who did it. The ruined cities are the places that lie in ruins, and the devastated lands are the areas that have been wasted and left empty. God promises to rebuild and to plant again, and he assures that he will do what he has said.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The land of Israel lay in ruins and the surrounding peoples mocked it. God promises to return the land to them and to give them a new heart, so that his name will be recognized among the nations.

For today: when your life or your family feels like it is in ruins, do not think that God can no longer do anything. He is able to rebuild what seems lost. Trust his word and give him time, while you keep walking with him in obedience.
exp.21:16:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel, meaning that God spoke to him again. The wording "came unto me" is an older way of saying "came to me." The important part is not in this verse but in what God says right after it.

The one speaking is God, and he does so through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, God had announced that he would scatter his people because of their sin and that in this way he would cleanse them of their impurity. Now a new message begins: God compares Israel to dross, the worthless residue left behind when metals are melted down.

For today: God continues to speak through his Word. Before reading it, ask him for a heart willing to listen, even when he corrects you, because his correction seeks to cleanse and restore you.
exp.20:6:
God tells Ezekiel to groan openly, and when the people ask him why, he will answer that it is because of the news that is coming. That news will bring terror: every heart will melt with fear, every hand will grow weak, every spirit will faint, and every knee will become weak as water. God assures them that it is coming and will be fulfilled.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. In this chapter he announces judgment on Jerusalem, pictured as a sword that God draws from its sheath. The prophet's groaning is a dramatized sign so that the people will understand how serious what is coming is. The exact details of how this was experienced are known only from what the text says.

For today: when God warns us, it is wise to take it seriously and turn back to him in time, rather than ignoring the sign. His word also invites us to feel the weight of sin with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.22:38:
The explanation says that the people sacrificed their children before their idols and that same day entered God's temple as if nothing had happened. "Defiling it" means making it dirty, making it impure. "The sanctuary" is the temple, the holy place. God points out the contradiction: one hand offered to the idols while the other claimed to worship him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 23 he uses the story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. With that image he denounces their unfaithfulness: they made alliances with other nations and worshiped false gods. This verse shows that their sin reached the temple itself.

For today: God is not content with a Sunday-only religion. We can ask ourselves whether our daily life, at work, at home, and in what we love, agrees with what we say at church.
exp.11:10:
The prophet Ezekiel is said to be a sign for the people. What he did, packing his belongings and going out like someone leaving for exile, is what will happen to them. "Captivity" means being taken away as prisoners to another land. The phrase about what will be done to them means they will truly live through it.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The people were rebellious and did not believe Jerusalem would be judged. So God commanded him to portray the exile through visible actions. The prince is the ruler of Jerusalem; the verses that follow announce that he will be captured and taken to Babylon. Many understand this to refer to King Zedekiah.

For today: when God warns us, it is wise to listen in time and not to mock or delay. His warning is a sign of patience, for it gives us the opportunity to return to Him before the consequences arrive.
exp.18:5:
He walked among the lions, that is, among the other powerful kings and nations. He became a strong young lion, he learned to catch and seize prey (he learned to hunt and trap victims), and he devoured men (he destroyed and abused people).

God speaks through Ezekiel and asks him to make a lament over the princes of Israel. The lioness represents Judah or its royal line, and the cubs represent its kings. Many believe this second cub is Jehoiachin or Jehoiakim, but this is not certain; some think of Zedekiah. The clear point is that he ruled with violence and fell.

Whoever holds power can learn to use it to harm. Today we can ask God to teach us to lead, work, and direct with justice and compassion, not with abuse.
exp.47:3:
It says that the land is divided into long strips, running from east to west. Next to the territory of Naphtali lies another strip, that of Manasseh. The word "border" means the boundary or edge of a territory. "The sea" is the Mediterranean Sea, to the west. "Another" means one more portion given to another tribe.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, toward the end of the book. He is describing a vision of the land restored for Israel, with an orderly division among the tribes and a temple at the center. Many interpret it in different ways: as a promise for Israel, as a spiritual picture, or as something yet to be fulfilled. What is certain is that it shows God cares for each tribe and each family.

God forgets no one, and He gives each person a place. Today we can trust that He also has a place and a purpose for you, and live thankful for what He gives us.
exp.20:28:
God says that the prophets and diviners of Ammon announce to them empty things and lies. Those false promises will not save them: the sword will fall upon them, along with other wicked people condemned to die. "Empty" means something without value. The sentence about the diviners, which in the source explained a word meaning "those who foretell for you," is removed. "The full measure of wickedness" refers to the final point, when sin reached its height.

God speaks through Ezekiel, at the time of the fall of Jerusalem. This part is a message against Ammon, a neighboring people who mocked Israel. Ammon trusted in its diviners, but God announces that its judgment will come anyway.

Today, do not let yourself be comforted by pleasant messages that do not come from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and respond to God with humility before it is too late.
exp.27:12:
This verse describes someone who was in Eden, the garden of God, covered with precious stones and gold. It speaks of beauty and of a splendor prepared from the day of his creation. "Thy covering" means that he was adorned; the instruments named in the verse are the tabrets and pipes, that is, drums and flutes; and "prepared" means made ready.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to raise a lament over the king of Tyre. Many believe the language goes beyond a human king and alludes to Satan; others understand it as a poetic image of that king's pride. Christians interpret it in both ways. The central theme is the fall of one who grew proud of his beauty and wisdom.

For today: everything good we have, whether talents, beauty, or success, is a gift from God. Let us thank him with humility and not allow it to lead us into pride.
exp.44:23:
It says that, along with each bull and each ram the prince offers, he must present a grain offering of one ephah, and for each ephah, a hin of oil. The "ephah" was a measure of capacity for dry goods, and the "hin" a measure for liquids. Its exact equivalent in liters is debated, but the ephah was considerably larger than the hin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of a renewed temple and worship. These rules regulate the prince's offerings during the Passover feast. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes something literal, something symbolic, or something future. What is clear is that God wants orderly worship.

For today: come near to God with order and generosity, not with what is left over. Sincere worship includes preparation and concrete giving.
exp.18:13:
It says that from one of the branches of the vine a fire came out and consumed its own fruit. No strong branch was left to serve as a scepter, that is, a staff of authority for ruling. "To rule" here means to dominate or reign. A lament is a sad song of mourning. The text says this is a lamentation and that it will continue to be remembered as one.

God commands Ezekiel to raise this lament over the princes of Judah. The vine represents the house of David, uprooted and carried off into exile in Babylon. The fire that comes from the branch itself is usually understood as the guilt of the rulers themselves, perhaps King Zedekiah. Scholars debate exactly whom each image refers to.

For today: whoever holds authority can destroy what they are meant to protect when they act with pride or injustice. Let us ask God for humility to lead with integrity in our family, our work, or our church.
exp.16:14:
It says that the king of Judah rebelled against the king of Babylon by sending messengers to Egypt to ask for horses and a large army. Then God asks, with a tone of reproach: Will things go well for the one who did this? Will the one who broke his covenant escape? A word like "covenant" means a firm promise or agreement, and "messengers" are official envoys.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. King Zedekiah had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, but he broke that oath and sought help from Egypt. God reminds him that a promise made in his name is serious, and that trusting in human power would not save him.

For today: keep your word, even when it is hard, and do not look for deceptive shortcuts. When you feel fear or pressure, instead of relying only on human resources, go first to God with honesty and ask him for wisdom to act with integrity.
exp.15:29:
God says that Jerusalem's heart is weak and unsteady. Some versions render the unusual Hebrew word here as "sick with passion" or "full of rage," and the reader's verse uses "weak." God accuses her of acting with the shamelessness of a powerful prostitute, that is, without shame or restraint.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he describes Jerusalem as a woman he cared for and made a covenant with, but who turned away from him. Her unfaithful dealings represent idolatry and alliances with Assyria, Canaan and Babylon, instead of trusting in God.

For today: our hearts can seek to be satisfied in things that do not fill them, such as success, money or the approval of others. Today we can stop, honestly acknowledge this, and return to God, who is faithful and forgives.
exp.38:14:
It says that while the land is being cleaned, those who travel through the country and come across human bones will set up a marker beside them, a heap of stones. In this way the place is marked until the burial workers, the ones assigned to bury the dead, carry the remains to the valley of Hamon-gog. The name "Hamon-gog" means something like "the multitude of Gog."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he announced the defeat of Gog, an enemy who attacks Israel. After the victory, the people must clear the land of corpses, because under Israel's law contact with death made a person unclean. Many understand this literally, and others as a symbol of the complete purification God will bring. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: God cares about what is clean and orderly. If we see something damaged around us, let us not ignore it. We can help with patience, step by step, until it is restored.
exp.26:19:
Ezekiel 27:20 says that Dedan traded with Tyre, supplying it with "precious clothes for chariots." The phrase seems to refer to fine cloths or blankets placed on horses or on chariots for riding. Some scholars think these were saddle blankets. The word "merchant" refers to the people or city that does the trading.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, the great trading city of the sea. A list of peoples is given who brought goods from many places. The purpose is to show Tyre's enormous wealth and pride, a city that would soon be judged. Dedan was a region of Arabia, although its exact location is debated.

For today: wealth and success can make us feel secure apart from God. Ask yourself what you truly trust in. Use what you have with gratitude and humility, remembering that everything comes from God and that our security is in him.
exp.35:15:
This verse says: "Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying." The word "came" is how this phrase is rendered in English. It is a phrase Ezekiel uses many times to signal that God is going to speak to him again.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who lived in exile with the people in Babylon. Earlier, God had promised the land of Israel that it would no longer suffer shame or the loss of its children. Now a new message begins, in which God explains why Israel was punished: they defiled the land with their sins, their idols, and the blood they shed. This helps us better understand the need for restoration.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before asking him for comfort or change, it is good to open the Bible with humility and listen also to what he says about our lives, even when it is difficult. His truth corrects us so that we may be healed.
exp.17:13:
Ezekiel 18:14 describes a man who is violent and sinful and has a son. That son sees all the sins his father has committed. The explanation notes that the word "beget" carries the sense of "have," and that the phrase "and doeth not such like" means that although he sees them, he does not copy them. This begins a third case: the son who decides to live differently.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. They were saying, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge," as if they were suffering only for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is responsible for his or her own life. The son is not condemned for the wickedness of his father if he does not follow it.

For today: your family past does not decide your future. If you grew up seeing bad examples, with God's help you can break that cycle and choose a different path, one of justice and mercy.
exp.13:13:
God says that even if three very righteous men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in a sinful land, they would save only their own lives. Saying they would deliver only "their own souls" means that they would save themselves. Saying they would be saved "by their righteousness" indicates that their faithfulness to God would protect them, but not others.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Judah. Some believed that Jerusalem would be saved because of the good people within it. God answers that the people's sin was so grave that neither the prayers nor the righteousness of others would rescue them. The three men were well-known examples of faith. About Daniel, some scholars think of the Daniel of the exile and others of an ancient figure; this is not entirely certain.

For today: faith is not inherited or lent. We can pray for others, but each person must respond to God. Seek out a sincere relationship with Him yourself.
exp.26:7:
Ezekiel 27:8 says that Tyre, a great trading city, was like a very splendid ship. The people of Sidon and Arvad, other Phoenician cities, worked as the crew who rowed. And the wise men of Tyre itself, that is, its skilled and capable experts, were the ones who piloted the ship. The "oarsmen" are those who move the oars; the "pilots" steer the course.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre. He describes her as a beautiful ship, built with the best of many nations. With this image he shows her wealth and her pride. Later on, the same ship sinks, and so he announces her fall.

For today: having good resources and capable people does not guarantee a secure future. We can be thankful for and make good use of what God gives us, but without trusting in those things as if they were our salvation. Let us place our trust in Him.
exp.35:7:
God speaks to the mountains of Israel as if they could hear him. He tells them that they will once again put out branches and bear fruit, and that this fruit will belong to his people Israel. "Branches" here means the limbs of the trees, and "the time for them to come home is near" means that the people's return is close at hand.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was in exile, its land lay desolate, and it was mocked by the neighboring nations. God promises to restore the land, bring his people back to it, and rebuild the ruined cities. Interpreters debate whether this was fulfilled only in the return from exile or whether it also points to a future fulfillment.

For today: when your life feels barren or in ruins, remember that God knows how to restore. Trust his promise, and while you wait, prepare yourself to bear fruit and to bless others.
exp.22:13:
Ezekiel 23:14 explains that Oholah, one of the two sisters in the story, did not stop at her first sin but increased it. When she saw men portrayed on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans (Babylonians) painted in red, she was drawn to them. "Whoredoms" here refers to unfaithfulness, not only sexual sin. "Pourtrayed with vermilion" refers to images in bright colors.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. With the image of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), he shows how his people were unfaithful to him by seeking foreign alliances and gods. This part describes Jerusalem, which copies the error of Samaria and goes even further, drawn to what she sees.

For today: what we look at can awaken desires that pull us away from God. Be careful about what you let into your eyes and your heart, and return to him quickly when you notice you are going astray.
exp.23:13:
God says that what he has announced will come to pass and that he himself will carry it out. He will not change his mind, will not feel pity, and will not relent.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, which is compared to a rusty, dirty pot. For years the people rejected the cleansing God offered them and kept on in their wickedness. That is why judgment is coming, and shortly afterward Ezekiel will lose his wife as a sign of that grief.

For today: do not take God's warnings lightly. If he shows you something you need to change, respond quickly with humility and repentance, because his forgiveness is offered, and it is better to accept it today than to harden your heart.
exp.45:19:
It says that in the vision there is a special place inside the temple where the priests boil or cook the meat of the sin offerings and the trespass offerings, and also prepare the meat offering. They do it there, inside, so as not to carry those holy things out into the outer court, where the people are. The phrase about the people being sanctified here means that what is holy should not improperly affect the people.

The one speaking is a guide who shows Ezekiel, in a vision, the future temple. He walks through its parts and its rules. The purpose is to teach that God is holy and that his service must be carried out with order and reverence. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

Today we can learn to treat what belongs to God with reverence and care. Before we speak, serve, or teach, it is good to approach with humility, remembering that God is holy and merciful.
exp.31:5:
It says that God will pour out the blood of the pharaoh of Egypt over the land, until it covers the mountains, and that the rivers will be filled with him. "Water" means to pour out or soak. "Swimmest" refers to the pharaoh being compared to a monster of the river. "Be full" means they will be filled completely.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. It is a lament against the pharaoh, who believed himself as powerful as a crocodile or dragon of the Nile. God uses this strong image to announce that his pride will end and that Egypt will fall. It is poetic and symbolic language, not a literal description.

For today: no one is so great that they stand above God. If today we trust in our power, money, or fame, this text invites us to humility and to place our trust in the Lord, who is just and has the final word.
exp.21:25:
Her priests have broken my law and profaned my holy things. They have made no distinction between what is holy and what is common, and they have not taught the difference between the unclean and the clean. They have ignored my Sabbaths on purpose, and so I have been dishonored among my people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, shortly before or during the fall of Jerusalem (around 590 B.C.). He is accusing the city's leaders: prophets, priests, and princes. The priests were supposed to teach the people to distinguish the sacred from the ordinary, but they did the opposite. That is why God announces judgment.

For today: if you teach or guide others, be faithful to God's Word and do not bend it to your own convenience. All of us can ask ourselves whether we give God the place that belongs to him.
exp.37:10:
Here God describes what Gog, an enemy leader, will think. He plans to attack a land of villages, a peaceful people who live at rest and feel secure, with no walls, no bars to secure them, and no gates. To Gog, that people looks like an easy prey.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that, at a future time, Gog will have an evil thought and will gather allies to plunder the people of Israel, who have been restored. Interpreters differ: some see it as a future historical event, others as a symbolic picture of evil's attack against God's people. What is clear is that God knows the hidden plans of the heart.

For today: do not confuse calm with weakness. If you are at peace, trust that God sees every intention against you, and guard your own heart too, so that no thoughts of taking advantage of others are born within you.
exp.33:1:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak firmly to the shepherds of Israel, that is, to its leaders. He calls them to account with a cry of grief and warning. Their failing is that they care only for themselves, feeding themselves rather than the flock. But a shepherd exists to feed and care for the flock.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. The people were suffering, and their rulers, and probably other leaders as well, had neglected them. The verses that follow describe in detail how they took advantage of the sheep instead of caring for them.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the family, the church, or at work, ask yourself whom you are really serving. Leading means caring, not taking advantage.
exp.21:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of addressing him as a simple human being. He asks him, insistently, whether he will not judge the city that sheds blood, that is, full of violence and unjust deaths. He also charges him to show her all her abominations, that is, her practices that are detestable in God's eyes.

The one speaking is the LORD, and the city is Jerusalem, as seen in the rest of the chapter. Ezekiel was a prophet and a priest, and he lived among the exiles in Babylon. God sends him to declare clearly the guilt of the city: violence, idolatry, and corruption, which would bring consequences.

For today: God expects us to call things by their name, with truth and humility. Let us ask him to show us first our own faults, and to help us speak with courage and love when there is injustice.
exp.42:22:
It says that, when the ceremony of purifying the altar with sin offerings is finished, a young bull and a ram, both without fault, must be offered. "Atone" means to cleanse or cover guilt. "Blemish" means a stain or flaw. "Herd of cattle" is the cattle of cows, and "flock" here is the group of animals.

God speaks to Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. After the exile, the people needed to understand that God is holy and that people must approach him with reverence. These rites dedicate the altar over seven days. Interpreters differ on whether this will be fulfilled literally or is a symbolic picture of restored worship.

For today: come to God with sincerity and respect. Christians believe that Jesus is the perfect sacrifice, so we can pray with confidence, without hiding our failures.
exp.42:18:
God tells Ezekiel to give a young bull from the herd to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok. They are the ones who draw near to God to serve him. The bull would be a sin offering, that is, an offering to cleanse sin.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the future temple. God gives instructions for consecrating the altar on the day it is made. Before it was used, it had to be purified with blood. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a spiritual image.

For today: drawing near to God calls for reverence and a clean heart. Before serving him, we need to acknowledge our sin and trust in the forgiveness that Christ offered for us.
exp.11:26:
The explanation says that the people of Israel were mocking Ezekiel. They said his vision was for many days ahead, meaning something that would happen very late, and that he prophesied of times that were far off, so distant a future that it did not concern them. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel.

God speaks to Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. The people used sayings to make light of the warnings of judgment and to stay comfortable in their rebellion. God answers that his words will not delay any longer: what was announced would be fulfilled in their own days.

For today: do not use "it is still a long way off" as an excuse to postpone your obedience. If God is speaking to you through his Word, respond today with humility, because his patience is an opportunity to return to him.
exp.44:10:
This verse says that the ephah and the bath, which are measures, must be of the same size. The ephah was used to measure dry things, such as grain, and the bath to measure liquids, such as oil or wine. Both were to equal the tenth part of a homer, which was the large reference measure. In this way everyone would use the same fixed standard.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel. He rebukes the princes of Israel because they oppressed the people with violence, robbery, and unjust taxes. He asks them to practice justice, and exact measures were part of that, since they were used for buying, selling, and offering to the Lord. Scholars do not agree on the exact value of these measures in liters.

For today: be honest in small things, such as prices, work, and accounts. God cares about how we treat others in everyday life.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "came unto me, saying" means that a message from the Lord came to me. It is the simple way the book announces that what follows is not the prophet's own ideas, but what God wants to say.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, along with other Jews taken captive. Here God begins a new message addressed to the people. The verses that follow compare Jerusalem to the wood of the vine, which is of little use except for bearing fruit. For that reason, this verse works as an introduction.

For today: before we look for what God wants to tell us, it is good to stop and listen. We can read the Bible calmly and ask, "Lord, speak to me," ready to receive even what is hard for us to hear.
exp.26:10:
It says that men of Arvad, together with Tyre's army, kept watch on its walls, and that the Gammadims were in its towers. They hung their shields on the walls, and so they made the city more beautiful. Helmets are the "helmets" of the verse, and the "galleys" are the large oar-driven ships; [the Gammadims are not certain: some believe they were a people, others think the word refers to guards or to a place.]

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and laments over Tyre, a wealthy and proud seaport city. The text describes its beauty like that of a great ship, built with the help of many nations. This praise prepares the announcement of its fall, because its trust was in its wealth and its power.

For today: everything that seems strong and beautiful, such as money, success, or prestige, can disappear. It is better to trust in God, who does not change, and to use what we have with humility and gratitude.
exp.23:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak a parable to the rebellious house, that is, to the people of Israel who had resisted God. He is to set a pot on the fire and pour water into it. The sentence about the old wording is removed, since the words it explained are not in the verse. The name of God here is the Lord God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. That same day the king of Babylon began the siege of Jerusalem, and God reveals it to him in advance. The pot represents the city, and what follows shows the judgment that would come because of its persistent rebellion.

For today: God speaks clearly before he corrects, and his warnings are a sign of patience. If you feel today that he is calling you back to his way, do not harden your heart; listen, acknowledge your error, and return to him, who is willing to forgive.
exp.13:9:
The verse says that both the one who inquires and the prophet will bear the consequences of their sin. "They shall bear their iniquity" means that each one will answer for his own guilt. "Iniquity" here means wrongdoing or sin, and "the one who inquires" is the person who goes to seek a word from God. The guilt of both will be the same.

God speaks through Ezekiel to Israel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders had idols in their hearts and yet still wanted to consult the prophet. God warns that whoever seeks answers with a divided heart, and whoever tells them what they want to hear, will fall together under judgment. The passage is difficult, and scholars interpret it in various ways, but its aim is to bring the people back to God.

For today: before seeking spiritual counsel, examine your heart. Ask God for honesty, and seek voices that tell you the truth, not only what pleases you.
exp.22:9:
The explanation says that the Assyrians, Aholah's former lovers, left her in shame: they uncovered her nakedness, took away her sons and daughters, and killed her with the sword. She became famous among women, because judgment was carried out against her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells a parable about two sisters: Aholah represents Samaria (the northern kingdom of Israel) and Aholibah represents Jerusalem. The sexual unfaithfulness in the parable stands for faithlessness toward God, through seeking alliances and idols from other nations. Samaria fell to Assyria, and here it is presented as a warning for Jerusalem.

For today: trusting in what is not God may seem attractive, but in the end it betrays us. Today we can ask ourselves where we look for security apart from Him, and return our trust to God.
exp.13:7:
God says he will set himself against the person who keeps idols in the heart and yet comes to ask him for an answer. "Setting my face against" means confronting that person with judgment. "A sign and a proverb" means that he will become a public example, something people will talk about as a warning. "Cut off" means removing him from the community. The purpose is that they will know that I am the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Some of the people's leaders were coming to consult him, but they kept idols in their hearts. God calls them to turn back and does not accept a religion that is only outward appearance. Some understand "cut off" as exclusion from the covenant people; the text gives no further detail.

For today: before seeking God's guidance, ask yourself what thing is occupying the place that belongs to him alone. Confess it honestly, turn away from it, and draw near to God with a whole heart.
exp.47:33:
This verse describes the west side of the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It measures four thousand five hundred reeds (a reed was a measuring rod, about three meters according to some scholars) and has three gates, named for Gad, Asher, and Naphtali, three of the twelve tribes of Israel.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting what God showed him. Israel was in exile and had lost its city and its temple. This vision, at the end of the book, gave them hope: God would restore his people. Christians interpret it in various ways, either as a promise for Israel or as an image of God's presence with his people. The city's final name is "The LORD Is There."

For today: each tribe had its own gate, so everyone had a place in the city. God reminds us that every person among his people is welcome and has their place before him.
exp.11:16:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel once again. "Moreover the word of the Lord came to me, saying" means that a message from the Lord came to him. It is the phrase the prophet uses to introduce a new message. What God will say comes in the following verses.

Here speaks Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. God uses him to warn the people that Jerusalem will be judged. Earlier, God said that some would survive and would recognize who He is. Now He gives Ezekiel a new sign: to eat and drink with trembling, to show the fear that would come upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

For today: God still speaks, above all through His Word. Before beginning the day, take a moment to read the Bible and ask Him to speak to you, with a heart ready to listen and obey.
exp.19:19:
God asks his people to set the sabbaths apart as holy days, that is, days dedicated to him. The sabbath would be a sign between God and Israel, a reminder of the relationship they shared. To make something holy means to set it apart for sacred use. The Lord is God's name, the Lord himself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel, during the exile in Babylon. He reminds them of what he told their ancestors in the desert, after bringing them out of Egypt. He asked for faithfulness and that they not follow idols. But they rebelled and profaned the sabbaths, and even so God showed patience for the sake of his name.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and remember who God is. Turn off the noise, pray, give thanks, and trust that he sustains your life, not only your effort.
exp.39:1:
He says that God, in visions, carried Ezekiel from Babylon to the land of Israel. He set him on a very high mountain, and from there he saw something that looked like the buildings of a city toward the south.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile. He speaks in the first person and tells what God showed him, fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem. His people were wounded and without hope. This vision of the temple and the city would give them encouragement. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: when everything seems lost, God can still show you hope. Ask him to let you see beyond your situation, and trust that he has not abandoned his promises.
exp.22:41:
It says that in Jerusalem (Aholibah) there was a noise of people gathered in festivity and wild revelry. Along with men of the common sort came also Sabeans from the desert, and the women were adorned with bracelets on their hands and beautiful crowns on their heads. Some scholars explain that the Sabeans were a trading people from southern Arabia; other translations read "drunkards," and not all agree on what the original text says.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), to show how his people allied themselves with foreign nations and their gods, leaving behind faithfulness to him.

For today: what adorns us on the outside does not replace loyalty to God. Ask yourself what things you seek to feel valuable or secure, and put God first again.
exp.35:32:
It says that when God cleanses the people from all their sins, He will also cause the cities to be inhabited again, and the places that were destroyed will be rebuilt. "Wickedness" refers to acts of evil, and the word for ruined refers to places left in ruins.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites who were in exile, far from their land, because they had turned away from Him. Before promising restoration, He tells them to remember their evil ways, but He makes clear that He acts for the sake of His own name and not because they deserve it. First comes the cleansing of the heart, and then the rebuilding.

For today: God does not only want to repair what looks broken in our lives, but He begins by cleansing the heart. Today you can honestly acknowledge what you have done wrong, ask Him for forgiveness, and trust that He can rebuild what seems lost.
exp.32:1:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to his people using a comparison. When God allows war to come upon a land, the people of that place choose a man from among them and set him up as a watchman, that is, a guard who keeps careful watch from a tower and warns of danger.

The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God gives him his task as a spiritual watchman for Israel. The image was familiar: a sentinel warned the city when the enemy drew near. In this way Ezekiel was to warn the people.

For today: if God places us near someone, we can speak to them with love and truth when we see that they are going down the wrong path. We should also listen with humility when someone warns us with good intentions.
exp.26:1:
God says to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," that he should take up a lamentation over Tyre. A lamentation is a funeral song, a mourning that is sung for someone who has fallen or is about to fall. Tyre was a great trading city by the sea.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile in Babylon. God announces judgment against Tyre for its pride and its wealth. What follows shows that Tyre boasted of its perfect beauty. The lamentation is ironic: it mourns a city that believed itself invincible.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success or appearance. All of that can disappear. We can receive with humility what God gives us and trust in him, who endures forever.
exp.38:13:
After the great defeat of Gog's army, men will be hired on a permanent basis to travel across the whole land. Their task will be to search for and bury the bodies that remain, so that the land is made clean. The explanation of the phrase about men hired for their work is that they are workers paid for their labor. The part about the land's surface means the face of the earth. After seven months, they will carry out a final inspection to make sure nothing is left behind.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapters 38 and 39 he announces that a great coalition will attack Israel and be defeated. The bodies would leave the land unclean, so a careful cleansing is required. Interpreters differ: some understand this as a literal future event, and others as a symbolic picture of God's judgment on evil.

For today: God takes cleansing seriously and does not settle for what is only partly seen. We can ask him to show us areas of our lives that need review and ongoing cleansing, and not leave them half-done.
exp.39:45:
This verse says that the chamber facing north was set aside for the priests who looked after the altar. They were descendants of Zadok, from the tribe of Levi, and they were the only ones who could draw near to the Lord to serve him. The word "chamber" means a room, and the word "keepers" refers to those who take care of and watch over the charge entrusted to them.

This is part of the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, who, while in exile, was taken in a vision to a new temple. A guide walks him through it and measures each part. Here the order and holiness of the place are shown: each group had its own space and its own task. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God values service done with order, reverence, and faithfulness. Whatever your task in your church or family, do it with care, as one who serves the Lord.
exp.47:13:
