It says that the portion of land set apart for the Levites could not be sold, exchanged, or passed into other hands. "Exchange" is what the verse calls changing one thing for another, and "passing it over to another" is giving it away to someone else. The "firstfruits of the land" are the best and the first of what is produced, offered to God. It was something holy, that is, dedicated to the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision about the restored people and the new division of the land, with the temple and the city. This holy portion lay at the center, for the service of God. Scholars debate whether this is to be fulfilled literally or symbolically, and it is honest to acknowledge that there are several interpretations.

Today we can ask ourselves what the first and best things we set aside for God are: time, money, or attention. What we dedicate to him should not be bargained away or traded according to our convenience.
exp.26:27:
It says that when the sailors of Tyre cry out in anguish, the people of the nearby lands and coasts will tremble with fear. The word "suburbs" in the verse refers to the areas around the city, and some translations understand it as the shores or the pasturelands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a city rich from its sea trade. The prophet compares it to a great ship that is sinking. Its pride and its wealth will not save it, and its fall will shake everyone who depended on it.

For today: nothing we build, whether money, success, or reputation, is a secure foundation on its own. It is wise to trust God and live with humility, using what we have with generosity and justice.
exp.15:11:
It says that God, like someone caring for a beloved person, adorned her with jewels. He put a ring or jewel on her nose, earrings in her ears, and a beautiful crown on her head. The jewels and earrings are the ornaments mentioned in the verse, and the crown is the royal band worn on the head.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl whom He found, cared for, and helped grow up, and with whom He later made a covenant, as in a marriage. That woman represents Jerusalem, that is, God's people. The passage first shows how much He gave them, and then points to their unfaithfulness. What they had came from God, not from themselves.

For today: remember that everything good we have is a gift from God. That leads us to live thankful and humble, and to be faithful to Him, instead of boasting or trusting in our own strength.
exp.38:6:
God says he will make his holy name known in the midst of Israel, his people. He promises that he will never again let that name be polluted, and the nations will know that he is the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, within the prophecy against Gog and Magog (chapters 38 and 39). Earlier, Israel had dishonored God's name through its idolatry and its exile. Now God promises to defeat a great enemy to show who he is. Interpreters differ: some see a future event, others see symbolic language of God's final triumph.

For today: let us take care how we live and speak, because our conduct can either honor or stain the name of God. Let us also trust that he guards his own honor and keeps his promises.
exp.12:6:
God asks the false prophets a pointed question: have they not seen worthless visions and announced false predictions? They said "The LORD says," but God makes clear that He had not spoken. A "lying divination" means an invented message presented as if it came from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some prophets gave false hopes of peace without calling the people back to God. For this reason they did not help to repair the breaches in the wall, that is, they did not defend the people like someone fixing the cracks in a wall. God announces that He will oppose them.

Today, before accepting a message said to come from God, it is wise to compare it with the Bible. And when we speak of God to others, let us do so with humility and truth, never putting into His mouth what He has not said.
exp.47:26:
Next to the territory of Zebulun, the explanation says, another strip of land would go to the tribe of Gad. That strip stretches from east to west, "from the east side unto the west side," that is, from the eastern side to the Mediterranean Sea. "Border" means boundary or limit. Gad is the last tribe named in this southern list.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile. In the final chapters of the book, God shows a vision of the land divided into equal strips among the tribes, with the Lord at the center. Interpreters differ on whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic. Either way, it gave hope of restoration to a people in exile.

God takes care that every family has its place. We can trust that He forgets no one, and give thanks for what He has given us, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.11:5:
God tells Ezekiel that, while the people watch him, he is to load his belongings onto his shoulders and go out at night. He must cover his face so that he cannot see the ground. His belongings are his baggage or luggage, and his act is meant as a sign or example for the people.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The Israelites refused to believe that Jerusalem would be judged. God uses this visible action, like a prophetic drama, to show that the king and the people would go into exile. Many understand that the covered face shows shame and the loss of their land, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings just because you do not like them or they seem distant. Listen to His Word with humility and respond in time, while there is still an opportunity to return to Him.
exp.31:19:
It says Egypt will fall among those who die by the sword. She has already been given over to the "knife," that is, to war and destruction. Then the command is given to draw her out, along with all her peoples, that is, her whole multitude, to the same end. The word "á," the old form of "a," is no longer used in modern writing, and "uncircumcised" refers to the peoples who did not belong to Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." He asks him to sing a funeral lament over Egypt, a powerful and proud nation. According to the text, God announces that this power will not save her. The image used is that of going down to the grave together with other nations already defeated. Many read this as poetic language about God's judgment.

For today: let us not trust in power, fame, or success, because everything is temporary. Let us place our security in God and live with humility.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to me" is the way the prophet announces that what follows is not his own ideas but a message received from God. It is how he signals that the words that come next are a message from God.

Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. Some elders of Israel came to seek the Lord, that is, to ask for a word through the prophet, and they sat down in front of him. Before Ezekiel says anything to them, God speaks first. His answer will be surprising: he will not listen to them, because their hearts were not right.

For today: before asking something of God, it is good to examine the attitude with which we approach him. He desires a sincere heart willing to obey, not only words or rituals.
exp.26:12:
This verse says that Greece (in Hebrew, Javan), Tubal, and Meshech traded with Tyre. They brought to its fairs, that is, to its markets, enslaved people and utensils or vessels of bronze and other metals. The "vessels" were containers, not only cups.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a city very rich because of its sea trade. The chapter lists its trading partners to show its fame and its pride. Then comes the announcement of its fall. Here the trade in people is also mentioned, something the Bible does not approve as an ideal, but presents as part of an arrogant economy.

For today: check where your earnings and your purchases come from. Prospering is not wrong, but God calls us to work with justice, without taking advantage of others or trusting in money more than in Him.
exp.27:19:
This verse says: "Again the word of the Lord came unto me, saying." The word "came" here means that the message arrived or was received, and it is a formula Ezekiel uses to introduce a new message from God.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, the prophet, who says he received the word of God. He has just finished the message against the king of Tyre, and now he begins a new one against Sidon, another neighboring city. God announces that he will judge the pride and injustice of the nations, and that they will know that he is the Lord.

God does not stay silent before wickedness, but he does not act in secret either: he speaks and warns. Today we can approach the Bible with attention, knowing that God still speaks to us through his word. Listening with humility helps us correct our course in time.
exp.36:1:
He says that God led Ezekiel through the valley full of bones, walking around among them. There were a great number of them, lying on the ground across the whole surface of the valley. Moreover, they were very dry: they had been there so long that no trace of life remained.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision God gave him. Later in this same chapter, God explains that the bones represent Israel, which lived in exile and felt that its hope had run out. God first shows him the worst of the situation before he acts.

For today: God is not alarmed by situations that seem hopeless to us. You can honestly bring to him whatever you feel is dry or beyond repair, and trust that he knows what he is able to do, as Ezekiel answered: "you know."
exp.26:28:
This verse describes the sailors of Tyre: the rowers and the pilots who guided the ships. They come down from their vessels and stand on dry land, as people who can no longer continue sailing. The rowers are those who handle the oar, and the pilots are those who directed the ship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who composes a lament over Tyre, a city made rich by its sea trade. He announces its fall because of its pride and its trust in riches. The sailors appear as witnesses of the disaster: they see what seemed unshakable sink, and they weep bitterly.

For today: examine where you place your security. Money, success, or reputation can disappear quickly. Trust in God first, and use what you have with humility and generosity.
exp.20:16:
God says that He too will "strike his hands together," that is, clap them. In that time, this gesture could express anger, grief, or that something is considered done. Then he says he will "rest" his fury, meaning he will let it settle once the judgment has been carried out. It ends with the seal of his authority: "I the Lord have spoken."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces that the sword of the king of Babylon would come against Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The verses before describe that sword as sharpened and ready. Some scholars understand the clapping as anger, others as the seal of a judgment that has been decided.

For today: God is serious and does not mock sin, but his anger is neither eternal nor capricious. We can heed his correction in time, return to him with humility, and trust that his justice has an end and a purpose.
exp.21:20:
God says that he will gather his people inside Jerusalem, the way someone puts metals into a furnace. Then he will blow the fire of his anger on them, and there they will be melted down. To be melted means to become liquid from the heat. Anger like this is very intense.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to the exiles in Babylon. Earlier he had said that Israel had become like dross, meaning the worthless remains left behind when metal is refined. The people were full of injustice, violence, and idolatry. Jerusalem would be the furnace where judgment would arrive.

For today: let us not take sin or God's patience lightly. If there is something in our lives that we know does not please him, we can acknowledge it today, ask for forgiveness, and change direction. God calls us to return to him before the consequences reach us.
exp.11:9:
It says God tells Ezekiel to give a message: what he has just acted out is a "burden," that is, a heavy word of judgment. That burden is for the prince in Jerusalem (the king, Zedekiah, as is commonly understood) and for all the people of Israel who live there with him.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The prophet had represented with actions, such as carrying his baggage, that Jerusalem would be taken into captivity. The people, called a rebellious house, asked with curiosity or mockery: "What are you doing?" God answers by explaining that the sign was a real warning.

For today: God does not leave his people without warning. When one of his words makes us uncomfortable, instead of mocking it or ignoring it, we can stop, sincerely ask what he wants to teach us, and correct our course in time.
exp.25:5:
This verse says that the "daughters" of Tyre, that is, the towns or villages that depended on her on the mainland, would be destroyed by the sword. The final result would be that they would know that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a trading city, proud of its wealth, and it rejoiced when Jerusalem fell (26:2). God announces judgment against her, and the following text names Nebuchadnezzar as the instrument. Scholars discuss how all this was fulfilled in detail, but the central message is clear: no human power stands above God.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success, or our own strength. All of that can disappear. Let us instead trust in God, and let us rejoice with humility, never with pride, when others suffer.
exp.16:10:
This verse says: "Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying". The word "came" here is the verb that introduces the new message. It is a transition phrase that announces that God is going to speak to Ezekiel again.

The prophet Ezekiel is speaking, and he is in exile in Babylon. He has just told a parable about a vine that does not prosper, and now God gives him a new message to explain it. The verses that follow make clear that the parable refers to the king of Judah and his alliance with Babylon, which he later broke. The people did not want to understand, so God calls them a "rebellious house."

For today: God does not leave his messages half-finished, but helps us understand them. We can come to the Bible with an open heart, asking him to explain what we do not understand and being willing to obey what he shows us.
exp.11:23:
He says that God will put an end to false prophecies in Israel. A "vain vision" is a vision with no truth or value, and "flattering divination" refers to false predictions that only pleased the people, telling them what they wanted to hear even though they did not come from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who prophesied among the exiles in Babylon. The people repeated a saying: "the days go on and no vision is fulfilled." In this way they mocked the warnings of judgment. In addition, false prophets gave them comfort with pleasant messages. God answers that his words will be fulfilled soon and that there will no longer be room for those lies.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek God's truth or only words that make us feel comfortable. Reading the Bible with humility helps us distinguish what is true, even when it sometimes corrects us.
exp.32:23:
Ezekiel reports that some of those who remained among the ruins of Israel, after the fall of Jerusalem, reasoned this way: "Abraham was alone and God gave him the land; we are many, so the land is all the more ours." The phrase about them speaking is simply a way of saying they kept saying this among themselves and to others.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Those who stayed in the land took pride in the promise made to Abraham, but they lived in violence, idolatry and immorality. In the verses that follow, God answers them that they cannot claim his promises while they despise his ways.

For today: relying on an inheritance, a family or a religious tradition is not enough to make us feel secure before God. God's promises are received with faith and sincere obedience. Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly live as his people.
exp.26:30:
This verse describes very intense signs of mourning. "They shall make themselves utterly bald for thee" means they will shave their heads as a sign of grief. "Gird them with sackcloth" means they will dress in rough clothing of mourning. "They shall weep for thee" refers to crying out in lament, and here it is "bitterness of heart and bitter wailing," full of deep sorrow.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a funeral song about Tyre, a seafaring city very rich from its trade. The sailors and the pilots, who lived by the sea and their business, mourn its fall. It is poetic language: Tyre is pictured as a great ship that is sinking. The passage shows that a nation's pride and wealth are not safe before God.

For today: do not put your security in money, success, or prestige, because all of that can disappear. Trust instead in God, who always endures, and use what you have with humility and generosity.
exp.25:16:
This verse says that when Tyre falls, others will raise a funeral song over her. They will say in astonishment: "How are you destroyed, you renowned city of the sea?" A funeral song is a lament for the dead. The word "success" here means "departure" or "end," not triumph. Tyre was admired, strong at sea, and her power made those who lived nearby afraid.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very rich and proud trading city, and she had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem (Ezek 26:2). God announces that she too will fall, and that the princes of the sea will be shaken when they see it.

For today: success, fame, and power are not a secure foundation. We can give thanks for what we have, but without trusting in it. Today is a good day to ask ourselves: where do I truly rest, and how do I use what God has given me with humility?
exp.24:12:
God says that he himself will punish Edom. "I will stretch out my hand" means that God will act with power to judge. The phrases for destroying and laying waste are rendered here as cutting off and making desolate, which match the wording of the verse above, and "they shall fall by the sword" means they will die by the sword. Teman and Dedan were known places, one within Edom and one nearby, and they are mentioned to show that the judgment would reach the whole region, from one end to the other.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at a time when Jerusalem had already been struck by Babylon. Edom, Israel's neighbor and distant relative, took advantage of Judah's fall and took revenge with cruelty. God responds to that attitude of resentment and lack of compassion.

Today, this text reminds us that we should not rejoice in the suffering of others or take advantage of someone who falls. If someone has wronged us, we can leave justice to God and ask him for a compassionate heart, instead of seeking revenge.
exp.23:19:
This verse is a transition phrase. Ezekiel answers the people's question and says that God spoke to him.

Ezekiel was a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God had told him that his wife would die and that he must not mourn for her in public. The people, puzzled, ask him what this means. His conduct was a sign: this is how they would react when the temple in Jerusalem fell. Scholars agree on the basics of this symbolism, although they debate some of the details.

For today: before giving answers to those who suffer or ask questions, it is wise to pause and listen to God. Praying and seeking his word helps us speak with truth and humility, not only with our own ideas.
exp.19:11:
God says that he also gave the Israelites his sabbaths. The sabbath would be a sign between him and them, a visible reminder of their relationship. His purpose was that they would know that the Lord is the one who sanctifies them, that is, the one who sets them apart as his people and makes them holy.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some leaders of Israel came to consult him, and he reminds them of their history: he brought them out of Egypt, gave them his law and the sabbath. But they rebelled and profaned the sabbaths, that is, they treated them as something common. Even so, God acted for the sake of his name and did not destroy them.

Today we can set apart a regular time to rest and remember that God sustains us and makes us his own. Resting is trusting that our life does not depend only on our own effort.
exp.24:4:
God says that Rabbah, the capital of Ammon, will become a place where camels rest, and that the Ammonite people will be like a field where sheep graze. The word for the sheep pen is not used here; rather, the verse speaks of a resting place for the animals. "Dwelling" here means a place of rest. In the end, God affirms that in this way they will know that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile of Judah in Babylon. The Ammonites, neighbors of Israel, rejoiced when the temple was defiled and the land lay in ruins. God judges them for mocking the suffering of his people. Rabbah was their main city, and the image of camels and sheep speaks of ruin and abandonment.

For today: God takes mockery in the face of another's suffering seriously. We can examine our hearts and ask ourselves whether we rejoice over the falls of others. It is better to pray, to help, and to show compassion, trusting that God is just.
exp.15:57:
It says that Jerusalem (speaking of her as an unfaithful wife) now bears the weight of her great wickedness and her detestable deeds. The word "lewdness" means a very great wickedness, and "abominations" are things that God loathes, above all idolatry. The phrase "thou hast borne" suggests that the consequences already rest upon her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 He compares Jerusalem to a wife whom He cared for, but who was unfaithful to Him. Before, she considered herself better than Sodom; now her sin has been exposed, and other peoples despise her. Even so, the verses that follow show that God will remember His covenant and offer an everlasting one.

For today: it is not healthy to hide or justify our faults. We can acknowledge them honestly before God, knowing that His judgment is not His final word, because He is faithful and offers forgiveness and restoration.
exp.42:19:
The explanation says that the priest was to take blood from the young bull and put it on the four horns of the altar, on the four corners of the upper ledge (the hearth) and on the whole border. In this way the altar was made clean and pure. The horns were the points that stood out at the corners of the altar.

God speaks to Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. After the exile, the people needed to understand that God was to be worshiped with reverence. Before the altar was used, it was to be consecrated with the blood of atonement. How this relates to the future is something Christians interpret in different ways.

For today: God does not come near lightly, and neither should we. Christians believe that Christ cleanses us by his blood. Before praying or serving, we can draw near with humility, thankful for his forgiveness.
exp.43:2:
It says that only the prince may sit in the eastern gate, which is closed, to eat bread before the Lord. He will enter by the passage of the gate from the outer court and leave by the same way. "Bread" here refers to a meal before God, probably a holy meal or a sacrificial meal.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel hears it in a vision of the new temple (chapters 40 to 48). The gate is closed because the glory of God entered through it. Interpreters differ on who the prince is and whether the temple is literal, symbolic, or prophetic. What is clear is that God is holy and sets the way we draw near to Him.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and gratitude. Even those who hold authority live under God's order, and eating "before the Lord" reminds us that we can live each day aware of His presence.
exp.15:33:
She behaved differently from other women who give themselves to unfaithfulness. Normally a prostitute receives payment, but she paid her lovers. Here "unfaithfulness" means adultery, and the lovers are the nations and idols she sought alliances with. The word "contrary" means that she did everything backwards.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Jerusalem, who were living in exile or on the verge of falling. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to show how Israel left God, trusted other peoples, and worshiped idols. It is harsh language, meant to awaken their conscience.

For today: examine what you pursue with so much effort, money, or time to feel secure or valued. Return to God, who does not ask you to pay for his love.
exp.26:22:
This verse lists cities and peoples of the ancient Near East who did business with Tyre. Haran, Canneh and Eden were places in Mesopotamia or nearby. Sheba and Asshur also appear as trading partners. Chilmad is a little-known place, and no one knows for certain where it was. The word "merchants" in the verse means that these peoples traded or dealt with the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a rich and proud seaport city. The long list of partners shows how much wealth and fame it had. But God presents it this way to announce that, however powerful it was, its fall would come.

For today: money, connections and success can give a sense of security, but they are not firm. We can be thankful for what God gives us and work with integrity, but we should place our trust in Him and not in what we have.
exp.23:4:
He says to take the best sheep from the flock, to build a fire with the bones under the pot, and to let everything boil well, until the bones are also cooked inside it. "Choice" means the best, and "boil" is the same as "cook" in the verse above.

God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to tell this parable to the rebellious house, the people of Judah. The pot represents Jerusalem, and the good pieces represent its inhabitants. Then it says the city is full of blood, that is, of violence and injustice. The fire announces God's judgment through the siege by Babylon.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. Let us ask that he examine our hearts, let go of what harms others, and seek repentance before sin consumes us.
exp.27:4:
It says that the king of Tyre was very skilled in business. With his wisdom in trade (the word translated as "traffick" means dealing or commerce) he increased his riches. But those riches led him to pride: his heart was lifted up, that is, it was filled with arrogance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the prince or king of Tyre, a city rich from maritime trade. God reminds him of his reputation for wisdom, but shows him that his success made him believe himself almost divine. For this reason, in the following verses, he announces judgment. Some believe the passage also alludes to a spiritual power behind the king, although it is interpreted in several ways.

We can work with intelligence and prosper, but it is good to remember that every good thing comes from God. Give him thanks, be generous, and examine your heart: may success not make you proud.
exp.44:14:
God commands the people to give one lamb out of every two hundred from the flock, choosing the best and healthiest animals of Israel. These offerings would be used for the sacrifices: the burnt offerings (offerings completely burned) and the peace offerings (offerings of fellowship), to make atonement, that is, to cover the sin of the people.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of a renewed temple and worship. The people bring the offerings, and the prince presents them at the festivals. Scholars understand this vision in several ways: some see it as something literal and future, others as symbolic, and others as fulfilled in Christ.

Today we can learn to give God our best with gratitude, and not what is left over. And we remember that only God can forgive; Christians trust in the sacrifice of Jesus.
exp.23:11:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to a rusty pot, has worn herself out with so much useless effort. Her scum is the dirt, the rust, or the wickedness stuck to her, and it did not come out. For that reason she will be burned in the fire. "Fraud" is understood as deceit or vain effort; some translators read "she hath wearied herself with lies," and the Hebrew text here is difficult.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. When the siege of Jerusalem begins, God uses the image of a pot to show that the city, full of violence and sin, will be judged. Before this, he had already called her to return, but she did not want to be cleansed.

For today: let us not hide sin or try to cleanse it with appearances or our own efforts. Let us ask God to truly cleanse us, and let us respond quickly when he calls us to change.
exp.35:4:
God says that he has spoken in the fire of his zeal, that is, in an intense love for his land and his people, against the neighboring nations and against Edom (Idumea). They took possession of the land of Israel as if it were their own, with joy and with malice, in order to plunder those who had been driven out of it. Malice means deep hatred or resentment, and plunder means the spoils taken from others.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while Israel is in exile and its land lies in ruins. The neighboring peoples mocked and took advantage of its fall. God responds by defending his people and his land, and announces that these nations will bear their shame.

For today: God sees injustice and does not rejoice with those who delight in another's misfortune. We can avoid mocking those who fall, and instead help and pray, trusting that God does justice in his own time.
exp.43:23:
It says the priests will be the judges when there is a dispute among the people. They must judge according to God's laws, not according to their own opinion. They must also keep God's laws and statutes at all his assemblies and set apart the sabbaths as holy days. "Controversy" means a conflict or legal dispute, and "solemn assemblies" are the appointed feasts.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a new temple. In this passage he describes how the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok must live: teaching the people the difference between what is holy and what is common, and being an example of obedience. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways, and there is no complete agreement.

For today: if God has given you some responsibility over others, as a parent, leader, or teacher, seek to decide with justice according to his Word, not according to your convenience, and live out yourself what you teach.
exp.15:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of saying "human being." He tells him to cause Jerusalem to know its abominations, that is, to make clear to her the detestable things she has done.

The LORD, the God of Israel, is speaking. Ezekiel was a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God wants Jerusalem to see her sin, and in the verses that follow he reminds her of her humble origins and how he cared for her. Many understand this to be a harsh message, but it is given in the hope that the people will recognize their error.

For today: God tells us the truth because he loves us. We can ask him to show us our faults, accept his correction with humility, and return to him, remembering that everything good we have comes from his grace.
exp.15:54:
This verse says that God will restore Sodom and Samaria, together with their daughters, to their former condition. He will do the same for Jerusalem and her daughters. Here "daughters" means the nearby cities and villages. The comment on the wording of "return" is not needed for this reader, so it is omitted.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, whom this chapter accuses of unfaithfulness, comparing her to a wife who betrayed her husband. Sodom and Samaria are called her "sisters," and Jerusalem turns out to be worse than they are. Scholars debate whether this restoration is literal or symbolic. Even so, punishment is not God's final word.

For today: when we honestly acknowledge our own failures, and not only those of others, God can restore us. Today we can draw near to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy.
exp.35:16:
God speaks to Ezekiel, called "son of man," and reminds him that Israel lived in its own land and defiled it by their conduct and their actions. The phrase about uncleanness of a removed woman refers to the ritual impurity of the law of Moses; God says that their way of living was as impure to him as that.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. God explains why the exile happened: it was not chance, but the result of violence and idolatry, as the following verses say. This reminder prepares the promises of restoration that come later in the chapter.

For today: God cares about how we live, not only about what we say we believe. We can ask him to show us the areas where we need to change, and remember that he also offers forgiveness and renewal to anyone who turns to him sincerely.
exp.22:19:
Here the prophet describes Aholibah (who represents Jerusalem) falling in love with her "lovers" or "allies" who used her. The comparisons to "donkeys" and "horses" are deliberately blunt: they speak of an unrestrained desire, almost animal in nature, and of the strength and power of those nations that attracted her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two unfaithful sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, to show how his people abandoned God and sought security in Egypt and other powers. The language is harsh so that the people would feel the seriousness of their betrayal. Scholars agree that this is a symbolic image, though they differ on the details.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust apart from God, such as money, prestige, or powerful people. Return to Him sincerely, because only He truly sustains you.
exp.31:0:
This verse marks the moment when God speaks to Ezekiel again. It says that it happened in the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" is old-fashioned language and means "I received a message from God." It is only the introduction to a new prophecy.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon along with other Jews. He tells that God gave him a message, and in the verses that follow that message is a lament against Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Many understand that the date corresponds to about twelve years after the deportation of King Jehoiachin, although scholars do not always agree on the exact calculation.

For today: God speaks at specific moments and does not forget history. You can trust that He sees the pride of the powerful and cares for His people. Take time to listen to His Word with attention.
exp.42:4:
It says that the Spirit lifted up Ezekiel and brought him into the inner court of the temple. There he saw that the glory of the Lord filled the house. The verse's wording refers to the inner court of the temple, which is the courtyard surrounding the main building.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, describes a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had seen the glory of God leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now he sees it return through the east gate. God promises to dwell again among Israel and asks His people to give up idolatry. Interpreters differ on whether this temple is literal, future, or symbolic.

For today: God desires to dwell among His people, but He looks for clean and faithful hearts. We can ask Him to remove whatever draws us away from Him and to fill our lives with His presence.
exp.47:28:
This verse says that the land mentioned will be divided by lot, that is, by casting lots, like a drawing, to give each tribe of Israel its inheritance. The portion each tribe receives is its share of the inheritance. Everything ends with God's own word: "saith the Lord God."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, toward the end of his book. It is a vision of restoration for Israel, who was in exile. God shows that his people will have a place and that each tribe will have its portion. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic.

For today: God cares for each of his own and forgets no one. You can trust that He has a place and a purpose for your life, and receive with gratitude what He gives you, without comparing yourself with others.
exp.12:15:
This verse says that there were prophets in Israel who spoke about Jerusalem and claimed to have seen a vision of peace. But there was no peace. God declares that those messages were false. The phrase about prophesying concerning Jerusalem means that they spoke on God's behalf to the city. The part about seeing visions refers to what they claimed to have seen from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The false prophets reassured the people with pleasant words, like someone covering a cracked wall with loose mud. God says that wall will fall, because it had no firm foundation.

For today: let us seek God's truth, even when it is uncomfortable, and not only what makes us feel at ease. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and when we speak with others, let us try to be sincere and kind.
exp.38:15:
It says there will be a city with the name Hamonah, which means "multitude," and that the land will be made clean. "They will cleanse" refers to burying the bodies of the dead so that the country does not remain unclean. Hamonah recalls the valley of Hamon-gog, where they would be buried.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He had already announced the defeat of Gog, an enemy who would attack Israel. After that victory, the people would have to spend months purifying the land. Scholars interpret this passage in several ways: some see it as literal and future, others as symbolic language of God's final triumph.

For today: God is interested in cleansing and restoring completely, not halfway. We can ask him to help us remove from our lives, with patience and steadiness, whatever contaminates us.
exp.25:10:
It says the invading army will enter the city with such force that its horses will trample all the streets. The people will be killed by the sword, that is, with a sword. The "pillars of your strength" were probably columns or monuments of the city, and they will fall to the ground. "Trample" means to stomp down under the feet.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, and addresses Tyre, a city rich and proud because of its trade. It rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own gain. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon is the instrument of judgment. Scholars debate how all of this was fulfilled, since Tyre resisted for a long time and the prophecy has several stages.

For today: wealth, power and pride do not protect us from God. We can examine whether we trust in what we have more than in Him, and rejoice with humility, never at another's misfortune.
exp.28:2:
God speaks through the prophet and declares himself against Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He calls him "the great dragon", an image of a water monster, perhaps a crocodile, that lies calmly in the middle of the Nile. Pharaoh boasted: "My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself." "Lieth" means that he is stretched out, resting.

The Lord speaks to Ezekiel around 587 B.C., when Egypt seemed a safe ally for Judah. God denounces the pride of a king who believed himself the owner of the source of his wealth and power. The verses that follow show his fall.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we boast of what we have, as if it were only our own merit. Everything we have comes from God. Recognizing this leads us to live with gratitude and humility.
exp.23:22:
The people will do the same as Ezekiel: they will leave their turbans or headdresses and their shoes in place, normal signs of everyday life, instead of the signs of mourning. They will not make public laments or weep aloud. Their grief will be internal: they will waste away because of their sins and groan among themselves.

God speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. God had just commanded him not to mourn the death of his wife, so that he would be a sign. In this way the people would understand that the fall of Jerusalem and the temple would be so painful that they could not even express their grief openly.

For today: let us not wait until the pain is so great before we recognize our faults. A sincere repentance, made in time before God, is better than mourning late over consequences we could have avoided.
exp.19:0:
It says that in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day, certain leaders of the people of Israel came to inquire of the Lord. They sat before Ezekiel to hear what God would say.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The "seventh year" is usually understood as the seventh year since the exile of King Jehoiachin, that is, around 591 B.C. The elders come looking for a word from God, but the following verse shows that God does not answer them as they hoped, because their hearts were not sincere.

For today: it is not enough to draw near to God in appearance. Before asking Him for direction, we should examine whether we are truly willing to obey Him. He looks for an honest heart, not merely a religious visit.
exp.15:32:
Ezekiel 16:33 says that prostitutes are normally paid, but Jerusalem did the opposite: she paid her lovers. She gave them gifts and bribes so that they would come to her from every side. The word "lovers" in the verse is what this passage calls the men who came to her, and the act described is unfaithfulness to her husband.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to accuse Jerusalem of abandoning God and seeking alliances and gods of other nations. Many understand that the "gifts" include riches and political dealings, although the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: examine what you are "paying" for with your time, money and heart in order to feel secure or loved. God does not want us to buy affection somewhere else, since He already offers us His faithful love. Return to Him with sincerity.
exp.36:25:
God promises to make with his people a "covenant of peace," that is, a binding agreement of well-being and reconciliation that will never come to an end. He says he will "establish" them, that is, set them securely in their land, and that he will multiply them. Furthermore, he will place his sanctuary, his holy place, in the midst of them forever.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people exiled in Babylon, discouraged and divided. Shortly before, in the vision of the dry bones, God had promised to restore them. Here he announces unity under a king from the line of David. How the promise is fulfilled is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can trust that God seeks to dwell near his people and to give them lasting peace. When you feel far away or without hope, pray and remember that his nearness does not depend on your strength, but on his faithfulness.
exp.15:21:
It says that Jerusalem, with all her idolatries and her spiritual unfaithfulness, forgot what she was at the beginning. "Youth" means the time of being young. She was "naked and bare" and "wallowing in her blood": weak, without help, and without worth of her own, like a newborn baby left abandoned.

God speaks here through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he uses the image of an abandoned girl whom he finds, cares for, and makes his wife. Then she is unfaithful to him with other gods, and even sacrifices her children. God reminds her of her origin to show her the seriousness of her ingratitude.

For today: remembering where God rescued us from keeps us humble and thankful. When we forget his grace, it is easy to feel self-sufficient and to look for security in other things. Today you can give thanks for one specific way God helped you.
exp.12:3:
It says that the prophets of Israel were like foxes among ruins. A fox roams among the wreckage, looking for what it can take for itself, and it takes no care of anything and protects no one. In the wording of the verse, "deserts" means abandoned or ruined places, not necessarily sand.

God speaks through Ezekiel, during the years when Jerusalem was near its fall. He accuses the false prophets, who claimed to speak for the LORD when they were only speaking from their own hearts. With comforting words, they did not help the people see their sin or repair the breaches in the wall. So the people were left without defense.

Today, before accepting a message as coming from God, it is wise to compare it with the Bible. And when we speak of God, let us do so with humility and truth, even when that is not the most comfortable thing to hear.
exp.32:8:
This verse says that if the watchman warns the wicked person (the one who lives in evil) to turn from his evil way, and even so the wicked person does not turn away, he will die for his own sin. The watchman, that is, the one who keeps watch and sounds the alarm, is free of blame.

God speaks to Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He appoints him as a watchman for Israel, like the lookout of a city who sounds the trumpet when danger comes. His duty was to speak faithfully; the decision to respond belonged to each listener. Then God makes clear that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but wants them to turn back and live.

For today: when you have the chance, speak with love and truth to someone who is going down a wrong path, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.29:6:
It says that Egypt and its allies will be destroyed and left empty. The word "desolate" means ruined, left in ruins. Their cities will be just like other cities that are already deserted, that is, without people and without life. Nothing will set them apart from the other fallen nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people of Israel are living in exile. He announces judgment against Egypt and the nations that supported it. Egypt was proud and trusted in its strength. God shows that no human power, not even its allies, can stop what he has decided. Scholars debate exactly who some of those peoples were, such as Chub.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in money, power, or human alliances. All of that can fall. Trust first in God, who remains firm.
exp.24:9:
He says that God will hand the land of Ammon over to the "sons of the east" (desert peoples to the east, probably nomadic tribes), together with Moab, to possess as an inheritance. The result would be that Ammon would no longer be remembered among the nations. The verse's wording of "hand over" and "possess" points to the same idea, and "the nations" are the peoples of the world.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile of Judah in Babylon. Ammon and Moab mocked Judah when it fell, saying it was just like any other people. God responds by defending his people and judging that contempt. Scholars generally agree that this is a historical judgment, though not all agree on exactly how it was fulfilled.

For today: God sees the mockery and pride that rejoice in the pain of others. Let us learn not to celebrate anyone's downfall, but to show compassion, and to trust that God cares for those who suffer.
exp.18:9:
It says that Israel's mother was like a healthy vine, planted beside the waters. Because she had water in abundance, she bore fruit and put out many branches. The new shoots mentioned here are the young branches. The phrase "in thy blood" is a difficult expression; some understand it as "in your lineage" or "in your vineyard," and others think the original text says something different.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament about the princes of Judah. The "mother" most likely represents Judah or Jerusalem, and the young lions of the earlier chapters are her kings, who were taken captive to Babylon. The passage recalls a former prosperity to show how much was lost.

For today: what we receive from God, such as blessings, family, or gifts, is not something to boast about or take for granted. A vine grows by the water it receives. Let us remain close to God with gratitude and humility, for all fruit comes from Him.
exp.15:50:
God tells Jerusalem that Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, did not commit even half of her sins. Jerusalem did more detestable things, and by doing so she made her sisters, Samaria and Sodom, seem righteous by comparison. Here, "justified" means that she made them look less guilty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to the exiles in Babylon. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman who forgot God. He mentions Sodom and Samaria, cities already judged, to show that Jerusalem, which had received so much light and so much of God's care, failed more gravely.

For today: it is easy to compare ourselves with others and feel better. But God looks at the heart and at what we have received from Him. Instead of pointing out other people's errors, let us ask Him to examine our own, and remember that He also promises restoration.
exp.22:10:
This verse says that Aholibah, the younger sister, saw what had happened to her sister Aholah. But instead of learning from it, she gave herself to her desires even more than her sister did. The phrase "ruined her love" means she corrupted her love, and "whoredoms" refers to her unfaithfulness. Her sins were worse than her sister's.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters as a picture: Aholah represents Samaria (Israel) and Aholibah represents Jerusalem (Judah). Both allied themselves with Assyria and with its idols instead of remaining faithful to God. Samaria had already been punished, and Jerusalem should have taken it as a warning.

For today: let us learn from the mistakes of others before repeating them. If we see someone suffering because they have turned away from God, it is an opportunity to examine our own hearts and return to Him in time.
exp.18:3:
The nations heard about what this young lion was doing. They caught him in their trap, and they brought him in chains to the land of Egypt. "Chains" here refers to iron shackles used to bind the feet or the hands, and "was taken" means that he was captured.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who sings a lament for the princes of Israel. The mother lioness is usually understood as Judah or its kingdom, and the cub as King Jehoahaz, whom Pharaoh Necho took captive to Egypt. Some scholars connect it to that historical event, although the text does not give the name. His violence led him to ruin.

Whoever uses their power to harm others does not remain safe forever. Today we can ask God for a just and humble heart, so that whatever we have, little or much, we use to serve and not to take advantage of others.
exp.35:3:
God speaks to the land of Israel as if it could hear him: to the mountains, hills, streams and valleys, and also to the ruins and empty cities. These places had been plundered and mocked by the surrounding nations.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile in Babylon. The land had been left in ruins, and neighboring peoples, such as Edom, rejoiced and wanted to take it for themselves. God answers that mockery and promises to act on behalf of his people and his land.

For today: when you feel that your life is like a place in ruins, and others mock or look down on you, remember that God sees you and speaks to you. He does not stay silent in the face of your pain. You can bring him your shame and wait for his restoration.
exp.21:18:
God says that all his people have become "dross," that is, the worthless waste left behind when a metal is melted down. For that reason, he will gather them inside Jerusalem, the way someone gathers metals into a furnace to melt them down. The word "became" in this verse means that they have become this.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. The people had fallen into injustice, violence, and idolatry. Jerusalem would be like a furnace where God would gather them to subject them to his judgment before the city fell. The verses that follow speak of anger, but the image of melting also suggests a purpose of purification.

For today: God sees the truth of our hearts, not just appearances. If you notice areas of your life that have filled up with "dross," such as lying or selfishness, do not wait for trials to arrive. Bring them to God today with humility and ask him to cleanse you.
exp.19:3:
God asks Ezekiel, called "son of man," whether he is willing to judge the people. It is a rhetorical question that invites Ezekiel to say yes and to act as God's spokesman. To "make known" to them means to let them know, or to make them aware. The detestable practices, above all idolatry, that their ancestors committed are what God wants them to recognize.

God speaks to Ezekiel when some elders of Israel come to consult him, probably during the exile in Babylon. God refuses to answer them because their hearts remain far from him. Before giving them any answer, he wants them to remember their history of rebellion and his own mercy from Egypt.

For today: before asking God for direction, it is wise to look honestly at our lives and repent of what we know displeases him. God listens to a sincere heart.
exp.15:20:
It says that Jerusalem took the children who belonged to God, killed them as an offering, and gave them over to idols. The phrase about causing them to pass through the fire refers to burning them as a sacrifice. The part about giving them over speaks of the images of false gods. The words about her children show that God regarded them as His own.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who received everything from Him and used it to worship idols. Sacrificing children was a practice of neighboring peoples, and God condemns it harshly. His accusation aims to show how serious the people's sin was.

For today: everything we have, family, time, and talents, comes from God. Let us ask ourselves whether we are sacrificing what is most precious, such as the care of our children, for things that promise success or security but are not God.
exp.35:6:
God says that he has lifted up his hand, that is, that he has made a solemn oath. He promises that the nations neighboring Israel will receive their own shame. The word "shame" in this verse is the insult or dishonor that they inflicted on Israel, and now they will have to carry it themselves.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at a time when the people were in exile and their land lay desolate. Nations such as Edom (Idumea) mocked Israel and wanted to take that land for themselves. God responds with a fierce, firm love that defends his people. Then he promises that the mountains of Israel will once again bear fruit.

For today: when you feel humiliated or unjustly treated, you can trust that God sees and that his justice is certain. Give him your pain, refrain from seeking revenge, and wait on his faithfulness.
exp.24:10:
God also says that he will carry out his judgments against Moab, the neighboring nation of Israel. To "execute judgments" means to apply his justice and punish wrongdoing. The expected result is that they will know that he is the Lord, meaning they will recognize that the God of Israel is the true Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile of Judah in Babylon. Moab had looked down on Judah, claiming that it was just like the other nations (v. 8). For this reason God announces that Moab will lose its border cities and will be handed over to the people of the east. The passage shows that God does not overlook contempt toward his people.

We can trust that God sees every injustice and that he will bring about justice in his own time. So we do not need to take revenge or mock anyone. Instead, we leave judgment in his hands and live with humility.
exp.20:11:
God tells Ezekiel to cry out and lament, because the sword of judgment will fall on the people and on their leaders. "Howl" means to cry out loudly in grief. "Terrors by reason of the sword" refers to the dread that war brings. "Smite upon thy thigh" was a gesture of pain and anguish, like striking one's leg or breast.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." Judah had rejected his warnings again and again. The "sword" is commonly understood to be the army of Babylon, used by God to judge. God does not want Ezekiel to announce this coldly, but with sincere sorrow.

For today: when we speak about sin and its consequences, let us do so with humility and tears, not with pride. And if God corrects us, let us take his voice seriously and return to him in time.
exp.42:23:
This verse says that the bull and the ram would be presented before God. The priests would throw salt on them and burn them whole as an offering to the Lord. A "burnt offering" means an offering that was burned entirely on the altar. The old-fashioned verb forms in the wording are archaic, but the meaning is clear.

Here God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, giving him instructions for consecrating the altar in the temple he saw in a vision. This takes place after the glory of God returns to the temple. Interpreters differ on whether these visions refer to a literal future temple or have a symbolic meaning. Salt was used in offerings as a sign of purity and of covenant (Leviticus 2:13).

For today: God deserves our best and our whole selves. We can ask ourselves whether we give our lives to him sincerely and without holding back, not just parts of them.
exp.32:22:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again. The opening phrase of the verse, "Then the word of the Lord came unto me," marks the start of a new message.

Ezekiel was a prophet exiled in Babylon. A survivor had just arrived with the news that Jerusalem had fallen, just as Ezekiel had announced. God had restored his speech, and now he gives him a message for those who had been left in the land and believed it belonged to them, even though they lived in injustice and idolatry.

For today: God still speaks through his Word, and it is wise to listen with humility, especially when he corrects us. Before claiming blessings, let us ask ourselves whether we are living in obedience and justice.
exp.25:0:
This verse says that in the eleventh year, on the first day of the month, God spoke to Ezekiel. The word "came" in the King James wording is the form that means "came to pass," and "unto me" means "to me." It is a simple way of opening a new message: God took the initiative and spoke.

The one speaking is God, and the one who listens is the prophet Ezekiel. It refers to the eleventh year of the exile, but the text does not give the month, so it cannot be known for certain. The next verse shows that God is going to speak against Tyre, a city that rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem because it expected to profit from it.

For today: God sees what happens in the world and also how we react to the suffering of others. We can ask ourselves whether we rejoice when someone falls, or whether we accompany them with compassion. Listening to God's word helps us look at others the way He looks at them.
exp.19:10:
God says that, after bringing Israel out of Egypt, he gave them his ordinances and explained to them his rights, that is, his laws and righteous decrees. He promises that whoever keeps them will live by them, meaning they will have a good life under his care. The words "gave them" are the meaning of the phrase, and "made known to them" is what the same phrase means in this context.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who recalls the history of Israel. God rescued them for the sake of his name and led them into the wilderness. There he showed them how to live as his people. But the text goes on to say that they rebelled. Some understand "live" as a full life in this present world; others understand it also as spiritual life.

Today, God's instructions are not a burden but a path toward a healthy life. Ask yourself: what teaching from the Bible can I put into practice this week, trusting that God guides me for good?
exp.29:0:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel once again. "The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying," is an older way of saying this, and "the Lord" is the name for God used in this translation. It is an opening phrase that is repeated in the book to mark a new message.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, and God called him to speak on his behalf. Here a new message begins, directed against Egypt and its allies, as the verses that follow and the rest of the chapter show. God is the one speaking, and Ezekiel only passes on what he receives. The verses that follow announce the day of the Lord, a time of judgment.

For today: God still speaks, today mainly through his Word. Before we give our opinion or make a decision, we can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible carefully and ask him to speak to us.
exp.33:30:
God tells his people that they are his sheep, the ones he himself cares for and feeds. The word for the place where sheep eat is the pasture. The verse also makes clear that they are people, that is, fragile human beings, and that he is their God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier, God rebuked the shepherds of Israel, that is, the leaders who took advantage of the people and neglected them. Now he promises to care for them himself and to give them a shepherd, here called a plant, which many Christians understand as a sign of the Messiah. He ends by reminding them of the relationship: they are his, and he is their God.

For today: even when you feel weak or have been neglected by others, God calls you his. Rest in his care, and help others with the same tenderness.
exp.17:4:
This verse begins to describe a righteous man. A "righteous" person is one who lives well before God. Acting with uprightness and treating others in a fair and honest way is what the verse points to. The sentence is left open, because the description continues in the verses that follow.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. The people kept repeating a saying that blamed their parents for their suffering. God answers that every person belongs to him and answers for himself. So he gives concrete examples of a righteous life: not following idols, not oppressing others, and helping the poor.

For today: God's justice shows up in everyday life. This week, look for one concrete act of honesty or generosity, such as paying what is fair, keeping your word, or sharing your food with someone in need.
exp.26:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Tyre, a city located by the sea, which traded with many peoples of islands and distant coasts. The verse calls her a merchant, which means a trader. The word translated here as "lament" refers to songs of mourning. Tyre had described herself as "of perfect beauty," that is, completely beautiful and without flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon with Israel. Tyre was a rich and proud port. God announces a lament over her, for her confidence in her beauty and wealth would lead her to fall. The passage that follows compares her to a great ship that was very well built.

For today: the good things we have, such as talent, success, or money, can make us believe we do not need God. We can be thankful for what we have, but place our security in Him and not in our achievements.
exp.22:26:
God says he will put an end to the impurity and the sexual unfaithfulness that Jerusalem brought with it from Egypt. Here the word for unfaithfulness is an image of spiritual infidelity. The people will no longer look back toward Egypt with longing or remember it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells the story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. They sought alliances and the gods of other nations instead of trusting the Lord. The punishment announced is severe, and it aims to bring an end to that unfaithfulness. Some scholars also see here a desire for the people to wake up.

For today: ask yourself in what things you place your trust instead of in God. Ask him to free you from whatever pulls you away from him, and do not keep idealizing a past that harmed you.
exp.15:41:
He says that when God finishes punishing, his anger will be satisfied. The phrase about his anger coming to rest means that his anger calms down. The phrase about his jealousy departing from you means that his jealousy, his pain at having been betrayed, is withdrawn. The phrase about no longer being angry means that he will no longer stay angry.

He speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, whom he presents as an unfaithful woman who forgot the love and care he gave her in her youth. The image of a prostitute describes idolatry and alliances with other nations. The punishments announced speak of judgment through enemy peoples. Even so, the chapter ends further on with a promise of restoration.

For today: God grieves when we forget him, but his anger is not eternal. Today you can remember what he has done for you and return to him sincerely before seeking comfort in other things.
exp.39:36:
It says that the gate on the north side had its posts (the columns on each side of the entrance) facing the outer court. Palm trees were carved on the posts on both sides. To go up to the gate there was a staircase of eight steps. The word for steps is the stairs leading up to the gate, and the court is the open yard around the temple.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide who looks like a man takes him through a new temple and measures every detail. Interpreters do not agree on its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, others of a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his people.

For today: drawing near to God is something that deserves care and reverence. Here even the entrance has steps and order. We can prepare our hearts before praying or meeting with other believers, without haste or carelessness, remembering that God is holy and at the same time invites us to draw near.
exp.40:22:
This verse says that the temple (the large hall, also called the holy place) and the sanctuary (the most holy place, the innermost part) each had a doorway, that is, an entrance with its frame and its doors. So there was one entrance for going into the temple and another for going into the sanctuary.

Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple. A guide shows him and measures each part. Shortly before, he was shown the wooden table that stands before the LORD. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of the restoration of Israel, or as a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: drawing near to God is both serious and beautiful. The doors remind us that we should come to Him with reverence, and today, in Christ, we have open access to His presence.
exp.19:32:
God says, swearing by his own life, that he will indeed reign over his people. He will do it with a mighty hand (power), a stretched-out arm (decisive action), and fury poured out (his anger expressed with firmness). These are words that recall the exodus from Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel, who were in exile. They wanted to be like the other nations and to serve idols of wood and stone. God answers that this plan will not succeed. He will not let them go: he will bring them out from among the peoples and confront them to correct them. His anger seeks to bring them back to himself.

For today: we cannot mix God with other gods, such as money or success. If he corrects us, it is not to destroy us, but because he loves us and wants to be our Lord. Today you can give him something that is pulling you away from him.
exp.40:18:
It says that on the temple walls there were carved figures: cherubim with two faces, one of a man and the other of a lion. The face of the man looked toward a palm tree on one side, and the face of the lion toward another palm tree on the other side. This was repeated all around the whole temple. The palm tree is a common decorative figure.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, describes a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. A guide showed him, with measurements, a new and orderly temple. The Israelites had lost the temple, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell among them. Scholars disagree about whether this temple was meant to be built literally or is a symbolic image.

For today: God is a God of order and beauty, and he wants to dwell with his people. We can prepare our hearts to worship him with reverence, remembering that his presence is the greatest treasure.
exp.15:43:
This verse says that everyone who uses sayings will use a saying about Jerusalem: "As is the mother, so is her daughter." Someone who quotes sayings or popular proverbs is the kind of person who would repeat such a thing. The idea is that the daughter is like her mother in her conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he describes Jerusalem as a woman whom He cared for and who later became unfaithful to Him, following idolatrous practices. The verses that follow explain the saying: her roots were Canaanite, and she resembled her neighbors Samaria and Sodom in their sin. God shows her her guilt in order to lead her to repentance.

For today: it is good to examine which habits and attitudes we inherit from our surroundings or family. What is good we thank God for, and what is harmful we hand over to God so that He may change us.
exp.39:21:
This verse describes the gate of the outer court of the temple that Ezekiel sees in his vision. Its windows, arches, and palm trees (decorations shaped like palm trees) had the same measurements as the east gate. One went up to it by seven steps, and the arches (probably a porch or entrance hall) stood in front of them.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts what God showed him. A guide with a measuring reed teaches him about the temple with precision. Many see here a promise of restoration and of God's presence; others interpret it differently, and there is no single agreement on whether it describes a literal or a symbolic temple.

For today: God cares about order and detail, and He draws near to His people with purpose. We can approach Him with reverence, with calm, and with the desire to grow step by step, like someone climbing stairs.
exp.47:24:
This verse says that, next to the territory of Simeon, lies the portion of the tribe of Issachar. Each tribe receives a strip of land running from east to west, reaching all the way to the sea, that is, to the Mediterranean Sea. A boundary or border is the line that marks where one area ends and another begins.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of the land being divided again among the twelve tribes, at the end of the book. The people were in exile, and this vision gave them hope of restoration. Interpreters differ: some understand it literally, others as a symbol of the restored people of God.

For today: God cares for each one and gives each a place. No one is forgotten. We can trust that he has a place for us, and live in peace with those who are beside us.
exp.19:31:
He says God knows what Israel has in mind: wanting to be "like the nations," that is, to live like the pagan peoples who worshiped idols of wood and stone. But God declares that this shall not be. It will not happen; he will not allow it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to some leaders of Israel who were in exile in Babylon. They were still following idols, as their ancestors had, and yet they wanted to consult God. He rejects this double life and announces that, with a strong hand, he will reign over them and gather them together again.

For today: let us not copy what most people do just to fit in. It is worth asking ourselves which things are taking God's place in our hearts, and giving them over to him with sincerity.
exp.39:32:
This verse describes the gate of the inner court, the one facing the east... actually, here it is the gate facing east. It had chambers (small rooms for guards), posts (the columns of the entrance), and arches (the porch or vestibule), all with the same measurements as the other gates. It also had windows all around. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide; a cubit was about half a meter.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, who in a vision is guided by a man with a measuring reed. He is in exile, and this vision of the new temple shows him order, holiness, and the presence of God. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual symbol.

For today: God is a God of order and of care for details. We can approach Him with reverence and, at the same time, trust that nothing in our lives escapes His notice.
exp.45:15:
It says that if the prince gives a portion of his property to one of his sons, that gift will belong to them forever, and it will pass to their descendants as an inheritance. The words "gift," "inheritance," and "possession" each name something: a gift is something freely given, an inheritance is the land or property kept within a family, and a possession is what someone holds as their own.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of the future temple and the life of the people. These rules protect each family's land. What the prince gives to his sons stays within the family, but what he gives to a servant returns to him in the year of liberty. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about justice and does not want those who hold power to abuse others. If you have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, use it with honesty and take care of what belongs to others.
exp.24:16:
God says he will punish the Philistines with force. The word "vengeance" here means a just punishment, not a hateful payback. "Furious rebukes" are harsh corrections, given with holy anger. The purpose is that they will come to acknowledge that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Philistines had acted with spite and had destroyed Israel out of old hostilities. God judges them for that wickedness. This is part of a series of messages against Israel's neighboring nations.

For today: let us not hold on to old grudges or look for a way to get even. God sees every injustice and is the one who judges with righteousness. We can hand our wounds over to him, forgive, and trust that he will do what is right, as Romans 12:19 teaches.
exp.21:24:
It says that the prophets of Jerusalem have joined together in a plot, like a roaring lion tearing apart its prey. "They have devoured souls" means they destroyed lives; "they have taken the treasure and precious things" refers to goods and possessions taken for themselves; and their abuses left many women widowed.

God speaks, telling Ezekiel to accuse Jerusalem shortly before its fall to Babylon. The leaders of the people, prophets, priests and princes, used their position for their own gain instead of caring for the people. That is why the judgment was just.

For today: if you have any influence, whether in the church, at work or in the family, use it to serve and protect others, not to get ahead. Ask God to examine your heart and give you integrity.
exp.19:18:
God presents himself as "the Lord your God", that is, the Lord who has a relationship with his people. He tells them to walk in his commands (his instructions), to keep his decrees (his just rules), and to do them, that is, to practice them and not only to hear them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel during the exile in Babylon. He reminds them of the history in the desert: he forgave the generation of their fathers and asked the next generation not to follow the idols and customs of those before them. Even so, the children also rebelled.

For today: God invites us to truly obey him, not only to know his Word. Today you can choose one clear command from the Bible, such as forgiving or being honest, and put it into practice, without copying without thinking what others do.
exp.16:16:
The explanation says that the pharaoh of Egypt will not truly help the king of Judah in the war. Even with a great army and many people, he will not save him when Babylon raises mounds and builds siege towers to cut off many lives.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Judah, Zedekiah, had sworn loyalty to Babylon, but he rebelled and asked Egypt for help. God calls him to account because he broke an oath made in God's name. Some scholars believe the passage also shows the uselessness of trusting in human powers.

For today: before seeking support in money, influence, or powerful people, ask yourself whether you are being faithful to your word and to God. Keeping what you have promised and trusting in Him gives more security than any army.
exp.46:7:
It says that the water of the river flowing from the temple runs toward the east, goes down into the valley of the Jordan (the plain, the Arabah) and reaches the Dead Sea, here called the sea. When it enters there, its waters, which are salty and lifeless, are made whole. "Healing" here means that the water becomes pure and good for life.

It is a heavenly guide who shows Ezekiel a vision. The prophet was living in exile and his people were discouraged. The vision promises that God will dwell with them again and that his presence will bring life. Some understand it symbolically, others as something yet to come; the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: where God acts, he can bring life even to what seems dead. We can bring Him our dry places, such as a broken relationship or deep weariness, and trust that his grace keeps healing us little by little.
exp.15:60:
It says that Jerusalem, the people of God, will remember her bad conduct and feel shame. On that day she will receive her other sisters, that is, other cities or peoples, both the greater and the lesser. God will give them to her as daughters, but not because Jerusalem has kept the covenant.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he has compared Jerusalem to an unfaithful wife who broke the covenant. Even so, he promises to remember his covenant with her and to give her an everlasting one.
