Scholars understand in various ways who the sisters are (Samaria and Sodom, mentioned earlier), but all of them see here a restoration that comes from the grace of God.

For today: when we remember our failures, shame can lead us to repentance and not to despair. God restores us through his mercy, not through our merits. We can return to him with humility and gratitude.
exp.39:14:
This verse gives a measurement: from the front of the entrance gate to the front of the porch of the inner gate, there are fifty cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters. So the gate passage measured about 25 meters, although scholars do not fully agree on the exact value of the cubit.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, is the one speaking. In a vision, a guide takes him to a new temple and shows him each measurement in great detail. Many believe this encouraged a discouraged people, but there are different interpretations about whether that temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about order and reverence when we draw near to Him. Before you pray or worship, take a moment to come in calmly and respectfully, without rushing.
exp.23:25:
He says that on that same day someone who managed to escape from Jerusalem will reach Ezekiel. That person will bring the news of what happened.

God speaks, addressing Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem had been besieged, and the Lord announced that the temple, the delight of their eyes, would be taken away. Ezekiel was not to mourn publicly for the death of his wife, so that it would be a sign to the people. When the survivor arrived, Ezekiel would speak again, and the people would recognize that God had fulfilled his word.

For today: God keeps what he says, even when his warnings hurt. If there is something he has shown you and you have been ignoring, take it seriously with humility and return to him before the difficulty arrives.
exp.20:17:
This verse is a short formula that is repeated throughout Ezekiel. "The word of the Lord came unto me again, saying," means that God spoke to Ezekiel once more. It is like saying: "A message from the Lord came to me."

The one speaking is God, and he gives the prophet a new message. Before this, God had announced judgment using the image of a sword. Now a new instruction begins: Ezekiel is to draw two roads along which the king of Babylon could advance, toward Rabbah of the Ammonites or toward Jerusalem. This shows that God works even within human decisions and political pressures.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before deciding something important, seek to hear him with humility, by reading the Bible and praying, rather than trusting only your own judgment.
exp.42:11:
This verse says that the "law of the house," meaning the main rule of the temple, is that the whole area on top of the mountain, all around its edge, is to be "most holy," that is, completely set apart for God. "Limit" here means the boundary or border. The verse repeats the phrase to give more force to what it says.

God speaks to Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. He tells him to show the people the vision of the temple so that they will be ashamed of their sins and understand what a life close to God should look like. How this vision will be fulfilled is interpreted in different ways: some see it as a future temple, others as a spiritual picture.

For today: God wants holiness to cover everything, not just certain moments. Today we can ask ourselves which areas of our lives we still keep far from Him, and hand them over to Him with humility.
exp.39:16:
He says that the man guiding Ezekiel brought him into the outer court of the temple he saw in the vision. There were thirty chambers there, that is, rooms or small halls, and a paved area around the court, that is, a stone floor. The chambers were arranged in a circle, next to that pavement.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he was living in exile in Babylon. In 573 B.C. he received this vision, in which a guide with a measuring reed showed him a detailed temple. Scholars do not agree on its meaning: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence and of the hope of restoration for his people.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and he values having a prepared place where people can draw near to him. We can set aside a space and an orderly time each day to seek him with reverence.
exp.42:24:
For seven days, the priests are to offer a male goat every day as a sin offering (atonement). In addition, they are to offer a young bull from the herd and a ram from the flock.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple. Before the altar could be used, it had to be purified and dedicated for seven days. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of restoration and of God's presence with his people.

For today: God draws near to us in holiness, and he deserves the best, not what is left over. We can prepare ourselves to worship him with a sincere heart, confessing our failings and giving thanks that Christ offered the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.28:6:
It says that Egypt is like a brittle reed. When Israel took hold of it with the hand to lean on it, the reed splintered and wounded the shoulder. When they leaned upon it, it broke and left their loins twisted.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the pharaoh of Egypt, who is compared to a great monster of the river. Judah was seeking help in Egypt against Babylon, instead of trusting in God. Egypt could not hold them up, and God judged it for its pride, for it said: "My river is my own."

Today we can ask ourselves what we lean on most: money, people, status, or our own strength. All of these can fail. It is good to use help and good resources, but our final trust must be in God, who does not break and does not let us fall.
exp.19:35:
He says that God will "contend" with his people, that is, bring them into a legal case and confront them face to face. He will do it in the same way he dealt with their ancestors in the wilderness after they left Egypt. "Your fathers" refers to the ancestors of Israel, and "the Lord God" is the name of the covenant God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The leaders of the people wanted to consult him, but they remained devoted to their idols. God reminds them that their rebellion is not new. The "wilderness of the peoples" can be understood as a place of testing and purification. The verses that follow speak of separating out the rebels, and interpreters see this in different ways.

For today: God's correction is not rejection, but a care that seeks to cleanse and restore us. When he confronts us, it is wise to listen with humility and return to him with sincerity.
exp.34:9:
This verse shows what Edom, represented by Mount Seir, was thinking. They said that the "two nations" and the "two countries" would be theirs. Nearly everyone understands this to mean Israel and Judah, the northern and southern kingdoms. They said they would possess them, as if God were not there or were not going to do anything. The phrase "whereas the Lord was there" means that God, present in that land, did not stop them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom had shown an old hostility toward Israel and wanted to take advantage of its fall to seize its territory. God answers that He heard those words and that He will judge that greed and that pride.

Today, we should not rejoice in the misfortune of others or want to profit from it. God sees what we say and think. We can ask Him for a humble heart, one that helps and does not covet.
exp.26:17:
1) What it says: Damascus traded with Tyre because Tyre produced a great many things and had great riches. Damascus brought wine from Helbon and white wool to Tyre. The word "merchant" refers to someone who trades. The "wares of thy making" are the goods that were made or worked by hand. Helbon was a place known for its wine, although scholars are not sure of its exact location. Some translate the "white wool" as wool from Zahar, but the sense is still good-quality wool.

2) Context: God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He asks him to sing a lament over Tyre, a city rich from its sea trade. This list of nations shows how great and proud Tyre was, before the announcement of its fall.

3) For today: Riches and success can seem secure, but they are not a firm foundation. Be thankful for what you have, work with integrity, and place your trust in God, not in your possessions.
exp.25:4:
It says that Tyre, the great trading city by the sea, will become a place where fishermen spread their nets to dry. A "place for spreading nets" is a place for drying fishing nets. "The sea" is the sea. God adds that it will be plundered by many nations, and stresses that he has said so.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud city, and this chapter announces its fall, partly for rejoicing at the ruin of Jerusalem. The following verses name Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon as the one who would come against it. As for how the detail about the nets was fulfilled, scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: riches and success are not a secure foundation. Trust God more than your achievements, and avoid rejoicing when others fall.
exp.32:18:
This verse says that if a wicked person turns away from his wickedness and begins to act with justice and righteousness, he will live because of it. "Wicked" describes someone who lives without respect for God. "Turn" means to leave or turn away from something. "Do that which is lawful and right" means acting in accordance with what is right and just.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was with the exiles in Babylon. Some of the people were saying, "The way of the Lord is not fair," that is, they were accusing God of being unjust. God answers that He judges each person according to their own way, and that the door of repentance is open. Soon after, news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen.

For today: no one is condemned by their past if they return to God. Instead of making excuses or blaming others, take one concrete step of change today, such as asking for forgiveness or letting go of a bad habit, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.35:25:
God promises to change his people from the inside. A "stony heart" is a hard heart, one that does not listen or obey; a "heart of flesh" is a tender one, one that responds to God. The phrases "I will give" and "your" are simply rendered as the verse above has them. Beyond a new heart, he also promises a new spirit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had been scattered because of their disobedience and idolatry. God promises to gather them, cleanse them, and bring them back to their land. The verses that follow explain that his Spirit will help them obey. Some Christians see here a foreshadowing of the new covenant.

For today: it is not enough simply to try harder to behave better. We can ask God each day to soften our hearts and help us listen to him with humility.
exp.19:22:
It says that God, while the people were in the wilderness, lifted up his hand, that is, he made a solemn oath. He promised that, if they kept rebelling, he would scatter them among the nations. The word "scatter" in the verse refers to this: it means to spread something out, as grain is tossed in the air so the wind carries away the chaff.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes to the exiles in Babylon. God reviews the history of Israel to show that the rebellion did not begin then. From the wilderness, after leaving Egypt, the people despised his commands and turned to idols. The exile was no surprise: God had warned them of the consequences. Scholars debate how best to understand this passage, but it shows that God is just and also patient.

For today: God warns out of love because he wants us to live. If you feel that he is calling you to correct something, do not put it off; respond today with humility and simple obedience.
exp.22:12:
God says that he saw that Oholibah, just like her sister Oholah, had become defiled, that is, she had dirtied herself morally. The two of them went the same path of unfaithfulness. Here, the word "whoredoms" refers to spiritual unfaithfulness, not only sexual sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. He uses the image of two sisters, who represent Samaria (Oholah) and Jerusalem (Oholibah). Both looked for alliances and gods of other nations, such as Assyria and Babylon, instead of trusting in Him. Jerusalem did not learn from Samaria's punishment.

For today: it is easy to repeat the mistakes we saw in others and think it will not happen to us. Let us learn from the falls of others, examine what we place our trust in, and return to God with sincerity.
exp.21:23:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Jerusalem. He says she is not a land that has been made clean, meaning a land that is pure and healthy. Nor has she received rain in the time of God's judgment. The image speaks of a land that is dry and polluted, with no freshness or cleansing.

The Lord is speaking, and the message is directed to the people of Jerusalem. Shortly before, God compared them to impure metals melted in the furnace. Then the text points out the sins of prophets, priests, and rulers: injustice, abuse, and contempt for what is holy. Scholars understand the image in different ways, but all of them see a city without repentance.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are letting God cleanse our hearts or whether we are hardening them. When God corrects us, it is better to respond with humility and return to Him soon.
exp.19:36:
He says that God will make His people pass "under the rod" and will bring them into the bond of the covenant. Passing under the rod was an image of shepherds who counted and inspected the sheep one by one as they entered the sheepfold. The phrase about the bond of the covenant means the tie or obligation of the covenant, that is, the commitment between God and His people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Israel had rebelled and kept following idols. God promises to examine His people, separate out the rebels, and draw the faithful back into His covenant. Some understand the rod as discipline, others as the shepherd's counting; both ideas fit.

For today: God knows us one by one, and sometimes He corrects us to bring us back to Himself. We can ask Him to examine our hearts and sincerely renew our commitment to Him, setting aside whatever has taken His place.
exp.20:24:
God addresses the king of Israel and calls him "profane," meaning one who does not respect what is holy, and "wicked," meaning one who lives without fearing God. He says his day has come: the moment when his wickedness has reached its limit and punishment will come. "Completion" means the final point or culmination.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Many understand this to refer to Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, who broke his oath to Babylon. The text does not give the name, so this is a common identification, not a completely certain one. God announces that he will remove the crown until the one "whose right it is" comes, which many Christians see as a promise of the Messiah.

For today: those who hold authority answer to God. Let us be honest and humble in what has been entrusted to us, and remember that Christ is the righteous King.
exp.43:14:
God says that the Levitic priests, descendants of Zadok, will be able to draw near to Him to serve Him. They faithfully guarded the sanctuary when the people turned away from God. They will be able to stand before Him and offer the fat and the blood of the sacrifices. "Near" means close; "to minister" means to serve Me.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the temple. Earlier, other Levites had gone after idols and were restricted to lesser tasks. The sons of Zadok, on the other hand, were faithful, and God gives them the privilege of serving Him up close. How this vision is to be fulfilled is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God values faithfulness when everyone around us is turning aside. Be steadfast in what He has entrusted to you, even when no one notices; God does see it, and He honors those who are faithful to Him.
exp.45:7:
When the prince comes in to worship at the temple, he will enter through the porch of the east gate and leave by the same way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes in a vision a temple and an order of worship. This follows the offerings for the new moon. The text does not explain every detail, and interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it as a literal description of the future, others as a symbolic picture. What is clear is that even the prince submits to the order God set.

For today: no one stands above the reverent way of drawing near to God. Come to Him with humility, without haste or pride, and let Him shape the way you worship.
exp.19:12:
God says that Israel rebelled against him in the wilderness. They did not follow his statutes, they despised his judgments (his righteous rules), and they profaned his sabbaths, that is, they treated them as ordinary days. That is why God said he would pour out his fury to consume them, that is, to destroy them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel who are in exile. He reviews their history to show that the rebellion did not begin today, but from the time they left Egypt. God had given them his law so that they would live and know that he sanctifies them. But the next verse shows that, for the sake of his name, God did not destroy them.

For today: do not see God's commands as a burden, but as a path to life. Today you can set aside a time of rest to be with God and remember that he is the one who sustains you.
exp.39:29:
It says that around the gate there were "arcos," which were probably porches or open galleries, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide. A cubit was an ancient measure, roughly half a meter, so these would be about twelve meters by two and a half meters. Some scholars think it refers to covered spaces beside the entrance.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision he received. A guide who looks like a man takes him through a future temple and measures each part carefully. Here it is in the inner court, at the south gate. Interpreters differ on whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both, and on when it would be fulfilled.

For today: God pays attention to details and cares that his people approach him with order and reverence. When you pray or gather with others, do not take it lightly. Prepare your heart with respect and gratitude.
exp.24:14:
God speaks here against the Philistines. They acted out of revenge, with a hateful, spiteful heart, and they brought ruin on others out of an old enmity that had lasted for generations. The word for ruining others means harming or destroying them without mercy.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he judges several nations that bordered Israel, including Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia. The Philistines were enemies of Israel for a long time, and here God calls them to account for their vengeance and hatred. The text gives no further details about each specific event.

For today: a grudge held for years can become destructive. Ask God to heal old wounds and help you forgive rather than take revenge. He is the righteous judge.
exp.31:8:
This verse says that God will cause many peoples to be saddened and distressed when news of Egypt's fall spreads. "Ruin" means destruction or collapse. The nations are the peoples of the earth, and the faraway lands are places distant from Egypt. The news of its downfall would reach even there.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over the Pharaoh of Egypt. Egypt considered itself powerful and secure, but God announces that Babylon would come against it. The images of darkened skies show how serious the judgment is. Scholars understand this language as poetic, not necessarily literal.

For today: no human strength, wealth, or fame is so secure that it can set God aside. Today we can examine what we truly trust in, and draw near with humility to the One who sustains all things.
exp.39:30:
It says that the gate of the outer court, on the north side of the temple that Ezekiel sees, had arches facing outward toward the court. The "arches" are probably porches or entrance halls. The posts (pillars) were decorated with palm trees, and one went up by eight steps. Some details of the Hebrew words are uncertain.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide, with the appearance of a man, leads him and measures the temple with a measuring rod. These measurements showed an orderly, holy place, already restored, to encourage a discouraged people. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: approaching God is not something done carelessly. The steps and the palm trees remind us that He deserves reverence and order. We can prepare ourselves calmly before praying or going to church, and remember that God cares even for the details of His house and of our lives.
exp.24:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying" is the verse's way of saying, in plain terms: "I received a message from God." Ezekiel uses this wording to mark the beginning of a new message. There is no content yet here, only the introduction.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. With this verse a new section of the book opens: messages against the nations that bordered Israel. The first message, according to the verses that follow, is aimed at Ammon, which rejoiced when Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed. God does not ignore that mockery.

For today: God keeps speaking and hopes we will listen closely. Before we speak or react, we can pause to hear his word in the Bible. This passage also reminds us that God sees how we treat those who suffer, and it invites us not to take pleasure in other people's pain.
exp.31:11:
God says he will bring down the people of Egypt by the swords of mighty men. Those warriors are called the most terrible of the nations, the strongest of all peoples. They will destroy Egypt's pride, meaning its haughtiness and arrogance, and all its great multitude will be laid low.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Pharaoh. The verse before says that the sword of the king of Babylon will come against Egypt. God uses one powerful nation to judge the pride of another. Scholars agree that Babylon is the main instrument, although the text speaks of the mighty in general.

For today: power, wealth, or number of people is not a safe foundation for life. Egypt trusted in its greatness, but God rules over all nations. Today we can examine whether our pride makes us trust in ourselves, and humbly return to depending on God.
exp.16:12:
The explanation says that the king of Babylon took someone from the royal family of Judah, made a covenant with him, and made him swear loyalty with an oath. He also carried off the mighty men of the land. "Seed of the kingdom" means a descendant of the king's family; "made him swear an oath" means that he forced him to take an oath.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon, whom he calls "a rebellious house." He explains to them the parable of the eagles. The king of Babylon is Nebuchadnezzar, and the royal descendant appears to be Zedekiah. God reminds them that Zedekiah swore loyalty, but then broke that covenant by seeking help from Egypt.

For today: God takes a given word seriously. Keeping our promises, even the difficult ones, is a way of honoring him, and trusting in him is safer than looking for easy escapes.
exp.29:17:
God says that in Tehaphnehes, a city of Egypt, the day will be darkened. There he will break the yokes of Egypt, that is, its power and its defenses, like someone breaking the bars of a door. The pride of its strength will come to an end. A cloud will cover it, a cloud of judgment, and the people of its villages will be taken away as prisoners.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt trusted in its power, and Judah sometimes sought support from it. God announces judgment on that nation so that it will be known that He is the Lord. Some scholars connect this with the Babylonian invasion, although the text gives no further details.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, work, reputation, or your own strength. All of these can fail. Entrust your plans to God with humility and trust Him first.
exp.17:19:
This verse says that each person is responsible for their own actions. The "soul" means the person themselves. "Carry" means to bear the guilt or the punishment. "Wickedness" means living without reverence for God. The son does not pay for the father's sins, nor does the father pay for the son's.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people kept repeating a saying: "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (v. 2). By this they meant that they were suffering because of their ancestors. God corrects that excuse and calls them to answer for themselves, and He shows them that they can always turn back to Him.

For today: do not use your family's past as an excuse, and do not stay trapped in guilt for other people's mistakes. Today you can choose to obey God and start over with Him.
exp.41:6:
It says there was a wall on the outside, facing the rooms, on the side of the outer court. That wall measured fifty cubits in length. A cubit was an ancient measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about half a meter, although scholars do not fully agree on the exact figure. The rooms were chambers or living spaces within the temple, and the court was an open yard.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting what he saw in a vision while a guide measured the temple. He was among the exiles in Babylon. These very detailed measurements showed that God cared about order, about the separation between the common and the holy, and that his presence would once again dwell among his people. Interpreters differ on whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God is concerned with order and with the boundaries that protect what is sacred. We can ask ourselves what healthy "walls" we need in order to guard our time with God.
exp.32:0:
This verse is an opening phrase.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God gives him a new assignment: to be like a watchman, that is, a lookout who warns of danger. With this phrase a section begins in which God reminds him of his responsibility to warn the people.

For today: before speaking, it is good to listen. If we want to encourage or advise others, let us start by reading the Bible and praying, so that our words come from God and not only from our own opinions. And when He shows us something, let us say it with love and truth.
exp.17:8:
The explanation says that the person who walks according to God's laws and keeps his commands faithfully and truthfully is considered righteous, and therefore will live. Words such as "statutes" are God's instructions; "judgments" are his righteous standards; "to deal truly" means acting with honesty and loyalty.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to the exiles in Babylon. They were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their fathers. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life. This verse closes the description of a righteous man: he helps the poor, does not oppress, does not rob, and judges with uprightness. Then comes the example of his son, who does not live this way.

For today: faith shows itself in everyday life. This week, look for one concrete way to act with honesty or to help someone in need, without excusing yourself by what others have done.
exp.13:14:
He says that God could send wild and dangerous animals over a sinful land. They would leave it so ruined and empty that no one would dare to cross it for fear of those beasts. The word for "ruined" means to lay waste or leave in ruins. The word for "desolate" means empty, without people. The phrase "because of the beasts" means that the beasts are the cause.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in exile, to a people who thought they were safe. God lists four judgments: famine, beasts, sword, and plague. With them he warns that a rebellious land is not saved by the merits of others, not even by righteous men such as Noah, Daniel, and Job. Each person answers before God.

For today: do not live on the faith of your parents or your church. Seek God yourself, with humility and repentance, because his mercy also invites you to return to him.
exp.13:19:
It says that even if three men famous for their righteousness, Noah, Daniel and Job, were in a land, they could not save their sons and daughters. They would only save themselves by their righteousness.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the exiles in Babylon. Some were thinking that Jerusalem would not be destroyed, because there were good people in it. God answers that the people's sin was so serious that neither the prayer nor the righteousness of others would prevent the judgment. Scholars debate who this Daniel was, but the text does not make it clear.

For today: faith is neither inherited nor lent. We can pray for our family, but each person must trust God for themselves. Take care of your own walk with Him.
exp.28:17:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army work very hard to attack the city of Tyre. The soldiers ended up with their heads bald from carrying helmets and with their shoulders raw from bearing loads. And despite all that effort, neither the king nor his troops received any pay or plunder from Tyre. "Wages" means reward or gain.

God speaks, addressing the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." We are in the twenty-seventh year of the exile, and God explains that Babylon, though it did not know it, was carrying out a purpose of his. Scholars believe that the long siege of Tyre left Babylon with little gain, and that is why God promises to give it Egypt as compensation.

For today: God sees the effort of every person, and nothing that is done lies outside his care. We can trust that he governs history and that he is just.
exp.28:12:
God says that, when forty years have passed, He will gather the Egyptians again, the very people He had scattered among the nations. The verse's wording for "gather" means to bring together, and the word for scattered means spread out, dispersed to different places.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt had thought itself very powerful and had been a source of false confidence for Israel. For this reason God announces judgment on its pride. But the punishment has a limit: afterward restoration will come, although Egypt will remain a humble kingdom. Scholars debate whether the forty years is a literal or symbolic figure, and it is not known with certainty how it was fulfilled.

For today: God corrects, but He does not destroy without hope. If you are going through a difficult season, remember that He sets limits on punishment and can restore. Learn humility and trust in God, not in your own power.
exp.17:16:
He says that the son who turns his hand away from harming the poor, who does not charge interest or excessive interest, and who keeps God's laws, will not die for the sins of his father. He will surely live. "Turn his hand away from the poor" means not mistreating them. Charging excessive interest to someone who needs help is the wrong being described. Keeping God's laws is what is meant here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life. Some interpret "die" as physical death, and others as separation from God; the text allows both ideas to be seen.

For today: do not live tied to the mistakes of your family. With God's help you can choose another path, treating those in need with justice and generosity.
exp.32:5:
This verse speaks of a watchman who sees an enemy army coming but does not sound the trumpet to warn the people. If the people die without having been warned, they still bear their own guilt, but God will hold the watchman responsible for his silence.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. He appoints him as a spiritual watchman over the people. His task was to warn them clearly on God's behalf, so that they could change their course before judgment came.

For today: if God has given you a truth that helps others, do not keep it silent out of fear or comfort. Share it with love, humility and clarity, and let each person decide.
exp.14:7:
God says that he will leave the land turned into ruins and desolation. "Desolation" means total destruction, an empty and devastated place. "Trespass" is betraying or being unfaithful to a commitment, like breaking a sacred promise. The phrase "I will make" simply means "I will turn" or "I will bring about."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the people's exile in Babylon. Earlier, he compared Jerusalem to the wood of a vine, which is useless for building anything and is used only as firewood. Jerusalem was not producing the fruit of faithfulness that God expected, and so judgment would come. God makes it clear that the cause was the people's unfaithfulness toward him.

For today: God expects our lives to bear the fruit of faithfulness, not just outward appearance. Today you can ask yourself, in prayer, where you have been unfaithful to God, and return to him with sincerity, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.39:4:
He says that Ezekiel saw a wall surrounding the house, that is, the temple. The man who was guiding him had a measuring reed of six cubits, and each cubit was "a cubit and a hand breadth": a long cubit, that is, an ordinary cubit plus a hand breadth (about 52 to 53 cm, although experts are not completely sure). With that reed he measured the wall: one reed for its width and another for its height.

Ezekiel was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, God took him to Israel, and a guide with the appearance of shining bronze showed him a new temple. He was asked to look, listen, and set his heart on what he saw, so that he could tell it later to the people. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol, or as a promise that God would dwell again with his people.

For today: God attends to the details and invites us to give attention to his Word calmly, not in a hurry. Today, read a passage slowly and ask him to speak to you.
exp.20:20:
He says that the king of Babylon stopped at a fork in the road, where the way divides in two, to find out which direction to take. He used three kinds of divination: he shook up and mixed marked arrows and drew one out, he consulted the household idols, and he looked at the liver of a sacrificed animal.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. One road led to Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and the other to Jerusalem. The lot pointed to Jerusalem. God uses this pagan decision to show that judgment on Judah for its sin was already coming.

For today: no one decides by chance or by superstition. God governs even the decisions of the powerful. Before choosing a path, let us seek his guidance in prayer and in his Word, and not in horoscopes or doubtful signs.
exp.22:37:
God says that, in addition to everything before, his people did another serious thing: "they have defiled my sanctuary in the same day," that is, they made the holy place unclean, and "have profaned my sabbaths," meaning they treated as ordinary the day of rest that God had set apart for himself.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses two sisters, Aholah and Aholibah, as an image of Samaria and Jerusalem, who turned away from God. The following verse explains the accusation: they offered their children to idols and then entered the temple that same day, as if nothing had happened. Their worship was a false mixture.

For today: we cannot serve God and other gods at the same time. It is worth examining whether our daily life agrees with what we say at church, and returning to God with a sincere heart, not only with rituals.
exp.39:47:
Here Ezekiel is still accompanied by a guide who leads him to the entrance of the temple, called the "porch." With a measuring rod, the guide records the thickness of each post (the pillars of the entrance): five cubits on each side. A cubit was roughly half a meter. He also measures the gate, three cubits on each side.

Ezekiel recounts this vision while he is exiled in Babylon. A man with the appearance of bronze measures the whole temple for him. Scholars interpret it in various ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of God's presence, or as a promise of restoration. No one knows for certain.

For today: God is a God of order, and he attends to the details of his house. We can draw near to him with respect and reverence, and trust that, even in times of discouragement, he has a plan to restore his people.
exp.19:25:
God says that he defiled them, that is, he left them stained by their own offerings, when they were making their firstborn children pass through the fire. "That I might make them desolate" means that they would be left horrified and devastated. The purpose was that they would recognize that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and recounts the rebellion of Israel. Because the people rejected his commands, God gave them over to the practices they preferred. The Law forbade sacrificing children, so many understand that God did not command this, but allowed that path as judgment. Some scholars interpret it in other ways, and the text is difficult.

For today: when we insist on living our own way, God may let us reap the consequences. Let us seek his word soon, before our paths hurt us and those we love.
exp.43:12:
God says that certain Levites will no longer be able to come near to him as priests. They will not touch the holy things or the most holy offerings. Those who "come near" are those who draw close, so they will bear their shame and the detestable practices they committed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of the new temple. Those Levites had served before idols and caused Israel to stumble. For this reason they lose the office of priest, but they continue serving in humbler tasks: guarding the gates and helping in the house. The sons of Zadok, who were faithful, will indeed draw near. Interpreters explain the final meaning of this vision in several ways.

For today: serving God is not only a position but faithfulness. Let us examine whether anything holds in our heart the place that belongs to God, and return to him with humility.
exp.38:2:
It says God will take away Gog's main weapon. The bow in the left hand and the arrows in the right hand show a warrior ready to fight. God declares that He will leave him without power and without defense. An old word from the context, which can be understood in several ways: some think it means "to guide," others "to leave with only a sixth part."

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog appears as a leader of enemy nations who will attack Israel. The prophecy announces that God Himself will intervene and defeat them. Scholars disagree about whether Gog refers to historical events, a future event, or a symbol of evil.

For today: when you feel you are facing something stronger than you, remember that God rules over all human power. Trust in Him, pray, and rest in the knowledge that justice and protection ultimately belong to Him.
exp.18:1:
It says that God tells Ezekiel to sing a lament, a sad song. It presents a mother lioness who lay down to live among other lions and raised her cubs there. The word "lament" means a song of mourning, and the word "raised" in the verse means she brought them up and helped them grow.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The song refers to the princes or kings of Judah. The lioness is usually understood as Judah or its royal line, although some see it differently. The cubs are kings who, surrounded by violence, learned to imitate it and ended up falling.

For today: what surrounds us shapes us. It is worth reviewing which environments, friendships and habits are shaping our family, and seeking God so that we raise our children in wisdom and not in the hardness of the world.
exp.22:31:
It says that Jerusalem, called by the name of Oholibah, will drink the same cup of punishment that her sister Samaria drank. The cup is a vessel for drinking, and here it stands for God's judgment. It is deep and wide, a huge cup full of suffering. The words that say the nations will mock her and scorn her mean that the peoples will laugh at her and bring her down to humiliation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel uses the image of two sisters to speak of Samaria (the northern kingdom) and Jerusalem (the kingdom of Judah). Both turned away from God and sought alliances and idols from other nations. Samaria had already fallen, and God warns that Judah, by following the same path, would face the same end.

For today: let us learn from the mistakes of others. If we see that someone suffered the consequences of turning away from God, let us not think that it will not happen to us. Today we can return to God with humility, because He offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.20:31:
God says that this people will be like wood for the fire. Their blood will be poured out in the middle of their own land, and no one will remember them anymore. The Lord himself, who speaks here, declares that this is his word.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this passage the judgment is directed at the Ammonites, who mocked the fall of Judah. God's sword, used by cruel men, would also fall upon them. Some scholars see here a general warning against the pride and violence of nations.

For today: do not rejoice when others suffer, and do not think yourself untouchable because of your success. God sees every injustice and every pride. With humility, let him correct you in time, and trust that his justice is true.
exp.47:14:
This verse describes a smaller strip of land, five thousand cubits wide, that is left over after the holy portion has been set apart. That part is "profane," meaning it is not sacred but for ordinary use. It will serve the city: a place where people can live and, around it, pasture and open ground. The city will stand in the center.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. In his final vision, God shows how the land of Israel would be divided: first what is dedicated to Him, then what is for common use. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic or spiritual.

For today: even when daily life is ordinary, like home and work, God wants it in order and at the center, with what is holy close by. Put God in the middle of your routines.
exp.20:29:
God asks whether he will return the sword to its sheath. "Return" means to put back, and "sheath" is the case that holds the blade. The understood answer is not yet: the judgment continues. God says he will judge Ammon in its own land, where it was born and lived.

God speaks through Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." Ammon mocked the fall of Judah, and its false prophets promised that it would be safe. God answers that this deception will not save it. Some scholars think the verse is addressed to the sword and others that it is addressed to Ammon, so the text is not entirely clear on that point.

For today: do not trust in words that only reassure you. Seek God's truth, and do not mock the suffering of others.
exp.30:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to deliver a message to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and to his multitude. The question is: "Whom art thou like in thy greatness?" In other words, with whom do you think you can compare yourself?

The message comes in the eleventh year of the exile, as it is understood, when Egypt felt powerful. Jehovah speaks through Ezekiel. Next he compares Assyria, once so great, to a very tall cedar that fell. In this way God warns Pharaoh that his pride will end in the same way.

Some scholars debate details of the image, but the message about pride is clear.

For today: when we feel strong because of our success, money, or position, it is good to remember that everything comes from God. We can ask him for a humble and grateful heart.
exp.38:27:
God says that the people of Israel will know that He is the Lord their God when, after having led them away captive among the nations, He brings them back together in their own land. Not one of them will be left behind. "Among the heathen" means "among the nations"; "the Lord" is God's name; "gathered" means "brought back together."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been exiled because of its rebellion, and this message promises restoration. The nearby verses speak of shame for sin, of living in safety, and of God pouring out His Spirit. Some believers see here the return from Babylon; others see a future fulfillment. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: even when we have failed or feel far away, God knows how to restore and gather His own. We can acknowledge our faults honestly and trust that He is faithful to lift us up again.
exp.43:0:
Ezekiel tells us that a guide led him back toward the outer gate of the sanctuary, the one facing east. That gate was shut.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, is in the middle of a long vision of a new temple, given to the exiles of Israel. The following verse explains that God himself says the gate will remain shut because he entered through it. It likely recalls the glory of God returning from the east (chapter 43). Interpreters differ on whether this vision should be read literally, symbolically, or as a prophecy about Christ.

For today: the holiness of God deserves respect. We can approach him with reverence, remembering that he opens the way, and we respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.21:7:
It says that Jerusalem has treated with contempt what God regarded as holy. "Holy things" refers to the temple and to the things dedicated to God. "Despised" means that you took away their value, treating them as something of no importance. "Profaned" means that what was holy was treated as common. The sabbaths were the day of rest that God set apart for his people.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time of exile in Babylon. He is accusing Jerusalem of serious sins: violence, injustice against orphans, widows and foreigners, and immorality. This verse shows that their wickedness was not only against people, but also against God, since they despised his worship and his day.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we take what belongs to God seriously, such as his Word, prayer, and the time of rest and worship. And let us notice that loving God and caring for the weak go together.
exp.20:10:
It says the sword is already ready to be used. "Furbished" means polished and made bright, as a weapon is. God had the sword made sharp and polished so that it would be at hand, that is, prepared, and given into the hand of the one who will carry out the punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and its people for their disobedience. The sword is often understood as the army of Babylon, although the text presents it as an instrument of God. The verses that follow show that the blow would reach even the princes of Israel.

For today: God speaks in earnest, but he warns so that there may be repentance. Today I can examine my life honestly, correct what I know is wrong, and return to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.46:17:
Here God describes the east boundary of the land Israel would receive. The border would run between the regions of Hauran and Damascus, and between Gilead and the land of Israel, following the Jordan River down to the eastern sea. The phrase "you shall measure" means "they will mark out" or "they will measure." The "eastern sea" is usually understood to be the Dead Sea, although some interpret it in other ways.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision about the restoration of his people after the exile. He divides the land with clear and fair boundaries for the twelve tribes. Scholars disagree: some see here a literal fulfillment in the future, while others see a spiritual picture of the kingdom of God.

For today: God is interested in the details of our lives and keeps his promises with order. We can trust that he knows how to give us what we need and to set good limits for our lives.
exp.33:17:
God asks the strong sheep whether it is not enough for them to eat the best pasture. Instead of leaving something for the others, they trample what is left over and foul the clean water. Here the water is described as still, clear water, and the trampling of the pasture is the same as treading it down with their feet.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had condemned the shepherds of Israel, who fed themselves and neglected the flock. Now God addresses the powerful sheep who take advantage of the weak. He promises to care for the injured and the lost, and to judge between one sheep and another. Some understand this to refer to the leaders and wealthy people of that time, though the text speaks in the language of shepherding.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use what God has given us only for ourselves. Sharing time, resources, and attention with those who have less is a concrete way of reflecting the heart of the good Shepherd.
exp.12:21:
This verse says that God accuses certain false prophetesses of doing two kinds of harm: with lies they filled the heart of the righteous with sorrow and discouragement, though God never wanted to make him sad, and they gave courage and encouragement to the wicked so that he would continue in his evil way. To "strengthen the hands" means to give him backing or support. An "evil way" is his sinful conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. Earlier in this chapter, God condemns prophets and prophetesses who invented messages and said they came from God. The details of the "pillows" and the "veils" are objects tied to their practices of divination; scholars are not entirely certain how they were used. God promises to rescue his people from their influence.

For today: before accepting or repeating a "spiritual" message, let us compare whether it is faithful to the Bible. A true word corrects the one who sins while speaking truth, and comforts the one who suffers without deceit.
exp.27:17:
He says the king of Tyre filled his life with wickedness through his injustice and his dishonest dealings, and so he defiled his holy places. Therefore God brought out a fire from within him that consumed him and left him reduced to ashes in the sight of all.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against the king of Tyre, a city rich from its trade. The language uses images of Eden and of a guardian cherub. Some see only the human king; others also see an allusion to Satan. It is debated, and the text does not fully settle it.

For today: wealth, beauty, or success can make us proud. Let us examine with humility how we earn and use what we have, and ask God for an honest heart.
exp.27:2:
God says to the prince of Tyre: "Behold, you think you are wiser than Daniel; you think no secret is hidden from you." Many read this as mockery: the ruler thought he was the wisest of all. The phrase "Behold" in the verse above means "look" or "take notice."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The ruler of Tyre, a rich and powerful city, had filled himself with pride and even compared himself to God. Daniel was famous for his wisdom, although some scholars debate whether Ezekiel means the Daniel of Babylon or an older righteous man. The central point is that God confronts his arrogance.

For today: intelligence, success, and money are gifts, not reasons to feel superior. Ask God for humility and acknowledge that all wisdom comes from Him.
exp.34:4:
It says that God judges Edom, called here "the mountain of Seir," for two reasons: it had "perpetual enmities," that is, a hatred that never ended, and it handed the Israelites over to the power of the sword, that is, to violence, when they were at their worst moment. The explanation of "you have scattered" is that Edom dispersed them. The phrase about "an extremely evil time" refers to the day of their ruin.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and descended from Esau, brother of Jacob. When Jerusalem fell, Edom did not help but took advantage. God responds by defending his wounded people and showing that he sees the injustice.

For today: do not hold on to resentment or rejoice in the pain of others. When someone suffers, offer them help and comfort, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.35:24:
God promises to cleanse his people completely. "I will sprinkle clean water" is an image of purification, like the washing done in the rituals of the temple. "Filthiness" refers to the impurities that keep people away from God, and "idols" are the false gods the people had worshiped.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had dishonored God's name with their idolatry and their injustice. Even so, God promises to restore them, not because they deserve it, but for the sake of the holiness of his name. This cleansing prepares the way for the "new heart" and the Spirit that come right after.

For today: we cannot cleanse ourselves alone of what harms us inside. We can come before God with sincerity, acknowledge whatever has taken his place in our lives, and ask him to purify and renew us. Many Christians see in this text a foreshadowing of forgiveness and of the work of the Spirit in Christ.
exp.40:1:
Here a man with a measuring rod walks through the temple and records each size. The entrance of the temple is ten cubits wide (a cubit was roughly half a meter), and on each side there is a wall of five cubits. Then he measures the main hall, called the sanctuary or holy place: forty cubits long and twenty cubits wide.

It is Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, a guide takes him through a new temple and shows him its measurements. Scholars do not agree on its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, while others see it as a symbol of God's presence among his people.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and he wants us to draw near to him with reverence. Today we can set aside a quiet moment to pray with respect and attention.
exp.17:24:
They said that some in Israel were complaining that God was not just. The word "crooked" means that their ways are not upright or honest. God answers with a question: is it really his way that is unjust, or are the ways of the people the ones that are crooked? The word "hear" is an invitation to listen carefully.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people said they were suffering for the sins of their fathers and that God was not just. God makes clear to them that each person answers for himself, and that He wants the sinner to turn back and live, not to die.

When something goes wrong, it is easy to blame God or others. This verse invites us to examine our own hearts honestly. God always leaves the door open to repentance, and we can return to Him today.
exp.40:15:
This verse continues describing the temple that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It mentions the door posts (the base of the doors), the narrow windows, and the side chambers on three levels all around. Everything was covered with wood from the floor up to the windows. The word "round about" means all around, and "in front" means at the front.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, recounts what he sees while a guide with a measuring reed shows him the temple. This takes place during the exile in Babylon. God shows him an orderly, measured temple, perhaps to bring hope to a discouraged people. Scholars interpret it in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbolic image, or as a sign of God's presence.

For today: God cares about order and detail. Pay careful attention to your prayer life and your community, so that they may be places where God dwells.
exp.35:20:
God says that he felt compassion, or that he was concerned, for his holy name, that is, for his reputation and his honor. That name was dishonored by Israel among the nations where they were taken. "Nations" means non-Jewish peoples, and "dishonor" means treating what is sacred as common or worthless.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile. Israel had been scattered because of its sin. But the nations, seeing the exiles, thought that the God of Israel was weak or unable to care for his people. For this reason God announces that he will act, not because of any merit on their part, but to show who he truly is.

For today: the way we live speaks of God before others. We can ask him to help us live in such a way that his name is honored and not shamed, trusting that his mercy remains greater than our failures.
exp.26:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "The word of the Lord came again unto me" is the opening phrase of a new message, and what God will say comes in the verses that follow.

The one speaking is God, and the one listening is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. With this verse begins a chapter devoted to Tyre, a rich and proud city that traded by sea. God instructs Ezekiel to raise a lament, that is, a funeral song, because it announces the fall of that city, which boasted of its beauty and its power.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before trusting in our riches or achievements, it is wise to stop and listen to him with humility.
exp.14:6:
God says that he will set himself against the inhabitants of Jerusalem. To set one's face against someone means to confront them with judgment. They have "come out from one fire," meaning they had already gone through earlier punishments, but the fire will consume them again. In this way they will recognize that God is the Lord, the true LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to the wood of the vine, which is of no use for making anything and is only valuable if it bears fruit. Because the people did not bear the fruit of faithfulness and rebelled (unfaithfulness means betraying or seriously breaking a covenant), God announces his judgment.

For today: God expects a life that bears the fruit of obedience and trust in him. We can honestly examine where we have turned away, and return to him sincerely, before pride hardens us.
exp.16:17:
He despised the oath and broke the covenant he had made, although he "had given his hand," that is, he had promised with a solemn gesture of commitment. Since he did all of these things, God declares that he shall not escape the punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is referring to Zedekiah, king of Judah, who swore loyalty to Babylon but rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God says that the oath, made in his name, was also God's own, and that is why the betrayal was so serious.

Today it reminds us that our word matters. Keeping what we have promised, in marriage, at work, or with friends, is a way of honoring God. If we have failed, we can come to him with sincerity and ask for forgiveness.
exp.13:0:
It says that some leaders of the people of Israel, called "elders," came to Ezekiel and sat down in front of him. Here "came to me" and "sat down" are older ways of writing the same ideas as "came to me" and "sat down" in the verse you are reading, so the comment on the wording can be left aside. This was the posture of someone who comes to listen or to ask for a word from God.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. These elders were probably seeking an answer from the Lord. But right away God shows Ezekiel that these men had idols in their hearts. They appeared to be seeking God, but their loyalty was divided.

For today: we can draw near to God with religious attitudes, such as praying, attending church, or asking for advice, and still hold on to something that takes his place. Today it is good to ask him to show us what we love more than him, and to surrender it to him sincerely.
exp.38:0:
God commands Ezekiel, whom He calls "son of man" (simply a human being), to prophesy, that is, to speak on God's behalf. The message is against Gog. God says: "Behold, I am against you". The phrase "chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" can be understood as the main leader of Meshech and Tubal, although some translate it as "prince of Rosh".

The Lord GOD speaks, in a prophecy given to the prophet Ezekiel for the people of Israel. Gog appears as a leader who attacks God's people. Scholars disagree about who he is: some see real nations, others a symbol of evil in the last times. What is clear is that God opposes whoever oppresses His people.

For today: when evil seems very powerful, remember that God is greater than any power. You can rest in Him and pray with confidence.
exp.19:14:
He says that God lifted up his hand, that is, made a solemn oath, in the wilderness. He swore that Israel would not enter the land he had given them, a land that is fertile and abundant, the most beautiful of all.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel, who were in exile. He reminds them of their history: even after being freed from Egypt, the people rebelled, profaned the Sabbaths, and followed their idols. God shows them that their present situation has deep roots. Even so, the text that follows says that God forgave them and did not destroy them.

For today: God's blessings should not be taken for granted. Today we can examine whether we obey him wholeheartedly or whether we still follow other "idols." And we can trust that his mercy continues to give us the opportunity to return.
exp.30:12:
It says that when the great tree falls and lies in ruins, the birds and the beasts of the field will settle on its fallen trunk and its broken branches. Before, they sought shelter in its shade; now they live only off what remains.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He compares Assyria, or perhaps Egypt (interpreters understand it in different ways), to an enormous and proud cedar. Because of its arrogance, God allows strong nations to bring it down. Its fall serves as a warning to other powerful ones.

For today: power, success, and prestige do not last if the heart is filled with pride. We can be thankful for what God gives us, live with humility, and remember that all our strength depends on Him.
exp.22:47:
He says God will put an end to the wickedness and immoral behavior that was in the land. The women, that is, those who hear or see this punishment, will learn the lesson (learning by punishment is what it means) and will not imitate that shameful conduct, which here speaks of disgraceful and immoral behavior.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter, Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two sisters, Ahola and Aholiba, who represent the unfaithfulness of Israel and Judah, since they joined themselves to other nations and their idols instead of remaining faithful to God. The judgment is a warning for other peoples.

For today: let us not take faithfulness to God lightly. If we see the consequences of idolatry and sin, let us learn in time and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.36:4:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to say to some dry bones: "I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live." The word "spirit" here also means "breath" or "breath of life."

God, the Lord, speaks in a vision that Ezekiel had. The bones represent the people of Israel, who were exiled in Babylon and felt they had no hope (Ezekiel 37:11). God promises to restore them to life and bring them back. Many also see here an image of spiritual renewal, though the text focuses on Israel.

For today: if there are areas of your life that feel dry or without a way out, do not stop talking with God about them. He can bring life where it seems impossible. Trust in His Word, even when you cannot see how.
exp.35:31:
God tells the people of Israel that he will not restore them because of anything they deserve. He wants them to understand this clearly. He asks them to feel shame and sorrow for their wrongful behavior. The words "let it be known" are rendered simply as "that it be clear to you." The word "iniquities" refers to acts of wickedness or injustice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people living in exile because they had abandoned him. Before and after this verse, he promises to return them to their land, make it fruitful, and rebuild the cities. Here he makes clear that he will do this for his own faithfulness and for his name, not because Israel has earned it. His grace comes first; repentance follows.

Today we can remember that God's forgiveness and blessings are a gift, not a payment. This leads us to honestly acknowledge our failings, without excuses, but also without despair, trusting in his mercy.
exp.35:29:
God promises that he will make the fruit of the trees and of the fields grow much more abundantly. The reason is that Israel will never again suffer the shame of going hungry before the other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people exiled because of their sin. In the neighboring countries, drought and famine were seen as a sign of divine abandonment. God promises to restore the land and also the heart of his people. He then makes clear that he does this for the sake of his name and his grace, not because they deserve it.

For today: God cares for our needs and also for our hearts. When you receive his help, do not see it as a reward for your effort, but as grace. Respond with gratitude, humility, and a sincere desire to live better.
exp.40:24:
It says that the doors of the temple had carvings of cherubim and palm trees, just like the walls. Also, there was a "thick planks" (a kind of beam or wooden overhang) at the front of the entrance, on the outside. "Carved" means cut or sculpted.

Ezekiel speaks, a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. God gave him a vision of a new temple, measured with great detail. This encouraged a defeated people to believe that God was still present and that there would be restoration. Scholars disagree about whether this temple should be understood literally, symbolically, or as something yet to come.

For today: the cherubim and palm trees remind us that God is holy, but He also wants us to live in His presence with life and hope. We can set aside a moment each day to draw near to Him with reverence and gratitude, without hurry.
exp.25:9:
It says that the enemy army will be so great that its horses will raise a cloud of dust that will cover the city. The noise of the horsemen, the wheels and the chariots will make the walls shake. The invader will enter through the gates as one who passes through a city wall that has already been broken down. "Breaches" are gaps or openings made in a wall; "horsemen" here means riders on horseback.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against Tyre, a very rich trading city. The text says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would come against it (v. 7). Tyre had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking only of its own gain. God announces judgment and shows that no powerful city stands above Him.

For today: let us not place our security in money, prestige or success, because all of that can fall. Let us seek our refuge in God, and avoid rejoicing in the misfortune of others.
exp.37:5:
This verse continues the list of nations that God says will join Gog. It names Gomer and the house of Togarmah, "from the far north," with all their troops, and adds "many peoples." The word for "troops" here refers to armies or groups of allies. Today people debate where these peoples lived; many place them in the region of Anatolia, north of Israel, but there is no complete certainty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that, in a future time, a great coalition will come against Israel, now restored. God says that He Himself leads it, to show that He is above all human power. Christians interpret this prophecy in different ways: literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: even when you see great threats and powerful alliances, remember that none of them escapes God's control. Trust in Him, pray, and live with calm, without letting fear rule you.
exp.45:11:
If the prince wishes to offer to God, of his own free will and not out of obligation, a burnt offering (a complete offering that is burned) or peace offerings (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving), the eastern gate of the inner court will be opened for him. There he will present his offering just as he does on the Sabbath. Then he will go out, and the gate will be shut after he leaves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a future temple and worship. Interpreters disagree about whether this is a literal vision, a symbolic one, or one tied to the Messiah. Here the emphasis is that even the prince must worship with order and reverence, under God's rules.

For today: God values an offering given freely and with joy. We can serve him and give him our time, prayer, or help to others, not under pressure, but with a willing and reverent heart.
exp.44:5:
Here it says that, alongside the portion set apart for the sanctuary, an area of land must be reserved for the city. It measures five thousand across and twenty-five thousand long (the units, probably cubits, are not stated here). That land is not for the priests or for the princes, but for the whole house of Israel. "Possession" means property or inheritance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of a restored temple and land. This vision comes to a people in exile. The territory is divided in an orderly way: first the holy portion, then the city, and then the portion for the prince. Interpreters differ on whether this is meant to be fulfilled literally or is symbolic.

For today: put God at the center and make sure what is shared belongs to everyone. We can arrange our time and possessions so that God has first place, and so that no one is left outside the blessing.
exp.16:3:
It says the eagle tore off the highest and most tender branch of the cedar, carried it to a land of merchants, and set it down in a city of traders. The new shoots are the fresh young growth of a tree; the word "carried" and "set" simply mean that the eagle took the branch away and placed it in that city.

God asks Ezekiel to tell a parable to Israel. Many understand that the eagle is the king of Babylon, and that the branch torn off is King Jehoiachin, taken into exile with other leaders of Judah. The "land of merchants" would be Babylon. God uses this image to show the people why they suffered that fall and what would happen next.

For today: even when we lose what seemed secure, such as a job or a sense of safety, God still governs. We can ask Him for wisdom to trust Him and not only human powers.
exp.40:17:
This verse describes the decoration of the temple walls that Ezekiel saw in a vision. Figures of cherubim and palm trees were carved into them, arranged in alternation: a palm tree, then a cherub, then another palm tree. Each cherub had two faces.

Ezekiel speaks here as a priest who was exiled in Babylon. A guide shows him and measures a new temple for him. The verses that follow say that the two faces were those of a man and a lion. Scholars do not agree on whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or future. The cherubim recall God's presence, and the palm trees may evoke life and beauty.

For today: God cares about the beauty and order of his presence. We can draw near to him with reverence, remembering that his house is a place of life and hope, even when we feel far away or in exile.
exp.19:45:
God tells Ezekiel to look toward the south and to proclaim a prophetic message against a "forest" of the south. "Son of man" is the way God addresses the prophet. "Noon" and "the southern part" both mean the south. "Pouring out the word" means speaking with force and holding nothing back.

God himself speaks and sends Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The verses that follow explain that the forest will be set on fire and that the fire will not go out. Many understand that the forest represents Judah and Jerusalem, and that the fire is God's judgment. Later on, Ezekiel himself tells that people were saying he only spoke in parables, so the message was not always understood.

Today we can learn to listen to God even when his message is uncomfortable. Before asking God to correct others, it is wise to ask him what he wants to correct in us.
exp.44:15:
This verse says that all the people of the land will have to give an offering for the prince of Israel. The word "obligated" means it was not optional: the whole people had to take part. The offering included goods such as oil, grain, and animals from the flock.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about a new temple and a new way of life for Israel. With these offerings, the prince could cover the sacrifices and the festivals on behalf of everyone. In this way, worship was a shared responsibility. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic or future.

For today: worship and service to God should not rest on just one person. Ask yourself how you can contribute faithfully, with your time, your gifts, or your resources, to support your community of faith.
exp.44:12:
It says the people were to give a grain offering: one-sixth of an ephah for every homer of wheat, and likewise one-sixth of an ephah for every homer of barley. An ephah was a measure for dry goods, and a homer was a large measure, equal to ten ephahs. So a small, well-defined portion was required, close to 1.7 percent.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of a temple and a renewed life for Israel. Before this verse, God calls for honest weights and measures. The offering was part of an arrangement in which the people supported the prince and the worship. The exact details of how this vision would be fulfilled are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God joins worship with honesty. We can give with order and generosity, and be fair in our work, in our prices, and in our agreements, because what we offer to God matters, and so does how we treat others.
exp.23:21:
Here God tells the people that they will do just what Ezekiel did: they will not cover the lower part of their face with a cloak or veil, as mourners did, nor will they eat the food that friends would bring to those in grief. Ezekiel's own mourning customs are the sign. The phrase "bread of men" most likely refers to the meal that friends brought to people who were mourning.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who had just lost his wife and was not allowed to mourn in public. That was a sign for Israel: Jerusalem and the temple would be destroyed, and the grief would be so great that there would be no way to express it through the usual customs. Some understand it to mean a silent, deeply shocked weeping.

For today: when God corrects us, it is better to respond with humility and sincere repentance, rather than mourning only when it is already too late.
exp.26:5:
The explanation says that the oars of Tyre's ship were made of oak wood from Bashan, a region known for its strong trees. The "benches" are the seats of the rowers, and they are described as inlaid with ivory brought from the isles of Chittim, that is, Cyprus or the shores of the Mediterranean. The phrase about the Ashurites is difficult to translate, and scholars understand it in several different ways.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre, a trading city, is presented as a beautiful and luxurious ship, proud of its wealth. This poetic lament prepares the announcement of its fall.

Today: we may have things that are very valuable and beautiful, but they must not be the center of our security. Ask yourself what you truly trust in, and thank God for everything you have, using it with humility and generosity.
exp.32:2:
This verse speaks of the watchman, the sentry who sees danger coming, blows the trumpet (a horn trumpet) and warns the people. "Warn" means he gives the alert in time. His job is to see and to sound the warning clearly.

God is speaking to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. God uses the picture of a city that appoints a watchman to explain Ezekiel's mission: to warn the people of the judgment that is coming. If the people hear the warning and pay no attention, the responsibility is theirs. If the watchman stays silent, he is the one who will answer for it.

For today: if God has shown you a truth that can help someone, do not keep it silent out of fear or shame. Speak it with love, with respect and with clarity, and let the other person decide.
exp.15:27:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to an unfaithful woman, also sought out the Assyrians to satisfy herself. Here "played the whore" means being unfaithful, above all seeking other gods or allies in place of God. To be "unsatiable" means never being satisfied. Even after doing this, she did not find what she was looking for.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, who were living in exile or near it. He uses a strong image to show how Jerusalem turned away from Him and trusted in alliances with powerful nations and in its idols. God wants the people to see how serious their unfaithfulness is, and in the same book He also promises restoration.

For today: when we look for money, success, or the approval of others to fill the emptiness of the heart, they never satisfy. We can return to God and ask Him to be our true satisfaction.
exp.12:16:

That is, they give messages made up by themselves, not received from God. "Set your face" means to address someone with determination. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, reminding him that he is a simple human being.

God speaks in the middle of the exile and Israel's crisis. He had already condemned the male prophets who promised false peace. Now the message is directed at women who were also deceiving the people. The following verses show that they did so for gain, in exchange for barley and bread. The exact details of their practices are not entirely clear.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I listen to what God says in his Word, or only to what comforts me? Comparing everything with the Bible protects us from messages that are pleasant but false.
exp.19:4:
