God tells Ezekiel to speak to the elders of Israel and remind them of the day he chose his people. The phrase "lifted up my hand" is an old way of saying he made a solemn oath or promise. The word "seed" means descendants, and "made myself known" means God revealed himself to them. In Egypt he declared to them: "I am the Lord your God."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Some elders had come to consult him, but God answers that he will not attend to them, because first they must face their history of unfaithfulness. That is why he begins by recalling how everything started: with his choosing and his promise.

For today: before asking something of God, it is good to remember who he is and how faithful he has been to us. That helps us come near with sincerity and humility, ready to correct what we need to change.
exp.47:34:
It says the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision measures eighteen thousand measures all around (a measure was a rod of about three meters, though the exact calculation is debated). And from that day the city shall be called "The Lord is there."

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, for he received this vision during the exile in Babylon. The people were far from their land, and the Temple had been destroyed. At the end of the book, God promises restoration and, above all, his presence. Some believe the vision speaks of a literal future, others that it is symbolic of the church or of heaven; Christians understand it in different ways.

The most valuable thing about a place is not its walls or its size, but that God is present. Today we can ask him to be the center of our home, our work, and our daily life.
exp.11:19:
God says that the cities where people live today will be destroyed and the land will be left empty and desolate. Seeing this, the people will recognize that the Lord is the Lord. "Laid waste" means reduced to ruins.

God speaks and gives this message to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Ezekiel was to act as if he were eating with fear, to show what would come upon Jerusalem. The text says the cause was the wickedness of its inhabitants. God gave the warning so that they would understand that He is serious.

Today we can learn not to take God's warnings lightly. If He shows us something we need to correct, it is a sign of His care. You can pray today with humility and ask Him, "Lord, what should I change?" and obey promptly.
exp.12:8:
God says he will act with force against the prophets who see empty things and announce lies. They will have no place in the assembly of his people, their names will not be written in the record of Israel, and they will not return to their land. The words "divine" and "vain" here refer to announcing supposed messages, and to something empty and without worth. In the end, everyone will recognize that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some false prophets claimed to speak for the Lord when God had not spoken to them, and they promised peace when judgment was coming. In this way they gave the people a false sense of security. Scholars understand in different ways exactly what "the book" was, but it seems to refer to the record of God's people.

Today we can examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, and if we teach, we should speak with honesty. A truth that makes us uncomfortable is better than a sweet promise that God has not made.
exp.46:3:
The explanation says that the man guiding Ezekiel continued measuring another thousand cubits along the river that flowed from the temple. In the first stretch, the water reached the knees. In the next, it reached the loins, that is, up to the waist. With each measurement, the water grew deeper.

Ezekiel is the one speaking, recounting a vision that God gave him. A guide, holding a measuring cord, leads him step by step through the water flowing from the temple. Many understand this water to represent God's life and blessing, which keeps growing without end. Some see it as a promise for Israel's future, others as an image of the Spirit. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God invites us to move forward in faith little by little, not staying only at the water's edge. Each step of trust brings us into a deeper life with Him.
exp.42:13:
This verse gives the measurements of the altar that Ezekiel saw in his vision. It speaks of the base, which was one cubit high and one cubit wide. From that base to the first ledge below there are two cubits, and from there to the next level, four cubits, with a width of one cubit as well. The word translated here as "settle" refers to a base or channel; scholars understand it in several ways. A cubit was roughly half a meter.

God himself shows Ezekiel the new temple and its altar through a guide. The people were exiled in Babylon, and this vision gave them hope: God would once again dwell among them. The precise measurements show that God is orderly, and that worship of him should be carried out with reverence and holiness. How this vision is fulfilled, interpreters debate.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we draw near to him. Come with reverence and sincerity, and remember that Christ has already opened the way for you.
exp.21:27:
These verses say that the prophets of Jerusalem covered over the people's sins with plaster that had not been prepared properly, like someone painting over a weak wall so that it looks solid. They announced empty and false things, and they said, "Thus saith the Lord God," even though God had not spoken to them.

God speaks through Ezekiel shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. God accuses all the leaders: priests, princes, and prophets. The prophets reassured the people with lies, and so no one repented. That is why God looked for someone to stand in the gap and did not find anyone.

Today we can examine what we hear and what we say in God's name. Let us compare everything with the Bible, and if we speak to others, let us do so with truth and love, without dressing up sin to please people.
exp.29:19:
This verse marks the date of a new prophecy. It says that in the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh day, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel. The phrase "in the seventh day of the month" simply names the day, and "the word of the Lord came unto me" means that a message from the Lord reached him.

Here the speaker is Ezekiel, the prophet, who was living in exile in Babylon. He introduces a message against Egypt and its king, the pharaoh. Many understand that the eleventh year is counted from the exile of King Jehoiachin, that is, around 587 B.C., although the text does not state this in full. Egypt seemed a secure source of help for Judah, but God announces that this power will be broken.

For today: God speaks at specific moments in history and is not caught off guard by anything. We can rest in Him and place our ultimate trust not in governments, money, or people, but in the Lord, who keeps His word.
exp.36:22:
God promises that his people will no longer defile themselves with their idols, with their detestable things, or with any of their rebellions. He will save them from all the places where they sinned, he will cleanse them, and the relationship will be restored: they will be his people and he will be their God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Israel was scattered and divided into two kingdoms. God announces that he will gather them into their land, under one king from the line of David. Many Christians see in that king a foreshadowing of Jesus, though some understand it in other ways.

For today: God does not only forgive, he also cleanses and restores. You can bring him those areas where you keep falling, trusting that he can heal you and draw you closer to him.
exp.15:23:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as an unfaithful woman, built for herself an eminent place and a high place in every street. An "eminent place" refers to a raised place for worship, and here it speaks of shrines of idolatry. The verse uses the image of building for herself, and "street" means the public places of the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of a girl rescued and cared for by Him, who then gives herself to other lovers. With this He shows that Judah abandoned God and sought idols and alliances with other nations. The tone is one of grief and judgment, not only of anger.

For today: we can ask ourselves what things we have placed in the place of God, such as money, fame, or approval. Remembering how He has cared for us helps us return to Him with humility and gratitude.
exp.47:25:
It says that, next to the territory of Issachar and running from east to west, Zebulun receives a strip of land. "The east side" is the east, "the sea" is the Mediterranean Sea (the west), and "border" means boundary or edge. They are parallel strips, one after another.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. In the final vision of the book, God shows how the land will be divided among the twelve tribes, with a clear order and with his presence at the center. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some as a promise of literal restoration, others as a symbolic picture of God's people restored.

For today: God does not forget anyone. Even a small tribe, mentioned in just one verse, has its assigned place. If you feel overlooked, remember that God knows you and has given you a place among his people.
exp.17:31:
He says that God takes no pleasure when someone dies because of their sin. The word "turn" means to turn around, to change direction. The word "live" speaks of a true life, one that begins when a person returns to God. The invitation is clear: change your way and live.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that God was unjust and that they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for their own life, but that He offers a way out: repentance. His judgment is serious, and His desire is that people be saved.

Today we can come near to God without fear, even though we have failed. If there is something you need to leave behind, ask Him for help right now. He does not wait to condemn you, but to receive you and give you a new heart.
exp.21:21:
This verse compares Jerusalem to silver placed in a furnace. Just as fire melts metal, God says his people will be melted within the city, meaning they will go through a harsh judgment. "I have poured out my wrath" means that God would let his punishment fall upon them. The result would be that they would recognize that the Lord is the one who acts.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time when Jerusalem was heading toward its fall. Shortly before, God describes Israel as dross, that is, worthless residue left when metals are melted down. The people were full of violence, injustice and idolatry, and God announces the consequences.

For today: let us not take sin or God's patience lightly. If the Lord corrects us, let us humble ourselves quickly and return to him, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.36:12:
God says that when he opens the graves of his people and brings them up out of the tombs, they will know that he is the LORD. "Graves" and "tombs" are burial places. Here God calls Israel "my people," even in its worst moment.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in the vision of the valley of dry bones. The bones represent Israel in exile, which said, "Our hope is lost." God answers by promising restoration and bringing them back to their land. Some see here only the restoration of Israel; others also see a hope of future resurrection.

For today: if you feel without strength or without hope, remember that God can give life where it seems everything has ended. Bring him your weariness honestly, and trust that he still calls you his own.
exp.37:2:
God tells Ezekiel to say to Gog: "Behold, I am against you." Gog is called "the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal." The wording "I am against thee" in the verse above is the same as the phrase in the explanation, so the old-form comment is deleted here, since "thee" already appears in the verse.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote during Israel's exile in Babylon. God announces judgment against Gog, a leader from distant lands, and his great army. Exactly who Gog and Magog are is understood in several ways: some see real nations of that time, others a symbol of the forces that oppose God.

For today: even when evil seems powerful and threatening, God remains the Lord of history. You can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his people and has the final word. Today, give him your fears and trust in his justice.
exp.44:8:
Thus says the Lord God to the princes of Israel: enough is enough. He tells them to stop using violence and taking by force what belongs to others. Instead, they are to practice justice and right judgment, and remove the unfair charges and burdens they had placed on the people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, within his vision of a future temple and a divided land. Before this, God had said that the princes would no longer oppress the people, and that they would have their own portion of land. This way they would have no excuse to abuse others. What follows is about honest weights and measures. Interpreters differ on how to understand this vision, but the call to justice is clear.

For today: if you have authority, whether at work, in the family, or in the church, use it to serve and not to gain advantage. Be fair in money matters and in how you treat others.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that the word of God came to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" means that a message from the Lord reached him. It is the formula the prophet uses to show that what follows does not come from his own opinion, but from God.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. Here God gives him a message for Jerusalem, and in the verses that follow he prepares him to confront the city for its sins. God speaks with clarity, but he does so as one who knows the history of his people from the beginning.

For today: before correcting or judging others, it is wise to first listen to what God says in his Word. Reading the Bible with humility helps us distinguish between our opinions and the truth of God, and to speak with love and honesty.
exp.44:1:
It says that, within the portion of land set apart for God, a square of five hundred by five hundred (reeds, according to the context) would be for the sanctuary. Around it there would be a strip of fifty cubits called "ejidos," which is an open, free space, like a buffer area of protection. A reed and a cubit are ancient measures of length.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who was exiled in Babylon. This vision of the temple and of the land divided among the people gave hope to the people. Scholars interpret it in various ways: some as a literal temple in the future; others, symbolically, as God's presence among his people. What is clear is that the center of everything is the holy.

For today: just as there was a space of respect around the sanctuary, we can cherish spaces of silence, prayer, and rest that protect our relationship with God from the rush and distractions of daily life.
exp.29:16:
The explanation says that the young men of two Egyptian cities, Aven and Pi-beseth, will die in war, and that the cities themselves, referred to as "these cities," will be taken away into captivity. The word "young men" is the sense of the verse's wording, and the phrase "by the sword" is what the verse means by "fall by the sword." Aven is usually identified with Heliopolis, and Pi-beseth with Bubastis, though this identification is made through historical study.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who announces judgment against Egypt. That country was powerful and proud, and Judah had put its trust in Egypt instead of trusting in God. The nearby text says that the Lord will break Egypt's strength so that they will know that He is the LORD.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in power, money, or human allies, for all of these can fall. Let us rest in God, who is faithful and just.
exp.23:16:
God tells Ezekiel not to show his grief in public: he is to sigh quietly, not to observe the customary mourning, to keep the headpiece on his head and his sandals on his feet, not to cover his lips, and not to eat the bread of men, that is, the food that neighbors would bring to those who were grieving.

The LORD speaks to his prophet. He announces that his wife, the delight of his eyes, will die suddenly. His behavior would be a sign for the people, who would soon lose the temple and Jerusalem. The verses that follow show that the people asked him what it meant.

For today: God can use even our most painful moments, and sometimes obeying him costs us a great deal. If you are suffering today, do not keep your pain silent before God; he understands you and walks with you.
exp.28:5:
It says that all the inhabitants of Egypt will know that the Lord is God. The reason is that Egypt was like a staff of reed to Israel. A staff is a stick for leaning on, and a reed is weak and breaks. Egypt seemed like firm help, but it failed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Judah had sought support in Egypt instead of trusting God. God compares Pharaoh to a great monster of the Nile and announces judgment on his pride. The verses that follow explain that Egypt broke when Israel leaned on it.

For today: review the things you lean on more than God, such as money, a position, or a person. They can help you, but they are fragile reeds. Rest first in the Lord, who never breaks.
exp.21:8:
It says that in Jerusalem there were people who invented false accusations so that innocent people would be put to death. They also ate on the mountains, that is, on the high places where rites were performed to false gods. The sins described as "filthy" refer to shameful sexual and moral conduct. Those who "carry tales" are the ones who slander others with lies.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. God accuses Jerusalem by calling it the city that sheds blood. The list of sins includes injustice, idolatry, and contempt for what is holy. Many understand that this explains why judgment would come upon the city.

For today: let us take care with our tongues. Speaking badly of someone or telling lies can seriously harm their life. Let us ask God to make us people of truth, who defend the innocent and do not let themselves be carried away by gossip.
exp.22:46:
It says that a crowd of people will come against these women: they will stone them, strike them with the sword, kill their sons and daughters, and burn their houses. "To cut down" means to strike or kill with a bladed weapon. "A company of people" is a crowd or an army.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The two women, Oholah and Oholibah, represent Samaria and Jerusalem, which were unfaithful to God by seeking alliances with other nations and by worshiping idols. The language is harsh and symbolic, and it announces the judgment that would come with the Babylonian invasion. The punishment follows what the law prescribed for adultery.

For today: God takes faithfulness seriously. It is worth asking ourselves what things are occupying the place that belongs to Him, and returning to Him sincerely before those things destroy us.
exp.29:20:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," that he has already broken the arm of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. That arm was not healed: no one applied medicine or a bandage to hold it together. So Pharaoh does not regain strength to take up the sword again, that is, to fight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the eleventh year of the exile (around 587 B.C.). Egypt seemed a secure power, and some hoped it would help Judah against Babylon. God announces that this power will be broken. The "arm" symbolizes military strength. The verses that follow show that the judgment will continue.

For today: let us not place our ultimate trust in human powers, such as money, positions, or alliances. All of these can be broken. Let us rest in God, whose care truly sustains and never fails.
exp.39:38:
It says that in the porch of the temple gate there were four tables, two on each side. On them the animals were slaughtered, that is, killed and prepared, for three kinds of offerings: the burnt offering (an offering that was burned up completely), the offering for atonement, and the sin offering, which sought forgiveness and cleansing.

This takes place within a vision that the prophet Ezekiel receives, years after the destruction of Jerusalem, while the people were in exile. A guide shows him in detail a future temple. Scholars interpret it in various ways: some see it as a literal temple yet to come, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence restored among his people.

For today: this careful order reminds us that drawing near to God requires taking sin seriously. Christians believe that Christ offered the final sacrifice, so we can come to God with humility, confessing our failures and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.38:10:
It says that, when that time comes, God himself will give Gog a burial place in Israel. It will be the "valley of the passengers," east of the sea (probably the Dead Sea or the Mediterranean; this is not known for certain). There will be so many bodies that they will block the way of travelers. There they will bury Gog and all his army, and the place will be called "Hamon-gog," which means "multitude of Gog."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog leads a great alliance that attacks Israel, and God defeats it. Interpreters disagree: some see a future event, others a symbolic language of God's final victory over evil. Chapters 38 and 39 show that God protects his people and is glorified.

For today: trust that God has the last word over all evil. You can rest in the knowledge that He cares for his own and will do justice in his time.
exp.38:12:
It says that all the people of the land, that is, the people of Israel, will be the ones to bury the dead of Gog's army. "Renown" means fame or something worth remembering. On that day, when God is honored, that is, when he shows his greatness and power, it will be a memorable day for them.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 describe a great invasion against Israel led by Gog, and the defeat God brings upon him. The burials cleanse the land and show that God keeps what he promises. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future event, others a symbolic picture of God's final triumph over evil.

Today we can trust that God has the last word over evil. When the world seems chaotic, remember that his justice will come and that he deserves our honor.
exp.40:25:
It says that the temple building had narrow windows, and that there were carved palm trees on both sides of the porch, on the walls of the house, and on the beams. The word "narrow" is the one the verse uses for the windows. The end of the verse is hard to translate, and scholars understand it in several ways.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest who was living in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide shows him and measures a new temple. God wanted to encourage his wounded people, reminding them that one day he would dwell among them again. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal or symbolic.

For today: God cares even about the details of where he dwells. Today the New Testament says that our body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Ask yourself: what small detail of my life can I care for today to honor God?
exp.37:13:
God gives Ezekiel a clear message to speak to Gog. When Israel is living "securely," that is, confident and at peace, Gog will notice it. The question "shalt thou not know it?" is a way of saying that Gog will see this and recognize his opportunity there.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel. Gog is the leader of a great northern coalition who intends to plunder Israel when he sees the nation at rest. Scholars interpret this passage in several ways: as future events, as a symbol of evil's attack against God's people, or as both. What is certain is that God knows what is coming and directs it to display his holiness.

Although at times it may feel that evil advances without control, God sees everything and continues to govern. We can rest in him and remain faithful, without letting fear overcome us.
exp.46:1:
It says that the guide brought Ezekiel out of the temple through the north gate and led him around the outside to the east gate. There he saw water coming out on the right side (the south). The phrases "brought me out" and "led me around" are the ones to note here, since they are the words in this verse that carry the movement.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received while in exile in Babylon. A man guides him and measures the temple. The east gate was shut, so they had to go around outside. The water comes from the temple, that is, from the presence of God, and then it grows. Interpreters understand it in several ways: as a future restoration of Israel, as a spiritual picture of the life God gives, or as both.

For today: the life God gives begins in his presence. Seek to spend time with him every day, and let that life flow out to others as well.
exp.44:2:
This verse says that, within the portion of land set apart for God, a plot would be measured twenty-five thousand reeds long and ten thousand wide. In it would stand the sanctuary, called the most holy place. A reed was a measuring rod, about three meters according to some scholars; the exact figures are debated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile. In his vision, the people return to the land and divide it, but first a portion is set apart for the LORD. The priests and the Levites would live near the sanctuary. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: before we divide up what is ours, let us put God first. We can set aside time, money and attention for him, and let his presence be the center of our lives.
exp.32:31:
This verse says that the prophet Ezekiel was to the people like a singer of love songs, with a pleasant voice and skill on an instrument. The people enjoyed listening to him, but they did not do what he said.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Some of the people would come to hear him the way someone goes to a show, remarking to one another, "Come, let us hear what the word is from the LORD." Their mouths showed affection, but their hearts were after gain. God makes clear that when what was announced came to pass, they would know that there had indeed been a prophet among them.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy a good message or a good sermon. After hearing the Bible, choose one specific thing God has asked of you and put it into practice this week. That is what truly hearing means.
exp.38:26:
This verse says that God will bring his people back from the nations where they were scattered. He will gather them from the lands of their enemies. The word "back" here comes from the phrase "I will bring them again," and "sanctified" means that God will show himself to be holy, that is, unique and worthy of respect. This will happen in the sight of many nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into exile because of its rebellion, and the nations could think that God was weak. By restoring his people, God shows that he is faithful and that he cares for the honor of his name. The context says that Israel would acknowledge its shame and that God would pour out his Spirit. Some believers see the fulfillment in the return from exile, others in the future, and others in both.

For today: even if you have failed or feel far from God, he can restore you. Trust in his mercy and let your life show his goodness.
exp.37:20:
God says he will call for a sword against Gog, the invading leader, throughout all the mountains of Israel. The result will be confusion: the enemy soldiers will turn against one another, and each man will raise his sword against his own brother. "Call for a sword" means summoning or sending destruction.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog and his allies come to attack Israel, and God acts to defend his people and to show his holiness. Interpreters differ on whether this prophecy speaks of a historical event, a future one, or a symbolic picture of the final judgment. All agree that God is in control.

For today: when the powers that oppose God seem unstoppable, remember that he still rules. Trust him instead of living in fear, and seek to be a peacemaker, not someone who raises the sword against his brother.
exp.33:16:
It says that God speaks to his people, whom he calls "my flock," and announces that he himself will judge between one sheep and another. The strong males of the flock are the "rams," and the "he goats" are the male goats. God distinguishes between one and the other within the same flock.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel, that is, its leaders, who took advantage of the people. Now God promises to care for his flock and also to correct the strong who trample on the weak, as the verses that follow show.

For today: God sees how we treat the weakest. If I have strength, influence, or resources, I can ask myself whether I use them to care for others or to take advantage of them. Today I can help someone who is tired or in need.
exp.39:22:
It says that, on the north side of the temple that Ezekiel sees in the vision, the gate of the inner court stood directly opposite the gate of the outer court. The same was true on the east side. Between one gate and the other there were a hundred cubits. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so the distance would be about fifty meters.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. A guide who appears as a man shows him the temple in vision and measures it with a reed. Scholars disagree about its meaning: some see it as a literal temple in the future, others as a symbol of God's presence and order among his restored people.

For today: God is a God of order and of clear access. Just as those gates were lined up, we can draw near to him with purpose and reverence, without confusion, and put our lives in order to receive him.
exp.18:11:
It says the vine, once strong and fruitful, was plucked up in anger and thrown to the ground. The east wind, a hot and dry wind from the east, dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were broken and withered, and the fire consumed them. "But" is the same as "yet," and "rods" are the firm branches or stems. "Rods" here refers to the strong branches of the vine, so the sentence is rewritten to name those branches directly.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to raise a lament, that is, a funeral song, over the princes of Judah. The vine is usually understood as Judah or its royal dynasty, and the "mother" as Jerusalem or the house of David. Scholars debate which kings are meant, but the message is clear: the kingdom lost its power and ended in exile.

For today: privileges and blessings do not replace a life rooted in God. Ask yourself what source you are drinking from, and nurture your relationship with Him before the drought arrives.
exp.38:17:
The explanation says that birds and wild animals will be invited to a great feast. They will eat the flesh of powerful warriors and drink the blood of the leaders of the earth. The animals named (rams, lambs, male goats, bulls) are pictures of those strong men. Bashan was a region known for its fine livestock. The word "fatlings" means well fed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces the total defeat of Gog and his armies, who would attack Israel. Many understand these images as strong symbolic language to show that God judges those who rise against his people. Interpreters differ on whether this is fulfilled in a historical event or in a future time.

For today: we can rest in the fact that God is just and has the final word. Faced with the violence and pride of the powerful, trust that He governs, and leave judgment in his hands.
exp.39:42:
Inside the entrance hall of the gate there were hooks, or ledges, a handbreadth long (about eight centimeters, more or less), set all around. On the tables the meat of the offering was placed. The word "hooks" is hard to translate; some think they were hooks for hanging up the animals, and others think they were edges or shelves.

The prophet Ezekiel receives a vision of a new temple, and a guide who looks like a man shows him and measures every detail. Here he describes where the sacrifices were prepared. Interpreters do not agree: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares even for the details of how He is worshiped, with order and reverence. We can draw near to Him with seriousness and gratitude, remembering that Christ offered the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.27:7:
The explanation says the king of Tyre will be brought down to "the pit," a phrase that means the grave or the place of the dead. He will die "the deaths of those who are slain in the midst of the seas," that is, with a violent death and without honor, like someone who dies far from his homeland and without a proper burial.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Tyre, a rich and powerful city built on sea trade, thought himself a god because of his wisdom and his riches. God announces to him that foreign nations will defeat him. Some see in this passage also a broader allusion to pride and the fall of Satan, though not everyone interprets it this way.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us believe we do not need anyone. Today you can thank God for what you have and recognize that everything is a gift from him.
exp.30:2:
The verse describes Assyria as a cedar of Lebanon: beautiful, with leafy branches that gave shade, very tall, with its top among thick boughs.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He tells him to warn the king of Egypt, who was proud of his greatness. God asks him what he is to be compared with, and he holds up Assyria as an example, a powerful empire that had already fallen. Some scholars doubt whether the original text says "Assyrian" or refers to a different tree, but the message is the same: if Assyria fell, Egypt will fall too.

For today: everything we have, whether strength, success or influence, comes from God, so there is no reason for pride. Whoever thinks himself invincible can fall; whoever lives in humility before God remains firm.
exp.42:5:
He says that Ezekiel heard someone speaking to him from inside the temple, while a man stood beside him. The old wording is simple: the "man" is simply a man, and "beside me" means "at my side."

Ezekiel is seeing a vision in which the glory of God fills the new temple. The one speaking from the house is the Lord himself, as the following words show ("the place of my throne"). The man at his side is a guide who shows him the temple; the text does not say who he is, and some think he is an angel. God speaks to promise that he will dwell among his people and to ask them to give up idolatry.

Today we can learn that God wants to be close to us and to speak to us. If we make room for him, through prayer and attention to his Word, we will be able to hear his voice and live with reverence.
exp.23:14:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" means that a message from God came to him. It is a phrase the prophet uses several times to announce that he is going to receive an important command or message.

Ezekiel speaks, writing down what God said to him. It comes after a harsh message of judgment against Jerusalem for its sin. Now God is preparing to give the prophet a painful instruction: the death of his wife, whom he was to mourn without the usual mourning, as a sign for the people.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before we act or judge what we are living through, we can stop and listen to him with humility, even when the message is hard. Obeying him, even with pain, is a way of trusting him.
exp.17:1:
God asks the people what they mean by a saying they kept repeating in Israel. They said, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." With this saying they were suggesting that the children were paying for the sins of their parents.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were suffering and used the saying to complain, as if the punishment were unfair and they bore no responsibility. God corrects that idea and, in the verses that follow, teaches that each person answers for their own life.

For today: do not use your family's past as an excuse, and do not sink into guilt over other people's mistakes. Recognize your own steps, return to God with sincerity, and trust that He offers you a new beginning.
exp.45:1:
The explanation says that the prince will enter through the porch of the outer gate and stand beside the post of the gate. While the priests prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, he will worship at the threshold of the gate. Then he will go out the same way he came in. The gate will not be shut until evening, so that others may also draw near.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a new temple. It describes how worship should be carried out there. Scholars disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally, or whether it is a symbolic picture of worship to God. What is clear is the order and the reverence with which a person should come near to Him.

For today: even someone who has authority approaches God with humility. Find a moment today to worship Him without rushing, recognizing that He is greater than you.
exp.12:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. "And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying," is the way the book usually introduces each new message from God, and it simply means: a message from the Lord came to me.

The one speaking is the Lord, and he addresses Ezekiel, a priest who prophesied among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. This message opens a new section. God will give a warning against false prophets, who claimed to speak in his name but only presented their own ideas. That is why Ezekiel must listen first and speak afterward.

For today: before teaching, offering an opinion, or giving advice in God's name, it is wise to listen to him first in his Word. This keeps us from repeating what comes only from our own hearts and helps us give a true message.
exp.23:26:
God tells Ezekiel that when a survivor (the one who "escaped") arrives with news from Jerusalem, his mouth will be opened and he will no longer be mute. Ezekiel will be a sign to the people, and so they will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He had announced that Jerusalem would fall, but many did not believe him. His silence as a prophet seems to have lasted until the news of the fall arrived (Ezekiel 33:21-22). Scholars debate exactly what that silence was like, but the message is clear: God keeps his word.

For today: God remains faithful even when his word takes time or we do not take it seriously. Today you can trust him and listen to his voice with humility, before circumstances force you to do so.
exp.30:5:
This verse describes a huge, leafy tree. In its branches all the birds of the sky made their nests, under its boughs the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and in its shade many peoples lived.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to speak to the pharaoh of Egypt. With the image of this tree, compared with Assyria, God shows the greatness of a powerful empire. Scholars understand the passage in several ways, but all of them see a warning: the tree grew proud, and for that reason it would be brought down.

For today: everything we have, such as strength, success, or influence, comes from God. If we use it to give shelter and help others, and do so with humility, we honor the Lord. Pride, on the other hand, makes us fall.
exp.38:7:
He says that what God had announced is already a certain fact. "Behold, it is come, and it is done" sounds like something already accomplished, though it speaks of something future. "This is the day" refers to the day of judgment on Gog and his army, of which God spoke earlier.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to a people who lived in exile and discouragement. He promises that a great enemy, called Gog of the land of Magog, will come against Israel and be defeated. Interpreters differ: some see it as a historical event, others as a vision of the last times, others as a symbol. In every case, the message is that God keeps his word and defends his holy name.

For today: when God's promises seem to take a long time, we can rest in the fact that he is faithful. What he has said, he will do in his time, and we can trust him with peace.
exp.41:7:
This verse gives measurements. It says that the chambers on the side of the outer court were fifty cubits long, and that the chambers on the side facing the temple added up to one hundred cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him a new temple with very precise measurements. These chambers were sacred spaces for the priests. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares about order and reverence. We can set apart careful times and spaces to draw near to him, without haste or carelessness, because his presence deserves our attention.
exp.35:37:
It says that, just as Jerusalem was filled with holy sheep that were brought for offering during the feasts, so the cities now in ruins will be filled with people. The religious feasts are the solemn gatherings, and the great crowds of people are the multitudes. Seeing this, they will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites in exile. Their cities were destroyed and their neighbors mocked them. God promises to restore the land and the people. He makes clear that he will do it, but he also wants his people to ask him for it: "Yet I will be sought by them."

For today: God can restore what seems empty or ruined, such as a family, a church, or a hope. We can pray with confidence and wait for his work, remembering that he does it so that we may know him better.
exp.46:0:
Ezekiel sees that a guide brings him back to the entrance of the temple. There he discovers water flowing out from beneath the threshold, that is, the base of the doorway. It runs toward the east, because the temple faced the east. The water flows down from the right side of the building, on the south side of the altar.

Ezekiel was a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. This vision of the temple comes to encourage a people who had lost everything. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see a promise for Israel, others an image of God's work that reaches to Christ and his Spirit. What is certain is that the water springs from the presence of God.

For today: true life does not begin in our own strength, but in God. Seek his presence every day and let it renew your heart.
exp.19:42:
God says that when the people return to their land, they will remember there their wrong ways and all the things that made them unclean before God. The word "defiled" means they were stained by their sins. "Ye shall loathe yourselves in your own sight" means they will feel shame when they see themselves honestly.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Israel, who was in exile. Earlier he reviewed the people's long rebellion. Now he promises to bring them back and accept them. This shame is not the final punishment but the fruit of his grace, for the following verse says that God acts for the sake of his name, not because of their merits.

For today: when God shows you your failures, do not run away or sink into guilt. Acknowledge them honestly, for his forgiveness and his kindness are greater than your sin.
exp.22:3:
It says there were two sisters with symbolic names: Aholah, the elder, and Aholibah, the younger. God says they "were mine," meaning they belonged to him, and that they bore sons and daughters. Then it explains the symbol: Aholah represents Samaria, and Aholibah represents Jerusalem.

The one speaking is God, and he is speaking to the prophet Ezekiel. He uses this image of two sisters to show how the kingdoms of Israel (Samaria) and Judah (Jerusalem) were unfaithful to him, seeking other gods and alliances. The language is harsh on purpose, so that the people would see how serious their sin was. The names sound alike in Hebrew, and their meanings are explained in several ways.

God does not overlook it when we give to others the place that belongs only to him. Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security, and return to trusting him.
exp.38:1:
God tells Gog that he will turn him back, leave only a sixth part of him, and bring him up from the north parts to the mountains of Israel. The word for "leave only a sixth part" is hard to pin down, and scholars read it in different ways: some think it means "lead" or "drag," others that it means "leave only a sixth part." Other versions read "I will drag you" or "I will guide you."

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. He orders Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, a leader of northern nations who will attack Israel. Christians understand this passage in different ways: some see it as a future event, others as a symbolic picture of the final confrontation against God's people. What is clear is that God directs the scene.

When the world seems out of control, remember that God still governs history. Hand over your fears to him today and trust in his care.
exp.27:5:
This verse begins the announcement of a judgment. God says: "Therefore thus saith the Lord God", that is, "for this reason." The reason is that the king of Tyre considered himself equal to God, "thou hast set thine heart as the heart of God." Here "heart" means his way of thinking and his pride.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the prince or king of Tyre, a city rich through trade. His wisdom brought him riches, and the riches filled him with arrogance. The verses that follow announce that powerful foreigners would come against him. Some scholars see here only a human ruler; others think the text also alludes to something more.

For today: what we have, whether talents or money, is a gift from God. Give thanks to God for it and ask him for humility so that you do not regard yourself as the owner of your life.
exp.37:6:
God speaks to Gog and commands him: "Be thou prepared, and prepare for thyself," along with the whole army gathered around him. He also tells him: "be thou a guard unto them," that is, their protector or leader.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that a great alliance of nations will attack Israel, a people gathered again in their land. The tone is ironic: God himself directs the scene, and those who think they are strong are in fact under his control. Scholars debate whether this passage refers to historical events, to something in the future, or to a symbol of evil rising against God's people.

For today: even when evil seems organized and powerful, it does not have the final word. Today you can rest in the knowledge that God governs history, and pray with confidence when you feel fear for the world or for your own life.
exp.31:16:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel on an exact date: the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month. The verse does not name the month, and some older copies have it differently, so it cannot be known for certain which one is correct.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. God gives him a new message, a lament over Egypt, which follows the announcements of judgment against that nation. The date shows that this word was real and came at a specific moment in history.

For today: God acts in real history and still speaks through his Word. We can read the Bible with confidence, and set aside a fixed time each day to listen to him.
exp.16:4:
It says that the eagle also took a seed from the land and put it in a good field for sowing. It planted it beside many waters, the way a willow is planted. The explanation's phrase "seed of the land," meaning a seed of that place, and the word "put it," both refer to the same act described in the verse above.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is in exile in Babylon. This is a parable or allegory. Later in the same chapter it explains that the first eagle represents the king of Babylon, and that the top of the cedar is the king of Judah, taken captive. The seed that was planted would be a descendant of the royal family, placed under Babylonian control. God wants to show that Judah rebelled and sought help from Egypt.

For today: even when a situation seems good and secure, we should not trust human powers more than God. Seek your security in Him and keep your promises faithfully.
exp.17:26:
It says that if a wicked person turns away from his evil and begins to act with righteousness and uprightness, he will save his life. "Wickedness" means living without respect for God and doing what is wrong. "Doing justice and righteousness" means acting uprightly and dealing fairly with others. "His soul" refers to his whole life.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They were saying that God's way was not fair, as if they were paying for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life, and that He offers forgiveness to whoever repents.

It is never too late to change. If today you recognize something you are doing wrong, stop blaming others or your past, ask God for forgiveness, and take a concrete step of justice, such as apologizing or correcting an unfair dealing.
exp.30:4:
It says that this great tree grew taller than all the other trees of the field. Its boughs were multiplied and its branches became long because it had plenty of water. The word "exalted" means that it rose up high. The boughs and branches are the limbs of the tree. "Shot forth" means that it had put out its growth.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to speak to the pharaoh of Egypt. He compares him with Assyria, pictured as a majestic cedar that was powerful and then fell. Many understand the comparison as a warning: if Assyria fell, Egypt too can fall. Some scholars debate certain details of the image, but the general message is clear.

For today: everything we have, such as talents, success, or influence, comes from the hand of God. If we forget this and fill ourselves with pride, we fall easily. Let us thank God and use what he gives us to bless others.
exp.34:8:
It says God will leave Edom, the mountain of Seir, completely ruined. "Perpetual desolations" means ruins that last forever, and "never be restored" means its cities will not be rebuilt. In the end, everyone will recognize that the Lord is the Lord.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The mountain of Seir is the region of Edom, the descendants of Esau. According to the text, Edom held an old hostility against Israel and wanted to take over its lands, as if God were not present there. For this reason the Lord announces judgment. Scholars debate how this was fulfilled in history, but the central message is clear.

For today: let us not hold grudges or envy toward others, nor think that God does not see what we do. Rather, let us ask him for a forgiving heart, and trust that he does justice.
exp.33:8:
It says that God calls the shepherds' attention and orders them to hear his word. The word "hear" here carries the sense of listening closely and paying attention. Here "shepherds" does not mean simple keepers of sheep, but the leaders of Israel. With this call, God prepares to say something serious to them.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to Israel, who was living in exile. The leaders had taken care of themselves and not of the people, who were like a scattered flock exposed to danger. For this reason God announces to them that he will call them to account and that he himself will care for his sheep.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the church, the family or the workplace, ask yourself whether you are seeking your own benefit or their good. Before leading, learn to listen to the word of God.
exp.33:15:
God promises to care for each sheep according to its need: he will seek the one that is lost, bring back the one that wandered off into the mountains and went astray, bind up the one with a broken leg, and strengthen the weak one. "Strengthen" is the word used in this verse for giving strength. The sheep that is "fat" and strong, that is, the one that abuses its power, he will destroy. Some older versions say "I will care for" in this place, but the common reading is "destroy." He will shepherd them "with judgment," that is, with justice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel's leaders, called shepherds, took advantage of the people and neglected the weak. That is why God says that he himself will be the shepherd.

For today: if you are wounded, lost, or weary, God seeks you. And if you have any power or influence, use it to care for the weak, not to take advantage of them.
exp.23:20:
God tells Ezekiel to announce to Israel that He is going to let His sanctuary be defiled, that is, allow the temple to be dishonored and destroyed. That place was their pride, the thing they trusted in, the thing they loved most, and the thing they wanted most. Their sons and daughters they had left behind in Jerusalem would also fall by the sword.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. People asked him what it meant that he did not mourn the death of his wife. That sign announced the grief that would come with the judgment on Jerusalem, caused by the people's persistent rebellion.

For today: let us not place our security in places, customs, or religious achievements, but in God himself. What we love most must be under his lordship.
exp.47:29:
This verse says that the city will have gates on its north side, and that this side measures four thousand and five hundred measures. The "measure" was a rod used for measuring, about three meters according to many scholars, although the exact calculation is debated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who received this vision during the exile in Babylon. The people were far from their land and discouraged. God shows them a well-ordered city, with a place for each tribe. Scholars interpret it in several ways: as a literal temple and city in the future, or as a symbol of God's presence and order among his people.

For today: God attends to every detail and has a place for each of his own. If you feel far away or without direction, trust that he continues to work with order and faithfulness. Pray today, giving thanks for the place you have among his people.
exp.17:11:
He oppresses the poor and needy, commits robbery, and does not return the pledge (something the poor person left as security for a loan). He also looks with longing at idols and does detestable things in God's sight.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying they were suffering for the sins of their fathers. God answers with an example of three generations: a righteous father, a wicked son, and a grandson who decides not to follow that evil path. Each person answers to God for their own choices.

For today: do not use your family past or your circumstances as an excuse. Today you can choose to treat with justice and kindness those who have less than you, and to break with bad examples.
exp.20:21:
He says that the king of Babylon cast lots to decide where to attack, and the sign fell into his right hand: he would go against Jerusalem. Then he makes all his preparations: he appoints captains, gives the order to kill, raises the war cry, sets battering rams against the gates, and builds up ramps and siege towers. Divination is the attempt to learn the direction of events through signs.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. God explains that, although the pagan king uses arrows, idols, and the liver of animals to decide, God is the one directing events to judge the sin of Jerusalem. Some scholars see here God using Babylon as his instrument.

For today: do not look for guidance in superstition or doubtful signs. Seek God with humility, in his Word and in prayer, and let him correct your heart before the consequences arrive.
exp.47:17:
It says that the land left over beside the holy portion, on the east and west sides, ten thousand on each side, will be used for farming. Its crops will be for those who work in service to the city.

Ezekiel, speaking for God in his final vision of a restored and well-ordered land, says these servants will come from all the tribes of Israel. Some believe this describes a literal temple and city, while others see it as a picture of God's kingdom. Christians interpret it in several ways.

For today: God cares for those who serve others and provides what they need. We can generously support those who work for the good of the community, both in the church and beyond it.
exp.16:7:
It was planted in good soil beside abundant water, with everything it needed to grow, to put out branches, to produce fruit, and to become a strong vine. The verse stresses that nothing was lacking for it to prosper.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells a parable about two eagles and a vine. Many understand the vine to represent Judah and its king Zedekiah, placed there by Babylon. Instead of remaining faithful, he sought help from another "eagle," which would be Egypt. God shows that this alliance would fail and that the vine would wither.

For today: having good conditions does not guarantee a firm life if we stop trusting God. When we face pressure or fear, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are seeking security in something human instead of remaining faithful to Him.
exp.39:13:
The verse says that the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the posts, that is, the pillars or columns on the sides of the gateway, and gave them sixty cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about half a meter.

Ezekiel tells of a vision he received while in exile, about twenty years after the temple was destroyed. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, and Ezekiel records each measurement carefully. Scholars disagree about whether this refers to a literal building, to something in the future, or to a symbol. Also, the Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and translations vary in the figures.

For today: God attends to the details and wants his people to draw near with order and reverence. This week, take a quiet moment to pray without hurry, preparing your heart before you ask.
exp.15:45:
Ezekiel 16:46 speaks of Jerusalem as having two "sisters": Samaria, the older, who lived to the north (on the left as you face east), and Sodom, the younger, who was to the south (on the right). The "daughters" are the villages or towns near each one. "Dwelling at your side" means they live beside you.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In a long account, God presents Jerusalem as a woman he had cared for, but who was unfaithful to him with idols and alliances with other nations. By comparing her with Samaria and Sodom, cities known for their sin and their judgment, God shows that Jerusalem had become even worse.

For today: we should not compare ourselves with others in order to feel better. When we believe we are better than other people, we can forget our own need to return to God with humility and ask his forgiveness.
exp.47:27:
This verse describes the southern border of the portion of Gad, the last tribe in the list. It runs from Tamar, passes by the waters of strife (Meribah-Kadesh), continues along Kadesh and the brook (probably the brook of Egypt), and reaches the Great Sea, the Mediterranean. The words "south" and "southward" in the verse both mean the south.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who receives this vision during the exile in Babylon. It is part of the vision of the future division of the land, with the tribes arranged from north to south. It is understood in several ways: as a promise of restoration for Israel, or as a symbolic picture of God's order. Scholars do not fully agree.

For today: God cares for every detail and forgets no one, not even in a list of borders. We can trust that he has a place prepared and a purpose for our lives, even when we are in times of waiting.
exp.33:10:
God says that he himself will go out to look for his sheep and take care of them. The phrase "I will search" is rendered here as "I will search for them carefully" and "I will seek them out" means he will know them, examine them, and attend to each one individually. It is a personal promise: "I, even I."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people of Israel are scattered and in exile. Their leaders, called shepherds, had taken advantage of the people instead of caring for them. That is why God confronts them and promises that he himself will rescue and gather his flock. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Jesus, the good shepherd.

If you feel lost, tired, or neglected, remember that God has not forgotten you. He seeks you and knows you by name. Open your heart to him today in prayer, and if you have responsibility over others, care for them with that same love.
exp.39:20:
It says the north gate of the outer court had three small rooms on each side, that is, small rooms for guards or for service. Its posts (the pillars of the entrance) and its arches (the porches or vestibules) had the same measurements as the east gate: fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. A cubit measures about half a meter, although scholars vary on the exact figure.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, who in a vision is carried to Israel and sees a guide who measures a new temple. This takes place during the exile in Babylon, when the temple had been destroyed. The repeated measurements show order and holiness. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and He wants us to draw near to Him with reverence. We can ask ourselves whether in our daily life there are well-kept gates for worshiping Him, such as set times of prayer and reading of His Word.
exp.39:19:
It says that the guide who accompanied Ezekiel measured the north gate of the outer court of the temple. He took its length and its breadth, just as he had done with the gate of the east. The outer court is the open yard that surrounds the main building, and the gate here is a large entrance with rooms and passageways.

Ezekiel tells of a vision he received in exile, years after the destruction of the first temple. A man with a measuring reed shows him a new temple in careful detail. Scholars debate whether it is a literal temple yet to come, a symbol, or both. What is certain is that the discouraged people receive the promise that God would dwell among them again, with order and holiness.

For today: God cares about order and care in drawing near to Him. Set aside a quiet, fixed time to pray and read His Word, preparing your heart with respect and gratitude.
exp.35:17:
God says that he poured out his anger on Israel for two sins: the unjust killings they committed in the land, and the idolatry that, according to the verse, defiled the territory. To "defile" means to make dirty what was holy. "Pour out" is used here both for the blood and for the anger, as something that falls with force.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He explains to the exiles why they lost their land: it was not chance or God's abandonment, but the consequence of their violence and their idols. Then the chapter announces that God will restore them for the sake of his holy name.

For today: God cares about how we treat people and whom we worship. We can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts and how that affects those around us. He corrects, but he also offers forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.35:19:
This verse says that when the people of Israel came to the nations where they were taken, they caused God's holy name to be treated without respect. "Profaned" means treating as common what is sacred. People were saying, "These are the people of the Lord, and they had to leave his land." In other words, their defeat made God seem weak or unfaithful.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he explains that he judged Israel for its violence and its idolatry. But now he shows his concern for his name: what the people did and suffered affected how the nations saw God. For that reason he promises to act, not because of anything they deserved, but for the sake of his holy name.

For today: those of us who say we belong to God represent his name. Today you can take care in how you treat others, in your honesty and in your words, so that others see in you a faithful reflection of him.
exp.44:22:
It says that during the seven days of the Passover feast, the prince was to offer a burnt offering to God each day: seven bullocks and seven rams without blemish. In addition, each day he offered a male goat as a sin offering. A burnt offering was one that was burned whole on the altar. "Without blemish" means without any physical flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of a renewed temple and worship (chapters 40 to 48). These instructions differ in several details from the law of Moses, and interpreters understand them in different ways: some see them as something literal in the future, others as a symbolic picture of restored worship. What is clear is that the people were to approach God with reverence.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can offer Him each day our time, attention, and obedience with sincerity, trusting that Christ has already covered our sin.
exp.32:14:
What it says: God affirms that if a wicked person truly turns back, he will live. Returning what was given as security for a loan is giving back what was held as a pledge. Giving back what was taken is repairing the harm. The commands of God that lead to a good life are the way forward. If he leaves his wrongdoing, he will not die.

Context: God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he appointed as a watchman to warn Israel. The people were in exile and said that God was unjust. God answers that his door is open to repentance and that each person answers for his own way. The exact meaning of "life" and "death" here is debated: they may refer to physical life, to the survival of the people, or to life with God.

For today: Repentance includes actions. If you have hurt or harmed someone, ask for forgiveness and, if you can, repair the damage. God offers a new beginning.
exp.17:22:
God asks a question that already contains its answer: does he take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? Clearly not. What he desires is that the wicked person turn away from his evil ways and live. "Wicked" is the person who lives with his back turned to God, and "turn away" means to repent and change direction.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some of the people were saying that God's way was not fair, and they felt punished for the sins of others. God answers that each person answers for himself, and that the door of repentance is always open.

For today: if you feel that your past condemns you, remember that God takes no delight in your ruin, but in your return. Today you can come back to him sincerely and begin to live in a different way.
exp.45:21:
This verse describes four small courts, one in each corner of the outer court of the temple. Each one measured forty cubits long by thirty wide (a cubit was roughly half a meter). The corners are the places where the four sides meet, and "of one measure" means that all four were the same size.

A guide speaks here, showing Ezekiel a vision of the future temple. These courts were kitchens, where the people's sacrifices and the priests' offerings were prepared, so that holy things were not carried out into the outer court. How this vision is fulfilled, whether literally or symbolically, is understood in several ways.

For today: God cares about order and respect in the way we approach Him. We can take care of what is sacred, such as prayer, the Bible, and meeting with other believers, by giving them a clear and set-apart place in our week.
exp.22:1:
This verse begins a parable. God calls Ezekiel "son of man," a way of addressing him as an ordinary human being. He speaks of two women who were sisters, daughters of the same mother. Later the passage makes clear that they represent two cities.

The one speaking is God, who gives his message to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The verses that follow explain that the sisters are Samaria (Aholah) and Jerusalem (Aholibah), that is, the northern and southern kingdoms. With this vivid story, God shows his people that they had been unfaithful to him by seeking help and gods from other nations.

For today: God desires our whole heart. We can ask ourselves in what things we are placing the trust that belongs only to him, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.11:20:
This verse is a transition phrase. "And the word of the Lord came unto me" means: "God spoke to me again." It is the way Ezekiel signals that a new message is beginning.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God has just announced that Jerusalem will suffer for its wickedness. Now a response begins to a popular saying, by which people claimed that the prophet's visions would never come true or would take far too long.

For today: God does not stay silent, and his word deserves attention, not mockery or delay. We can ask ourselves whether we are putting off what God has already told us. Today is a good day to listen and to obey with humility.
exp.22:36:
Aholah and Aholibah, names that represent Samaria and Jerusalem, were unfaithful to God. Here "committed adultery" and "played the harlot" are used as an image of idolatry, that is, leaving God to serve other gods. "Blood is in their hands" speaks of violence and death. And "caused to pass through the fire" is understood as sacrificing their children to the idols by burning them.

God speaks, and gives his message to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. God compares his people to two unfaithful women to show how much pain their betrayal caused him. In accusing them, he notes that they mixed those sacrifices with visits to the temple, as if nothing were wrong.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your life. Do not try to mix faith with what God rejects; give him your heart completely.
exp.21:30:
This verse says that God let his anger fall on the people and destroyed them like a fire. The phrase "poured out" is like emptying out a container, and "consumed" means to finish off completely. The phrase "I have recompensed their way upon their heads" means that he gave back to them the consequences of what they had done.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Before this, the passage explains the people's sins: they oppressed, they stole, and they mistreated the poor and the foreigner. God looked for someone who would stand in the breach of the wall, that is, who would intercede and defend the land, and he found no one. In this way, the judgment is presented as a fair response to injustice that had spread widely.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat the weak. We can ask ourselves who near us needs justice or help, and be someone who prays and intercedes for others and acts with kindness.
exp.45:3:
It says that the prince must present to God, on the sabbath day, a complete burnt offering: six lambs and a ram, all without blemish. A burnt offering is an offering that was entirely burned on the altar. Without blemish means without any harm or flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the restored temple (chapters 40 to 48). There it is described how the people would worship with order and reverence. Interpreters do not agree on whether this will be fulfilled literally or whether it is a spiritual picture of future worship. What is clear is that even the prince draws near to God as one worshiper among others.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not the leftovers. We can give him first place with our time, our attention and our heart, especially on the day of rest, regardless of our position.
exp.26:26:
This verse says that everything that made Tyre great would go down with her: her wealth, her trade, her sailors, her pilots and even her soldiers. "Trade" means business or commerce. The "repairers of your breaches" were the ones who fixed the cracks in the ship. The "occupiers of your merchandise" were the merchants who handled the deals. "To fall into the midst of the seas" means to be swallowed up in the deep sea.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a rich seafaring city. Ezekiel describes her as a great, beautiful ship sinking in a storm. It is prophetic poetry: it announces that her pride and commercial power would not save her from judgment.

For today: money, success and strength can disappear suddenly. It is worth asking where we have placed our security, and trusting first in God, who does not sink.
exp.15:52:
He says that God will bring back, that is, return or restore, the captives of three groups: Sodom with her daughters (her villages or nearby cities), Samaria with her daughters, and the captives of Jerusalem, to whom he is speaking. The captivity refers to the situations of ruin and slavery into which they had fallen.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman who turned away from God and committed more wickedness than Samaria and Sodom. Before announcing restoration, he shows her her shame. Scholars understand in different ways how this promise would be fulfilled for Sodom, but it is clear that God promises mercy after judgment.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to make yourself feel better. Acknowledge your failures with humility, and trust that God, who corrects, also restores those who return to him.
exp.45:0:
God says that the east gate of the inner court of the temple will be shut during the six working days. It will be opened only on the Sabbath and on the day of the new moon, when the month begins. The inner court is the courtyard closest to the temple, and the new moon was a monthly festival.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. In chapters 40 to 48 he receives a vision of a restored temple and worship. Interpreters differ about its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, while others see it as a symbolic picture of restoration and God's presence. What is clear is that worship was to be carried out with order and reverence.

For today: work has its place, but God deserves set-apart time. Keep a regular moment, such as on Sunday or each morning, to draw near to Him with calm and gratitude.
exp.47:9:
1) What it says: God marks out a portion of holy land for the priests. It measures twenty-five thousand in length (north to south) and ten thousand in breadth (east to west). The portion is the share allotted to someone in the division of the land, and the measure is a unit of length. In the middle of that portion will be the sanctuary of the Lord.

2) Context: This is part of the vision God gave the prophet Ezekiel about the land divided again and a future temple. The people were in exile and needed hope. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future event, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people. The Bible does not fully explain it.

3) For today: God wants to be at the center, not at the edge. We can ask what place He holds in our decisions, our time, and our home, and set aside room for Him each day.
exp.29:7:
It says that when God sets a fire in Egypt and all its allies are destroyed, people will recognize that the Lord is God. The phrase about setting fire is an older way of saying it, and the word for "destroyed" means defeated or broken down. The "helpers" are the nations that supported Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around the time when Babylon controlled the region. Egypt was a proud power, and many people trusted in it. God announces that its power will fall, and the passage that follows says Babylon would be the instrument. The "fire" is usually understood as an image of judgment and destruction.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in power, money, or human alliances, because all of these can fall. Let us rest in God, who remains faithful and is still the Lord of history.
exp.43:21:
It says that the priests were not to marry widows or women who had been divorced. They were to choose virgins from the people of Israel, or the widow of another priest. The word "repudiated" as used there means a woman who was sent away or divorced by her husband.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. He gives special rules for the priests, who were to live in a very set-apart way because they served near what is holy. This rule is similar to the one in Leviticus 21, though here it is stricter, since it allows widows only if they were the widows of a priest. Interpreters differ on how to understand this vision: some read it literally, others symbolically.

For today: God values a life of service that is whole and careful. Although we are not under these rules today, we can ask ourselves whether we are guarding our witness and our commitments, especially if we serve others in the church.
exp.35:22:
God says he will show that his great name is holy. That name had been profaned, that is, treated as something common and without respect, among the nations. Israel had dishonored it by the way they lived. When God acts, the nations will know that he is the Lord, seeing his holiness displayed in his people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was scattered among the nations because of its sin, and its bad conduct made others think poorly of God. He makes clear that he will restore his people, not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his own name. Then he promises to cleanse them and bring them back to their land.

For today: our lives speak of God before others. We can ask him to cleanse us and help us live in a way that lets others see his goodness, trusting that his grace, and not our merits, sustains us.
exp.29:23:
