This verse says that God will strengthen the hands of the king of Babylon and put his own sword in the king's hand. But God will break the arms of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. The "arms" stand for power and the ability to fight. The phrase about groaning like a man mortally wounded means that Pharaoh will cry out like someone seriously injured.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt was a great power, and Judah had put its trust in Egypt instead of trusting in God. God announces that Egypt will fall and that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will be the instrument of that judgment. The final purpose is that they will know that He is the LORD.

For today: no human strength, whether money, work, or influence, can give us complete security. God rules over all powers. Today you can hand Him your fears and lean on Him before anything else.
exp.35:21:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to say to the people of Israel that what he is going to do for them is not because they deserve it. He will do it for the sake of his holy name, that is, his reputation and his character, which Israel stained among the nations where they were scattered.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The nations saw Israel defeated and driven out of its land, and they thought poorly of the God of that people. For this reason God will act, and the text that follows promises to gather them and bring them back to their land.

For today: Our lives speak well or badly of God before others. When we fail, we do not depend on our merits but on God's grace. That grace invites us to live in a way that honors his name, with humility and gratitude.
exp.36:9:
He says that Ezekiel obeyed what God commanded him: he spoke to the breath, and it entered the bodies that had been lifeless before. Then they lived and stood up on their feet, like a huge army. The word for "breath" here can also mean "wind" or "spirit," and in Hebrew it is the same word (ruach). To "prophesy" means to speak on God's behalf.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of dry bones. He then explains them right away: they are Israel, a people discouraged by the exile in Babylon, who said they had lost all hope. God promises to restore their life and bring them back to their land. Many understand this as a national restoration; some also see a sign of the future resurrection.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, do not stay in discouragement. Obey what God shows you, pray, and trust that He can give new life where today you see only weariness or loss.
exp.40:9:
It says that, between the side rooms of the temple and the other buildings around them, there was an open space twenty cubits wide, all the way around the house on every side. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers (about 45 to 50 centimeters). The rooms were small chambers built against the main building.

Here Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide showed him and measured a new temple in great detail. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic message of hope and of the holiness of God.

For today: just as the temple had spaces that separated and protected what was sacred, we too need to leave room for silence and prayer in our routine, so that God does not get squeezed in among so many occupations.
exp.32:9:
God tells Ezekiel to repeat to Israel what the people are saying: their rebellions and sins weigh on them, they are wasting away little by little, and they ask how they will be able to live. It is a complaint mixed with despair.

Ezekiel was a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God had appointed him as a watchman, someone who warns of danger. Here Israel was already suffering the consequences of its sin and felt there was no way out. God answers right after, in the next verse, that He does not want anyone to die, but wants them to turn back to Him and live.

For today: if guilt makes you think there is no hope, do not stay lamenting. Turn back to God with sincerity, because He offers forgiveness and a new life to those who return to Him.
exp.15:58:
God asks Jerusalem a serious question: should He treat her the way she treated Him? She despised the solemn promise she made to God, and she broke the covenant as if it meant nothing. God announces that there will be consequences for that unfaithfulness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 16, God describes Jerusalem as a woman He cared for and made a covenant with, but who betrayed Him through idolatry and alliances with other nations. This verse connects the judgment with what follows: God will remember His covenant and offer an everlasting one.

For today: God takes promises seriously, and we should too. When we fail, we should not harden ourselves or despair, but return with humility, trusting that His mercy is greater than our failure.
exp.38:25:
The explanation says that when the people of Israel live peacefully in their land again, they will feel shame as they remember their rebellion. The word "trespassed" in the verse means that they betrayed or were unfaithful to God. Living "safely" means living without danger. "Afraid" means that no one will frighten them. There will be peace, and no one will make them afraid.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into captivity because of its idolatry and disobedience, and God explains that this punishment was just. But now he promises to restore them out of mercy and out of concern for his holy name. Some see here the return from Babylon; others, a fulfillment still in the future.

For today: when God forgives and restores us, it is good to remember our failings with humility, not to sink into guilt, but to give thanks for his grace and to live with greater faithfulness.
exp.22:34:
It says God is speaking to Jerusalem (Aholibah) because she forgot Him and turned her back on Him. "Cast behind the back" means ignoring and despising God. "Filthiness" and "whoredoms" refer to her spiritual unfaithfulness, that is, following idols. That is why God says she will now bear the consequences of that conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. In chapter 23, Samaria (Aholah) and Jerusalem (Aholibah) are presented as two unfaithful sisters. Samaria had already fallen, and Jerusalem, instead of learning from this, followed the same path. The language is harsh, but it shows the pain of a broken covenant.

For today: when I notice that God has been pushed to the background, I can return to Him without delay. A simple practice is to begin the day by speaking with God before attending to anything else.
exp.22:30:
It says that Jerusalem (called Oholibah) followed the same path as her sister Samaria (Oholah), that is, idolatry and alliances with other nations. That is why God says he will place in her hand the same cup as her sister's. The cup was a vessel that represents the judgment and suffering she would have to drink.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He uses a story about two sisters to show the unfaithfulness of Samaria and Jerusalem. Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, had already been destroyed. God warns that Jerusalem, by repeating her sin, would receive a similar consequence.

For today: learn from the mistakes of others. If we see that a certain path leads to pain, there is no need to walk it. Today you can ask God to show you where you need to return to him, before the consequences arrive.
exp.32:17:
It says that if a person who was living uprightly leaves that path and begins to do evil, that person will face the consequences of that evil. "Righteous" is one who lives according to God's will; "iniquity" is wickedness or injustice; "turneth" means that he turns away or abandons the path.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who is the watchman of Israel. The people, in exile, said that the way of the Lord was not fair, that is, that it was not just. God answers that He judges each person according to how they are living now, and that both forgiveness and consequence depend on where the heart turns. Christians read this together with other texts about perseverance.

For today: let us not live confident in the good we did yesterday. Each day it is wise to return to God, keep a humble heart, and ask Him for help to keep walking in what is right, without blaming Him when we face the consequences of our decisions.
exp.46:20:
The land promised to Israel is to be divided among the twelve tribes. After describing the southern and western borders, God commands that everyone receive a portion. The word "divide" here means "to share out" or "to split up," and "you" refers to the people as a whole.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He gives them a vision of restoration: the land will once again be their inheritance, with clearly defined boundaries. The verses that follow add that foreigners living among them will also receive an inheritance. Some interpret this vision literally, others as a spiritual picture of God's kingdom; opinions vary.

For today: God cares that there be justice and a place for everyone. We can ask ourselves whether we share what we have generously and whether we welcome the stranger who arrives, as God does.
exp.20:8:
God commands the prophet Ezekiel to announce a message: a sword is ready to act. The sword is described as having a sharp edge and being polished and bright, prepared for use. It is an image of judgment that is already about to fall.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Jerusalem and its people because of their disobedience. Many understand that the sword represents the army of Babylon, although the text presents it as an instrument in God's hands. The people would feel fear and discouragement when the news arrived.

For today: God is serious, but He also warns before He acts. If there is something in your life that He has pointed out to you, do not put it off. Respond with humility and change today.
exp.29:10:
The explanation says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his army, described as the most fearsome of the nations, will be brought to lay Egypt waste. The verse's phrase about drawing swords means taking them out of their sheaths. Filling the land means covering it. The image is of a land covered with the dead from war.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt had been a proud power, with its idols and with allies who trusted in it. God announces judgment on that pride and that idolatry. The verses that follow show that God directs history, for he says: "I, the LORD, have spoken." The Babylonians are an instrument in his hand, though that does not excuse their cruelty.

For today: do not place your security in what seems strong, such as money, power or influence. All of that passes away. Trust in God, who is just and rules over every nation.
exp.20:4:
It says that all people will see that God himself drew out his sword, that is, that he brought judgment. "All flesh" means every human being. The sheath is the case that holds the sword. "It shall not return any more" means that this time the judgment will not stop until it has accomplished its purpose.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment against Jerusalem and the land of Israel for their persistent sin. The sword is usually understood as the invasion by Babylon. The text says that "the righteous and the wicked" would fall, and scholars explain this in several ways: as the scale of the disaster, or as the shared experience of a nation under judgment.

For today: God is serious, but he also warns before he acts. If we sense he is calling us to change, let us not postpone it. Today we can pray sincerely and correct something concrete.
exp.39:39:
It says that, on the outer side of the steps, beside the entrance of the north gate of the temple, there were two tables. On the other side, also beside the entrance, there were two more. The word for "steps" means the stairs or ascent leading up to the gate, and the form of writing used in the old text is simply the ordinary word "at," which appears in the verse above as "at the side." These tables were used to prepare the sacrifices, such as the burnt offering and the sin offering.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide, holding a measuring rod, shows him a new temple in detail. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal temple in the future, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people. The details aim to show order and holiness.

God cares about the way we draw near to him. Today we can give God an orderly place in our lives, with times of prayer and reading, remembering that Christ has already made the sacrifice for our sins.
exp.11:11:
He says the prince of Jerusalem will be carried on his shoulder, that is, borne upon the shoulders, and will go out in the dark. They will make an opening in the wall to take him out secretly. He will cover his face so that he does not see the ground he is leaving.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Ezekiel had acted out the flight and the exile with his own actions. God warns that the ruler will try to escape from Jerusalem, but he will not succeed. Many understand this to refer to King Zedekiah, and the following passages show that he would be captured and taken to Babylon.

For today: we cannot hide our decisions or escape the consequences through cunning. It is better to listen to God humbly and in time, to trust Him and obey Him, rather than depending on our own plans.
exp.28:1:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," to set his face against Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and to deliver a message from God against him and against all of Egypt. To set one's face against someone means to confront them with determination. Here, to prophesy means to declare what God says.

The Lord speaks, and the message comes in the tenth year of Ezekiel's exile, while Babylon was pressing on the region. Egypt was a proud power. Later, Pharaoh appears as a great dragon who boasts: "My river is my own, and I made it for myself." God answers that pride.

Today we can remember that everything we have comes from God, not only from our own effort. We can thank him this week for something specific and avoid the attitude that everything depends on us.
exp.32:3:
If someone hears the sound of danger, the alarm (the "trumpet" was a horn or trumpet blown to give warning), but pays it no attention, and then the enemy's sword arrives and takes his life, the blame is his own. "His blood shall be upon his own head" means that he is responsible for his own ruin. "Taketh not warning" means that he does not get ready or take any precautions.

God speaks to Ezekiel, whom He appoints as a watchman, for the people of Israel who were living in exile. God uses the image of a city that chooses a lookout. If he gives warning and the people do not respond, the responsibility falls on them. If he does not warn them, the watchman answers for it.

For today: when God warns us through His Word, or through someone who speaks to us with love and truth, let us not ignore it. Listening in time and correcting our course is a sign of wisdom and humility.
exp.32:13:
God tells Ezekiel that when he warns the wicked person, "You will surely die," that sentence is not final. If the wicked person turns away from his sin and does what is lawful and right (that is, acts uprightly and deals fairly with others), the warning changes course. "Wicked" means someone who lives without taking God into account.

God speaks to Ezekiel, whom He set as a watchman over the people of Israel during the exile in Babylon. Some of the people thought they had no remedy for their past sins. God answers that His warning seeks to lead to repentance, not only to condemn. The following verse shows what that change involves: returning what was stolen and living in obedience.

For today: no one is so far away that they cannot return to God, and no one should feel secure because of their past. If anything in your life pulls you away from Him, today you can change course with concrete actions, such as asking forgiveness, making right a wrong, and treating others justly.
exp.20:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the land of Israel. The message is harsh: "I am against you." God will draw his sword from its sheath, meaning he will unsheathe it to judge, and he will cut off both the righteous and the wicked.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The people had persisted in idolatry and injustice, and God announces judgment on Jerusalem. That the righteous would also be struck is understood in several ways: the judgment would fall on the whole nation, and the righteous would suffer along with everyone else, though not because they were guilty as the wicked were.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also calls us to live faithfully in the midst of a society that is turning away from him. We can pray for our surroundings and return to God with humility.
exp.39:37:
This verse describes a room next to the temple gate, with its own entrance. There the burnt offering was washed, that is, the parts of the animal that would later be offered whole on the altar.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him. A guide showed him a new temple with very exact measurements. The Israelites were in exile in Babylon, and this vision spoke to them of order, purity, and the presence of God among them. Scholars interpret it in different ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol, or as a hope of restoration.

For today: drawing near to God requires preparation and a clean heart. Before praying or serving, we can pause and ask him to cleanse us and teach us to give him our best with reverence.
exp.36:14:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again. The phrase "The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying," is an older way of saying that God's message is starting. It marks the beginning of a new message.

The one speaking is God, and He speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. Just before this, God had promised to restore life to His people, like dry bones coming back to life. Now He continues with another lesson: that of the two sticks, which represents the joining of Judah and Israel into one people. Many understand this as a promise of unity and restoration.

For today: before you act or speak, take a moment to listen to God in His Word. He continues to guide and heal His people, even when there is division.
exp.41:10:
This verse describes the chambers on the south side of the temple. It says that the open passage in front of them was the same as that of the chambers on the north: the same length, the same width, with the same exits, doors, and entrances. A space that was open and clear beside the building is called the courtyard area, and the exits are the ways out.

The one speaking is the angel who guides Ezekiel through a vision of the temple, during the exile in Babylon. The verses that follow explain the purpose: these chambers were holy, and there the priests ate the offerings and stored them. Scholars disagree about whether this temple was meant to be built literally or whether it is a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares about the details and desires order and holiness in worship. We can ask ourselves whether we set aside time and space to draw near to Him with reverence and with simplicity of heart.
exp.36:0:
It says that God took control of Ezekiel and carried him "in the spirit" to a valley or field full of bones. "The hand of the Lord" is an expression meaning that God's power acted upon him. The words "carried me out" and "set me down" are the verse's own wording, and they simply describe Ezekiel being taken out and placed in the middle of the valley. It does not make clear whether this was a vision or a physical transport; the most common understanding is that it was a vision.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who was living in exile in Babylon. The people of Israel were discouraged and felt there was no hope of returning to their land. God shows him this scene to speak to that wounded people. The dry bones represent a nation that felt lifeless.

For today: when your situation seems dry and without a way out, do not ignore it or sink into it. Bring it honestly before God, and trust that He can give life where we no longer see anything.
exp.27:6:
God says he will bring against the ruler of Tyre "strangers," that is, foreigners, and "the most ruthless of the nations," meaning the most violent peoples among the nations. They will draw their swords against what he admired so much: his wisdom and his beauty. Their coming will ruin his fame and his glory.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The message is addressed to the prince of Tyre, a city rich from trade. He became so proud of his success that he considered himself a god. Many think it refers to an actual king of Tyre; some also see an echo of something greater, but the text does not fully make this clear.

Everything we have, whether intelligence, talents, or money, is a gift. If we use these to feel superior, we move away from God. Today we can give thanks and serve with humility.
exp.21:17:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him that the people of Israel have become like dross, that is, the worthless waste left behind when a metal is refined. Although they are all like brass, tin, iron and lead (common metals), in the middle of the furnace they are only the waste of silver, not pure silver. "Has become to me" means "has turned into."

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God accuses Israel of corruption and sin, and announces that he will gather his people in Jerusalem, as someone gathers metals into a furnace, to submit them to the fire of judgment and purify them.

For today: it is not enough to look valuable on the outside. We can ask God to examine our hearts and cleanse us, humbly accepting his corrections, because his goal is that we be pure and not that we be lost.
exp.45:17:
This verse says that the prince may not take anything from the people's inheritance, so as not to leave them without their property. Whatever he wants to give to his sons must come from what is his own. In the verse above, the words "oppression" and "possession" carry this same meaning.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the restored land. The chapters before this one show a just order for worship and for government. God protects each family in its land and sets limits on those who hold power. Some understand this literally, and others as a picture of God's just rule.

For today: if you have authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, do not use it to benefit yourself at the expense of others. Use what is yours with generosity, and respect what belongs to other people.
exp.17:7:
He says that the righteous man does not lend money at interest and does not take any profit from it. Those old words refer to charging abusive interest, especially to a needy brother. He also withdraws his hand from wickedness, that is, he turns away from doing evil. And "executes true judgment between man and man": he settles disputes with justice and honesty, without favoring anyone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life. Here he describes how a righteous person lives: it is not merely keeping rituals, but treating one's neighbor well.

For today: review how you handle money and agreements. If you lend, do not take advantage of others' need. If you have to decide something between people, be just and honest, even when no one is watching.
exp.41:13:
They say that when the priests entered the holy place, they were not to go straight out into the outer court wearing the garments they used for ministering. First they had to leave those garments there, because they were holy, and put on other clothes. Only then could they approach the people.

This is part of the vision of the temple that the prophet Ezekiel received, while a guide showed him the building and measured it. The priests' chambers were holy, because there they ate the sacred offerings. The rule protected the difference between what was set apart for God and the ordinary life of the people. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision refers to a literal future temple or has a symbolic meaning.

For today: serving God deserves respect and reverence. At the same time, whoever serves should draw near to others with simplicity and humility. We can cultivate a life of sincere prayer and then go out to treat people with warmth.
exp.33:9:
It says that God himself sets himself against the shepherds who failed. "Behold, I am against the shepherds" means "here I am, against the shepherds." God will require the flock at their hand, will take away their charge of caring for the sheep, and will deliver his flock from their mouth, that is, from being used as food. To feed the flock means to care for and nourish it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile in Babylon. The "shepherds" were the leaders of the people, especially the rulers. Instead of caring for the people, they sought their own gain, and the people were scattered and left unprotected. God responds by defending his sheep and promising to care for them himself.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the family, the church, or at work, ask yourself whether you are serving or only seeking your own advantage. And if you have been hurt by bad leaders, remember that God sees and cares for his own.
exp.45:22:
It says that around each of the four small courtyards there was a stone wall, and that underneath, along the walls, there were places for cooking. The word for the cooking places in this version probably refers to hearths or ovens; the original is uncertain, and some translations call them "boiling places."

Ezekiel recounts a vision of the new temple. A guide takes him through the outer court and shows him the kitchens, where the temple servants boiled the meat of the people's sacrifices. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence restored.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life, such as shared meals. We can make our table, our kitchen, and our simple service a place where others are fed and welcomed with gratitude.
exp.29:2:
It says that God's judgment is very near. "The day of the Lord" is a time when God acts to judge. "Cloudy" speaks of darkness and distress, like a sky covered with clouds. "A day for the nations" means a day for the nations, that is, the peoples who were not Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The message announces judgment against Egypt and its allies, such as Ethiopia and Libya, who trusted in their power and their military strength. The text presents the sword as a sign of that judgment, and scholars often connect it with Babylon.

For today: let us not put our security in money, power, or human alliances. All of that can fall. Let us live with humility, trusting in God, and listen to his call to turn back to him while there is still time.
exp.47:10:
The explanation says that the holy portion of land is for the priests descended from Zadok. God calls them "sanctified," that is, set apart for himself. "Which have kept my charge" means that they faithfully carried out their service and his commands. When Israel went astray, they did not stray, unlike the Levites, who did go astray.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision of the future: the land divided up and a sanctuary in the center. This holy portion rewards the faithfulness of the Zadokites. The Levites receive their own place apart, alongside them. Scholars disagree about whether this vision should be understood literally, symbolically, or as something still to be fulfilled.

For today: God sees and values constant faithfulness, especially when many around us turn away. Ask him to help you follow him with firmness, even if you are one of the few who do.
exp.42:16:
This verse continues describing the measurements of the altar. The upper part, the platform where the offerings were burned, was a square fourteen cubits on each side. It had a border of half a cubit, and a base of one cubit all around. The stairs, or steps, faced east.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple, while the people are living in exile. He gives exact measurements and rules for worship. Scholars debate whether this vision will be fulfilled literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something spiritual. Here there is no certainty.

For today: God cares about the details of how we draw near to Him. We can approach Him with respect, preparing our hearts with reverence, and remember that today we trust in Christ as our way to God.
exp.19:16:
Ezekiel 20:17 says that, although the people deserved a harsh punishment, God had compassion. "Nevertheless mine eye spared them" means that God looked on them with mercy. "From destroying them" and "neither did I make an end of them" mean that he did not completely destroy them in the wilderness, even though they rebelled.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel who are in exile. He reminds them of their history: from Egypt and the wilderness, their ancestors rejected God's laws, broke the Sabbaths, and followed idols. Even so, God did not wipe them out and kept speaking to his children, inviting them to obey him.

For today: God is patient and does not treat us according to what we deserve. His mercy is not an excuse to keep doing the same things, but an invitation to return to him. Today you can respond with gratitude and let go of something that pulls you away from God.
exp.11:15:
God says that from the judgment coming on Jerusalem, he will leave a few people alive. They will be spared from the sword, from famine, and from plague. These survivors will tell, among the nations where they go, all the wicked deeds of his people, that is, their serious sins, above all their idolatry. In this way they will come to know that God is the Lord.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Before the fall of Jerusalem, God announces the fate of the king and his people, who will be scattered. Even in judgment, God leaves a group that bears witness to the truth.

For today: when we honestly acknowledge our mistakes, without hiding them, we make room for God to correct us and teach us. We can ask him for the courage to admit our failures and learn from them.
exp.31:13:
He says God will make the waters of Egypt settle, that is, become calm and still, and that its rivers will flow slowly and smoothly, "like oil." Before, those waters were stirred up by the feet of men and animals. Now they will be clean and tranquil, because no crowd will be left to stir them.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against Pharaoh and Egypt. Egypt depended on the Nile and felt powerful. God announces that this pride will fall through judgment, and that everything will fall silent. Some understand the image as a symbol of desolation; the text gives no further details.

For today: power and human pride are not secure. We can trust in God, not in our achievements, and live with humility.
exp.32:20:
Ezekiel recounts that, in the twelfth year of their exile in Babylon, a survivor who had fled from Jerusalem brought him news. A person who managed to get away is one who escaped. "The city is smitten" means the city was struck down and defeated.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who was exiled along with his people. For years he had warned that Jerusalem would fall, but many did not believe him. This news confirms that his words came from God. The verses that follow say that God opened his mouth so that he could speak again. Some manuscripts and scholars debate the exact date, but the meaning remains the same.

For today: God keeps what he says. We should not wait for the consequences to arrive before listening to him. Today we can respond to his Word with humility, turn back to him, and trust that his mercy is still open.
exp.31:24:
This verse describes a powerful people who now lie dead in Sheol, the place of the dead. The phrase "they have set her a bed" means that a resting place has been prepared for them among the fallen. Their graves surround them. Here "uncircumcised" points to those who died without belonging to the people of God. They once spread terror among the living, but now they bear their shame along with those who go down to the grave.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt, which runs through the chapter. Many understand the "bed" to be for the pharaoh and his multitude. He announces to them that, like other violent nations, they will end up defeated. The language is poetic, not a literal description of the afterlife.

For today: power used to intimidate others does not last. It is worth more to live with humility and justice, because God sees how we treat people.
exp.22:8:
This verse says that God handed Aholah, a symbolic woman, over to her lovers, the Assyrians, the ones for whom she had become passionate. "Lovers" refers to those she sought out instead of remaining faithful; "became passionate" describes an attraction that took control of her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this allegory, Aholah represents Samaria, the northern kingdom of Israel, and Aholibah represents Jerusalem. The adulterous acts symbolize unfaithfulness to God: seeking political alliances and foreign idols. When Assyria conquered Samaria, God presents this as the consequence of that choice.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether success, money, or approval, ends up controlling us and hurting us. Today you could identify what you are trusting in more than God, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.32:30:
God tells Ezekiel that the people come to hear him as a crowd, as if they were his people and wanted to obey. But they do not put into practice what they hear. Their mouths say one thing, but their hearts run after their own gain.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some from Jerusalem had already been taken away, and the people went to hear him with curiosity, almost as someone enjoys a song. The verses that follow compare him to a pleasant singer. God warns them that when what was announced comes to pass, they will know that a prophet was among them.

For today: it is not enough to listen to sermons or to read the Bible with enjoyment. Ask yourself this week what specific teaching of God you can put into practice, even if it costs you, and decide to do it.
exp.30:0:
This verse marks the moment when God speaks to Ezekiel. The text says it happened in the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month. It is the exact date of a new message.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, who receives God's message. It is generally understood that the eleventh year corresponds to the exile of the people in Babylon, around 587 B.C., although the text gives no further detail. The message that follows is for Pharaoh and Egypt, and it warns them with the image of a great cedar, the one of Assyria, which fell.

For today: God speaks at concrete and real moments in history. We can approach his Word with confidence, knowing that he is interested in our time. It also reminds us that no human power is eternal; only God remains.
exp.28:19:
This verse says that God gives the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for his military labor against Tyre. God affirms that, although the king did not know it, that effort was done for me. The phrase saith the Lord God stresses that the one speaking and deciding is God himself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. According to the passage, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre with great exhaustion, but did not receive the spoil he expected. God compensates that effort with Egypt, which was already under judgment. Historians debate how exactly this was fulfilled, but the text shows God directing the nations.

For today: even when the world seems to move by human interests, God continues to govern history. We can trust that he sees every effort and that his plans advance, even when we do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.31:27:
God tells Pharaoh of Egypt that he will be destroyed and will lie down among the uncircumcised, that is, among pagan peoples who did not belong to the covenant with Israel. "Shalt lie" means you will be lying down, dead. "By the sword" means by the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and pronounces a lament over Egypt. That kingdom was powerful and proud, and it had caused terror to other peoples. The prophet describes it in the place of the dead, alongside other nations that also fell. In this way he teaches that no empire escapes God's judgment.

For today: power, fame, and strength do not protect us before God. It is wiser to live with humility, to treat others well, and to trust in Him, not in our own resources.
exp.19:39:
God promises that one day all of Israel will worship him on his holy mountain, in the land he gave them. There he will receive them with favor and ask for their offerings, the firstfruits (the first and best of the harvest) and everything set apart, that is, dedicated to him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to an exiled and rebellious people who mixed the worship of the Lord with idols. First he rebukes them and says he will separate out the rebels. Then he announces hope: he will gather his people and restore them, so that they worship him sincerely and it is shown that he is holy.

For today: God does not want divided worship but a whole heart. Think about what idol competes with him in your life, and give God the best of your time, your strength, and your possessions, trusting that his grace accepts you and restores you.
exp.39:12:
He measured the gate from the roof of one small room to the roof of the room across from it, the total being twenty-five cubits (a cubit is roughly half a meter, so about twelve meters). The small rooms were little chambers inside the entrance. The phrase "door against door" seems to mean that he measured from one opening to the other.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him during the exile, about fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem. A man with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, and Ezekiel records each measurement. Scholars disagree on whether it is a literal future building or a spiritual picture of God's presence. The measurements show order and care.

For today: God pays attention to details, and he cares that his people approach him with order and reverence. Ask yourself what "gate" you need to tend in order to draw near to God each day.
exp.41:4:
It says that the rooms on the upper floor were narrower than those below and in the middle. The reason is that the galleries, that is, the open walkways or terraces that surrounded the building, took up more space on the upper floors. So the upper chambers had less room left.

The prophet Ezekiel is seeing a vision of the temple, and a guide shows him and measures each part. These chambers were next to the outer court and were for the priests. The exact details of the construction are not easy to understand, and scholars interpret them in different ways. What is clear is that God wants an orderly and holy place for his service.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can ask ourselves whether we are leaving enough room in our daily lives to pray, read his Word, and serve him, or whether other things are filling up all the space.
exp.38:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel will spend seven months burying the dead of the defeated army, in order to cleanse the land. At that time it was believed that an unburied body defiled the place. "Cleanse" here means removing that uncleanness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This part describes the defeat of Gog, an enemy leader who attacks Israel, and how God overcomes him. Interpreters differ: some see it as literal and future, others as a symbol of God's final triumph over evil. What is clear is that God protects his people and restores the land.

For today: God does not only defeat evil, he also wants to cleanse its consequences. We can ask him to help us patiently repair what sin has damaged in our lives and in our surroundings.
exp.21:12:
God says that he "struck his hand," meaning that he struck the palms of his hands together. In that time it was a strong gesture that showed anger, indignation, or a firm decision to act. The "greed" is the desire to gain money unjustly, and "your bloods" refers to the murders and violence within Jerusalem.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people lived in sin: injustice, immorality, abuse of their neighbors, and forgetfulness of God. For this reason he announces that judgment will come and that the people will be scattered.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek gain at the expense of others, even in ways that seem ordinary or accepted. God sees injustice and calls us to live with honesty, compassion, and respect, remembering that he is the one who holds us accountable.
exp.35:9:
God promises that the people of Israel will grow in number again, and that it will not be only a part, but the whole house of Israel. The empty cities will once again have people living in them, and the ruins will be rebuilt. The word "á" is an old form of "a," and "vosotros" means "you all."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He speaks to the mountains of Israel, which had been left desolate and mocked by the neighboring nations. God announces that he will restore the land and his people. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also see it pointing to a future and more complete restoration.

For today: if there are areas of your life that seem to be in ruins, remember that God knows how to rebuild. Trust in him and take small steps of obedience while he works.
exp.13:5:
God tells the people of Israel, through Ezekiel: "Repent, turn yourselves from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations." The word "turn" here means changing direction, and "abominations" are practices that God detests.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some leaders of the people came to consult God, but they carried idols in their hearts. God answers them that it is not enough to appear faithful; first they must truly return to Him. His call is an invitation to restore the relationship.

Today we can ask ourselves what thing occupies in our heart the place that belongs to God: money, success, the opinion of others, or something else. Before asking Him for direction, let us prepare our heart, acknowledge that thing before Him, and decide to turn away from it with His help.
exp.27:16:
His heart was lifted up with pride because of his beauty. His wisdom was ruined by his brightness, that is, by his fame and splendor. That is why God says he will cast him down to the ground and set him as a spectacle before kings, so that they may see him. Here "lifted up" is clearly the pride in view, and "brightness" refers to his glory or splendor.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the king of Tyre. Many believers see in the images of Eden and the guardian cherub also an allusion to Satan; others understand it only as poetic language about the king. This is debated, so it is good to read it with humility. In either case, the theme is the fall that comes from pride.

For today: what God gives us, such as talents, success, or good looks, is a gift. Be thankful for it and use it to serve, not to boast, because pride pulls us away from God.
exp.27:3:
It says that the prince of Tyre used his intelligence and his skill in business, and with that gathered great wealth. "Wisdom" means good judgment in managing things, and "thine understanding" refers to his skill at making sound decisions. "Treasures" are the places where he kept his goods, and "hast gotten" means that he acquired gold and silver.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a city made rich by its trade at sea. Its ruler thought of himself as almost a god because of his wisdom and success. God does not say that riches are evil, but that pride made him forget he was only a man. The verses that follow show that his wealth led his heart to become proud.

We can be thankful for and make good use of our abilities, but without thinking we own everything. Everything we have, whether talent or money, is a gift from God, and humility keeps us grounded.
exp.29:21:
God says he is against Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He announces that he will break his arms, both the one that is still strong and the one that was already broken, and that he will make the sword fall from his hand.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile of Judah in Babylon. Egypt seemed like a possible ally, but God announces that its power will come to an end. The "arms" represent military strength. Pharaoh had already been struck down, and now a greater blow would come, while Babylon would be used by God as an instrument of judgment.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in money, power, or human alliances, because all of these can fail. Trusting in God gives us a support that does not break.
exp.22:20:
It says that Aholibah (Jerusalem) remembered again the lewdness of her youth, that is, the sins of her younger years. The verse's word "youth" is the one that matters here, and "remembered" means that she recalled those things with desire. "Bruising thy teats" is blunt, graphic language about abuse or improper relationships in Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses a strong image of two unfaithful sisters to show that Judah sought foreign alliances and idols instead of trusting in Him. Egypt was one of those temptations. Then comes judgment: those allies would turn against her.

For today: when we feel nostalgia for a past that hurt us, let us remember where it led us. Better to hand those desires over to God and seek in Him our security and rest.
exp.20:25:
God says to the king of Israel that he should take off the turban (the royal headdress) and the crown. Things will not stay as they are: God will lift up the humble and bring down the one who thinks himself high. "Bring down" means to pull down or humble.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The message is directed to the ruler of Israel, whom many understand to be King Zedekiah. Because of the sins of the people and their leaders, God allows judgment to come upon Jerusalem. The following verse speaks of one who holds the rightful claim, and many Christians see in it a sign of the Messiah, though others interpret it in other ways.

For today: let us not cling to power, position, or pride, because everything is in God's hands. Let us ask him for a humble heart and trust that he is the true King.
exp.31:4:
It says that God will leave the dead body of the pharaoh lying on the mountains, and that his remains will fill the valleys. The word "flesh" refers to his body, to what is left of it. "Fill" is the word for what will be done with the valleys. The phrase "with thy height" is hard to translate: some think it speaks of his great size or of his pride, and others believe the original text says something different, such as "your remains." That is why there are different interpretations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against the pharaoh of Egypt. The pharaoh thought of himself as a mighty monster of the Nile, and God announces that he will trap him like an animal in a net. It is a poetic image of judgment on a proud nation that oppressed others.

For today: power, fame, or success do not make us untouchable before God. We can examine whether there is pride in our hearts and ask Him for humility, remembering that all our strength comes from Him.
exp.32:15:
This verse says that when a wicked person turns away from his sins and changes the way he lives, God no longer holds those sins against him. "Judgment and justice" means acting with uprightness and doing what is right toward others. "He shall surely live" means he will have real life, without any doubt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom He appointed as a watchman for His people, who were in exile in Babylon. Some were saying that God's way was not fair. God answers that He offers forgiveness to whoever turns back to Him, and that the change must be seen in actions, such as giving back what was stolen.

For today: if there is something you need to correct or give back, do it with humility. God invites you to start again, and His forgiveness is real.
exp.12:17:
God speaks against certain women who claimed to be prophetesses. They sewed bands for the wrists and made head coverings, which were probably veils or head wraps for people of every height and age. With these they hunted people, that is, they trapped and manipulated others. God asks whether they do it to save their own lives, that is, to earn their living.

God speaks through Ezekiel, during the time when Jerusalem was falling. Many false prophets promised peace when judgment was coming. These women deceived the people with practices that seem like divination or magic. Scholars do not know exactly what those objects were like.

Today we should be wary of anyone who uses spiritual things to gain advantage or to control others. And if we speak on God's behalf, let it be with truth and not to gain money, fame, or power.
exp.22:7:
It says that Oholah (Samaria, the kingdom of Israel) never gave up the unfaithfulness she learned in Egypt. There, in her youth, others lay with her, handled her virgin breasts, and used her sexually. "Youth" is the time of her early years; the handling of her breasts speaks of abuse and forced intimacy; and the "whoring" here is an image of idolatry and alliances with other nations.

God speaks through Ezekiel, using a parable of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem). With very harsh language, he wants to show that Israel gave itself over to Egypt and Assyria, trusting in them and in their idols instead of trusting in him. Many understand that Egypt is mentioned as a pattern of unfaithfulness from an early time.

For today: examine the things you place your trust in apart from God, whether money, approval, or old habits. Bring them to him honestly and ask for his help to truly let them go.
exp.39:0:
He describes Ezekiel receiving a new vision on a precise date: the twenty-fifth year of the exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month. Fourteen years had passed since the city was struck down. Then the hand of the Lord came upon him, that is, he felt the power of God guiding him, and he was brought to a place.

Ezekiel was a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. With this verse begins the last great vision of the book (chapters 40 to 48), in which God shows him a new temple. It was a message of hope for a discouraged people. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: even when a loss has hurt for years, God has not forgotten you. He can speak hope to you at the exact time. Ask Him to help you look ahead with confidence.
exp.45:12:
Every day, in the morning, a lamb one year old and without fault was to be offered to God as a burnt offering. A burnt offering was a gift burned whole on the altar. "Without fault" means the animal had to be healthy, with no spots and no defects.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a new temple and an orderly worship (chapters 40 to 48). Before this, he speaks of the prince and of the offerings at feasts and on the Sabbath. This verse establishes the daily offering. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a spiritual picture of worship to God.

For today: God deserves the best of our day, and the beginning is a good time for it. Today we do not offer lambs, but we can dedicate the morning to him with prayer and devotion. Many Christians see in the lamb without fault a sign that points to Christ.
exp.44:21:
It says that on the day of the Passover (the fourteenth day of the first month), the prince will offer a young bull as a sin offering, both for himself and for all the people of the land.

Ezekiel's words about the sin offering are drawn from the verse above, so the explanation of what the offering does is given in plain terms: it is a way of covering over guilt and cleansing it, and it is meant for those who sinned without meaning to.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a restored temple and worship. The prince is a leader of the people, distinct from the priests. It is striking that he must also make an offering for himself: no leader stands above the need for forgiveness. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is fulfilled literally, symbolically, or in Christ.

For today: if you lead in your home, church, or workplace, acknowledge your own failings with humility. Before guiding others, draw near to God to ask for forgiveness and help.
exp.39:6:
It says that in the east gate of the temple there were small rooms for guards, each one square, one reed on each side. Between one room and the next there were five cubits of wall or space. The threshold or doorpost of the gate, on the inner side, also measured one reed. A "reed" here equals six long cubits (about three meters, although the exact measure is debated). The rooms are the small chambers, and the doorpost is the frame of the gate.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting his vision. A man with a measuring reed guides him through a new temple and measures it carefully. This takes place while Israel is in exile, and God shows him that his presence and his order have not been lost. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God cares about details and values order and holiness. Ask yourself which small area of your life you can put in order and offer to him with care.
exp.15:53:
She says that Jerusalem must bear her shame and feel humiliated for everything she has done. As she sees her sin, she ends up being a comfort to Sodom and Samaria. "Shame" here means dishonor or disgrace, and "a comfort to them" means that her case brings them relief.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, who is compared to an unfaithful woman. She had proudly judged her "sisters," Sodom and Samaria, but her sin was worse. God promises to restore all three. Some think the comfort comes from seeing that God treats everyone with equal justice; others, from seeing that their restoration includes Jerusalem.

Today we can look at our own failings before we judge others. When we acknowledge our sin with humility, God opens the door to restoration and to treating others with compassion.
exp.11:24:
God says that what He speaks will come to pass, and that there will be no more delay. He says it to Israel, whom He calls a rebellious house, and He assures them that everything will happen in their own days.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people were repeating a saying that the visions took a long time or never came to pass, and others thought they were meant for distant times. In this way they justified themselves for not taking the warning of judgment seriously. God answers that His word is neither empty nor far away.

For today: do not use God's patience as an excuse to put off your obedience. If you sense that God is speaking to you through His Word, respond today with humility, because He is faithful both in His promises and in His warnings.
exp.44:0:
It says that when the land was divided among the tribes by lot, a special portion first had to be set apart for God. It would be a rectangle twenty-five thousand reeds long and ten thousand wide. "Inheritance" is what is received as a heritage, and "holy" means set apart for God. The reed was a measuring rod; its exact length is debated, but it was about three meters.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the future of the people, after the exile in Babylon. He shows a new order for the land, with the sanctuary at the center. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as something literal, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: before dividing what we have, whether time, money, or energy, we can first set a part aside for God. In this way we put him at the center of our life.
exp.15:22:
This verse says that, after all the wickedness of Jerusalem, God gives a cry of grief: "woe, woe unto you!" It is like a parenthesis full of pain. The word "it came to pass" simply means "it happened." The sentence is left open and continues in the verses that follow, where even more sin is described.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an abandoned girl whom He rescued, cared for, and adorned. She, however, was unfaithful to Him with idols and with other nations. The "woe" is not only anger; it also shows sorrow and a warning before judgment.

For today: when God corrects us, He does not do so with coldness, but with a Father's pain. If today you have drifted away from Him, remember where He brought you from and return with humility. His warning seeks your return, not only that you feel condemned.
exp.34:2:
God commands Ezekiel to deliver a message against Mount Seir. God says that he is against that place, that he will stretch out his hand to punish it, and that he will make it most desolate, a total ruin with no one living there.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Seir was the land of Edom, a people descended from Esau and a neighbor of Israel. According to the verses that follow, God judges them for their lasting hostility and because they handed the Israelites over to the sword when they were suffering. Here "Mount Seir" stands for the whole people of Edom.

God sees how we treat those who suffer. It is not good to hold on to old grudges or to take advantage of the fall of others. Today we can choose compassion, help someone going through a hard time, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.37:3:
God tells Gog that he will turn him around, like an animal with a hook put in its jaw that is pulled wherever one wishes. He will bring him out together with his whole army: horses, horsemen, fully armored, and a great crowd with bucklers (large shields) and shields, all armed with swords.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces judgment against Gog, a leader from Magog, Meshech and Tubal. Interpreters debate who Gog is and when this is fulfilled: some think of a historical event, others of something still in the future, and others of a symbol of the final opposition against God. The central point is that God governs, even over the nations that attack his people.

For today: when evil seems strong and organized, remember that God still has control. You can rest in Him and pray with confidence.
exp.33:4:
They were scattered because they had no shepherd to watch over them. Without protection, they became easy prey for any wild animal. The words that describe them as scattered mean dispersed, without direction and without unity.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He accuses Israel's leaders, here called shepherds, because they took advantage of the people instead of caring for them. The sheep are the people. Many understand the beasts as the nations or the threats that harmed Israel, though the text uses figurative language.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, such as in your family, church, or workplace, ask yourself whether you serve those you look after or use them for your own benefit. And if you feel without guidance, remember that God himself promises to seek out his sheep (Ezekiel 34:11).
exp.23:24:
God tells Ezekiel that a day is coming when he will take away from the people what they value most: their strength, the joy of their glory, the desire of their eyes, and what they care for with their whole heart, their sons and their daughters. The "strength" refers to the temple, which was their pride and their security. "The desire of their eyes" is what they loved most. The sentence is left unfinished and is completed in the next verse.

The Lord speaks to Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. God had just announced the fall of Jerusalem and the death of Ezekiel's wife, which was a sign of the loss of the temple. Ezekiel was not to mourn publicly. The people would not be able to weep openly either, because the calamity would come because of their own sins.

For today: examine what your security depends on. Everything good we have is a gift from God, but only He should be our firm foundation.
exp.35:36:
God, the Lord, says that he will let himself be sought by Israel in order to do one more thing: make his people grow in number, like a flock. "Responding when asked" means that God will answer when they seek him and ask him. "I will multiply them" is the same idea put plainly. "People like a flock" is an image: very many people gathered together, like sheep.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The people were living in exile, and their land lay in ruins. God had just promised to restore cities and fields. Here he adds that he will also restore the people, and he will do it in response to his people seeking him in prayer.

For today: God promises, but he also invites us to ask him. Even when something in your life, your family, or your church seems ruined, you can pray with confidence and wait for God to restore it. Today, take a few minutes to ask him for something that needs to be lifted up.
exp.37:18:
God says that he has spoken out of his zeal, that is, his steadfast love for his people and his holy name, and out of the fire of his wrath, his anger against evil. He announces that in that time there will be a great shaking, an earthquake or strong tremor, over the land of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this prophecy, Gog, a leader from the north, attacks Israel, and God intervenes to defend his people. The verses that follow show that all of creation will tremble before him. Interpreters disagree about whether this will be fulfilled literally in the future or whether it is symbolic language.

For today: God is not indifferent to injustice, nor does he forget his own. We can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his people, and at the same time live with reverence, trusting in his justice rather than taking it into our own hands.
exp.39:7:
It says that the man who guides Ezekiel measured the inner porch of the gate, the one that opens toward the temple courtyard, and that it was one reed in width or depth. "Reed" was a measuring rod, about three meters long, though its exact length is debated. The phrase "inner side" means toward the inside. Some older versions read this verse differently, and scholars explain it in various ways.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision from God. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, beginning with the east gate. Such precise measurements gave a defeated people hope that God would restore his presence among them. How that temple should be understood is a debated question.

For today: God cares about details and works with order. We can trust that nothing in our lives escapes his notice, and we can draw near to him with reverence and hope.
exp.29:11:
God says he will dry up the rivers of Egypt, that is, take away the source of its wealth and its life. He will hand the land over into the hand of the wicked (violent and cruel people), and will destroy it, with everything it holds, through foreigners. The phrase "everything it holds" refers to all that the land has. Finally, God declares that he himself has spoken it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The message announces judgment on Egypt, which was proud and trusted in the Nile and in its idols. The text says that God would use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, as the instrument of that judgment.

For today: what seems most secure, such as money, power, or prestige, cannot replace God. Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our trust, and return to rest in him.
exp.43:27:
This verse says that the priests will not have a piece of land of their own in Israel, as the other families do. God himself will be their inheritance, that is, what they receive as their heritage, and their possession, what belongs to them.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of the new temple. He is giving rules for the Levite priests who serve in the sanctuary. Because their work was the service of God, they lived from the offerings and sacrifices that the people brought, as the following verses describe.

For today: we can ask ourselves what it is that most assures us of life. Even if we have work, a home, or money, our greatest wealth is God himself. Trusting in him frees us from anxiety and helps us to be generous.
exp.22:39:
This verse says that the two women, Oholah and Oholibah, sent for men from distant lands, and when those men arrived, she bathed, painted her eyes with a dark powder used for makeup, and put on jewelry. She did all of this to please them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, to show how his people sought alliances and foreign gods instead of remaining faithful to him. The passage presents this as a very painful betrayal, since they were also mixing their idols with worship in the sanctuary.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we arrange and prepare with the most care to win the approval of others, while we neglect our faithfulness to God. He invites us to return to him with sincerity.
exp.41:9:
This verse says there were more chambers or rooms on the east side of the court, along the wall. They were across from the separate place, which is the open space or set-apart area beside the temple, and across from the main building. They are rooms set apart for use by the temple.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, recounting a vision God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him the temple and its measurements in great detail. These chambers, according to the context, were for the priests (Ezekiel 42:13). Interpreters disagree about whether the vision describes a literal future temple or has a symbolic meaning of God's presence and holiness.

For today: God cares about the details of his house, and he cares that there be order and set-apart spaces for worshiping him. We can set aside a time and a place each day, even a simple one, to be alone with him.
exp.37:7:
It says that after many days God will call Gog to account. The phrase "you will be visited" here means that God will act against him. This will happen "in the latter years," when Israel is living in a land freed from war and gathered from many peoples. Its mountains had been in ruins for a long time. Now its inhabitants live "in safety," that is, with a sense of security.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces a future attack against Israel, after its restoration, led by Gog with many allies. Christians interpret this in several ways: as something still to come, as a symbol of the evil that attacks God's people, or as something partly fulfilled already. There is no single view that is universally accepted.

For today: the firmest security does not depend on the peace we see, but on the faithfulness of God. We can rest in Him, while still remaining watchful.
exp.19:34:
It says that God will bring his people into the "wilderness of the peoples," a meeting place set apart from the nations. There "I will plead with you" means he will enter into direct judgment or discussion with them, "face to face," without go-betweens or excuses.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The elders of Israel had come to consult him, but the people were still attached to their idols. God promises to bring them out from among the nations and compares this to what happened in the wilderness after they left Egypt. Interpreters debate whether the "wilderness of the peoples" is a literal place or an image of a time of testing and purification. Its purpose is to restore, not to destroy.

God sometimes draws us away from the noise to speak to us clearly and without disguise. If you feel a season of solitude or correction, do not run away: it may be his way of cleansing you and drawing you near to him. Come with sincerity and listen to him.
exp.47:30:
This verse says that the city will have twelve gates, and each one will bear the name of a tribe of Israel. Here the three gates on the north side are described: Reuben, Judah, and Levi. A measure of length was a reed, and an inheritance is the land received as a family's portion.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at the end of his book. It is a vision given to a people in exile, to encourage them with the promise that God dwells in the midst of his people. Interpreters differ: some see it as a promise for Israel, others as a picture of God's people in general.

For today: in that city everyone has access, from the tribe of Judah to the tribe of Levi. God counts on every person. Today we can welcome with warmth those who seem different in our church.
exp.25:15:
The explanation says that the rulers and leaders of the coastlands and the cities of the sea, who were allies of Tyre, will come down from their thrones. They will take off their robes and their embroidered garments, that is, their signs of power and wealth. Instead, they will clothe themselves with trembling: they will sit on the ground, shaking, and be astonished, that is, greatly amazed, as they see the fall of Tyre.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and powerful city of maritime trade. God announces its judgment, among other reasons because of its pride. The rulers who depended on it are frightened because they see that their security is collapsing.

For today: wealth, position, or prestige are not a firm foundation. We can be thankful for what we have, but we should place our trust in God and live with humility.
exp.21:19:
God says he will gather his people inside Jerusalem, the way someone puts metals (silver, iron, lead, tin) into a furnace and lights the fire to melt them. "Anger" and "wrath" speak of his righteous displeasure. "Leave you there" means he will keep the fire burning over them until they melt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He says Israel has become dross, meaning the worthless waste left behind when silver is refined. That describes their injustice, their idolatry, and their violence. The judgment on Jerusalem would be severe, and its purpose was that they would come to recognize that the LORD is Lord.

For today: let us not take sin or God's patience lightly. If he corrects us, let us listen quickly, repent, and return to him in humility, trusting in his justice and his mercy.
exp.25:12:
God says he will silence the music of the city of Tyre. The noise of its celebrations and songs will come to an end. The stringed instruments that accompanied them, which were something like ancient harps or lutes, will be heard no more.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very rich trading city, and it had rejoiced over the fall of Jerusalem, thinking it would profit from it. God announces that Tyre too will be torn down by an invading army. The verses that follow say it would become like a bare rock where fishing nets are spread out to dry.

For today: riches and festivities may seem secure, but they do not last. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, give thanks to God, and live with humility, without mocking the suffering of others.
exp.39:5:
He says that the guide, a man whom Ezekiel sees in the vision, went to the gate facing east of the temple. He climbed its steps and measured with his rod the two posts of the gate, that is, the columns on each side of the entrance. Each post was one reed wide. The steps are stairs, and the reed was a measuring rod of six long cubits.

Ezekiel is in exile, and God gives him a detailed vision of a temple. The guide asks him to look, listen, and set his heart on what he sees, so that he can then tell it to Israel. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as something symbolic, or as a hope of restoration.

For today: God cares about details and asks for the attention of the heart. When we read the Bible, let us not rush; let us listen calmly and let his Word shape us.
exp.27:0:
This verse is an introductory formula. It says that a message from God came to Ezekiel. The sentence "The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying," is the reader's guide here, so the translation should match that wording. The key point is that the message does not come from the prophet himself, but from the Lord, the God of Israel.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel is the messenger. This verse opens a new message, addressed to the ruler of Tyre, a rich and powerful city by the sea. According to the text that follows, God confronts him because his heart has been lifted up with pride and he has considered himself to be a god.

For today: before we speak or judge, it is wise to listen to God in his Word. And if we receive success or power, let us remember that everything is a gift and that we are still people who depend on him.
exp.17:23:
This verse says that if a person who had been living uprightly abandons their good path and commits wrongdoing, copying the detestable things the wicked person does, they cannot rely on their past goodness. The word "trespass" in the verse refers to betraying or failing in one's duty. "Shall die" speaks of the consequence of turning away from God; many understand it as physical death or separation from God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. They were saying that God was unjust and blaming their ancestors for their suffering. God answers that each person is accountable for their own way, and that He takes no pleasure in anyone's death, but desires that all turn back to Him.

For today: do not live on yesterday's faith. Keep your heart close to God every day, and if you have strayed, return to Him, because His mercy remains open.
exp.45:6:
He says that the prince, at the festival of the new moon, was to offer a grain offering: an ephah (a measure of about 22 liters, though the exact calculation is debated) with the bull, and an ephah with each ram. For the lambs he would give whatever he was able. In addition, a hin of oil (about 3 or 4 liters) for each ephah.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the temple and its worship (chapters 40 to 48). God gives orderly instructions for worshiping him with reverence. Christians interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture.

For today: God values orderly worship, and also giving according to what we are able to give. With whatever you have, whether time, talents, or resources, offer God your best with a sincere heart.
exp.22:5:
The explanation says that the Assyrians, the lovers of Oholah, were men of impressive appearance: clothed in blue (a deep blue or violet cloth, a luxury fabric), captains and rulers, attractive young men, and horsemen riding on horses. "Desirable young men" means young men who were attractive.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses a harsh parable about two sisters: Oholah represents Samaria (the northern kingdom) and Oholibah represents Jerusalem. Their unfaithfulness symbolizes the spiritual infidelity of Israel, which sought alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting in God. The verse shows what dazzled them: power, beauty and prestige.

For today: the glitter of what the world admires can draw us away from God without our noticing. Before trusting in something, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God or takes God's place.
exp.32:16:
Some of the people of Israel say that God is unjust. They claim: "The way of the Lord is not equal." The word "way" here means the path or manner of acting. But God answers that the crooked way is theirs, not his.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who had been set as a watchman to warn the people. Those exiled in Babylon thought God was unfair because he said he would forgive the wicked person who repented and would judge the righteous person who turned away from good. God shows them that his dealings are fair and that he always offers a way to return.

For today: before blaming God for what we do not understand, let us examine our own hearts. His invitation remains open: if we repent and walk in his truth, he receives us and forgives us.
exp.47:12:
This verse says that the Levites will receive a portion of land next to that of the priests. It measures twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth. A measuring rod was the unit used for measuring; in this vision it comes to about three meters, though scholars do not fully agree on its exact measure. The border is the limit or boundary line.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision about the land being divided again. Earlier it was said that the priests, the sons of Zadok, were faithful, while the Levites went astray with Israel. Even so, the Levites are given a place and a service. There are different ways to understand this vision: some see it as something literal and future, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares for the place of each servant, even for one who has failed and turns back to him. Serve where he places you, with faithfulness and humility.
exp.46:8:
It says that wherever the waters of this river reach, every living creature will flourish. There will be a great many fish, because these waters arrive and heal, and everything that enters the river will live. "Living creature" means a creature that is alive, and "swim" is the sense of the word "nade." Here, "streams" refers to the two branches of the river.

Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of the restored temple. An angel guides him and shows him a river flowing out from the temple and down toward the Dead Sea, whose salty waters are made healthy. Scholars understand this in several ways: as a promise of restoration for Israel, as a spiritual picture of the life God gives, or as a foretaste of a future renewal.

Today we can remember that where God acts, there is new life. Ask him to heal the dry places of your heart and of your surroundings.
exp.39:46:
