He says the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the inner courtyard: a perfect square, one hundred cubits on each side, roughly fifty meters. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, measured from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. The altar was before the house, that is, in front of the temple, at the center of that space.

Ezekiel is in a vision he received from God, and a guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple. The priests, the sons of Zadok, look after the altar and serve the Lord. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something in the future. What is clear is that God wants an orderly place for people to draw near to Him.

For today: the altar stands at the center, before one enters the house. We can make drawing near to God with sincerity and humility the center of our lives, before any other activity. Today, begin the day in prayer.
exp.47:32:
This verse describes the south side of the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It measures four thousand five hundred reeds (a reed was a measuring rod, about three meters according to some calculations) and has three gates, named for the tribes of Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun. The south side is the one that faces toward noon, the direction the sun is highest.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting what God showed him during the exile in Babylon. This is the close of the book: a vision of restoration, with a city whose twelve gates carry the names of the twelve tribes. Scholars understand it in different ways: as a literal temple and city yet to come, or as a symbol of God's presence with his people. The following verse calls the city by a name that means the LORD is there.

For today: God leaves no one outside his plan. Each tribe has its gate, and each person has a place. You can rest in the knowledge that God knows you by name and welcomes you.
exp.15:42:
God says to Jerusalem that she did not remember the days of her youth, when He cared for her and rescued her. Instead of being thankful, she provoked Him to anger. For this reason God brings the result of her own way down upon her head. The word for youth in this passage means the time of being young. "Bringing the way upon the head" means she will receive the consequences of her actions. Moreover, she did not even reflect on her abominations, that is, her detestable practices.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout this chapter, Jerusalem is presented as a young woman rescued by God who later became unfaithful to Him, above all through idolatry and alliances with other nations. The judgment comes because of that ingratitude and lack of repentance.

For today: remembering with gratitude what God has done in your life guards you against pride and forgetfulness. Take a moment this week to write down and give thanks for how God has cared for you.
exp.27:13:
It says this figure is called "great anointed cherub, covering," meaning an angelic being who covered or protected. God himself placed him on the holy mountain of God, and there he walked among the stones of fire, an image of brilliance and of God's holy presence.

God speaks through Ezekiel, addressing the king of Tyre, known for his wealth and pride. The language is poetic and very elevated. Some believe it is only a figure for the human king. Others think Satan is also reflected behind that pride. Christians have interpreted it both ways, so it is wise to speak with humility.

For today: everything we are and have was given to us by God. When we remember that, pride loses its place, and we can live thankful and simple.
exp.27:23:
It says that Israel will stop suffering the pain its neighbors caused it. A "pricking brier" is a thorn that wounds, and a "grieving thorn" is a threat that hurts. To "despise" means to look down on someone with contempt. God promises that these nations will no longer be a constant wound to Israel, and that everyone will acknowledge that He is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. First He announces judgment against Sidon, a neighboring city that harassed Israel. Then He promises to gather His scattered people so they may live in their land in safety. The text gives no further details about how this would happen; some read it as a hope for the return from exile, and others also see it as a promise still to be fulfilled.

For today: when contempt or injustice wounds you, remember that God sees and defends His people. You can rest in the knowledge that He has the last word, and entrust your pain to Him with confidence.
exp.24:3:
God tells Ammon that he will hand them over to "the people of the east," that is, to nomadic tribes of the desert to the east. They will take his land as their inheritance, set up their sheep pens and their tents there, eat the crops of his fields, and drink his milk. It is a picture of total loss.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Ammonites, neighbors of Israel, rejoiced when the temple was defiled, the land was laid waste, and Judah was taken into captivity. God answers that mockery by announcing judgment. The text does not say precisely which peoples "the people of the east" would be; it describes them in general terms.

Today: let us not rejoice in the pain of others, not even when someone seems to deserve it. God sees the heart and cares for those who suffer. Let us rather pray, help, and show compassion.
exp.23:9:
This verse describes someone who adds more wood and fans the fire to cook the meat until it is consumed. "Spice it well" refers to making the broth thick and rich, and in the end even the bones are burned. It is an image of judgment that grows more and more intense.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to a cooking pot and calls it a "city of bloodshed" because of its violence and injustice. With this image he announces that judgment will come upon her and that she will no longer be overlooked.

For today: God takes injustice and harm done to others seriously. We can humbly examine what things in our lives we need to recognize and leave behind, and turn to God in repentance, trusting in his mercy.
exp.19:15:
It says that God did not allow Israel to enter the promised land, because that generation rejected his judgments, did not live according to his ways, and did not honor his sabbaths. The word "judgments" in the verse can be understood as his decrees or rulings; "statutes" are his commands; "polluted" means they treated as common what was holy. The root of the problem was that their heart went after idols.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes in exile in Babylon. God reviews the history of Israel from the desert, after leaving Egypt. He wants to show the elders of the people that their present situation comes from a very ancient rebellion, and that He, even so, acted with patience for the sake of his name.

For today: our actions grow out of what we love. Ask yourself what truly occupies your heart, and ask God to draw it back to himself, so that obeying him becomes a response of love and not merely an obligation.
exp.38:20:
He says that God will show his glory, that is, his greatness and his power, before all the peoples. The nations that were not Israel will see the judgment of God, that is, his justice in punishing evil, and the hand of God laid upon his enemies, which means his power at work.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapters 38 and 39 he announces the defeat of Gog, an enemy who attacks Israel. The images of the feast and the blood are very strong language, and scholars understand them in different ways: some take them literally and others as symbol. The purpose is seen in the verses that follow: that Israel and the nations may know that God is the Lord and that he is just.

For today: God is not indifferent to evil or to his people. We can trust that he will do justice, and in the meantime live with humility and acknowledge his holiness.
exp.13:3:
God tells Ezekiel to warn the Israelites who have idols "in their heart," meaning they love and obey them inwardly, even though they come to consult the prophet. "The stumbling block of their iniquity" is that which makes them fall into sin. God says he will answer that kind of person "according to the multitude of their idols," which can be understood as a severe answer, one of judgment, in keeping with their divided heart.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to some elders of Israel who were in exile. They appeared to be seeking God, but their hearts remained bound to other gods. God does not look for religion that is only outward appearance; he wants them to truly turn back to him, as shown by the call to repentance.

Today we can ask ourselves what, in secret, occupies the place of God in our heart. Before asking him for anything, it is good to be honest, let go of that idol, and return to him with all our heart.
exp.15:9:
God says that he clothed the woman in fine garments: embroidered cloth, footwear of leather, and linen and silk. The leather he mentions is uncertain. Some think it was a fine, strong hide, and it is not known for sure what animal it came from. The same is true of the fine cloth in the verse, which may have been a fine fabric.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as an abandoned girl whom he rescued, cared for, and took as his wife. The clothing shows his care and generosity. Later in the chapter, it shows how she forgot that love and was unfaithful to him.

Today we can remember that all the good we have comes from God's grace, not from our own merits. Ask yourself: what has God done for me? Respond to him with gratitude, humility, and faithfulness.
exp.20:27:
God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the Ammonites, who mocked Israel. The message is that the sword of judgment is already drawn from its sheath. It is polished and sharpened, ready to slay, that is, to kill, and to destroy with a glittering flash like lightning.

The Lord God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier he had announced that the sword of Babylon would fall on Jerusalem. Now the judgment also reaches Ammon, a neighboring people who rejoiced at Israel's pain. Scholars discuss some details of the scene, but the central message is clear: God judges the nations.

For today: do not rejoice when others fall, and do not mock their suffering. God sees pride and mockery, and he also calls you to treat others with humility and compassion.
exp.17:28:
The people of Israel kept repeating: "The way of the Lord is not equal." God answers with a question: are my ways unequal? And He concludes that the unequal ways are theirs. "Just" here means fair, upright. "Transgressions" are rebellions or serious offenses against God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors and that God was not just. God makes it clear to them that each person answers for himself, and that the one who turns away from evil can live. His desire is that they repent.

When things go wrong, it is easy to blame God or others. This verse invites us to look honestly at our own way, to recognize what we need to change, and to return to God, who always offers forgiveness and a new heart.
exp.44:19:
It says that on the seventh day of the first month the ceremony of cleansing the temple should be repeated. This time it is for "those who have gone astray and been deceived," that is, for those who sinned without realizing it, through carelessness, or because they were led down the wrong path. "To make atonement" means to cleanse or cover guilt through a sacrifice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the future temple and worship (chapters 40 to 48). Before this verse, on the first day, the sanctuary was purified with the blood of a young bull. This second purification includes sins committed unintentionally. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes something literal, symbolic, or yet to be fulfilled; the Bible does not fully clarify this.

For today: God is also concerned with our hidden or unintentional faults. We can pray with humility, "Search me, Lord," and trust that his forgiveness reaches us too.
exp.19:9:
He says that God brought Israel out of Egypt and led them into the wilderness. The phrase "I caused them to go forth" and the word "brought" are the verse's own wording, so this is a brief fact, but a very important one: God took the initiative to rescue his people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who addresses the leaders of Israel who are in exile. God reminds them of their history to show that his people rebelled from the beginning, even in Egypt, since they kept following their idols. Even so, God rescued them for the sake of his name, that is, out of faithfulness to himself and not because of anything they deserved.

For today: God rescues us by his grace, not because we deserve it. If you feel unworthy today or have failed, remember his faithfulness and respond with gratitude, letting go of whatever has taken his place in your heart.
exp.34:12:
Ezekiel 35:13 says that Edom (Mount Seir) spoke proudly and poured out many words against God. The phrase "ye have boasted with your mouth" means they bragged and became arrogant. The phrase "ye have multiplied your words" means they spoke without restraint. And God declares: "I have heard them." None of that went unnoticed.

God himself is speaking here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom had held an old hostility toward Israel, and it rejoiced when Israel was laid waste, even saying that their lands were theirs to devour. By speaking this way about the land and the people of God, they spoke against God. That is why the judgment announced in the following verses comes.

For today: our words matter, and God hears them, including those we speak in private or in mockery. Before we speak with pride or rejoice in another's misfortune, let us ask him to guard our mouths.
exp.34:3:
It says that God will leave the cities of Mount Seir in ruins, and that this place will be destroyed and empty. In the end, the people will know that the Lord is Jehovah, that is, the true God who does what he says.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Seir was the region of Edom, a neighboring people of Israel. According to the text, Edom held a long-lasting hostility and handed the Israelites over to the sword when they were suffering. For this reason God announces judgment against them.

For today: do not rejoice in or take advantage of the pain of others, and do not hold a grudge for years. God sees injustice and also sees how we treat those who suffer. Ask him to give you a compassionate heart that is willing to forgive.
exp.34:5:
God swears by his own life that Mount Seir, that is, Edom, will be given over to bloodshed. "Assign" means to appoint or to sentence. "Hate" here means refusing or declining to shed blood. Because Edom did not hate violence, violence will overtake Edom itself. The punishment fits what Edom did.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, kept up an old hostility against Israel, and when Jerusalem fell, it handed many Israelites over to the sword. God responds by defending his wounded people and showing that he sees the injustice. The text does not say how each detail was fulfilled; that is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can examine whether we hold on to resentment or take pleasure in the misfortune of others. God calls us to reject violence and hatred, to leave justice in his hands, and to ask for mercy for others.
exp.39:41:
This verse describes four more tables, made of hewn stone, which measured about half a meter long and half a meter wide, and about 50 centimeters high (a cubit is roughly half a meter). There they would place the instruments used to slaughter, that is, to kill, the animals of the burnt offering and the sacrifice.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile, in which a guide shows him a new temple with very precise measurements. Interpreters do not agree: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence among his restored people. What is certain is that the text stresses the order and holiness of worship.

For today: God cares about the details when we worship him. We can approach him with order, reverence, and preparation, not in a hurried or careless way.
exp.13:16:
It says God could send war ("sword") upon a land and command it to pass through. The result would be that people and animals die. Here "cut off" means to cut down or remove, the way a tree is cut down.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. God explains that Jerusalem had fallen so deep into idolatry that not even the prayers of righteous men like Noah, Daniel and Job would save the city. Those men would save only themselves. This is the third of four warnings: famine, wild beasts, sword and pestilence.

For today: the faith of others is valuable, but it does not replace my own. Each person must turn to God personally and not trust in the spiritual reputation of parents or friends. God also always invites us to return to Him.
exp.15:6:
It says that God made Jerusalem grow like a girl left abandoned: he multiplied her like the plants of the field, made her grow, and made her beautiful. Even so, she was still bare and exposed, that is, without covering or dignity of her own, still in need. The phrase about coming to adornment speaks of reaching maturity, and the phrase about her breasts growing shows that she was already a young woman.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned baby, whom He rescues, to remind Jerusalem of her humble origin and the grace she received. Then He covers her and makes a covenant with her. Many understand that the account sets up an accusation about her unfaithfulness.

For today: do not forget where God took you from. Everything good you have is His gift, so respond with gratitude and faithfulness, not with pride.
exp.43:30:
The priests were not allowed to eat the meat of animals or birds that had died on their own ("carrion") or that had been torn apart by other beasts ("torn"). They could eat only the meat of animals that had been slaughtered in the proper way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the rules for the priests. Earlier, rules had already been given about their purity and their food. This law is similar to Leviticus 22:8, where priests are also forbidden to eat such animals. Their service was to show care and holiness, and their food was part of that.

For today: let us take care with what we allow into our lives, not only at the table but also in our minds and hearts. Whoever serves God seeks to live with integrity, even in everyday matters.
exp.15:48:
This verse tells us what the sin of Sodom was: pride, eating until full, and living with much free time and comfort. She and her daughters (the nearby towns) did not help the poor or the needy. "Abundance of food" means plenty of food. "Idleness" means a comfortable life without work. The phrase "did not strengthen the hand" means that they did not support or sustain the one in distress.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. She believed herself better than others, but God shows her that her sin was even greater than Sodom's. The passage goes on to say that Sodom also committed abomination, so this verse is not the full list of her sins, but one aspect that God emphasizes here.

For today: when I have more than I need, pride and comfort can harden my heart. Today I can ask myself whom I can help with my time or my resources.
exp.28:10:
It says that Egypt will be so empty and ruined that no one will pass through its land, neither person nor animal, and that it will have no inhabitants for forty years. "No one will walk there" means that no person will walk through it. "Laid waste" means left in ruins or destroyed.

The passage records God speaking through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Egypt had considered itself very powerful, and the pharaoh claimed that the Nile River was his. God answers that he is the true Lord. Scholars debate whether these forty years were literal or symbolic, since history does not clearly confirm it. The text goes on to say that God would later gather Egypt back together.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, such as money, success, or strength. All of that can fall. Let us place our trust in God, who sustains all things and also knows how to restore.
exp.38:3:
The explanation says that the enemy army will fall dead on the mountains of Israel, together with its troops and allied peoples. Their bodies will be left as food for the birds and the wild beasts.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 announce a great invasion against Israel, led by a leader from the land of Magog. God promises to step in and defeat them, to show that he is the Lord. Christians interpret these chapters in different ways: as a future event, as a symbol of God's final victory, or as something partly already fulfilled.

For today: even when evil seems strong and well organized, God is still greater. You can rest in him and entrust your fears to him, while continuing to do good.
exp.12:14:
God says he will finish pouring out his anger on the wall and on those who covered it with loose mortar, that is, with a weak mixture that holds nothing up. Covering a wall with a coat of plaster is what the mortar was for. In the end, God says that neither the wall nor its builders will continue to exist.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The wall represents the false security that the false prophets offered, since they promised peace to Jerusalem when there was no peace. They decorated a weak wall instead of calling the people to turn back to God. For that reason the judgment would come like a storm and would tear down everything.

For today: let us not build our lives on pretty but empty promises. Let us seek words that are true, even when they make us uncomfortable, and let us build on Christ and his word, which do withstand any storm.
exp.11:6:
Ezekiel tells us that he obeyed God to the letter. He brought out his "belongings," that is, his baggage or travel things, like someone going into exile. He did it by day, so that people would see. At evening he "dug through the wall," that is, he made an opening in the wall with his own hands. He went out at night and carried the load on his shoulders, in full view of everyone.

Ezekiel is a prophet who lives among the exiles in Babylon. God commanded this action as a sign, an acted-out prophecy, for the rebellious people. It represented what would happen to Jerusalem and its people: they would go into exile secretly and in haste. Many did not want to believe that the punishment would come.

For today: Ezekiel obeyed even though it seemed strange and exposed his reputation. Let us ask God for the courage to do what He shows us, without waiting for everyone to understand or approve.
exp.26:32:
It says that when Tyre's ships returned loaded with goods, many peoples were satisfied. Its wealth and its trade even made the kings of the earth rich.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Tyre, a city famous for its sea trade. The nearby verses describe other peoples mourning over its fall. Here its past glory is remembered, to show how great it was and how hard its ruin would be. The text does not say that trade is bad; the underlying problem in the chapter is pride.

Today we can be thankful for what God gives us, but without trusting in money or success. If you work or own a business, try to make sure your profit also blesses others, and remember that what matters most is not lost in a storm.
exp.21:0:
It says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" is an older way of saying "the Lord spoke to me," and this formula is repeated throughout this book to mark that a new message is beginning. What follows does not come from the prophet's own opinion, but from what God tells him.

The speaker is the Lord, and the receiver is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. This message is about Jerusalem, which is called "the city that sheds blood." God confronts it for its violence and its idolatry. This brief phrase sets the stage: what follows is a serious accusation, but given with the purpose of truth and of a call to return to God.

For today: before we speak, it is wise to listen to God. We can open the Bible with humility and ask him to show us the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, so that he corrects our hearts and not only points out the mistakes of others.
exp.40:7:
He said that Ezekiel looked at the height of the temple on every side and noticed that the side chambers had a firm base. That base measured "a full reed," a measuring rod that here equals six cubits (a cubit is roughly half a meter, so about three meters). The base where the chambers rested is what is meant here by the foundations.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile, in which a guide showed him a new temple and measured every part of it. The precise details stress order and holiness. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares about what seems small, like a foundation measured with care. Ask yourself what foundations hold up your daily life, such as prayer, the Word, and community, and strengthen one of them this week.
exp.20:5:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to groan in public. He must do it with the breaking of his loins, that is, with his body bent over by deep pain, and with bitterness, before the eyes of the people. It is not a quiet weeping but a sign that everyone can see.

God speaks to his prophet. Jerusalem was under judgment, and God announces that his sword, an image of destruction by war, will come against everyone. Ezekiel must groan so that, when people ask him why, he can announce the news that is coming and the people will understand how serious it is. Scholars agree that it is a symbolic gesture.

For today: when God shows us the pain of sin and its consequences, let us not speak with coldness. Let us ask him for a sensitive heart, one that feels compassion for others and warns them with love and sincerity.
exp.40:20:
It says the posts of the temple entrance were square in shape. A "post" is the column that holds up the door. The "face" is the front or facade. So the front of the sanctuary, the most holy part, looked the same as the front of the main temple, with the same measurements and the same order.

Here Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, tells of a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him a new temple in detail. The Jewish people were discouraged because the first temple had been destroyed. This vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell with his people. Interpreters disagree about whether it is a literal temple or a symbolic one.

For today: God cares about order and harmony, and he wants our lives to be steady and consistent, the same inside and out. Let us strive to be the same in private and in public.
exp.35:34:
It tells that the people, on seeing the restored land, will remark with amazement that the place which had been ruined now looks like the garden of Eden, and that the cities which were ruins are today fortified and secure.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites in exile. Their land had been left in ruin because of judgment, but God promises to cleanse them from their sins and restore them. The neighboring peoples will see the change and recognize that it was the work of God, not of men.

For today: God can restore what seems lost, whether a life, a family, or a relationship. He begins by cleansing the heart. We can come to Him with hope, and when He restores something, we can give Him the credit.
exp.30:8:
It says that God himself made this giant tree beautiful, giving it many branches. It was so impressive that even the trees of Eden, the garden of God, felt envy. The phrase "I made him" means "I made him," and the phrase about envy means that they envied him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the pharaoh of Egypt. He compares him to an enormous tree, as he does with Assyria, to show his greatness. Many scholars understand that the tree represents a powerful nation. But the passage warns that pride would lead him to his fall, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: everything good we have, whether talents, success, or influence, comes from God. Remembering this helps us give thanks instead of boasting, and not to trust in our own greatness.
exp.41:2:
The chambers of the temple rose in three stories, one facing the other. On one side they stood opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, and on the other side opposite the pavement (the stone-paved floor) of the outer court. A cubit measures about 45 to 50 centimeters. The outer court is an open yard around the temple.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him. A guide takes him through the temple and shows him very precise measurements. These chambers, according to the chapter, were located next to the area of the sanctuary. Scholars debate whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people. The people were then in exile.

For today: God cares about order, space, and detail when it comes to worshiping him. We can give God an orderly place in our week, with set time for prayer and Bible reading.
exp.47:8:
This verse says that the portion of land that the people were to set apart for the Lord would measure twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth. The unit of measure is not specified in this translation, and its exact size in meters is debated, but it was a measure used in that time.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the final vision of the book. There it describes how the land would be divided among the tribes and a holy area set aside, with the sanctuary in the middle. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: some see it literally, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God deserves the center and the first place. We can ask ourselves what real space, of time, attention and resources, we are setting aside for Him in our daily life.
exp.39:44:
He says the guide shows Ezekiel a room in the inner court, the one facing south. That room is set aside for the priests who are in charge of caring for the temple. "Chamber" means a room or hall, and "south" is the direction the room faces. "Keepers of the charge" means they are responsible for caring for and watching over the house.

Ezekiel is in a vision, about twenty-five years after the fall of Jerusalem. A man with the appearance of bronze leads him and measures the temple. Each space has a purpose. Here a distinction is made between those who care for the temple and those who serve at the altar. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God values faithful service, whether visible or quiet. There are those who care for, order, and sustain the life of the church without applause. Ask yourself what task you can do steadily, as for the Lord.
exp.25:17:
This verse says that when Tyre falls, the islands and the coastal lands will tremble in fear. "Shall tremble" means they will shake with fright. Here "departure" refers to her leaving or ending, which the King James Version renders as "departure"; other translations say "fall" or "disappearance." What frightens them is seeing how the end of a city that seemed so powerful unfolds.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich seaport that lived by trade and felt secure. God announces her judgment, and the rulers of the coasts mourn her fall with a funeral song. Scholars debate how it was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: no human power stands without God.

For today: do not place your security in money, success, or prestige, because all of that can disappear. Trust instead in God, who remains firm.
exp.21:10:
It says that in Jerusalem the people were committing serious sexual sins within their own families and with their neighbors. Doing something detestable in the eyes of God describes what the phrase means. Shamefully dishonoring a daughter-in-law is what is meant by the sin of defiling her. Taking sexual advantage of someone by force refers to abuse. It also mentions abusing a sister, a daughter of the same father.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem. He accuses the city of violence, injustice, idolatry, and sexual wickedness. These behaviors broke the law given to Israel (Leviticus 18 and 20). The people had forgotten God, and for that reason judgment would come.

For today: God is concerned with how we treat our family and our neighbor. We can guard purity, protect the vulnerable, and not stay silent in the face of abuse. If we have failed, there is forgiveness in Christ, who calls us to change.
exp.27:10:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel once again. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me, saying" means that a message from the Lord came to him. It is the way the prophet marks the beginning of a new message.

The one speaking is God, and he speaks to Ezekiel. Before this, the message was against the prince of Tyre, who considered himself a god. Now God asks the prophet for a lament, a song of mourning for the king of Tyre. Some understand the words that follow only as referring to that human king; others also see an echo of Adam or of Satan. The Bible does not fully clarify this here.

For today: before you speak or act, be quiet and let the Word of God speak to you first. What he says matters more than what we think of ourselves.
exp.23:23:
God tells Ezekiel that he will be a sign to the people. What he did, they will do too. When what has been announced comes to pass, they will know that God is the Lord.

The phrase "will be a sign" means that Ezekiel serves as a living example. The phrase "you will know that I am the Lord God" means that they will recognize that God had truly spoken.

God speaks to the exiles of Judah through Ezekiel. The prophet's wife suddenly dies, and God forbids him to mourn in public. By this, He shows that Jerusalem and the temple would be destroyed, and the grief would be so great that the people would not even be able to express their mourning. Interpreters see here a judgment for their sins, but also a warning so that they would respond.

For today: let us not wait until the crisis arrives to take God's voice seriously. If He warns us through His Word, let us listen in time, acknowledge our failures, and return to Him in humility.
exp.45:2:
This verse says that the people of the land, that is, the ordinary people of Israel, will worship God at the entrance of the gate of the inner court, on the sabbaths and on the new moons. The new moons were the first days of each month. To worship means to bow down and acknowledge God as Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of a restored temple and worship. The east gate was opened on special days, and the prince and the people worshiped there, while the priests offered the sacrifices. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision describes something literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God values constant and orderly worship, offered together with his people. Set aside a fixed time each week to worship him, whether you are a leader or an ordinary person.
exp.46:14:
This describes the northern border of the promised land. The line begins at "the great sea," which is the Mediterranean Sea, and continues along the way of Hethlon until it reaches Zedad. The verse uses "border" for the boundary or limit of the land. These are places in the north of Israel, and today it is not known with certainty where all of them were.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In a vision of restoration, the Lord marks the limits of the land he will divide among the twelve tribes. He reminds them that he swore to give it to their fathers. That promise still stands, even though the people have gone through exile. Scholars disagree about whether this vision should be understood literally or symbolically.

For today: God keeps his promises in detail, even in what seems small. You can trust that he is faithful to you, and you can thank him for what he has given you.
exp.27:9:
It says that the ruler of Tyre will have a shameful death, like that of the uncircumcised, that is, the death of those who did not belong to God's people. He will die at the hands of strangers, that is, at the hands of foreigners. And this is not simple chance: God says he has already declared it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the king of Tyre, who believed himself to be a god because of his wealth and wisdom. The verses before remind him that he is only a man. Some think the passage speaks only of a human king; others also see a broader background about pride. Scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us feel untouchable. We can be thankful for what we have, recognize that everything comes from God, and live with humility before him.
exp.47:7:
It says that, right next to the territory of Judah, running from east to west, there will be a special portion set apart. It measures twenty-five thousand reeds wide, and long like the other parts, from east to west. In the middle of that portion will be the sanctuary.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, records a vision God gave him near the end of the book. The people were in exile, and the vision showed a restoration with the land divided in good order. Scholars interpret this in different ways: some read it literally, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people. The central point is that the sanctuary holds the center.

For today: ask yourself what occupies the center of your life. We can arrange our time, our work, and our family around God, so that his presence becomes the reference point for everything else.
exp.22:42:
This verse speaks of a woman who is already old and worn down by her unfaithfulness. God says that those who pursue her will keep to their immoral ways, and that she will keep on with them. "Long practiced in adultery" means that she had been living that way for a long time. Her unfaithfulness is what is meant by the harlotries.

God speaks through Ezekiel. In this chapter, Aholah and Aholibah represent Samaria and Jerusalem, who turned away from God to seek alliances and idols from other nations. It is language of strong images to show how serious their unfaithfulness was. Some interpreters see here a sad persistence in sin, and others a warning of judgment.

For today: bad habits, if not confronted, become custom and harden us. Today you can return to God sincerely, before sin becomes your normal way of living.
exp.41:17:
He says the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the south side of the temple area, and it came out to five hundred reeds. "Midday" is an old way of saying south. The "measuring reed" was a long rod used as a ruler. In this vision, with a reed about six long cubits (the exact length is debated), the whole side would be enormous, more than a kilometer on each side.

Ezekiel describes a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed. A heavenly guide measures the whole enclosure: east and north, south and west, and all of them come out the same. The text says the wall served to separate the holy from the common. Scholars disagree about whether this is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness. We can set healthy boundaries to protect what is sacred in our lives, such as time with God, and not let everything else crowd it out.
exp.17:29:
God says that he will judge each person according to their way of living. Then he makes an invitation: "Repent, and turn yourselves," that is, change direction and leave sin behind. "Transgressions" are the wrongs people commit, and "ruin" is destruction. If they repent, their sin will no longer destroy them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who were living in exile. The people were saying that God was unjust and blaming their ancestors for their situation. God answers that each person is responsible for their own choices, and that he offers a way out: to return to him and live.

Today, we do not have to remain tied to past mistakes or blame others. Think of one habit or attitude that pulls you away from God, and today ask him for forgiveness and for help to change. He gladly welcomes the one who returns.
exp.24:2:
God tells Ezekiel to deliver a message to the Ammonites. They shouted "Aha," an expression of mockery and delight at the misfortune of others. They laughed because the sanctuary was defiled, the land of Israel was left in ruins, and the people of Judah were taken away as captives. "Hear" means "listen," and "desolate" means "laid waste."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Ammon was a neighboring people of Israel, and God judges them for rejoicing when Judah fell. The verses that follow announce that peoples from the east would take their land.

For today: God notices how we react to the pain of others. Even when someone has failed or is suffering the consequences of their mistakes, we should not mock or rejoice. Instead, let us pray, help, and show compassion.
exp.27:25:
This verse promises that Israel will live in its land in peace. They will build houses, plant vineyards, and not be afraid. The word "confidently" here means without fear, with security, so the rewrite is: "dwell with confidence" means living without fear, with security. The verse also speaks of those who plundered them, meaning those who took what was theirs by force. God says he will judge the neighbors who harmed his people. The result will be that Israel acknowledges that the Lord is their God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had announced judgment on Sidon, a neighboring city that had been hostile to Israel. Then he promises to gather his scattered people and bring them back to the land given to Jacob. Some see here the return from exile; others also see a future fulfillment. Christians have understood it in different ways.

Today we can trust that God cares for his people and does justice in his time. When you suffer or feel threatened, do not carry revenge or fear: hand them over to God and keep working with hope, like someone who plants a vineyard.
exp.45:8:
In the solemn feasts, the people of the land who came into the temple through the north gate were to leave through the south gate, and those who came in through the south gate were to leave through the north gate. They were not to go back out the way they came in, but were to leave through the gate facing it. "Midday" means south, and "solemn feasts" are Israel's sacred celebrations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a new temple and of how worship was to be arranged. Scholars explain the reason for this rule in several ways: perhaps it was meant to keep order among the crowds, or to show that no one came before God and left the same way they arrived. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when you come before God, try to leave different from how you came in, with a more renewed heart, and do not repeat the same old path.
exp.19:44:
This verse says: "Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying." The phrase "came unto me" is the verse's own wording, so the reader can see it. Ezekiel announces that God is speaking to him again and that a new message is about to be given.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. With this phrase, which is repeated many times in the book, he marks the start of a new prophecy. Earlier, God had promised to restore Israel for the sake of his name and not because of their merits. Now the message shifts to judgment: the image of a forest that will be burned appears. Some scholars connect it with Jerusalem and Judah, although it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before reading the Bible, we can pray and ask him for an attentive heart, ready to listen both to what comforts and to what corrects.
exp.42:12:
The explanation says that the altar of the temple Ezekiel saw in vision was to be measured in long cubits: a common cubit plus a handbreadth, that is, a little more than the normal measure. The "hollow" was a base or channel in the ground, a cubit high and a cubit wide. The "border" was a rim around the edge, a span wide (the width of the hand). That rim and its base formed the "higher place," that is, the lower part of the altar.

God speaks to Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He shows him a new temple with its exact measurements, so that the people will be ashamed of their sin and learn to live with order and reverence. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares about the details of how he is worshiped. Come near to him with respect and sincerity, and not lightly.
exp.41:0:
He brought me out into the outer court, on the way toward the north. There he led me to some chambers, that is, rooms or chambers of the temple. They were in front of an open space that lay beside the building on the north side. The sentence about the quoted words is removed, since the reader's verse uses "brought me forth" and "brought me into," which correspond to those phrases directly.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received from God, in which a guide shows him a new temple and measures it with great detail. This takes place while the people are living in exile in Babylon. Interpreters differ on what this temple represents: some think of a literal temple in the future, others of a spiritual picture of God's presence. What is clear is that God desires to dwell among his people, with order and holiness.

God cares even about the details of how we worship him. Today we can draw near to him with reverence, and also with the confidence that God does not forget us, even in difficult times.
exp.17:25:
It says that if a person who lived in righteousness leaves that path and begins to do evil, they will suffer the consequences of their wickedness. "Iniquity" refers to wickedness or injustice, and the word "die" refers to death as the result of sin, probably both physical and spiritual.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who were in exile. Some were saying, "The way of the Lord is not fair," blaming God or their ancestors for their situation. God answers that each person is accountable for their own choices, and that He always offers the opportunity to turn back to Him.

Today it reminds us that it is not enough to have walked well in the past; we need to keep trusting God each day. If we become careless, let us ask for forgiveness, for His desire is that we live.
exp.26:35:
The explanation says that the merchants of other peoples will hiss over Tyre, that is, they will make a sound of astonishment or mockery when they see her fall. A "terror" is something dreadful that causes fear. The city will be destroyed and will no longer exist.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a city rich and powerful through its sea trade. Earlier, the text describes her as a great ship full of riches that sinks. It says that Tyre filled herself with pride because of her wealth. Some understand the "never again" as a final blow to her power of that time.

For today: riches and success can be lost quickly. If we place our trust in money or prestige, we become fragile. We can be thankful for what we have, live with humility, and trust in God more than in our possessions.
exp.26:15:
It says that Syria traded with Tyre because of the great quantity of goods Tyre produced. In return, Syria offered at its fairs (markets) pearls, purple cloth, embroidered garments, fine linen, coral, and a red gemstone. Some of these words are hard to identify with certainty; the red stone could refer to another kind of red gem. "Merchant" means trader.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Tyre, a very rich seafaring city. This list of nations shows its enormous network of trade. But the chapter prepares the announcement of its fall: its wealth and pride would not save it from God's judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves what we trust in most: what we have, or God. Enjoying our work and possessions is not wrong, but they must not take God's place in our hearts. Let us ask him to teach us to be thankful, generous, and humble.
exp.39:2:
He brought me there, and I saw a man whose appearance was bright, like bronze or polished metal. The man had a line of flax in his hand and a measuring reed, and he was standing by the gate. "Man" means a male person, "appearance" is how he looked, and the "measuring reed" was a rod used for taking measurements.

Ezekiel wrote this in the twenty-fifth year of his captivity, while already in exile, about fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem. God carries him in vision to the land of Israel and to a very high mountain. This guide will show him a temple and ask him to tell everything to Israel. Scholars disagree about whether that temple is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: even when everything seems destroyed, God still has a plan and ordered measurements for restoration. We can trust Him and pay attention to what He shows us in His Word.
exp.15:17:
It says that Jerusalem took her embroidered, colorful garments and used them to cover the images she had made for herself. She also set before those images the oil and the incense that God had given her as offerings. The comment that "covered them" refers to the same act, and "fornicate" here speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness; these words are not used in the verse you are reading, so they are left out.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he describes Jerusalem as a young woman whom he rescued, cared for, and adorned. Instead of being grateful, she used those gifts to worship idols. In this way God shows the seriousness of her ingratitude and betrayal.

For today: everything we have, such as time, money, and talents, comes from God. We can ask ourselves whether we are using these things to honor him or to serve other things that have taken first place in our hearts.
exp.39:15:
It says that the temple gate Ezekiel sees had narrow windows in the small rooms, in the entrances, and in the passageways, all on the inside. Also, each post, or pillar, was decorated with palm trees. The small rooms are little chambers, and the entrances are the gateways with their structures.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he lived in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide takes him through a new temple, measuring it with great detail. Scholars interpret this in different ways: some see a literal future temple, while others see a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his people. Palm trees are often associated with life and victory, but the text does not explain that here.

God cares even about the details of his house and of how we draw near to him. Today you can approach God with reverence and order, without rushing, trusting that he is concerned with both the great and the small things in your life.
exp.12:19:
God says he is against the "pillows" or charms with which certain women trapped people, as one hunts birds. The "veils" were coverings they used in those rituals. God promises to tear those bindings from their arms and to let free the souls they were hunting.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some women pretended to prophesy and practiced spells to gain bread and barley. With lies they discouraged the righteous and encouraged the wicked to keep to their evil way. The exact meaning of the objects is uncertain, but the deception is clear.

For today: do not follow anyone who manipulates your faith with lies for their own gain. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and trust that God defends his people and sets them free.
exp.23:6:
It says that Jerusalem, called the "city of bloods," has blood spilled in the midst of her. That blood was not hidden: it was set upon a smooth rock, that is, a bare, exposed stone. They did not pour it on the ground to cover it with dust, as was done to hide blood.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. With the image of a boiling pot, He denounces the violence and injustice of Jerusalem. According to Leviticus 17:13, spilled blood was to be covered with earth. Here, by being left uncovered, the crime is in plain view and cries out for justice. Interpreters explain the detail of the rock in various ways, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees what we try to hide. If we have harmed someone, the best course is to acknowledge it, ask forgiveness, and make amends where possible, rather than covering it up.
exp.16:19:
God says he will throw his net over the king, the way an animal is caught, and the king will be trapped in his mesh. He will be taken to Babylon, and there God will call him to account for his trespass that he hath trespassed against me, which means breaking his word and failing to keep a commitment, because he rebelled against God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is referring to King Zedekiah of Judah, who had sworn loyalty to the king of Babylon in God's name and then broke that covenant by seeking help from Egypt. For God, breaking that oath was a way of despising his own name.

For today: When we give our word, God takes it seriously. Try to keep your promises, at work, in your family, and in the church, and if you fail, acknowledge it with humility and ask for forgiveness.
exp.17:20:
If a wicked person turns away from all the sins they have committed, keeps everything God commands, and acts with justice and righteousness, they will surely live and not die.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people complained that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is responsible for their own life, and that the way of repentance is always open. Many understand that "live" here speaks of life and favor before God.

For today: you are not condemned by your past or by the mistakes of your family. If you turn back to God today, you can start over, and He welcomes you gladly.
exp.43:26:
He says that when a priest, after having been unclean from touching a dead body, returns to serve in the sanctuary, in the inner court, he must offer a sacrifice for sin, that is, for the sin or for cleansing. The word "minister" means to serve. The Lord GOD says so.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the future temple. He gives rules for the priests descended from Zadok, so that they guard the holiness of the place. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes something literal, symbolic, or yet to be fulfilled.

For today: God values that whoever serves others does so with a clean heart. Before serving in your church or family, take a moment to confess your faults and receive the forgiveness of Christ.
exp.32:25:
God asks those who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem: how will they possess the land if they live by violence? "Ye stand upon your sword" means that they trusted in strength and violence. "Abomination" refers to practices that God detests, such as idolatry. "Defile every one his neighbour's wife" means that they dishonored their neighbors' marriages through adultery.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. Those who stayed among the ruins of the land claimed it belonged to them, since Abraham was one man and received it, so they, being many, had even more reason. But God shows them that their conduct contradicted that confidence, and announces judgment.

For today: it is not enough to claim God's blessings; He expects a faithful life. Examine whether your confidence rests on inherited promises or on sincere and humble obedience.
exp.15:13:
It says that Jerusalem's fame spread among the nations because of her beauty. That beauty was perfect, but it was not her own merit: God says it was his splendor, which he had placed upon her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he describes Jerusalem as an abandoned girl whom he rescued, cared for, and enriched, and with whom he made a covenant, as in a marriage. All of this prepares the accusation that follows: she forgot who had given her everything, trusted in her own beauty, and gave herself to idolatry, which the text calls "harlotry."

For today: everything good we have, such as talents, successes, or a good reputation, is a gift from God. If we remember this, we live with gratitude and humility, and we do not turn away from him out of pride.
exp.22:27:
God says he will hand Oholibah, the woman in the story, over to those she hated, that is, to the very people she grew weary of and whose appeal to her wore out. The word "wore out" here means they were used up or grew distasteful to her; she had desired them, but then she rejected them.

Ezekiel tells a parable about two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, who represent Israel and Judah. Oholibah is Jerusalem, who sought political and religious alliances with Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt instead of trusting in God. He announces that these same nations will become the instrument of her judgment, and that this will end her habit of depending on Egypt.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether money, approval, or power, usually ends up failing us. Today you can identify what you are seeking security in and hand it back to God in prayer.
exp.44:4:
This verse says that the Levites, those who serve in God's house, were given a portion of land measuring twenty-five thousand in length by ten thousand in breadth. It was a possession for them, and it had twenty chambers. Some older translations read differently here, which is why the detail of the twenty chambers is understood in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the land being divided again. First comes the holy district of the sanctuary, then the portion of the Levites, after that the city and the prince's share. Scholars debate whether this is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his name. We can support, with gratitude and generosity, the pastors, teachers, and servants of our church, so that they can devote themselves to their work with peace of mind.
exp.43:25:
It says that a priest who had become defiled by touching a dead body, such as when he buried a close relative, could not return to service right away. First he had to be purified, and afterward wait seven full days. The phrase "they shall reckon unto him" means that the days would be counted before he returned to his duties.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. He is giving rules to the priests descended from Zadok. Because they served in a holy place, they had to guard their purity. The law of Moses also required seven days of purification after touching a dead body (Numbers 19). Then the priest would offer a sin offering before returning to the sanctuary.

For today: God values our seeking him with a prepared heart. After a failure or a loss, we should not rush. We can give ourselves time to heal, repent, and return to God with sincerity.
exp.21:4:
It says that all the nations, both those near and those far away, will mock Jerusalem. The phrase "stained in reputation" means that the city's name is ruined and its reputation is spoiled. The phrase "great turmoil" speaks of a great disorder and confusion within the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. She shed innocent blood and filled herself with idols. The verses that follow show that her leaders abused their power, despised parents, and oppressed the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. Therefore God announces that this sin would bring public shame and chaos.

For today: our secret decisions end up affecting our witness and others. Let us ask God to help us live with justice and to care for the most vulnerable, so that our lives honor his name.
exp.34:13:
This verse says that God himself speaks and announces judgment against Edom, here called the mountain of Seir. When the whole earth rejoices, God will make Edom desolate, that is, a wasteland, empty and ruined. Some understand that the rejoicing is that of the nations who will see God's justice; the text does not make this completely clear.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom had mocked Israel when it was destroyed, and had spoken with pride against God. The Lord says that he heard everything. Therefore, what Edom did to others, God will repay to him.

Today we can learn that God hears our words, including those we say with mockery or pride. We should not rejoice when others fall. Rather, let us ask God for a humble and compassionate heart, and leave justice in his hands.
exp.22:17:
Ohola and Oholiba, the two sisters who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, did not hide their unfaithfulness; they displayed it openly. "Whoredoms" here speaks of unfaithfulness, and "nakedness" refers to their exposed shame and sin. "My mind was alienated" means that God felt rejection and turned away from her, just as he had earlier turned away from her sister.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses a very harsh image: two sisters who were married to Him. Through her, he shows how Jerusalem abandoned God to trust in Babylon, Egypt, and other nations, and in their idols. Many understand this as a warning before judgment.

For today: do not play with whatever draws you away from God, thinking nothing will happen. If you have placed your trust in anything more than in Him, return to Him with sincerity; God still calls people to repentance.
exp.36:15:
God tells Ezekiel to take two sticks, or pieces of wood, and write on one "For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions", and on the other "For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions". Here "stick" means a rod or a piece of wood, and "companions" refers to the tribes joined to each one.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel lives among the exiles. After the vision of the dry bones coming back to life, God announces a restoration. The kingdom had been divided in two: Judah to the south and Israel, with Ephraim as its leader, to the north. This gesture prepares the promise to bring them back together.

For today: God heals divisions that seem impossible. We can ask him to help us seek unity with other believers, without waiting for the other person to take the first step.
exp.17:17:
This verse speaks about the father in the previous example. He deceived and mistreated others, took what belonged to his brother by force, and did wrong among his people. For this reason, God says, that father will die because of his own wickedness. "Wrong" means harm or injustice, and "took by force" means that he stole using violence.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were repeating a saying: that the children paid for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person answers for himself. The righteous son would not be punished for his unjust father, and the unjust father would be judged for what he himself did.

For today: do not use your family's history as an excuse for wrongdoing, and do not live tied to the guilt of others. God invites you to seek justice, to be honest, and to treat others well, starting today.
exp.33:28:
He says God will raise up for his people "a plant of renown," that is, something famous and fruitful that grows and bears fruit. Because of it, the people will no longer go hungry in their land nor suffer the shame and contempt of the nations. To "raise up" here means to bring forth or set up. The "nations" are the foreign peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile in Babylon. Earlier he has criticized the bad shepherds who neglected the sheep, and he promises to be their Shepherd himself. Many Christians see in this "plant" a sign of the Messiah, such as Jesus; others understand it as the prosperity God would give his people. Both ideas can coexist, but the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when you feel empty or ashamed, remember that God cares for his own. You can bring that burden to him in prayer and trust that he knows how to sustain you and restore your hope.
exp.44:7:
It says the land set apart in the vision will be the prince's portion in Israel. And it promises that the princes will no longer mistreat my people. They will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel, according to their tribes. The word "mistreat" here means to treat others harshly and unjustly, and "portion" is the share of property that is received.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel, with a temple, a city, and a land divided in an orderly way. The leaders had previously abused the people, and for that reason the following verse orders them to stop the violence and practice justice. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is fulfilled in a literal or symbolic way.

For today: if you have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them. God is concerned with justice and honesty.
exp.43:5:
God commands Ezekiel to speak with firmness to the people of Israel, whom he calls "rebellious." The phrase "let it suffice you" means "enough is enough." God says he will no longer put up with their "abominations," that is, their detestable practices that offended him.

The Lord speaks in a vision of the new temple, just after Ezekiel sees the glory of God fill the house. God is about to give rules about who may serve in the sanctuary, and first he recalls how the people had defiled that place, letting in foreigners of uncommitted heart and neglecting their covenant.

For today: God calls us to say "enough" to what we know displeases him. We can come near to Him with sincerity, acknowledge our failures, and return to Him from the heart, not merely in appearance.
exp.33:29:
It says that the people of Israel will come to know clearly that God is with them and that they belong to him. The sentence about knowing it "by experience" is rewritten for the verse's own words: "Thus shall they know" means they will come to know it through what they experience. The name of God and the phrase about the whole people are not explained here, since those words do not appear in the verse above.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was scattered and wounded because its leaders, called shepherds, had neglected it. God promises to be the Shepherd who cares for, protects, and gives security to his people. This promise of peace and food is one that he would fulfill, and that trust would be born from seeing his faithfulness.

For today: when you feel alone or insecure, remember that God promises to care for his own. You can set aside a few minutes today to pray, thank him for his care, and hand over the worry that weighs on you most.
exp.39:26:
It says the inner court of the temple had a gate on its south side. The one who guided the measuring measured the distance between that gate and the south gate of the outer court, and it came to one hundred cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. A "court" is an open yard, and here "south" means the southern side.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him. A man who looked like bronze led him through a new temple and measured everything with a measuring reed. The Jewish people were exiles in Babylon and the temple had been destroyed. Scholars disagree about whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

God is a God of order and of detail, and his presence deserves reverence. Today we can ask ourselves whether we prepare our hearts carefully to draw near to him, without haste or carelessness, with respect and gratitude.
exp.18:0:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel: "Take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel." A lamentation is a sad song, the kind that was sung at funerals. To "take up" a lamentation means to begin singing it aloud. The princes are the kings or rulers of Judah.

The speaker is God, and he gives the task to Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. What follows is a poem with images of lions and a lioness. Many scholars think it refers to the last kings of Judah and their fall, though not all agree on exactly which kings are meant. The poem does not celebrate; it mourns a loss.

For today: God grieves over the fall of leaders, even when they have failed. We can pray and lament with sincere sadness, without mocking, for leaders who go wrong, and ask God to give us just rulers.
exp.39:43:
In the inner court, near the north gate, it says there were rooms for the singers. Those rooms faced south. Another room was beside the east gate and faced north. The "court" is an open yard around the temple. The "chambers" are rooms.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple. A guide who looks like a man shows him and measures each part. Scholars disagree: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence restored. What is certain is that the text gives room for singing within the order of the temple.

For today: praise is not an ornament. God gave it a place of its own in his house. We can care for our worship with consistency, preparation and reverence, not only when we feel like it.
exp.22:44:
It says that righteous men will judge Aholah and Aholibah according to the law that punishes adulterous women and women who kill. "Shed blood" means they commit murder. God accuses them of both things: of being unfaithful and of having their hands stained with blood.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he uses the story of two sisters, Aholah and Aholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. They had given themselves to other nations and to their idols, forgetting their covenant with God. Some understand the "righteous men" to be nations that God would use as an instrument of judgment, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: God expects total faithfulness, not a divided heart. Today we can ask ourselves what things we are giving to the place that belongs to Him alone, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.46:13:
It says the land will be divided into equal shares among the tribes: "one as well as another." God recalls that he lifted up his hand, that is, he made a solemn oath, to give this land to Israel's forefathers. "Shall fall unto you for inheritance" means it will come to them as an inheritance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of restoration for his people after the exile. Before this comes the image of the river that flows out from the sanctuary and gives life. Then the boundaries of the land are marked out. Interpreters differ: some see a literal fulfillment for Israel, others a spiritual picture of God's final blessing.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when a long time passes. We can trust his word in our hopes, and also be just and generous, without favoritism, with what he gives us.
exp.47:15:
It says the city will be a perfect square: each side measures four thousand five hundred, that is, the north, south, east and west sides are all the same length. A measure of length was the one the verse gives as "the measures thereof," used here in plain terms of about three meters, though scholars do not fully agree on its exact value. "South" means the south side, and "east" is the east side.

God shows the prophet Ezekiel a vision of the land divided again, with a sacred area at the center. The city lies in the common, non-consecrated part. This vision comforts the exiled people, for God promises to be with them. Christians interpret it in several ways: literally, symbolically, or as a foretaste of the new creation.

For today: the equal measure on all four sides reminds us that God loves order and justice. We can ask ourselves whether, in our lives, we give God the central place and put everything in order around Him.
exp.44:13:
God sets how much oil is to be given as an offering: a bath, which is the tenth part of a cor. Ten baths equal a homer. The bath, the cor, and the homer were ancient measures; their exact amount in liters today is not known for certain, and scholars give different figures.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a restored temple. There he gives clear rules for worship and also tells the rulers to stop oppressing people and to use honest measures. Some see something literal here, others something symbolic.

For today: God cares about order and honesty. Offer to God what is yours with sincerity, and be fair in your everyday dealings, without tricks or crooked measures.
exp.35:10:
God promises that the mountains of Israel will again be filled with people and animals. He says that they will multiply and grow. He also promises that the people will live there as before, and that things will go better for them than at the beginning. The phrase "used to" is the meaning of the old wording, so it is rewritten here as "used to live." Livestock, such as cattle, are the animals meant here. In the end, the people will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into exile, its land lay in ruins, and its neighboring nations mocked it. Here God addresses the mountains of Israel and promises to restore the land and its people, not because of anything they deserved, but to show who He is.

For today: when your life feels like it lies in ruins, remember that God knows how to rebuild what has been destroyed. Trust that He can restore, and wait for His work with patience and faith.
exp.25:14:
God asks Tyre whether the coastlands will not tremble at the sound of its fall. He speaks of the cries of the wounded and of a great slaughter inside the city. "Thunder" is a very loud noise, and the "coastlands" refers to the shores and distant peoples that traded with Tyre.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich city, proud of its sea trade, and it had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own gain. The text announces its judgment, and the kings of the sea will be astonished when they see it. There are different opinions about how it was fulfilled, since Babylon is mentioned and then other conquerors.

For today: power and wealth do not give us true security. It is wise to live with humility, without rejoicing in the misfortune of others, and to trust in God rather than in what we have.
exp.39:33:
It says that the arches (the porch or vestibule) of this gate of the inner court faced toward the outer court. The posts (the pillars of the entrance) were decorated with palm trees, one on each side. To go up, there were eight steps.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting his vision. A guide leads him and measures the temple with a measuring reed. This takes place about twenty-five years after he was taken captive to Babylon, when the temple had already been destroyed. Scholars disagree about whether this temple was meant to be built literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something in the future. All agree that it shows order, holiness, and the presence of God.

Even the details of a gate matter: the palm trees and the steps suggest that approaching God is something worthy of care and reverence. Today we can come near to Him without haste, with respect and gratitude, knowing that God receives us.
exp.19:13:
He says that God, for the sake of his name, decided not to destroy Israel in the desert. In this way he kept his name from being dishonored before the nations that had seen him bring them out of Egypt. The phrase "I acted so that it would not be defiled" means that he acted so that his name would not be stained or despised. The nations are the pagan peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel during the exile. He reminds them of their history: although the people rebelled in the desert, despised his laws, and profaned the Sabbaths, God held back his anger. His reason was to protect the honor of his name before the other peoples, not because of Israel's merits.

For today: our lives represent God before others. We can ask him for help to live with integrity, and trust that his mercy is greater than our failures, but without taking it lightly.
exp.22:40:
She is described as sitting on a splendid couch of honor, with a well-prepared table set before her. The word translated as "couch" here refers to an elegant seat or divan. On that table she placed the incense and the oil that belonged to God. In other words, she used for shameful purposes what rightfully belonged to Him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In a parable, He compares Samaria and Jerusalem to two unfaithful sisters, Oholah and Oholibah. Through this, He denounces that His people sought foreign alliances and idols, and even mixed that idolatry with worship in the temple. Some scholars think the incense and oil recall sacred offerings, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: examine whether you are using for other purposes what God has given you, such as your time, your talents, or your possessions. Place them again at His service with gratitude and sincerity.
exp.15:49:
It says that Sodom and her daughters (the nearby cities) became full of pride and did detestable things before God. The reference to becoming proud means they grew haughty, and the word for "abomination" is something God hates. The phrase about God taking them away as he saw good means that God removed them from the scene according to his just judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. She thought herself better than others, but God shows her that her sin was even worse than Sodom's. The previous verse highlights pride, abundance without generosity, and failing to help the poor.

For today: when we have comfort and well-being, it is easy to forget those in need. Let us ask God for a humble and grateful heart, and this week let us look for one concrete way to help someone who needs it.
exp.16:21:
It says that God himself will take a tender branch from the top of a tall cedar and plant it on a high and lofty mountain. The tender top of the tree is what the verse calls the shoot taken from its highest twigs, and the new growth is the fresh sprouts. God does not leave the future in the hands of human kings; he acts himself.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Before this, King Zedekiah rebelled and was judged. Now God promises a new beginning. Many Christians see here a promise of the Messiah, a descendant of David, although the text speaks directly of the restoration of Israel.
