For today: when you feel that everything is over, remember that God can bring life out of what seems cut off. Trust that he knows how to begin again.
exp.25:20:
God says he will make Tyre into something that causes terror. "Terror" here means a ruin so great that it amazes and frightens everyone. It says she will no longer exist, that people will look for her and never find her. The phrase "though thou be sought for" speaks of a total and final disappearance.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud city, which rejoiced when Jerusalem fell, thinking it would gain more trade. God announces his judgment. The verses before this one use the image of the sea covering her. Some scholars see here a gradual destruction, and others see poetic and exaggerated language, because the region of Tyre remained inhabited afterward.

For today: do not put your security in money, success, or power, because none of these is firm. If you feel proud, ask God for a humble and grateful heart, one that trusts in him and cares for others.
exp.36:6:
He says that Ezekiel obeyed God and spoke to the dry bones. As he spoke, there was a noise, there was a shaking, and the bones began to come together, each bone with the one that belonged to it.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of a valley full of bones. According to the same chapter, those bones represent Israel, which in exile felt that its hope had died. God promises to restore their life and to rebuild them as a people.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, we can obey what God asks of us, even if it means speaking his word in faith, and trust that he can give life where we see only ruin. He works step by step.
exp.33:12:
God promises to bring out his sheep, who are his people, from the nations where they were scattered. He will gather them and bring them back to their own land. There he will care for them and feed them on the mountains of Israel, beside the streams and in all the inhabited places of the country.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel, that is, its leaders, because they abandoned the people. Now God says that he himself will be the one who cares for his flock. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of Jesus, the good shepherd, although this is interpreted in different ways.

If you feel lost or far away, remember that God seeks you and wants to care for you. Open your heart to him in prayer and look for a community of faith where you can be accompanied.
exp.47:4:
It says that the portion of land belonging to the tribe of Ephraim lies right beside that of Manasseh. Each strip runs from east to west, from the east side to the west side. The sea mentioned at the far end is the Mediterranean Sea.

Ezekiel's text is the same verse as the English reading above; "border" is the word used for the boundary or limit between the strips.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. In this final vision, God shows how the land would be divided among the twelve tribes, in orderly strips. Interpreters do not agree: some see it as something literal for the future, others as a symbol of restoration and of God's presence with his people.

For today: God takes care that each person has a place and a portion. You can rest in the assurance that He does not forget you, and also make room for others with generosity, without envy.
exp.37:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," an expression that identifies him as an ordinary human being. He is commanded to set his face against Gog, that is, to look at him directly and declare a message of judgment. Magog, Meshech and Tubal are names of peoples or regions; the phrase "chief prince" means the principal leader.

Who Gog is exactly is debated, and there is no single certain answer.

The Lord speaks, and he does so through Ezekiel, who was prophesying to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. This message announces that God will oppose a power that will come against his people. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some as historical events, others as something future or symbolic.

For today: God remains Lord over every power that may seem threatening. We can trust that he cares for his people and rest in his justice, without letting fear dominate us.
exp.46:6:
The explanation says that Ezekiel, as he came back along the edge of the river, saw that on both sides there were a great many trees. "Returning" means going back, "bank" is the edge of the water, and the "stream" here is the river that flows from the temple. "Very many" means a large number.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, who describes a vision God gave him. A guide led him to measure a river that flowed out from the temple and grew deeper and deeper. After he had seen it grow, he returned to the bank and discovered the trees. Many see in this an image of the life and healing that come from the presence of God, although it is understood in several ways. Some take it literally, others symbolically.

For today: just as trees grow beside water, we can seek God every day in prayer and in his Word. If we stay close to him, our lives can bear fruit and be a blessing to others.
exp.45:4:
It says that along with each ram offered, the prince was to present an ephah of grain offering. With the lambs he gave what he was able to, "as he shall be able to give," that is, according to his generosity. In addition, a hin of oil was added for each ephah. An ephah was a measure of dry goods (roughly 20 to 40 liters, according to estimates), and a hin was a measure of liquids, much smaller.

God speaks through Ezekiel in the vision of the new temple (chapters 40 to 48). There he gives rules for worship, the Sabbath, and the new moon. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence with his restored people.

For today: worshiping God includes order, but also a generous heart. Think about what you can give this week, according to your means, with joy and without pressure.
exp.15:35:
It says God speaks to Jerusalem, whom He presents as an unfaithful woman. Her shame and her exposure are her sin, which was uncovered before her lovers, that is, the nations she allied herself with. It was also uncovered before her idols, to whom she even offered her own children in sacrifice. Here "whoredoms" means spiritual unfaithfulness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The whole of chapter 16 uses the image of a marriage: God cared for Jerusalem, and she betrayed Him with other nations and gods. The verses that follow announce judgment for that unfaithfulness.

For today: examine what you give your trust to that belongs only to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Bring them to Him honestly, because He forgives and restores those who return to Him.
exp.38:16:
God commands the prophet Ezekiel to call the birds and the wild beasts to come to a great feast on the mountains of Israel. He calls the defeat of his enemies a "sacrifice," and the birds and beasts will eat flesh and drink blood.

The Lord God speaks to Ezekiel, and he does so with strong, vivid imagery. This is in the prophecy about Gog, a leader who would attack Israel. Scholars understand this in different ways: some see it as a literal future event, others as a symbol of God's final judgment against evil. In both cases, God has the last word.

For today: we can rest in the fact that God will do justice. So, instead of seeking revenge, let us trust in Him and keep doing good.
exp.42:26:
It says that when the seven days of preparing the altar are over, from the eighth day onward the priests may offer upon it the burnt offerings (offerings that were completely burned up for God) and the peace offerings (offerings of fellowship or thanksgiving). Then God promises: "and I will accept you, saith the Lord God."

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, within his vision of a new temple. First the altar had to be purified for seven days and set apart as holy. After that, the people could worship with confidence. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God does not accept us because of what we do, but because He himself prepares the way for us to draw near. Christians see that way fulfilled in Christ. We can pray without fear and without pretense, knowing that He receives us with pleasure.
exp.43:20:
It says that no priest was allowed to drink wine when he was about to enter the inner court of the temple, which was the place where they served directly before God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes in a vision a future temple. There he gives rules for the priests, so that they would guard the holiness of their service and not confuse what is sacred with what is ordinary. Christians interpret this vision in different ways: some see it in a literal way, others in a symbolic way. A similar rule appears in Leviticus 10:8-11.

For today: when you serve God, whether by praying, teaching, or helping others, do it with a clear mind and an attentive heart. Ask Him to help you avoid anything that clouds your judgment or distracts you from Him.
exp.45:10:
This verse states how much grain offering was to be given at the feasts and solemn assemblies: one ephah of flour for each bullock, and one ephah for each ram. For the lambs, each person gave what they were able to give. In addition, one hin of oil for each ephah. The ephah was a measure of capacity for dry goods, and the hin a measure for liquids. Its exact equivalence is debated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile, in his vision of a renewed temple and worship. These instructions set out how the people, together with the prince, were to worship. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways, and not all of them agree.

For today: God cares about orderly worship, but also about generous and sincere worship. Today we can give God our best, according to our means, with a grateful heart.
exp.11:12:
God says he will catch the prince like an animal in a net. The word for the net's trap is not used here; the verse simply speaks of the net. He will be brought to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, but he will not see it, and there he will die.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was living in exile among the captives. He acted out the exile that was coming upon Jerusalem. Nearly everyone understands the prince to be King Zedekiah. According to 2 Kings 25, he was captured, had his eyes put out, and was taken to Babylon. In this way what was said came true, that he would not see it.

For today: God's warnings are serious, but they aim to bring us to recognize him. It is not wise to trust our own plans when God calls us to obey. Today you can ask him to help you listen to him in time.
exp.32:10:
God swears by his own life that he takes no pleasure when a wicked person dies. What he desires is that the wicked person change direction and live. A "wicked" person is one who lives without honoring God; to "turn" means to come around and go back the other way. Then God calls his people with urgency: "Turn ye, turn ye," and asks with grief: "Why will ye die?"

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls a watchman, a sentinel who warns of danger. The people were in exile and were saying, "Our sins are wasting us away; how can we live?", almost without hope. God answers that there is a way forward: repentance. The verses that follow show that neither past goodness nor past wickedness decides everything, but the direction in which a person walks today.

For today: if you feel that your mistakes can no longer be remedied, God invites you to return to him now. Pray with sincerity and take one concrete step of change today.
exp.12:10:
He says God commands that warning be given to those who plaster it with loose mortar, that is, those who cover a weak wall with a thin layer of mud so it looks solid. That wall will fall. A heavy rain will come pouring down, along with hailstones and a stormy wind that will tear it down.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The false prophets said there was peace when there was no peace, and the people built a weak wall, the wall of false security. They decorated it with pleasant lies. God warns them that their deception will be exposed when judgment comes.

For today: it is not enough for something to look good on the outside. Ask yourself whether your life, your decisions, and what you believe are built on the truth of God, even when it hurts, and not on comforting words that only soothe for a moment.
exp.26:23:
The passage says that merchants from various peoples came to the city of Tyre to sell goods of great value: cloaks of deep blue-violet, embroidered work, bundles of fine clothing tied with cords, and cedar wood. Merchants are traders, and to trade means to carry on business.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a great trading city by the sea. This list of goods shows its enormous wealth and influence. But the text that follows announces that this glory will sink like a ship broken by the wind. God warns against the pride that grows out of prosperity.

For today: We can enjoy and work with what God gives us, but without setting our hearts on money or success. Ask yourself: is my security in my possessions or in God?
exp.40:0:
He says that the guide of the vision brought Ezekiel to the temple, that is, to the part called the holy place or sanctuary. There he measured the posts, which are the columns on each side of the entrance. Each post measured six cubits in width. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about half a meter. The word for the tent is understood here as a reference to the width of the ancient sacred tent, though some scholars explain it in other ways.

Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. In a vision, God shows him a new temple, and a guide measures it carefully. This takes place after Jerusalem was destroyed, to give the people hope. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: God is a God of order and of promises. Even when everything seems to have fallen apart, you can trust that He has a plan and that He desires to dwell among His people.
exp.24:8:
He says God will "open the side" of Moab, that is, leave its border without defense. The border cities, which were its pride and "desirable lands" (beautiful and valuable), would be left exposed: Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim. "Border" here means the boundary or edge of the territory.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Moab said that Judah was just like the other nations, as if their God had nothing special with them. By this, it looked down on Judah and on the Lord himself. So God announces judgment. The texts that follow speak of peoples from the east who would take the region, though the text gives no further details about who they would be.

For today: God takes seriously the contempt shown toward his people and his name. We can avoid mocking the faith of others or rejoicing when someone falls, and trust that God is just and cares for his own.
exp.20:13:
God tells Ezekiel to deliver a message and to strike his hands together, a gesture that shows anger or grief. The sword is to be "doubled the third time," meaning it will strike with full force again and again. It is a sword of death and great slaughter, from which no one will be able to escape. "It will enter their private chambers" means that it will reach everyone.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The people and their leaders had rejected God, and judgment would come by the sword of Babylon. Interpreters explain the gesture of the hands and the "doubling" of the sword in different ways, but the general meaning is a severe and certain judgment.

For today: God speaks seriously about sin, but he also gives warnings so that we will return to him. Today we can listen to his voice with humility and correct our course before it is too late.
exp.40:11:
It says that, on the west side of the temple, there was another separate building that measured seventy cubits in width. Its walls were five cubits thick, and its length was ninety cubits. The word "separate place" refers to the open ground or area set apart that surrounded the temple. A cubit was an ancient measure, about 45 to 50 centimeters.

Ezekiel recounts what he saw in a vision, while a guide who looked like a man measured the temple for him. He was among the exiles in Babylon. Scholars debate whether this vision speaks of a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence and his order among his people. The details of this verse are difficult to interpret with certainty.

God cares about order, holiness, and his presence among his people. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is a cared-for and set-apart place for him in our lives. Setting aside a fixed time each day to pray and read his Word is a simple step.
exp.26:24:
The explanation says the ships of Tarshish were like the trading caravans of your commerce: they carried your merchandise over the sea. "Companies" here is understood as groups or fleets of ships that traveled together. Thanks to them, Tyre was filled with riches and grew greatly, standing in the midst of the seas. Tarshish was probably a distant port, though it is not known for certain where it was.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Tyre, a very rich and proud port city. The passage describes its great trade with many peoples. But the verses that follow announce that this greatness will sink like a ship destroyed by a storm.

Today we can ask ourselves what our security rests on. Having work, possessions, or success is not wrong, but trusting only in these is fragile. Let us first place our trust in God and use what we have with humility and generosity.
exp.33:24:
God promises to make a "covenant of peace" with his people, that is, a firm commitment to protect them and give them tranquility. He will remove the "evil beasts" from the land, that is, wild and dangerous animals. Because of this, his people will be able to live in the wilderness safely, which means with security and without fear, and even sleep peacefully in the woods.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, he has criticized the bad shepherds of Israel, who abused the sheep. Now he promises a faithful shepherd, called David. Many Christians see here a reference to Jesus, a descendant of David. Some interpreters understand the beasts literally, and others as a symbol of enemies and threats.

For today: if Christ is your shepherd, you can rest in his care even in places that seem dangerous. Speak to him about your fears tonight and hand them over to him before you sleep.
exp.19:37:
It says that God will separate the rebels from the rest of his people. "I will separate" means to take out or set apart. He will bring out of the countries where they live in exile those who rose up against him, but he will not let them enter the land of Israel. In the end, the people will recognize that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. He reminds them how he corrected their ancestors in the wilderness after they left Egypt. He will do the same now: he will bring them under the rod, like a shepherd who counts and examines his sheep, to tell the faithful apart from the rebels. His goal is a people who truly serve him.

For today: God is not satisfied with a faith that only looks good on the outside. Examine your heart honestly and ask him to help you obey him, knowing that his correction seeks to restore you.
exp.12:1:
God says to Ezekiel: "Son of man," a way of addressing him as an ordinary human being, that he should prophesy against the prophets of Israel. These prophets spoke "out of their own hearts," that is, from their own ideas, not from what God was saying. Even so, God commands them: "Hear ye the word of the Lord." They too were to listen. The word "Hear" means "listen."

The Lord is speaking, and his messenger is Ezekiel, who prophesied during the exile in Babylon. God confronts those who announced comfortable and false messages, claiming they came from him. The verses that follow call them "foolish" because they followed their own spirit and "saw nothing."

For today: before we repeat or teach something as "the word of God," let us compare it with the Bible. And when we speak of God, let us do so with humility, without confusing our opinions with his voice.
exp.42:0:
He tells us that a guide brought Ezekiel to the gate of the temple area that faces east. It is a short step, but it prepares what comes next.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks and recounts a vision he received. Earlier, in chapter 10 and following, he saw the glory of God leave the temple because of judgment on the people. Now, in a vision of the new temple, he is brought to the east gate, the gate through which that glory returns, as the verses that follow show. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple points to a literal future temple or to a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: God knows how to lead us step by step, even when we feel that He has withdrawn. We can pray and look with hope toward where He may yet work in our lives.
exp.25:6:
God announces that he is going to bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, against the city of Tyre. He comes "from the north," and he is called "king of kings" because he ruled over other kings. He arrives with a full army: horses, chariots, horsemen, companies, and many people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a wealthy city, proud of its trade, and it had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 26:2). God declares that he will judge that pride and that lack of compassion. Babylon would be the instrument of that judgment.

For today: God rules over the nations and the powerful, even when they do not acknowledge him. For that reason it is wise to avoid pride and not to rejoice in the misfortune of others. We can trust that God is just and that he is in control.
exp.46:21:
It says that, when the land was divided, the people were to cast lots to give inheritance to the Israelites and also to the foreigners who lived among them and had already had children there. Those foreigners would be treated "as those born in the country," that is, as if they had been born in Israel. The phrase "as those born in the country" means they are treated as native-born, and "had children among you" means they have built their family there.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel and the division of the land among the tribes. The preceding verses set the boundaries, and the following one clarifies that the foreigner would receive his share in the tribe where he lived. Interpreters debate whether this is fulfilled literally or whether it announces, in symbolic terms, the inclusion of all peoples in the people of God.

Today it reminds us that God opens the door to those who seem to be outsiders. We can welcome the immigrant or the newcomer into the church and the community, and treat them as one of the family.
exp.42:9:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to show the people of Israel the plan of the new temple that he has seen in a vision. He wants them to be ashamed of their sins and to measure the pattern, that is, to study the design and the measurements of the building. The plan is the blueprint or design.

He speaks himself, during the exile in Babylon. Before this, the kings and the people had placed their idols and their tombs next to the temple, and so they had defiled it. Now God promises to dwell with them forever. Interpreters differ on whether this temple would be built literally, whether it is an image of hope, or whether it points to the future.

For today: sincere shame over sin is not meant to crush us, but to turn us back to God. We can ask him to show us what things we have placed close to him and to help us let them go, so that we may live near him with a clean heart.
exp.46:5:
Here the guide asks Ezekiel, "Son of man, hast thou seen this?", that is, "did you really take in what you have just experienced?" Then he takes him back and causes him to return along the brink of the river.

Ezekiel is in a vision of the future temple. A guide, who looks like a man with a measuring reed, leads him along a river that flows out from the temple. At every thousand cubits the waters are deeper, until it can no longer be crossed on foot. The question invites him to reflect before he sees the trees and the healing that come afterward. Some see here a symbol of God's blessing; others expect a literal fulfillment.

For today: do not rush past what God shows you. Stop and meditate, and ask yourself what he is teaching you. His work in us often grows slowly, and he invites us to trust him more deeply.
exp.31:3:
God says he will leave Pharaoh lying on dry land, abandoned out in the open field. There the birds of the sky and the wild animals will feed on him. The phrase about the surface of the field is explained as the ground's surface, and the word for filling him completely means he will be satisfied with them completely. It is a strong image of total defeat.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to raise a lament over Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He is compared to a crocodile or sea monster that stirred up the rivers. Scholars understand this as announcing God's judgment against the pride and violence of Egypt, which believed itself invincible. The image is poetic, not a literal description.

For today: no human power or success is above God. If we ever feel tempted to trust in our own strength or to treat others badly, let us remember that God resists the proud. We can rest in Him with humility.
exp.19:28:
God asks with irony: "What is the high place whereunto ye go?" The word "Bamah" in Hebrew means "high place," and here it sounds as if he were saying, "What is this so-called high place you go to?" He says that the name remained "unto this day," that is, until the days of Ezekiel. The verse's own wording "whereunto" is simply the King James way of saying "to which."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel who are exiled in Babylon. He reminds them that their ancestors, as soon as they entered the promised land, worshiped on hills and under leafy trees. The high places were pagan sanctuaries. God shows them that their children are repeating the same sin, even offering their children to the fire.

For today: God invites us to examine where we go looking for help, peace, or meaning. If we have inherited customs that do not honor God, we can leave them behind and worship him his way, with sincerity and obedience.
exp.36:24:
It says that the people of Israel will live again in the land that God gave to Jacob, the same land where their ancestors lived. There their children and grandchildren will live forever, meaning for a very long time or permanently. Also, "my servant David" will be their prince, or ruler, forever.

The words are spoken by God through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. The people were scattered and discouraged. God promises to restore them, cleanse them from sin, and make with them a covenant of peace. Many Christians see in "David" a reference to Jesus, a descendant of David. Others see a promise for Israel as a nation. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God keeps his promises even when everything seems lost. If you feel far from him or defeated, remember that he restores, cleanses, and guides. Trust in Christ, the Shepherd, and seek to obey him with hope.
exp.23:15:
God tells Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," that he is going to take away suddenly "the delight of your eyes," that is, the person he loved most and whose presence gladdened him. Here it refers to his wife. He also orders him not to wail with mourning songs, not to weep, and not to let his tears fall.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in the middle of the exile in Babylon. Earlier he has announced judgment on Jerusalem. The death of his wife would be a sign for the people: in the same way they would lose the temple, which they valued so highly. God speaks with firmness, but the text also shows Ezekiel's pain.

For today: when we go through losses we do not understand, we can bring our pain honestly to God, trusting that he is with us and that our suffering does not go unnoticed by him.
exp.22:15:
She saw the images of the Chaldeans painted on the wall, and immediately fell in love with them. Then she sent messengers to Chaldea to invite them. "As soon as she saw them" means "as soon as she saw them." The Chaldeans are the Babylonians.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), as an image of an unfaithful people. Oholibah sought alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting the LORD. The "harlotry" here describes spiritual and political unfaithfulness. Scholars agree on this, although they debate some historical details.

For today: what we gaze at persistently can awaken desires that pull us away from God. Be careful what you let in through your eyes and your heart, and when you feel drawn to something that separates you from Him, stop and ask Him again to be your greatest treasure.
exp.20:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," that is, simply a human being. He tells him to set his face toward Jerusalem, meaning to look toward the city with firmness, like someone about to deliver a serious message. To pour out a word means to preach with force. The holy places were the sites of worship, and to prophesy means to announce what God says.

The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had fallen into idolatry and injustice. This message opens an announcement of judgment: God will compare his judgment to a sword that will come out of its sheath.

For today: God does not delight in remaining silent before sin, but he always gives warning first. If you hear his correction today, do not harden your heart; draw near to him in humility, and change in time what he shows you.
exp.18:7:
The explanation says that the neighboring nations joined together against the young lion, that is, the king the chapter is about. They set a net for him, as one does with wild beasts, and he was caught in the pit or trap they had dug. The phrase about being caught is simply "he was taken," that is, he was captured. The nearby regions are the surrounding areas.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament over the princes of Israel. Many understand that this young lion is Jehoahaz or Jehoiachin, kings of Judah who were carried into captivity, although the text does not give a name and this is debated. The song shows that his violence and pride ended in defeat and exile.

For today: what we sow with our power or our character sooner or later reaches us. Let us ask God for humility to use well whatever authority we have, caring for others instead of taking advantage of them.
exp.37:14:
Gog will come from his place, from the far northern regions, accompanied by many peoples. They all come riding on horses, forming a great multitude and a mighty army. The phrase about riding on horses is simply a reference to horses. The "far northern regions" refers to the outermost limits or borders of the north.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing Gog. Israel lives in peace, and God announces that a huge army will attack it. The verses that follow say that God himself allows this in order to show his holiness before the nations. Interpreters disagree: some see a historical event, others a future event, and others a symbolic language of the final conflict between evil and God.

For today: even when the powers of the world seem enormous, God remains in control. We can rest in him and not let fear of the news take control of us.
exp.19:30:
It says that Israel kept presenting its offerings and even made its sons pass through the fire, that is, offered them in sacrifice to idols. By doing this they defiled themselves, and they were still doing it up to this very day. For this reason God asks: "Shall I be enquired of by you?" He swears by his own life that he will not answer them, meaning that he will not listen when they come to seek him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders of Israel had come to inquire of him, but God reminds them of their history of idolatry going back for generations. He does not want them to seek him while they continue serving other gods.

For today: we cannot mix the worship of God with whatever takes his place in the heart. Ask God to show you what competes with him, and surrender it to him sincerely.
exp.18:4:
This verse tells how the lioness, seeing that her hope in her first whelp had been lost, chose another of her whelps and made him a strong young lion. The phrase "made him a young lion" means that she set him up as a young lion, that is, as a king. The idea of a long wait is shown by her long time of waiting.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over the princes of Israel. The lioness is usually understood as the nation or the mother of the royal line of Judah, and the whelps as kings, such as Jehoahaz, who was taken to Egypt. The second whelp is identified in several ways: as Jehoiakim or Zedekiah. Scholars do not agree on this.

When a hope falls apart, it is wise to seek God's direction before placing trust in another human solution. A new plan made only on impulse can repeat the same mistakes.
exp.28:13:
God says he will bring back the Egyptians who were taken captive and scattered. He will return them to Pathros, the region of southern Egypt, which was their land of origin. The phrase "I will bring again" is the same as "I will bring back," and "a base kingdom" means a humble kingdom, without greatness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt had been proud and unreliable for Israel, which at times sought its help instead of trusting in God. For this reason God announces judgment, but also a limited restoration. The forty years can be understood literally or as a symbolic period; scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God corrects pride, but he can also restore in humility. If today you trust your money, your strength, or your connections more than God, ask him to teach you to depend on him. His discipline is not always the end of the story.
exp.44:6:
The explanation says the prince will have his own portion of land on both sides of the district set apart for the sanctuary and of the city's allotted plot. That land stretches from west to east, from one end to the other. The word "separated" refers to the portion set apart for God, and "allotted land" refers to a parcel assigned to a particular use.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He divides the land in an orderly way: first the sanctuary, then the Levites, the city, and the prince. The verses that follow explain the reason: that the princes should stop oppressing the people, because they now have their own land. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision is to be read literally, symbolically, or as referring to the future.

For today: whoever has authority or resources should be content with what God has given them and use their position to serve with justice, never to take advantage of others.
exp.32:11:
This verse says that the good someone did in the past will not save them if they now turn away from God in rebellion. Nor does the past wickedness of a wicked person condemn them forever if they turn away from it. "Ungodliness" is living without reverence for God; "hindrance" is an obstacle; and "turns" means that a person repents and changes direction.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a discouraged people. The Israelites, already in exile, were saying that their sins were crushing them and that there was no hope left. God answers that he does not desire the death of anyone, but that all should turn back to him and live.

For today: do not live either on your past mistakes or on your past merits. If you have failed, God invites you to return today. If you are walking well, keep trusting and obeying each day, without boasting of what you have already done.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying," is an older way of saying what the verse states plainly: a message from the Lord came to him. It is how Ezekiel usually introduces what follows, showing that it does not come from his own ideas but from God.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel is the messenger. He lived among the exiles of Judah in Babylon. In this chapter, God uses the story of two sisters to speak about Samaria and Jerusalem, and about their unfaithfulness to Him. It is strong language, meant to awaken the conscience of the people.

For today: before we speak or give our opinion, it is worth pausing to listen to God. We can read the Bible with humility, willing to receive even uncomfortable messages, because God speaks to correct us and also to heal us.
exp.23:17:
Ezekiel says he spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening his wife died. The next morning he did what God had commanded him: he did not weep openly or observe the usual mourning. The sentences explaining the old spellings and the words "bonnet" and "veil" are removed here, since those words do not appear in the verse you are reading.

Ezekiel is a prophet and speaks in the first person. God took away his wife, "the delight of his eyes," and asked him not to show mourning. His silence was a sign for Israel: soon Jerusalem and the temple would be destroyed, and the grief would be so great that there would be no way to express it. The people asked him what all this meant.

For today: God sometimes asks us to obey in the midst of very deep sorrow, and we do not always understand why. We can be honest with Him about our pain and ask Him for strength to keep trusting Him, even when the path costs us a great deal.
exp.23:10:
It says that, after the meat has been cooked, God will set the empty pot on the coals. It gets so hot that its bottom burns, and the dirt stuck to it melts and the scum is consumed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Jerusalem is compared to a pot, full of violence and injustice (the "city of bloods"). With this image, God announces that the city will be purified by the fire of judgment, because it did not want to cleanse itself beforehand.

For today: we should not ignore God's calls to change. If he shows us something dirty in our hearts, such as resentment or deceit, let us respond quickly with repentance, trusting in his forgiveness and his grace.
exp.16:23:
God says that all the trees of the field, that is, all the nations and peoples, will recognize that He is the Lord. He brings down the one who is very high and lifts up the one who is low. He dries up the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish. He ends by saying that what He has said, He will do.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel at a time when Judah was in crisis and many were in exile in Babylon. The kings of Judah had trusted in political alliances and not in God. God promises to take a tender shoot from a cedar and plant it on the high mountain of Israel. Many Christians see here a hope that points to the Messiah, although the text speaks first of the restoration of God's people.

For today: even if you feel small or dry inside, God can give you new life. Trust in Him, not in your own strength, and do not think of yourself as more than you are.
exp.11:17:
God tells Ezekiel to eat his bread trembling and drink his water with shaking and anxiety. That is, he must eat and drink like someone who is afraid.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. This action is a visible sign, a message acted out. As the verses that follow explain, it represented how the inhabitants of Jerusalem would eat in fear when judgment came and the land was left desolate because of the violence of its people. God wanted them to understand the consequences of their wickedness.

Today we can remember that God speaks in earnest, but also that he warns so that we will turn back to him. Ask yourself: is there something God is pointing out to me that I have ignored? Answer him today with humility and obedience.
exp.37:21:
God says that he himself will take up the case, that is, enter into judgment and fight, against Gog, the enemy leader. He will use disease, violent death, and a huge storm: heavy rain, hail, fire, and burning stones, as at Sodom. This will fall on his armies and on the allied peoples as well.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapters 38 and 39 he announces that a great alliance will attack his restored people, and that he will defend them. Interpreters disagree: some see it as a future historical event, others as a symbolic picture of God's final victory. The purpose, according to the next verse, is that everyone will know that he is the LORD.

For today: when evil seems strong, remember that final justice belongs to God. Trust him, pray, and do not repay evil with evil.
exp.15:38:
God says he will hand Jerusalem over to her former allies. They will tear down her "high place" (the site where she worshiped idols) and pull down her altars. They will also strip her of her clothing and her jewels, and leave her completely naked and exposed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter He compares Jerusalem to a woman He cared for and clothed, but who was unfaithful to Him by seeking idols and alliances with other nations. Those nations she turned to would become the instrument of judgment. Many understand this as a reference to Jerusalem's fall to Babylon.

For today: What we put in place of God does not protect us, and sooner or later it leaves us exposed. Today you can ask yourself what you trust more than Him, and return to God with sincerity. His judgment aims to lead to repentance.
exp.31:28:
This verse says that Edom (Idumea), with its kings and all its princes, will also be in the place of the dead. Although they were powerful and strong, they fell by the sword and will lie down with those who were not part of Israel, the peoples outside the covenant, and with those who go down to the grave, that is, those who die.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt and Pharaoh. Ezekiel describes a place of the dead where the powerful nations that fell are gathered together. Edom appears as an example: its strength did not save it. Scholars understand the details of this place in different ways, since it is poetic language.

For today: power, fame, and money do not protect us from the end of life. It is wise to live with humility, to use well what we have, and to trust in God, who alone endures.
exp.27:24:
God says that one day he will gather his people Israel, who are scattered among the nations. When he does, he will show his holiness, that is, that he is pure and worthy of respect, before the eyes of all the peoples. Israel will live again in the land God gave to Jacob, whom he calls "my servant."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had announced judgment on Sidon, a neighboring city that had mistreated Israel. Now he moves on to a promise of restoration. Some believers understand that it was already fulfilled in part with the return from exile; others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: even when we feel that everything is broken or far away, God keeps what he promises. We can wait on him with patience, trusting that he knows how to gather and restore what seemed lost.
exp.16:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying," is the familiar way the prophet introduces a new message.

The one speaking is the Lord, and he is addressing Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon together with other Israelites. This verse opens a new message. As the following passage shows, God will ask him to tell a parable about eagles and a cedar, directed to the house of Israel. The full meaning is explained later in the chapter.

For today: before we speak or make a decision, it is good to pause and listen to God. We can read his Word with attention and humility, knowing that he wants to speak to us and guide us, even when circumstances are difficult.
exp.44:11:
God establishes that the shekel, the basic unit of weight, will equal twenty gerahs (a gerah was a very small weight). He then adds 20, 25 and 15 shekels, which make 60, and says that this will be a maneh. This verse is difficult, and some older translations understand it differently, so there is no single certain explanation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a restored people and a new temple. Shortly before, he had rebuked the princes of Israel for their violence and abuse. For this reason he requires fair weights and measures, so that no one cheats when buying, selling or giving offerings.

For today: God cares about honesty in everyday life. Be just in your work, in your accounts and in your dealings, without deceiving or taking advantage of anyone. That too is a way of worshiping him.
exp.29:18:
God says he will bring punishments on Egypt, and the result will be that they recognize who he is. The words "I will execute judgments" mean that God will pronounce sentence and carry it out. The phrase "they shall know that I am the Lord" is one that Ezekiel repeats many times: God acts to make himself known.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. Egypt was a nation proud of its strength, and Judah had trusted in Egypt instead of trusting in God. Before this verse, the fall of its cities, the captivity of its people, and the end of its pride are announced. Scholars agree that this is a historical judgment against Egypt, although the details of how it was fulfilled are debated.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, work, or people. All of that can break. Rest in God, who is the only one who never fails.
exp.44:24:
It says that in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day, when the feast arrives, the prince must offer the same things as during the seven days before it (those of the Passover). That includes the sin offering, the burnt offering (what was burned up entirely), the grain offering, and the oil. Measures of quantity are the ephah and the hin, which are not mentioned here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a new temple and an ordered worship (chapters 40 to 48). This feast of the seventh month seems to be the Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths. Scholars understand this vision in several ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of restoration and of Christ. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God values consistency and order in worship. We can seek Him faithfully, not only in special moments, but in a regular and sincere way.
exp.21:11:
It says that in Jerusalem people accepted bribes to kill innocent people, lent money charging abusive interest (the words for "usury and increase" refer to excessive profit on a loan), and robbed their neighbors through violence. All of this happened because they had forgotten God.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He is accusing Jerusalem of serious sins: injustice, sexual abuse, violence, and greed. The verse shows the root of the problem: forgetting God. When they stopped keeping him in mind, they stopped seeing people as valuable and used them for their own gain.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in our work, our businesses, or our debts, we treat others with justice. Remembering that God sees us helps us to earn our living honestly and not to take advantage of those in need.
exp.26:20:
It says that Arabia and all the princes of Kedar traded with Tyre. They sold her lambs, rams, and male goats, that is, small livestock. "Fairs" are markets, and "merchants of your hand" means they dealt directly with her. Kedar was a nomadic tribe of the desert, a descendant of Ishmael.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a very wealthy port city. He describes her trading relationships with many peoples to show her greatness and her pride. Later in the same chapter, he announces that this glory will sink like a ship in the sea.

For today: wealth and success may seem like a firm foundation, but they are not. Today we can thank God for what we have, work with honesty, and place our trust not in money but in Him.
exp.19:20:
The explanation says that the children of that generation, who came out of Egypt, also rebelled against God. They did not follow his ordinances (his commands), nor did they keep his rights (his righteous laws). Those laws gave life to whoever practiced them. They also profaned the sabbaths, that is, they treated them as common. For this reason God said he would pour out his wrath on them in the wilderness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel during the exile in Babylon. He recounts their history to show that their rebellion is not new. Even so, the following text says that God held back his hand for the sake of his name.

For today: obedience to God is not an empty burden but a path of life. Today you can ask him for help to obey him in something specific, trusting in his patience and his mercy.
exp.33:3:
The explanation says that Israel's leaders failed to care for the weakest people. They did not strengthen the weak sheep, did not heal the sick one, did not bind up the one with the broken leg, did not bring back the one that had wandered off and was lost in the hills, and did not search for the one that was lost. Instead, they ruled over the people with harshness and violence.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He calls the kings and leaders the shepherds, who took advantage of the people instead of caring for them. God rebukes them because the sheep are his, and he saw them scattered and without protection.

For today: if you lead others, in your family, your church, or your work, ask yourself whom you have neglected. This week, reach out to someone who is weak or discouraged, listen to them, and help them with tenderness, not pressure.
exp.43:4:
God speaks to Ezekiel and asks him to pay close attention: to set his heart, look with his eyes, and listen with his ears. What the Lord is going to tell him concerns the rules (the instructions) and the laws of the house of the Lord. He must also notice carefully who may enter the temple and who must leave the sanctuary.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel has just seen the glory of God filling the temple in a vision, and he fell face down on the ground. Right away comes a message of correction to Israel, which had allowed foreigners who were uncircumcised in heart to serve in the sanctuary. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways, but all of them see the theme of holiness.

For today: when you read the Bible or pray at church, do not do it distracted. God asks for complete attention: heart, eyes, and ears. Before you read, offer a brief prayer asking him to speak to you and to help you obey.
exp.33:18:
The explanation says that the weaker sheep have to feed on trampled grass and drink muddied water, because the strong sheep first ate the best and then spoiled what was left.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel, who looked after themselves and not after the flock. Now he addresses the strong sheep, who were also mistreating the weak. God promises to judge between one sheep and another. Many understand the sheep to represent the people, and the passage to criticize the powerful who took advantage of the most needy.

For today: it is not enough to take only what is ours. Ask yourself whether what you do, buy, or waste leaves something good for others. This week, look for a concrete way to share with or care for someone who has fewer resources.
exp.19:17:
God says that, while the people were in the wilderness, he spoke to the second generation, the children. He asked them not to follow the customs and the rules of their parents, and not to make themselves unclean with their idols. "Ordinances" are rules or customs; "defile" means to become spiritually dirty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The leaders of the people come to consult him, and God reminds them of their history: their parents rebelled in the wilderness, but God was patient and did not destroy them. Now he calls the children to choose another path, the path of obeying him.

For today: not everything we inherit is good. We can be thankful for the good in our family, but we can also examine, with humility, the harmful habits or customs that pass from generation to generation. With God's help, we can decide to walk differently and to follow his Word.
exp.23:7:
God says that, because Jerusalem has provoked his anger, he will do justice. The blood she spilled will not stay hidden: he will set it upon a smooth, hard rock, where no one can cover it. Here "vengeance" means justice that answers evil, not a whim of anger.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to a dirty pot, full of violence and injustice. In the law, spilled blood was covered with earth (Leviticus 17:13). But Jerusalem left her blood in plain sight, as if defying God, and he leaves it in plain sight so that her guilt may be seen.

For today: God sees what we try to hide. Instead of covering our faults, we can confess them honestly and seek his forgiveness, for he is faithful to cleanse us (1 John 1:9).
exp.39:35:
This verse describes the measurements of the north gate of the temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. It mentions its little chambers (the side rooms), the posts of the entrance, the arches (the covered passageways), and the windows. The whole structure measured fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. One cubit was roughly half a meter, though its exact length is debated.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives this vision from God. A guide with a measuring rod leads him through the temple, gate by gate. Many see in this a promise of hope and restoration for a broken people. Scholars disagree on whether the temple should be understood literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: God cares about details and does things with order. We can trust that He is also interested in the details of our lives, and draw near to Him with reverence and hope.
exp.28:7:
God himself declares a punishment against Egypt: he will bring a sword, that is, war and invasion, and he will cut off both people and animals. It is strong language to describe a great destruction.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the pharaoh and Egypt. Egypt had been like a fragile reed on which Israel leaned when seeking help, and it failed them. In addition, the pharaoh felt he owned the Nile, as if everything were his own doing. Scholars often connect this prophecy with the invasions of Babylon, though the text does not give all the details.

For today: trusting in power, money, or human alliances as if they were the safest things can leave us wounded. We can be thankful for what we have, but place our final trust in God, who does not fail.
exp.43:3:
In this verse, an angel leads Ezekiel to the north gate, in front of the temple. There the prophet looks and sees that the glory of the Lord, his bright and powerful presence, filled the house. Before that vision, Ezekiel falls on his face in a sign of reverence and humility.

Ezekiel writes this in exile, within a vision of the temple. Earlier, the glory had entered through the east gate, and for that reason that gate was shut. Shortly after, God commands him to pay attention to the rules of the temple and to confront Israel for its abominations. First he sees God's holiness; then comes the call to correct.

For today: before asking something of God, or correcting others, take a moment to acknowledge who He is. Standing in His presence with humility prepares us to listen and to obey.
exp.20:12:
God says that the sword of judgment has already been tested, meaning it is ready and proven. He asks what will happen if that sword despises even the scepter, which is the symbol of the king and his authority. The answer is that the scepter "shall be no more": not even royal power will be spared.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and its princes because of their sin. This verse is difficult in the original, and scholars translate and interpret it in various ways. Even so, the general message is clear: neither power nor titles deliver anyone from God's judgment.

For today: do not rely on your position, your success, or your merits to feel secure before God. In humility, ask him to correct your heart before sin grows.
exp.37:15:
It says that Gog, an enemy leader, will advance against Israel like a dark cloud covering the whole land. This will happen "in the latter days," that is, at a time still to come. God himself says he will bring Gog, so that the nations will know him when he shows his holiness before their eyes. The holiness and power of God will be recognized by all.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to a people in exile. He promises them that they will live safely in their land, but that there will be a final attack. Interpreters differ about Gog: some see a literal future event, others a symbol of evil against God's people. In the end, God appears as the one who is in control.

For today: when the world seems threatening or confusing, we can trust that God still reigns and will accomplish his purposes. Rest in him instead of living in fear.
exp.20:30:
God says he will pour out his anger on the people, like a fire that is kindled. He will hand them over to men who are "reckless," that is, violent and brutal, and to people who are "skilled in destruction." It is a very harsh sentence of judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, and the message is directed to the Ammonites, who were rejoicing at the fall of Jerusalem. Some scholars think the text also refers to Jerusalem itself. False prophecies had given empty confidence, and God responds with justice because wickedness had reached its limit.

For today: do not cling to comfortable messages that keep silent about the truth. Examine your life with humility, and if there is anything crooked in it, return to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.39:9:
This verse describes the eastern gate of the temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. On each side of its passage there were three small chambers, or little rooms, and all six were of the same size. The "posts" are the pillars or uprights that formed the entrance, and they too were the same on one side and on the other. The "measure" refers to the exact size they had.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision from God. A man with a measuring reed guides him through a new temple and shows him every detail. This happens in a time of grief, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways.

God is a God of order, and He cares about the way we draw near to Him. We can ask Him to bring balance and steadiness into our daily lives, so that we live with integrity in the small things and in the great ones.
exp.42:6:
God tells Ezekiel that the temple is the place of his throne and of the soles of his feet, that is, where he reigns and makes his presence known. He promises to live there with Israel forever. He also says that the people and their kings will no longer defile his holy name with their whoredom, which here means idolatry and unfaithfulness to God, nor with the carcasses of their kings, probably their tombs or idols near the temple (this is understood in several ways).

God speaks in a vision that Ezekiel receives after the exile in Babylon. His glory fills the house. Before, the people had placed their impure things right next to the temple, and that is why judgment came. Now God promises a new beginning with pure worship.

For today: God wants to live close to you, but he wants a clean heart with no rivals. Ask him today what you have placed beside him, and ask for help to remove it and give him first place.
exp.34:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase that the reader sees in the King James Version, "Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying," is the way the book marks the start of a new message. The name God is given in the text is the Lord, the name of God.

The one speaking is God, and the one receiving the message is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles from Judah in Babylon. The verses that follow show that the message is about Mount Seir, that is, the region of Edom. The Edomites lived there, neighbors of Israel, who according to the book acted with hostility against God's people. God announces that he is going to judge them.

For today: God speaks, and we can hear him in his Word. Before we give our opinion or react to injustice, let us begin by opening the Bible with attention and humility, trusting that God sees everything and acts with justice.
exp.30:9:
God says that, because this great tree grew very tall, it set its top among the thick boughs, and its heart was filled with pride because of its height. The phrase "you lifted yourself up" means that you rose up or thought yourself superior. The "top" is the highest part, the crown of the tree.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He directs this message to the pharaoh of Egypt, who is compared to a huge cedar, just as Assyria was before. Many understand the tree to represent the power and glory of a nation that believed itself invincible. God reminds him that his greatness was a gift from God, and for that reason He announces that his pride will bring his fall.

Everything good we have, such as talents, success, or position, comes from God. When we begin to feel superior, it is wise to pause, give thanks, and serve with humility.
exp.15:61:
He says that God himself will establish, or make firm, his covenant with Jerusalem, the unfaithful people he is addressing. "I will establish" means to make something sure and secure. The result will be that she "shall know" that God is the Lord, meaning she will truly know him through his faithfulness and his forgiveness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The whole of chapter 16 describes Jerusalem as a wife who abandoned her Lord. Even so, at the end God promises to remember his covenant and renew it, not because she deserves it, but out of his grace. The verses around it say that she will feel shame when she remembers her sin.

For today: when you fail, do not run from God or sink into guilt. Acknowledge your wrong with humility and trust that his faithfulness is firmer than yours. His forgiveness leads us to know him better.
exp.47:2:
The explanation says that the tribe of Naphtali receives a strip of land next to that of Asher, and that it stretches from east to west, from the eastern side to the sea (the Mediterranean). "Border" means boundary or edge. "Other" means "another part" of the land that was divided out.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. In his final vision a restored land is described, divided into horizontal strips for the twelve tribes, running from north to south. Naphtali is the third from the north. Interpreters differ: some see it as a promise for the restored Israel, others as a spiritual or future picture.

God does not forget anyone; each tribe has its assigned place. Today we can trust that God also has a place and a purpose for you. Rest in his care and serve with joy where he has placed you.
exp.42:1:
Ezekiel says he saw the glory of God coming from the east. Its sound was like the sound of many waters, something strong and awe-inspiring, and the earth shone with that glory. The word "glory" speaks of God's bright and majestic presence.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, speaks during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, in another vision, he had seen the glory of God leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now, in a vision of a restored temple, he sees the glory returning through the eastern gate. It is a message of hope: God did not abandon his people forever. Interpreters debate whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God wants to dwell among his people. If you feel you have drifted away from Him, you can return with humility, trusting that He draws near with forgiveness and new life.
exp.13:22:
God says that the exiles who arrive in Babylon will be comforted when they see how the survivors of Jerusalem live. The phrase "they shall comfort you" is rewritten here as "you will be comforted." When they see their way of life and their actions, that is, their conduct, they will understand that God did not act without reason in everything he did against the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had fallen into idolatry and injustice, and God announces judgment. Even so, he leaves a remnant that comes out of the city. Their conduct would show that the punishment was just. Some scholars see comfort here because God was not arbitrary; others stress that God preserves a small group.

For today: when we do not understand our pain, we can trust that God is just and good, and that he does not act without cause. He also keeps hope for his people.
exp.41:11:
The explanation says that the chambers on the south side of the temple had a door at the start of the passage, next to the wall facing east, through which people entered. It explains that "midday" means south, "east" means the east, and "courtyard" means an open space or yard beside the building. The south chambers were the same as those on the north.

Ezekiel recounts a vision of the temple that a guide shows him while the people live in exile in Babylon. The guide explains that these chambers were holy: there the priests ate the offerings and changed their clothes before going back out to the people. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God cares that what is holy be treated with respect and order. Before serving others, we can pause for a moment to pray and prepare ourselves with a clean and humble heart.
exp.26:21:
This verse says that the merchants of Sheba and Raamah came to Tyre with the best of their goods: the finest spices, every kind of precious stone, and gold. "Spices" in the verse refers to aromatic spices and perfumes, and "fairs" refers to the markets. They traded all of this in the city's markets.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a seaport city very rich from its trade. The list of peoples shows how great its fame and wealth were. The prophet describes it as a beautiful ship that would soon sink because of its pride. Many scholars place Sheba and Raamah in southern Arabia, although their exact location is debated.

For today: wealth and success can make us feel secure without God. Examine where you place your trust, and thank God for what you have by using it with humility and generosity.
exp.31:20:
From the realm of the dead, the mightiest warriors will welcome the Pharaoh as he arrives. With them are his allies, who have already gone down and lie among the uncircumcised, that is, the peoples who were not part of Israel's covenant, slain in war. "Hell" here translates Sheol, the grave or dwelling place of the dead, not necessarily a place of eternal punishment.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt and its Pharaoh. The language is poetic: Egypt, proud and feared, will end the same way as other mighty nations that fell. God shows that no empire escapes his judgment.

For today: power, success, and fame do not make us invincible. It is wise to live with humility before God, because He is the one who upholds or brings down the great, and our true security is in Him.
exp.27:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, calling him "son of man," and tells him to deliver a message to the ruler of Tyre, that is, the leader of that city. He accuses him of having a heart that has been lifted up, meaning he had become proud. He claimed to be a god and to sit in the seat of God in the midst of the seas. But God reminds him that he is only a man.

Tyre was a rich and powerful city on the Mediterranean coast, famous for its trade and its ships. Here the Lord speaks through Ezekiel, in a prophecy of judgment against that ruler. His wealth and success led him to think himself greater than he was. The verses that follow mention his wisdom and his riches.

For today: achievements and money can make us forget that we depend on God. Today you can thank Him for what you have and acknowledge that every gift comes from Him.
exp.28:18:
God says that he will hand Egypt over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Babylon will take the wealth and goods of the land, and this will be the payment for his army. "Multitude" here refers to Egypt's riches and population, and the spoil and prey are what is taken in a conquest.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the twenty-seventh year of the exile (around 571 B.C.). Babylon had besieged Tyre for a long time, and its soldiers were worn out without receiving any plunder. God says that Egypt will be the reward for that effort. Scholars debate how much of this was fulfilled and in what way, since the historical information is limited.

For today: God rules even over powerful kings and nations, though they do not acknowledge him. We can trust that he continues to guide history and our circumstances, even when everything seems confusing.
exp.16:13:
It says that Babylon left the kingdom of Judah brought low and unable to lift itself up. But there was a way out: if it kept the covenant it had made, it could remain standing under it. The words "brought low" and "covenant" are not used in the verse above, so I will not explain them here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar carried off King Jehoiachin and placed Zedekiah on the throne, and Zedekiah swore loyalty. Afterward Zedekiah rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God holds him to account because he broke an oath made in God's name. Some understand this as a call to humility under punishment.

For today: keeping one's word is a serious matter before God. Even when we go through times of humiliation, faithfulness and humility are worth more than seeking shortcuts or misplaced support.
exp.21:28:
The explanation says that the common people of the land also took part in the injustice. They practiced oppression and robbery, mistreated the poor and the needy, and treated the foreigner badly without any justice.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time when Judah was about to fall to Babylon. Earlier, God had accused the princes, the priests, and the prophets. Here he shows that the guilt reached down to the people. Then he says that he looked for someone to stand in the gap, and found no one.

Today we can ask ourselves who near us is in a disadvantaged position: an underpaid worker, an immigrant, a poor neighbor. God calls us to treat them with justice and not to remain silent in the face of abuse.
exp.24:5:
This verse explains the reason for God's judgment against Ammon. Clapping the hands and stamping the feet are gestures of mockery and joy at another's misfortune. Rejoicing from the heart, with all their scorn toward the land of Israel, means they were glad within themselves, with complete contempt for Israel's land.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Ammon, a neighboring people of Israel, mocked when Jerusalem and the temple were struck by Babylon. God did not overlook that attitude. The judgment that appears before and after this passage follows from this accusation: God takes contempt for his people seriously.

For today: when someone stumbles or suffers, even someone with whom we have had problems, let us avoid rejoicing in secret. Better to pray for that person and help if we can, remembering that God looks at the heart.
exp.22:22:
This verse lists the lovers who will come against Aholibah: the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, along with the Assyrians. They are described as attractive young men, noblemen, and horsemen. "Young men" refers to their youth; "desirable" means appealing; "stewards" is understood here as governors or officials.

God speaks through Ezekiel. Using the image of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), he denounces his people for being unfaithful to him by seeking alliances with other nations instead of trusting him. Those who attracted them will become the instruments of their punishment. Interpreters see Babylon here as the nation that would come to judge Judah.

For today: what draws us away from God often looks bright, but it can end up hurting us. Examine the things you place your trust in, and return to God, who is faithful.
exp.24:15:
It says that God himself will act against the Philistines. The sentence about "stretching out my hand" means he will intervene with power to punish them. To "cut off" means to wipe out or cut down completely. The Cherethites were a people linked to the Philistines, and "the sea coast" is the shore of the Mediterranean, where they lived.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a series of messages against the nations that bordered Israel. The Philistines had acted with spite and revenge, driven by an old enmity. God promises to answer that wickedness. Some scholars also see here God's defense of his people.

For today: let us not hold on to old grudges or seek revenge. We can leave our wounds in the hands of God, who is just, and ask him for the strength to forgive.
exp.21:3:
God tells Jerusalem that she is guilty because of the innocent blood she has shed and the idols she has made, which have made her unclean. In this way she herself has hastened her judgment, and now the end of her years has come. That is why God allows the nations to mock her. Disgrace and mockery both mean public shame and ridicule.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God commands him to confront the city, that is, to show her clearly her sins. The verses that follow point to the leaders of Israel, who abused their power. God does not act without warning: first he declares the wrong.

For today: sin is never small or private when it harms others or when we put something in the place of God. Ask him to show you which idols have taken his place in your heart, and return to him with humility while there is still time.
exp.33:19:
It says that God himself, the Lord GOD, will act personally. He will judge between the fat sheep, who are the strong and well-fed, and the lean sheep, who are the weak and mistreated. Some old words are explained here: "trample" means to push down under the feet, and "still waters" are calm, clean waters.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the people's exile in Babylon. In this chapter he rebukes the shepherds of Israel, that is, their leaders, who took advantage of the flock instead of caring for it. Some of the strong sheep also pushed the weak ones aside. For this reason God promises to defend the mistreated and to be the one who establishes justice.

For today: if you have some place of influence, in the home, the church or at work, use it to care for the weakest and not to gain advantage. And if you feel trampled, remember that God sees and promises to bring justice.
exp.21:13:
God asks Jerusalem whether her heart will hold up and whether her hands will stay strong when He acts against her. These are rhetorical questions: the answer is no. At the end, God affirms that He has spoken and that He will carry it out.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Jerusalem had given herself over to violence and theft, had taken unjust gain from loans, and had forgotten God. Therefore He announces that He will scatter her among the nations and purge her uncleanness, so that they will know that He is the Lord.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are living with honesty and justice, without taking advantage of anyone. Let us not trust in our own strength; it is better to turn back to God in time, with humility, and let Him cleanse our hearts.
exp.34:6:
God says that he will leave Mount Seir, the region of Edom, turned into a ruined and empty place. "Total destruction" is what the wording of the verse conveys, and an "empty place" is a land without inhabitants. The phrase about cutting off anyone who passes through means that no one will be able to go in or out of that land, because there will be no travelers and no life.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, had held an old hostility against Israel, and took advantage of Israel's fall, when Israel was at its worst moment. That is why God announces this judgment: Edom did not turn away from violence, and now it will receive it. In the end, God says that in this way they will know that he is the LORD.

For today: let us not rejoice in the pain of others or take advantage of their downfall. Let us ask God for a compassionate heart, one that helps those who suffer and leaves justice in God's hands.
exp.43:24:
It says the priest was not to go near a dead body, because that made him unclean according to the law. There was only one exception: if a very close relative died, such as his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, or an unmarried sister. In those cases he could become defiled, that is, ceremonially unclean, in order to attend to the mourning and the burial.

God speaks through Ezekiel, in the vision of the new temple. He is giving rules to the priests, so that they may teach the people to distinguish between what is holy and what is common. Death was regarded as an uncleanness that set a person apart from service in the sanctuary. This rule is similar to the one in Leviticus 21.

For today: God cares about holiness, but he also allows us to love and to grieve for our family. We can serve him with reverence without neglecting our own in their times of sorrow.
exp.26:25:
They say that Tyre's rowers brought her into deep, open waters, and there the east wind, the wind from the east, broke her to pieces in the middle of the sea. Tyre appears as a great ship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a city rich from its sea trade. Earlier the text describes her as full of pride and wealth. Now it announces that her power will not save her. The east wind is often strong and destructive, and here it represents God's judgment. Interpreters see it as an image of the city's fall, not as a literal storm.
