For today: we may have success, plans and resources, but none of that gives us final security. Let us trust in God more than in what we have achieved, and live with humility.
exp.36:27:
This verse says that the nations will recognize that the Lord is the one who sets Israel apart as his own people, because his sanctuary, that is, the place where God dwells among them, will be in the midst of them forever. The word "sanctify" in the verse means setting apart as holy, belonging to God. The "heathen" are the other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, in the vision of the dry bones, God promised to restore his people and unite them under one king. Here he promises an everlasting covenant of peace and his permanent presence. Christians often see this fulfilled in Christ and in the Church, though others understand it as a promise still future for Israel. There are different interpretations.

For today: God not only forgives us, he also wants to live close to us. We can set aside a few minutes each day to pray, remembering that his presence accompanies us and that the way we live can show others who he is.
exp.15:24:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, set up her altar at every corner of the roads. She ruined the beauty God gave her and gave herself to every man who passed by. "The head of the way" is the start of a street or a crossroads. "Infidelity" here means unfaithfulness to God, above all idolatry and alliances with other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he presents Jerusalem as a young girl whom he rescued, cared for, and adorned. She, however, used those gifts to seek other gods and other nations. God confronts her to call her to acknowledge her sin.

For today: what God has given us, such as talents, blessings, or faith, must not be placed at the service of other things that seek our heart. Think about what "altars" you are raising in your life, and return humbly to God, who remains faithful.
exp.26:29:
They who lived from the sea and from trade with Tyre, such as sailors and pilots, cry out their grief aloud. They weep bitterly, throw dust on their heads, and roll in ashes. These were common signs of deep mourning in that time.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very rich port city, and here the prophet describes it as a great ship that is sinking. Those who profited from it now mourn its loss. The passage shows that its power and its trade could not save it. Some also see in it a warning against Tyre's pride.

For today: wealth and success can disappear quickly. It is worth examining where we place our security and trusting in God, who remains. Let us use what we have with humility and generosity.
exp.31:26:
The verse says that these mighty warriors will not receive an honorable burial alongside the fallen heroes of other peoples. They went down to the grave with their weapons, and their swords were placed under their heads, as a sign of military glory. But "their iniquities shall be upon their bones": their violence goes with them into death. The phrase "uncircumcised" here refers to the peoples who were not Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he announces judgment against Egypt and describes it going down to the place of the dead, where other nations that spread terror are already present, such as Assyria, Meshech, and Tubal. The passage is prophetic poetry, with strong images. Not all scholars agree on the details of how that scene should be understood.

For today: power that is used to oppress and cause fear does not leave a good record before God. It is better to use whatever strength we have to serve and protect others.
exp.19:41:
This verse says that the people of Israel will truly come to know who God is when he brings them back to the land he promised to their ancestors. "I lifted up my hand" is an old expression for making a solemn oath.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, God had recalled Israel's rebellion throughout its history. Now he promises restoration, not because the people deserve it, but because of the faithfulness of his name and his word. Some understand this as the return from Babylon, and others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: when God fulfills what he has promised, we learn what he is like. If you have failed, remember that his goodness does not depend on your merits. Trust his word and respond with gratitude and obedience.
exp.36:18:
Here God tells Ezekiel to explain the sign of the two sticks (pieces of wood). God will take the stick of Joseph, also called Ephraim, together with the tribes of Israel who are with him, and join them to the stick of Judah. He will make them one stick, that is, one people, and they will be united in God's hand. The verse says God will "put them" and "make them" one stick, meaning he will bring them together and form them into a single people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. After the kingdom was divided, Israel and Judah were separated. With this sign, God promises that he will gather his people, bring them back to their land, and make them one nation.

For today: God wants to unite his people. Think of some division in your family or your church, and ask God to help you take a step toward reconciliation.
exp.40:4:
Here the heavenly guide continues measuring the temple that Ezekiel sees in the vision. First he measures the thickness of the wall of the house, which is six cubits (a cubit was about half a meter, so roughly three meters). Then he measures the side chambers, small rooms that surrounded the whole building, each four cubits wide (about two meters).

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he lived in exile in Babylon. God shows him this detailed vision when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed, to give him hope and to remind him that He wants to dwell among His people in holiness and order. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about order and details. We can give our daily lives the same careful attention, understanding that every part of them can be a place where God dwells.
exp.29:5:
God himself declares the fall of Egypt. It will not only be Egypt that falls, but also its allies, those who supported it. Its pride and its power will be brought low. The phrase "by the sword" means in war, that is, through battle.

The place names "from the tower of Migdol to Syene" are usually understood as from one end of Egypt to the other, from north to south, although some locate Syene differently.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Egypt was a power in which Judah trusted for its defense. God warns that this security was false and that he is the one who governs the nations. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment.

For today: examine where you place your ultimate security, whether money, reputation, or people. All of these can fail. Trust first in God, who does not change, and live with humility.
exp.30:16:
It says that the allies and defenders of this great tree also went down with him to the grave. The "pit" is the grave or the place of the dead. "Those slain with the sword" are those who died in war. "His arm" refers to those who supported him with their strength, and "his shadow" to those who lived protected by him among the nations.

God speaks through Ezekiel and compares Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to a towering cedar of Lebanon. Like Assyria before, Egypt trusted in its greatness, but it falls because of its pride. The text is poetic and symbolic: it does not describe a literal place, but shows that no empire escapes God's judgment. Its allies fall with it.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in power, money, or influential people. All of that can fall. Rest in God, who endures, and be humble with what He has given you.
exp.13:21:
It says that although the judgment on Jerusalem will be severe, a group of survivors will be left, sons and daughters, who will come out of the city. The word "remnant" is used for those who are left behind. They will come to where the exiles are in Babylon, and those exiles will see their way of life. Seeing how they live, the exiles will be comforted, understanding that the punishment on Jerusalem had a reason.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, God said that neither Noah, Daniel, nor Job could save others by their righteousness. The exiles thought Jerusalem was suffering for no reason. Many understand that the conduct of the survivors would show that the city was guilty, though the text gives no further details.

For today: when you do not understand pain or correction, do not stay only with your questions. Ask God for humility to see his justice and his mercy, which always leaves open a door of hope.
exp.28:15:
This verse says that Egypt will no longer be a place where Israel puts its trust. In the past, when Israel looked to Egypt for help, that reminded them of their lack of faith in God. Looking back to the Egyptians for support was a sign of turning away from God. In the end, Israel will know that the Lord alone is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Egypt had been an ally that Israel turned to instead of trusting God. Here God announces that Egypt will be humbled and weakened, so that no one will see it as a source of salvation.

For today: it is worth asking ourselves where we place our security, such as money, people, or plans. All of these can fail. God invites us to trust Him first, for He does not change and does not disappoint.
exp.37:22:
God says that He Himself will be magnified and recognized as holy before many nations. The idea of being "sanctified" means that His holiness, that is, His greatness and purity, will be displayed for all to see. The phrase about being "known in the eyes of many nations" means "in plain view of many peoples." The final result is that they will know that He is the LORD.

God is speaking through the prophet Ezekiel. He has just described judgment on Gog and his allies, who come against Israel: sword, plague, heavy rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur. Scholars interpret Gog in several ways (a historical enemy, a future enemy, or a symbol of evil), and there is no full agreement. What is clear is the purpose: that God be recognized.

For today: even when the world seems dominated by evil, we can trust that God has the last word. Today we can live with calm and honor Him in our everyday lives.
exp.40:6:
It says that the side chambers of the temple grew wider as they went up. A spiral staircase, that is, one winding round in a spiral, went around the building on the inside and rose very high. That is why the house was wider at the top. One passed from the lowest chamber to the highest through the middle one.

The speaker is the prophet Ezekiel, who in a vision is led by a man holding a measuring reed. He is in exile, and the earlier temple had been destroyed. The vision describes a new temple with very exact measurements. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people.

For today: this passage shows a space that opens up more as one climbs. We can ask God to make our spiritual life grow, step by step, and to give us more room for his presence, prayer, and service.
exp.43:15:
The explanation says that the faithful priests, the sons of Zadok, will be the only ones who may enter God's sanctuary. They will draw near to his table, that is, to the altar where the offerings are presented, in order to minister to him. The phrase about drawing near is explained by the word "approach," and the phrase about what God commanded to be kept is explained as the duties God gave them to guard.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. Earlier he had rebuked the Levites who went astray after idols. By contrast, he rewards the descendants of Zadok, who remained faithful when Israel turned away. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or symbolically.

For today: God values faithfulness when almost no one practices it. We can ask ourselves what God asks of our lives and obey him steadily, even when others drift away. Drawing near to him is both a privilege and a responsibility.
exp.29:12:
God says he will take away from Egypt the things it trusted in. The "images" and "idols" are the religious figures they worshiped, and Memphis was one of their most important cities. He also says there will no longer be a ruler of their own, that is, a leader born in that land, and that he will put dread, meaning fear and awe, on the whole country.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The message is a judgment against Egypt for its pride and its idolatry. The text connects it to the Babylonian invasion, but how exactly it was fulfilled is interpreted in several ways.

For today: nothing we put in place of God, whether money, power, or fame, can sustain us forever. Today you can examine what you trust in most and surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.31:1:
God tells Ezekiel to raise a lament over Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He compares him to a young lion among the nations and to a sea monster, which in Hebrew is a large creature of the water, perhaps a crocodile. This creature stirred up the rivers with its feet, muddied the waters, and trampled the banks.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. Egypt believed itself powerful and untouchable, but God announces its fall. The image shows a proud ruler who stirs up everything in his path.

For today: power and success do not give us the right to trample on others. If God gives us influence, let us use it to care for others, not to muddy their lives. Examine today how you treat those who depend on you.
exp.28:9:
God says to Egypt that he is against it and against its rivers, that is, against the Nile, the source of its wealth. He promises to leave the country devastated, like an empty desert. Where the verse says "utterly waste," the sense is ruin and destruction. "From the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia" is usually understood as from one end of Egypt to the other (Syene is identified with Aswan, though not everyone agrees). "Ethiopia" here refers to the region to the south, called Cush.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Egypt and its pharaoh believed they owned the river and its power, and they had been a deceptive support for Israel. God judges that pride so that they will acknowledge that he is the Lord.

For today: everything we have comes from God, not only from our own effort. Ask him to free you from pride and thank him every day for what he has given you.
exp.22:29:
This verse explains the reason for the punishment announced: Jerusalem, here pictured as a woman, "gone a whoring" after the nations, that is, she was unfaithful to God by seeking alliances with pagan peoples. "Thou art polluted with their idols" means she took on their false gods and became unclean before God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 23 he tells the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem). Samaria had already fallen into the hands of Assyria because of her unfaithfulness. Oholibah saw that, but she followed the same path. For this reason God hands her over to the peoples she once admired and later despised.

For today: God calls us not to give our hearts to things that take his place, such as money, fame, or influence. Ask yourself today: what am I trusting in more than in God? Return to him with sincerity.
exp.46:18:
This verse describes the southern boundary of the land that God promises to divide among the tribes of Israel. The line runs from Tamar, passes by the waters of strife (Meribah-Kadesh), follows the brook of Egypt, and reaches the great sea, the Mediterranean. The phrase "the south side southward" simply means the south.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. In his vision, He shows them a restored land, with clear borders and a division among all the tribes. It was a message of hope for a people without a home. Scholars understand these boundaries in different ways: literally, symbolically, or as tied to the future.

For today: God cares about the details and keeps His promises, even when everything seems lost. Today you can entrust your dreams and your waiting to Him, asking Him to guide you step by step.
exp.38:19:
It says that God invites the birds and the wild beasts to a great feast. The phrase "to be filled" means eating until one is satisfied. God's "table" is the battlefield, and what is eaten are horses, brave riders, and warriors of the defeated armies.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 describe Gog, an enemy leader who attacks Israel and is defeated by God. The image of the feast is poetic and very strong, and it shows a total defeat. Interpreters differ: some see it as something literal in the future, others as symbolic language of God's final triumph.

For today: God has the last word over all human power, however great it may seem. We can rest in the knowledge that he does justice, and so leave vengeance in his hands and trust him when evil seems strong.
exp.39:28:
This verse describes the south gate of the inner courtyard of the temple. It says that its small chambers (little rooms used for guards), its posts (the side columns), and its arches (porches or entryways) had the same measurements as the other gates. It had windows all around, and it measured fifty cubits long by twenty-five cubits wide. A cubit is about 45 to 50 centimeters.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision. A guide takes him through a new temple and measures each part for him. This happens during a time of exile and pain, when the temple had been destroyed. Interpreters differ: some see a literal temple in the future, while others see a symbolic picture of God's presence and his order.

For today: God is a God of order, and everything in his house has its place and its measure. We can bring order into our own lives so that we approach him with reverence, caring for the details of our faith and of our everyday life.
exp.40:5:
It says that around the temple there were three stories of side rooms, and that on each story there were thirty-three chambers, according to some interpretations. Beams or projecting supports were used to hold them up. Those supports went into the wall of the temple, but the rooms rested on them and were not attached directly to the holy wall.

Ezekiel describes a vision he received during the exile. A guide, described as a man with a measuring reed, shows him a new temple with very exact measurements. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple, a symbol, or both. Here the emphasis is on order and on reverence for the most holy place.

For today: God values order and reverence for what is holy. We can rest our daily life on good supports, such as prayer, the Word, and community, without trying to carry everything on just one thing.
exp.19:6:
God reminds Israel of what he asked of them in Egypt: that each one throw away the "abominations of their eyes," that is, the images and detestable things they worshiped. He warns them not to defile themselves, meaning not to make themselves spiritually unclean, with the idols of Egypt. And he seals it by saying: "I am the Lord your God."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile. He tells them the story of Israel to show that their rebellion goes back a long way. From Egypt, God chose them and promised them a good land, but they did not let go of their idols. Even so, God acted for the sake of his name.

For today: ask yourself what thing captures your gaze and competes with God in your heart. With his help, let it go, remembering that he is your God and remains faithful to you.
exp.15:40:
This verse says that the enemies of Jerusalem will burn her houses and carry out judgments against her in the sight of many women, meaning the other nations. The figure of a prostitute is used to speak of unfaithfulness. The verse says God will make her stop her unfaithful ways, and that she will no longer give gifts to her lovers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to a wife who, after being cared for and blessed by God, abandoned him to follow other gods and alliances. Scholars understand this judgment as a reference to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. God does not speak lightly: he shows grief and justice before a very serious betrayal.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. If we notice that our heart is going after other things, let us return to him quickly and with humility. His correction seeks to awaken us.
exp.26:14:
Dedan was a people of merchants who did business with Tyre. Many islands, that is, distant lands along the sea, bought their goods. They brought ivory tusks (here called "horns") and a fine wood of uncertain identification. Some versions translate this word as "ebony." Here, "present" means payment or goods handed over.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is mourning the fall of Tyre, a city rich and proud because of its trade. The long list of peoples who sold to it shows its enormous fame and power. But the chapter announces that all that wealth would not save it from God's judgment.

Today: Money and success can grow a great deal, but they are not a secure foundation. Use what you have with gratitude and generosity, and trust first in God, who does not change.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "The word of the Lord came unto me" is the way Ezekiel often introduces a new message. Here it does not yet say what the message is; it only announces that God is going to speak.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon with other Jews. God gives him a message about Jerusalem and the land of Israel, and in the verses that follow it speaks of judgment, using the image of a sword. The verse serves as an opening: what comes next is not the prophet's own ideas, but the word of God.

For today: before we speak or decide something important, it is good to stop and listen to God in his Word and in prayer. God still speaks, above all through the Bible, and he asks for our sincere attention and obedience, even when the message is not easy to hear.
exp.18:2:
It says the lioness raised one of her cubs until it became a strong young lion. It learned to hunt and to "devour men," that is, to attack and destroy people. "Catch prey" means to seize its victim. "Brought up" means she raised it.

God speaks through Ezekiel and tells him to chant a dirge, a song of mourning, over the princes of Israel. The lioness is usually understood as the mother of the kingdom of Judah, and the cub as one of its kings, probably Jehoahaz, who was taken to Egypt. Scholars debate exactly which figure represents whom. The point is that the rulers used their power to oppress, and in the end they fell.

For today: power without justice harms others and also the one who wields it. Whether at home, at work, or in the church, let us ask God to teach us to use our influence to serve and care, not to take advantage.
exp.35:30:
It says that when God carries out his work of restoration, the people will remember their past misconduct. By recalling their evil ways, their deeds that were not good, their sins, and their abominations (detestable things, above all idolatry), they will feel shame for themselves.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks for God to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. Earlier God had promised them a new heart, his Spirit, and abundant harvests. Now he makes clear that he restores them not because of anything they have earned, but by his grace. The shame described here is the result of receiving that undeserved forgiveness.

For today: when you remember your mistakes, do not sink into hopeless guilt. Let that memory lead you to humble repentance, and to thankfulness that God's goodness does not depend on what we deserve.
exp.19:8:
God says that, despite Israel's rebellion, he brought his people out of Egypt for the sake of his name, that is, for his honor and reputation. He did not want his name to be dishonored before the nations where the Israelites lived, since those nations had seen that he made himself known to his people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to some elders of Israel who were consulting him. He reminds them of their history: from Egypt onward the people rebelled and followed idols. Even so, God acted out of faithfulness to his own name and his promise, not because of anything they had earned.

For today: our salvation rests on God's faithfulness, not on our good performance. Trust his grace, acknowledge your failures with humility, and live in such a way that his name is honored, not dishonored, by your conduct.
exp.13:10:
God says he wants Israel to stop straying away from him and stop defiling themselves with their rebellions. His ultimate goal is to restore the relationship, so that they will be his people and he will be their God. To "go astray" means to wander off the path and lose one's way. To be "polluted" means to become unclean, made impure by sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile. Some leaders and elders had idols in their hearts, yet they came seeking a word from God while still holding on to their sin. God says he will judge both the false prophets and those who seek them out. The phrase about God deceiving the prophet is difficult; many understand it to mean that God allows, or gives over, to deception the one who has already chosen error. His judgment aims to correct and cleanse.

Today: even when God corrects, his purpose is to draw us near to him. Examine what things occupy your heart, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.16:2:
He says God tells Ezekiel to tell a parable. A great eagle, strong, with broad wings and feathers of many colors, comes to Lebanon and takes the highest top of a cedar tree. The highest, most tender shoot of a tree is the top branch. The word "long-winged" here refers to its long feathers or wings.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. This image is directed at Israel. Later in the same chapter, God explains that the eagle represents the king of Babylon and the cedar the royal house of Judah, whose king was taken captive. God wants the people to understand what happened and why.

For today: God sees history and the powers of this world with clarity. When life feels out of control, we can trust that he still rules and listen to his word with humility.
exp.41:5:
It says that the chambers of this temple building were built in three stories, but they did not have pillars like those of the courts (the open yards). For that reason, the upper floors were narrower than the lower and middle ones, because the galleries (the passages or balconies) took up part of their space. The phrase "from the ground" probably refers to the fact that the difference could be seen from the base of the building.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, describes a vision that God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him the new temple and its chambers, with exact measurements, chambers that were used by the priests. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic message of hope and restoration.

For today: God cares about the details and wants His presence to be holy and orderly. We can ask Him to bring order into our lives, even in small things, so that we may live near Him with reverence and hope.
exp.20:14:
This verse says that God allows the sword of judgment to reach the gates of the city. The result is fear in the heart, many deaths, and destruction. "Faint" means that courage runs out. "Ruin" refers to damage and slaughter. "Made bright" means made ready. "Slaughter" means to kill with the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem because of its rebellion and idolatry. The sword is commonly associated with Babylon as the instrument of that judgment. God commands Ezekiel to act out the message with his hands to show how serious it is.

For today: let us take God's voice seriously before the consequences arrive. If He points out something in our lives, it is better to listen and repent today, trusting in His mercy.
exp.42:21:
He says that on the second day of the dedication of the altar, a male goat without defect would be offered as a sin offering. With it the altar would be cleansed once more, just as the day before it had been cleansed with the bullock. "Atonement" means covering over or taking away guilt; "cleanse" means making clean for the service of God.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple. After the exile, God gives him instructions for dedicating the altar, over seven days in a row. Interpreters differ on whether this temple would be built literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something in the future. What is clear is that God desires a holy and clean place where people can draw near to Him.

For today: let us not take lightly sin or the holiness of God. We can come to Him sincerely, confessing what is wrong, and trust that Christ, according to the New Testament, offered the perfect sacrifice that cleanses us.
exp.15:14:
Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, stopped trusting in God and put her confidence in her own beauty and fame. Here "played the harlot" means being unfaithful, giving herself to others instead of remaining faithful to her husband. "Renown" means fame or reputation. "Pouredst out thy fornications on every one that passed by" indicates that she offered herself to anyone who came along.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of a wife who was rescued, adorned, and enriched by her husband, but who used those gifts to betray him. It is a way of showing how Jerusalem abandoned God for idols and alliances with other nations, forgetting that her beauty and prosperity came from Him.

Today we can ask ourselves what blessings, talents, or achievements make us feel secure. Everything good comes from God. Let us thank Him and use His gifts to honor Him, not to trust in ourselves.
exp.20:26:
God says he will completely overturn the kingdom of Judah. "Overturn, overturn, overturn" repeats three times that everything will be torn down. "It" refers to the crown or the kingdom. That power will not be restored to what it was until the one who has the rightful claim comes, the one with legitimate authority. God says he will give it to him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses King Zedekiah, whom he calls the wicked prince. Babylon was about to conquer Jerusalem. Many Christians see in "the one whose right it is" a promise of the Messiah, Jesus, a descendant of David. Others explain it more broadly, but the underlying idea is the same.

For today: no human power lasts forever. We can entrust our future to Christ, the rightful King, and live with humility.
exp.15:62:
This verse says that Jerusalem will remember her wrong way and feel shame. Because of this, she will no longer have anything to say in her own defense or to boast about. This will happen when God forgives her. The phrase "pacified toward you" means that God makes peace with her and covers her guilt. Having no way to boast or make excuses is what it means to be unable to speak up for oneself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, who was unfaithful to him like a wife who betrays her husband. After announcing judgment, God promises to restore her and confirm his covenant. The forgiveness is not based on what she deserves, but on God's faithfulness.

For today: when God forgives you, remember your failures without being crushed by them, and let his grace make you humble. In this way you stop making excuses or boasting, and you can treat with mercy those who also fail.
exp.20:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" is used many times by the prophet to announce that he is about to receive new instructions from God.

Here Ezekiel is speaking, and the one addressing him is God. He has just been told to groan with grief before the people, as a sign of the tragedy approaching Jerusalem. Now God continues with another message: the image of the sharp sword is introduced, which represents judgment. Some understand that sword to refer to the army of Babylon, and the Bible itself makes this clear later in the chapter.

For today: God continues to speak through his Word. Before acting or offering opinions, it is good to pause and listen humbly to what he says, even when the message is not easy to hear.
exp.32:7:
God says that if He warns the wicked person that he will die because of his evil way, and the watchman does not speak to turn him from it, that wicked person will die for his sin. But God will hold the watchman responsible for that death. To hold someone responsible means to make them answerable for what happened.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. He appoints him as a watchman for the people. Just as a sentinel sounds the horn when the enemy comes, Ezekiel was to warn of judgment and call people to repentance. The responsibility to speak was his; the responsibility to respond belonged to each person.

For today: do not stay silent out of fear or comfort when you can speak with love and truth to someone who is turning away from God. Do it with humility, prayer, and patience, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.47:21:
The explanation says that the prince's land lies on both sides of the sacred zone, which includes the portion of the Levites and that of the city. That zone is in the center, and the prince has his portion between the territory of Judah and that of Benjamin. Here "portion" means a designated share of land. "Boundary" means limit or border.

This is the final part of the vision that God gave to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. God shows him how the land would be divided, with the sanctuary at the center. It is interpreted in several ways: some see it as a promise for a restored Israel, others as a spiritual or future picture. What is clear is that God places his presence at the center of the people.

For today: ask yourself what occupies the center of your life. Just as in this vision everything is organized around the holy place, we can arrange our time, work and family around God.
exp.19:40:
God promises that he will accept Israel like a pleasing aroma. This will happen when he brings them out from among the nations and gathers them out of the countries where they have been scattered. In this way, God will show his holiness through them, in the sight of the other peoples. "I will be sanctified" means that God will be recognized as holy.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, God rebukes Israel for their idolatry and disobedience. But here he promises to restore his people to their land, so that they will worship him truly again. Interpreters apply this to the return from exile, and some also to a future restoration.

Today we can remember that God does not give up on us when we turn away. His forgiveness seeks to restore us, and a changed life can show others who he is. If you have wandered away, you can return with confidence.
exp.17:27:
The explanation says that the person who recognizes his error, turns away from all his transgressions and changes his way will not be condemned, but will live. Now, "considereth" means that he thought it over and opened his eyes. "Transgressions" are rebellions or serious offenses against God. "Turneth away" means that he turned away from them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They were saying that God was unjust, since they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is responsible for himself and that He always offers an opportunity to return to Him. Some understand "live" to refer to life on earth, others also to life with God.

For today: no matter what you have done, God invites you to stop, recognize your error and return to Him. Today you can speak with God sincerely and take a concrete step of change.
exp.14:2:
God asks whether the wood of the vine is good for anything useful. Can any piece of furniture or tool be made from it? Can a peg, that is, a wooden nail or hook, be taken from it to hang a vessel on? The expected answer is no. The wood of the vine is weak and is not fit for building.

God speaks, giving His word to the prophet Ezekiel, who is called "son of man." In this chapter, the vine represents Jerusalem and its inhabitants. A vine is valued for its fruit, not for its wood. If it does not bear fruit, it has no worth. God uses this image to show that the people, unfaithful to Him, had nothing to boast about.

For today: our worth does not lie in how we appear, but in remaining joined to God and bearing fruit. Jesus said something similar in John 15. Let us ask Him to keep us close to Him.
exp.39:31:
He brought me to the inner court on the east side, and there he measured the gate. He used the same measurements as the gates before it. The inner court is an open courtyard of the temple. The word for the measure used here is an old unit, roughly the length of the forearm.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. A man with a measuring reed guides him through the temple and measures everything with care. Scholars disagree about the purpose: some see a literal future temple, others see a symbol of God's orderly presence and of the hope of restoration.

For today: God is not disorderly or careless; He cares about the details of His work. When you find yourself in a time of ruin or waiting, remember that He continues to build with patience and purpose. Draw near to Him with reverence and trust.
exp.35:5:
God commands the prophet Ezekiel to speak to the land of Israel, as if the mountains, hills, streams and valleys could hear him. God says he speaks in zeal (a fierce love that will not tolerate injustice) and in anger (strong wrath), because the land has borne the shame and contempt of the neighboring nations.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel during Israel's exile. The surrounding peoples, especially Edom, mocked Israel and tried to take its land for themselves. God promises to defend his name and his people, and afterward to restore the land.

For today: when you feel ashamed or looked down upon, remember that God sees your pain and does not ignore it. Bring that humiliation to him in prayer and trust that he knows how to restore what others tried to destroy.
exp.15:19:
Here God says that Jerusalem took the sons and daughters that He had given her and sacrificed them to the idols, so that they would be devoured, that is, consumed by fire. "Whoredoms" speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness, of leaving God for other gods. The final question shows grief: was it not enough, all that unfaithfulness?

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter, Jerusalem is like a wife whom God cared for, clothed, and fed from her humble beginnings. She used those same gifts to worship idols. Sacrificing children was a pagan practice that God forbade.

For today: everything we have comes from God, and we can put it in the wrong place. Ask yourself which things, such as success or money, receive the best of your time and your heart, and place them again under God's care.
exp.39:27:
He led me into the inner court through the south gate, and he measured the south gate with these same measurements. The guide brought Ezekiel into the inner court by entering through the south gate, and he measured that gate by the same measures as the other gates. A "cubit" was an ancient unit of length, roughly the length of the forearm.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who was in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a man with a measuring reed guides him through a new temple and shows him every detail. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his restored people. For a discouraged people, it was a promise of hope.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can draw near to him with reverence and trust that he has a plan to restore what seems lost.
exp.18:12:
It says that the vine, which once was strong and full of branches, is now planted in a wilderness, in a dry land without water. The word "dry and thirsty ground" describes hard soil with no moisture, where nothing grows well. It is a picture of loss and weakness.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. This chapter is a lament, a song of mourning over the kings of Judah. The vine is usually understood as Jerusalem or its royal line, uprooted and carried into exile. Scholars disagree about exactly which kings are meant, but the general sense is clear: pride and injustice brought their consequences.

For today: when you go through a dry season, do not ignore it. Humbly ask what God wants to teach you, and seek again the fountain of living water, which is Christ.
exp.31:31:
This verse says that God allowed Pharaoh and his great army to spread fear in the land of the living, but in the end they themselves will lie among the dead, killed by the sword. The phrase about those who were not circumcised refers to foreign peoples who did not bear the sign of the covenant with Israel, and the phrase about lying down means they will lie there, without life.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. It is a lament over Egypt, part of a series of messages against the nations. God shows that Pharaoh, though powerful and feared, will end up like other proud kingdoms that have already fallen. Scholars understand some details of these images of the grave in different ways, but the central message is clear: no human power escapes the judgment of God.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed or frightened by human power, and do not trust in your own strength. God is the one who has the last word. Live with humility and trust in him.
exp.15:31:
This verse says that Jerusalem is like a married woman who betrays her husband and takes other men in place of him. The word "strangers" means people who are not her partner. In addition, the phrase "a wife that committeth adultery" describes someone who is unfaithful within marriage.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of a marriage to show how the people of Israel left Him and sought other gods and alliances with other nations. It is strong language, meant to awaken the conscience of the people and call them to repentance.

For today: ask yourself what things are occupying the place that only God should have in your heart, such as money, fame, or a relationship. Bring them to God in prayer with honesty, and ask Him for help to return to Him with all your heart.
exp.15:30:
Ezekiel 16:31 says that Jerusalem built her places of worship at the head of every road and made her high places in every street. Here "high places" means sites of false worship. Then the verse compares her to a harlot, but worse: an ordinary harlot takes her pay, while she scorned payment, because she paid her lovers instead of receiving anything in return. The phrase about scorning the reward means she was not seeking gain, only following her own desire.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to show that Israel abandoned God and gave herself to other nations and their gods. It is strong language, meant to awaken repentance in a people who had become accustomed to their sin.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts: money, fame, pleasure, or approval. If we are honest and return to Him, God remains faithful and forgives those who come to Him sincerely.
exp.47:19:
The verse says that the whole set-apart portion measures twenty-five thousand by twenty-five thousand, that is, a perfect square. That land is set apart "by lot," meaning by allotment or assignment, for three things together: the sanctuary, the priests, and the city. The reed was a unit of length; interpreters calculate it at about three meters, although there is variation.

The prophet Ezekiel receives this vision during the exile in Babylon. God shows him how the land will be divided when his people return. The tribes receive equal strips, and the center is reserved for what is holy. Christians interpret this vision in different ways: as a literal restoration, as a symbol of the Church, or as an image of the coming kingdom.

For today: just as this land places what is holy at the center, we can order our week and our finances by giving God the principal place, setting aside time and resources for Him first.
exp.23:8:
God declares judgment on Jerusalem, which he calls "the bloody city," meaning a city full of violence and unjust deaths. He says that he himself will make the pile for fire great, a large fire like one used for cooking, and in this way he will show that he will not overlook so much wickedness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem was under siege, and God uses the image of a pot set over the fire. The blood on the smooth rock shows that the crime was in plain sight, not hidden. God sees what is done, even when no one punishes it.

For today: God cares about justice and about those who suffer harm. Let us not hide or excuse injustice. Let us ask him to cleanse us from all evil and help us to defend and care for the lives of others.
exp.19:23:
This verse explains why God decided to scatter Israel. The people did not keep his commandments, rejected his laws, and dishonored the day of rest, and their eyes went after the idols their ancestors had worshiped.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes among the exiles in Babylon. He reviews Israel's history to show them that their punishment was not unjust: from the wilderness onward, generation after generation repeated the rebellion. The verses that follow are difficult and have been understood in several ways; many think God handed them over to the consequences of their own choices.

For today: what we look at with persistence ends up guiding our hearts. We can ask God to help us fix our eyes on him and to take care over what things occupy our attention.
exp.26:16:
It says that Judah and the land of Israel traded with Tyre. They sold it wheat from Minnith, and also pannag, honey, oil, and balm (or resin). "Merchants" are traders; "traded in your market" means they offered their goods there. It is not known for certain what "pannag" was; some think of a kind of sweet or cake, others of a different product.

God speaks through Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a city made rich by sea trade. The list of nations shows its great fame and wealth. Shortly afterward, the message announces that this greatness would not save it from judgment.

Today: We can work and trade honestly, but without placing our security in money or success. What we have is a gift to manage well and share, because only God is a firm foundation.
exp.33:5:
It says that God's sheep wandered and were scattered over mountains and hills, and across the whole earth. No one went out to look for them or to ask after them. The phrase "upon all the face of the earth" means the surface of the earth. The word "search" in the verse means to look for them with real concern, or to ask after them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He accuses the leaders of Israel, called shepherds, of caring for themselves and neglecting the people. The sheep are God's people, who were left scattered and exposed to harm because of the lack of good leadership.

For today: God pays attention to those who wander or are hurt. We can ask ourselves who we know that has drifted away or is alone, and seek them out with a phone call, a visit, or a prayer, without waiting for someone else to do it.
exp.15:56:
The verse says that Jerusalem did not realize her own wickedness while it remained hidden. Once it was finally exposed, she became an object of mockery to her neighbors: the daughters of Syria and of the Philistines. "Despise" means to look down on or treat with contempt. "Round about" means "on every side."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful wife who forgot everything God had done for her. She came to think herself so superior that she did not even mention Sodom, and yet her sin ended up being worse. Some scholars understand that the shame came with the defeats at the hands of those neighboring peoples.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to make yourself feel better. Ask God to show you your heart honestly, and return to Him before sin grows in secret.
exp.44:9:
God commands that there be just balances, and that the ephah and the bath, which were measures for dry goods and liquids, be accurate and honest. The balance is the scale; the ephah measured grain, and the bath measured liquids such as oil or wine. Both had the same volume, according to the following verse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He speaks to the princes, who had abused their power, and asks them to give up violence and unjust demands. Fixed measures protected people from deception in daily trade.

For today: be honest in small things, such as a fair price, work done well, a promise kept, and clean dealings with employees and customers. God cares about justice in everyday life, not only in religious matters.
exp.15:36:
God says he will gather all of Jerusalem's "lovers," both those she desired and those she despised, and set them against her. They will see her "shame" (her nakedness, her disgrace) and her "vileness" (her filthy and indecent conduct).

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to describe Jerusalem, who left God and sought alliances with other nations and with idols. The "lovers" probably represent those nations. God announces that the same people she trusted will be the ones who expose and judge her.

For today: whatever we put in God's place, whether money, approval, or power, never protects us in the end. We can return to God sincerely today, trusting that his faithfulness is more secure than anything else.
exp.15:15:
It says that Jerusalem took some of the fine clothing God had given her and used it to decorate shrines on high places, where she practiced idolatry. "Playing the harlot" here speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness. "High places" were sites of pagan worship. The final sentence says that something like this had never happened before and would never happen again: it was an extreme case.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as a wife whom he rescued, clothed, and honored, but who used those gifts to give herself to other gods. It is a powerful image, deliberately harsh, to show God's grief over the unfaithfulness of his people.

For today: everything good we have, talents, possessions, and opportunities, comes from God. Let us ask ourselves whether we use them to honor him or to serve other things that take his place.
exp.13:6:
It says that anyone at all, whether an Israelite or a foreigner living among them, who has turned away from God and set up idols in his heart, and then goes to the prophet to ask something on God's behalf, will receive a direct answer from the Lord himself. The stumbling block of their wickedness is what causes them to fall into sin. Turning away from following after me means ceasing to follow God.

God speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders of Israel came to consult him, but God saw that their hearts were still attached to idols. First he calls them to turn back. The answer he promises is not one of comfort but of judgment (in the verses that follow). Some scholars understand the phrase about answering by himself in this way.

Today: before seeking direction from God, let us examine what occupies first place in our heart. God invites us to return to him sincerely, not merely to ask him for advice.
exp.33:11:
This verse says that God compares himself to a shepherd who, among his sheep scattered about, knows each one. In this way God promises to know his people and to rescue them from all the places where they have been scattered. The phrase "in the cloudy and dark day" refers to a time of misfortune and confusion, probably the time of judgment and exile.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The leaders of Israel, called shepherds, had taken advantage of the people instead of caring for them. Because of this, God says he will take the sheep away from them and will himself seek them out. It is a promise of comfort for a people exiled and scattered.

For today: if you feel lost, forgotten, or far from home, remember that God knows you and seeks you out. You can approach him with confidence, knowing that you are not invisible to him.
exp.46:12:
This verse says that God himself gives an instruction: the people must divide the promised land among the twelve tribes of Israel. An inheritance is property that is received as a family's heritage. The boundary is the limit or border of the land. Joseph receives two portions, because his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, counted as separate tribes.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. After the vision of the river that flows from the temple and brings life, God shows how the land will be divided when his people return. It is a promise of restoration. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as something literal, others as a picture of God's future.

For today: God cares that there is a place for each of his own. You can trust that he has an inheritance prepared for you, and live with generosity, without envy for what others receive.
exp.24:7:
This verse begins a message from God against Moab and Seir (another name for Edom). They were saying that Judah was like all the other nations, meaning that it had nothing special and that its God did not protect it in any way different from other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Judah had already been struck by Babylon, and its neighbors were mocking it. By saying this, they despised God's covenant with his people. That is why God announces judgment on Moab, which would lose its border cities. Note: the text names Seir together with Moab, but the punishment that follows focuses on Moab.

For today: when others mock faith or those who are suffering, do not join them. God sees the contempt and cares for his own, even in difficult times. Respond with humility and compassion.
exp.21:15:
The verse says that Jerusalem will be like someone who receives an inheritance, but a shameful one, in plain view of all the nations. The word "inheritance" here carries the sense of possession. Some modern translations understand God to say that you will be defiled through your own guilt before the eyes of the peoples. The Hebrew text is difficult and is translated in several ways. In the end, the result is that they will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, which had filled itself with violence, idolatry, and injustice. Before this verse, God announces that he will scatter her among the nations to put an end to her uncleanness, that is, her sin. The punishment aims at the people coming to recognize who God is.

For today: God does not let us ignore the consequences of our decisions, but his goal is that we come to know him. If today you are going through a correction or a loss, ask him humbly what he wants to teach you, and seek him.
exp.34:14:
God says to Mount Seir, that is, to Edom (Idumea), that it will suffer the same thing it rejoiced over. Edom was glad when the land of Israel was laid waste, and now God says that Edom too will be left desolate. The inheritance is the land God gave to his people; the word "desolate" means ravaged and left in ruins. In the end, everyone will acknowledge that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a neighbor and distant relative of Israel, mocked its fall and spoke proudly against God. He heard it, and therefore he announces judgment. The text presents this sentence as a response to that attitude.

Today, this verse invites us not to rejoice in the misfortune of others, not even in that of someone we dislike. We can pray for those who suffer and help them, remembering that God sees our words and attitudes, and that He is the one who judges with justice.
exp.45:13:
Ezekiel 46:14 says that every morning, along with the lamb for the burnt offering, a grain offering was to be presented: one sixth of an ephah of fine flour (about a liter and a half or two, depending on how it is calculated), mixed with one third of a hin of oil (roughly a liter and a half). The verse calls this a meat offering, meaning an offering of grain. It is also a perpetual ordinance, a rule that was to be kept at all times.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and its worship. The regulations aim at a worship that is orderly for Israel, and the daily offering shows that communion with God was not occasional. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is to be fulfilled literally, symbolically, or in Christ.

For today: we can give God the first fruits of each day. Before rushing into our tasks, a moment of prayer and simple gratitude can set the tone for the rest of the day.
exp.46:22:
It says that foreigners living among the people of Israel will also receive a plot of land as an inheritance. Each one will receive it in the tribe where he is living. The word "sojourneth" is the same as "to live as a stranger," and an inheritance is land received as a family's property.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in the final vision of the book about the restoration of Israel and the division of the land. It is remarkable that foreigners whose children were born there are treated as native-born, that is, as part of the people. Some see here a picture of God's kindness toward all nations; others read it more literally. Both readings recognize His generosity.

For today: God invites us to make room for newcomers, whether immigrants or people new to the church. We can offer them not only help, but a true place among us.
exp.36:21:
God promises that he will unite his people into one nation in the mountains of Israel. There will be one king over them, and they will no longer be two separate nations or two divided kingdoms.

The phrase "one king will be king over all of them" means that a single king will rule over everyone. Older wording like "shall be" is simply said today as "will be."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Earlier, the kingdom of Israel had been split into two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Ezekiel took two sticks, one for each part, and joined them together in his hand as a sign. God promises to gather and cleanse his people. Many Christians see in this a promise that points to Christ, a descendant of David, although there are different interpretations.

For today: God is a God who reconciles what is divided. Ask him to help you seek peace and unity in your family or your church, beginning with forgiving someone.
exp.12:18:
This verse is an accusation from God against certain women who claimed to speak on his behalf but were in reality making up messages. God says they dishonored him among his people for a few handfuls of barley and pieces of bread, that is, for small payments. With their lies they declared innocent people doomed to die, and promised life to guilty people who would not live. And the people believed them.

It is God, speaking through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. These women practiced forms of divination with cushions and veils, whose exact use is not known with certainty. God confronts them because they deceived his people to earn their living.

Today it invites us not to trade in the truth, and to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, without being carried away by comfortable words.
exp.35:13:
It says that the land of Israel will no longer "devour" its people or take away their children. "You shall devour" and "you shall kill" are strong words: they speak of a land that seemed to swallow up its inhabitants. The phrase "your nations" means "your peoples" or "your inhabitants." God promises this firmly: "saith the Lord God."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the mountains and the land of Israel, which had been left in ruins by judgment and exile. Other nations mocked, saying that the land consumed its people. God promises to restore the land and return his people to it, removing that shame. Interpreters differ on how this is fulfilled: in the return from exile, in the future, or in both.

For today: when you feel that your story is marked by loss or shame, remember that God knows how to restore. Bring that pain to him in prayer and trust that his word has the final say over your life.
exp.12:13:
God says that he will tear down the wall that the false prophets plastered over with loose mud, that is, with a weak mixture. When it falls, its foundation will be laid bare, and those who built it will be destroyed along with it. The result is that they will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a time of crisis for Jerusalem. Some prophets announced peace when there was no peace. They were like someone painting a fragile wall so that it looks solid. God shows that their lies will not survive judgment, like a storm that brings down what was badly built.

For today: it is not enough that something looks good on the outside. Let us examine whether our faith and our decisions are firm in God's truth, even when that truth is uncomfortable. Let us build on his Word, not on pleasant words.
exp.15:59:
It says that God will not forget the covenant he made with Jerusalem when she was young, that is, at the beginning of her history as a people. Although she broke it, God promises to establish with her a covenant that is eternal, without end. The word that is rendered as "everlasting" here is what the reader needs to understand, so it is enough to note that the covenant lasts forever.

The words are spoken by the Lord through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16, God describes Jerusalem as a woman he rescued and cared for, but who was unfaithful to him through idolatry. After announcing the punishment, God declares that his faithfulness is greater than her unfaithfulness. Many Christians see here a sign of the new covenant, though interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: even if you have failed, God does not reject you forever. Return to him with humility and trust in his faithfulness, not in your own.
exp.15:5:
He says that God passed by a newborn girl, abandoned in the field and covered in her own blood. No one cared for her, but God saw her and commanded her, "Live!" and repeated it with force. The "blood" mentioned here refers to the blood of childbirth. "I said unto thee" means the same as "I told you."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. He uses the image of an abandoned girl to remind her of her humble beginnings: everything she became, she received from God's compassion. Afterward God cares for her, covers her, and makes a covenant with her. This prepares the later charge of her unfaithfulness. Scholars agree that this is a symbolic image, not a literal historical account.

For today: when you feel worthless or carry a shameful past, remember that God looks on you with compassion and calls you to live. Respond to him with gratitude and faithfulness.
exp.15:51:
Ezekiel 16:52 is about Jerusalem, which looked down on Samaria and Sodom, and now must bear its own shame. Its sins were worse, so much so that those sisters appear "more righteous" by comparison. The idea that she "justified" her sisters means that by sinning more, she made the others look less guilty. "Confounded" means dishonored or put to shame.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. In this chapter He compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman who forgot God's love. Samaria and Sodom are the "sisters," well-known examples of judgment. God wants the people to see how serious their sin is, and the verses that follow announce restoration.

For today: before pointing out the faults of others, let us examine our own hearts. Humbly acknowledging our guilt brings us closer to God's mercy, which humbles in order to heal and restore.
exp.33:27:
It says that God's people will no longer be the victims of the nations or of wild beasts. "Prey" is what an animal hunts in order to devour. "They will dwell safely" means they will live in peace and confidence, and "no one shall make them afraid" means that no one will frighten them or make them flee.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time of Israel's exile. He had earlier rebuked the shepherds who mistreated the flock, and now he promises that he himself will care for it. This peace is part of a covenant of blessing: rain in season, fruit, and freedom from oppression. Some see here a future fulfillment, and others see a foretaste in Christ, the good Shepherd.

For today: if your fears weigh you down, remember that God cares for his own. Bring to him in prayer what frightens you, and trust in his protection.
exp.20:15:
It says the sword of judgment receives a command: "Position yourself to one side, go either to the right hand or the left, wherever your face is set." The words for left and right in the source are "left" and "right," so the sword is like a living weapon that goes where it is sent.

God is speaking, who has asked Ezekiel to announce a judgment on Jerusalem and its people for their rebellion. The sword is usually understood as the army of Babylon, although the text presents it as an instrument of God. Some think God is speaking to the sword, others that he is addressing the prophet; the general sense is that the judgment is not by chance, but is directed. Afterward, God says he will cause his wrath to rest.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also is in control and sets limits on his judgment. Today we can come to him with humility, trust in his justice, and let him correct our heart in time.
exp.26:9:
It says that Tyre had foreign soldiers from distant places: Persia, Lud and Phut (probably a region of Africa, though it is not known exactly). They hung their shields and helmets on the city's walls. With this, according to the text, they gave Tyre fame and splendor.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a rich and trading city. He describes it as a great, beautiful ship, full of riches and of people from many nations. The poet highlights its pride and its confidence in its power, before announcing its fall.

For today: it is not wrong to have resources, preparation or good allies, but we should not place our security or our identity in them. Let us put our trust in God, who sustains everything we have and gives us true worth.
exp.19:29:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the house of Israel. He asks them a question that sounds like a rebuke: are you not defiling yourselves in the same way your fathers did? Going after their abominations means being unfaithful to God, chasing after idols and detestable practices, the way a person betrays a spouse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the leaders of the people in exile. He reminds them that since they entered the promised land, they worshiped on the high places. The high places refers to the shrines on hilltops where they worshiped. God shows that the children were repeating the sins of their fathers, and yet they still wanted to consult him.

For today, it is worth asking ourselves what harmful customs we have inherited without questioning them. God invites us not to repeat what is wrong simply because it has always been done that way, but to turn back to him with sincerity.
exp.12:2:
God says woe, that is, that pain and judgment are coming, upon the prophets who are "foolish," meaning those who have no wisdom. These men followed their own spirit: they spoke what came out of their own minds and desires, not what God had told them. And they "have seen nothing": they received no true vision from Him.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, whom He calls "son of man." He tells him to speak against prophets of Israel who invented messages out of their own hearts. The verses that follow compare them to foxes among ruins: they sought their own gain and did not protect the people or defend their spiritual walls when danger came on the day of the Lord.

Today we can compare what we hear, even from leaders we like, with what the Bible says. And if we speak on God's behalf, let us do it with humility, without presenting our own ideas as if they were His voice.
exp.39:17:
It says that the pavement of the outer court, beside the gates, was the same length as the gateways, and that it was the "lower pavement." The word translated as "pavement" refers to a floor made of stone. This suggests that the court had a lower part near the gates and a higher part toward the temple, although the text gives no further detail.

Ezekiel describes a vision he received during the exile, about twenty years after the fall of Jerusalem. A man with a measuring reed guides him through the future temple and measures each part with care. At this point he walks through the outer court, with its chambers and its pavement. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about details, even the floor we walk on to draw near to him. If he arranges his house with such care, we can approach him with reverence and also bring order to our daily lives, faithfully attending to the small things.
exp.39:48:
It says that the porch, that is, the entrance of the temple, was twenty cubits long and eleven cubits wide. One went up to it by steps or stairs. On each side of the entrance there was a pillar beside the posts, which are the frames or supports of the door. A cubit was roughly half a meter.

Ezekiel records what he sees in a vision. A guide who looks like a man leads him and measures each part of a new temple. This takes place while the people are exiled in Babylon. Scholars understand this vision in several ways: some see it as a literal temple in the future, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people.

Coming into the place where God is involves going up, not just passing by. We can draw near to him with attention and reverence, setting aside time for prayer and for his Word, and not in a hurry or in a casual way.
exp.36:26:
He says that God will set his dwelling place in the midst of his people. The "tabernacle" is the tent or dwelling where God lived among the Israelites. The phrase "I will be their God" appears here, and "they shall be my people" expresses the same promise from the other side. It is a promise of closeness and mutual belonging.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had just lost their land and their temple, and they felt hopeless. Shortly before, God showed him the valley of dry bones that came back to life. Here he promises restoration, peace, and his lasting presence. Some understand this as the future of Israel; many Christians see it fulfilled also in Christ and in the church.

For today: even when you feel far away or defeated, God desires to be with you. Seek him every day in prayer, knowing that you belong to him.
exp.13:4:
It says that God will answer those who seek him with hearts full of idols, in order to reach the heart of Israel. Reaching them "in their heart" means getting to the very core of who they are. God knows that all of them had drawn away from him because of their idols, and he wants to wake them up.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some leaders of the people came to consult him, but they kept idols within themselves. God does not answer them with a comfortable piece of advice, but with a call to return to him. Scholars agree that this is about inward idolatry, though not everyone agrees on how much outward idolatry was also involved.

For today: before asking God for direction, ask yourself what thing is occupying the place that belongs only to him, and surrender it to him sincerely.
exp.22:43:
This verse says that the men sought out Aholah and Aholibah the way one seeks a prostitute. A "harlot" is a woman who sells her body, and "lewd" means corrupt and without shame. "Went in unto her" means they approached them in order to use them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Aholah and Aholibah represent Samaria and Jerusalem, two kingdoms of God's people. With this harsh image, God accuses them of having abandoned him to seek foreign alliances and gods. For that reason he announces judgment, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: faithfulness to God is lost little by little when we look for security, pleasure, or approval in other things. Today you can ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart, and return to him sincerely before that thing enslaves you.
exp.30:15:
It says that the fall of this great tree made the nations tremble when God brought it down to the place of the dead. "Pit" and "grave" refer to the tomb or the place of the dead. "Nether parts of the earth" is the world of the dead. The other trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, and those that "drink water," were comforted down there on seeing that the mighty one was also falling.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He compares Pharaoh and Egypt to a huge, proud cedar, as a warning to Egypt, which believed itself invincible. The trees represent nations and rulers. Scholars understand the part about comfort in different ways, but the central idea is that no human power escapes God's judgment.

For today: pride and power do not protect us. We can live with humility, remembering that everything we have comes from God and that He is the one who exalts or humbles.
exp.38:28:
God promises that he will no longer turn his face away from his people, meaning he will no longer withdraw his nearness or his favor from them. The reason is that he will have poured out his Spirit upon Israel. The phrase "hide my face" is an old way of saying that God pulls away or stops helping. "Pour out" suggests something abundant and generous.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into exile because of its sin, and God had kept silent toward them. Here he promises to gather them, bring them back to their land, and renew them within. Some see this fulfilled in the return from exile, others in the future, and others in the Spirit given in Christ; Christians have understood it in different ways.

For today: even though we sometimes feel God is distant because of our failures, his desire is to draw near and give us his Spirit. We can return to him with confidence and ask him to renew us.
exp.41:12:
It says that the north chambers and the south chambers, which stand beside the temple courtyard, are holy chambers. There the priests who draw near to the Lord will eat the most holy offerings, and they will keep the grain offerings, the sin offerings, and the guilt offerings. Everything is done there because the place is holy.

Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of the temple. A guide shows him and measures each part. These chambers are for the priests. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic message about the holiness of God and his presence with his people.

God takes care that what is sacred is treated with reverence. Today we can approach him with respect and gratitude, setting aside time to pray and read his Word, not doing it in a hurry or out of mere habit.
exp.16:6:
It says that a second eagle appeared, a great one, with broad wings and many feathers. The vine, which was low but full of leaves, bent its roots and stretched its branches toward this new eagle, hoping that it would water it. The "furrows of her plantation" are the rows of ground where it had been planted.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a parable or riddle addressed to Israel. Many understand that the first eagle represents Babylon, the vine represents the kingdom of Judah and its king, and the second eagle represents Egypt. Judah broke its covenant with Babylon to look for help in Egypt. God shows that this trust was a mistake.

Many times we look for security in the wrong places, when we already have everything we need where God has planted us. Before running to a "second eagle," whether it is money, influence, or human promises, ask God and trust in Him.
exp.26:4:
They say the builders of Tyre made this "ship" from the finest materials. The "boards" are the planks that form the hull. They used fir wood (some translators say cypress or pine) from Senir, another name for Mount Hermon. For the mast they took cedars from Lebanon, known for their strength and quality.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is commanded to raise a lament over Tyre. The trading city is presented as a magnificent ship. Tyre boasted of its beauty, and the image shows its wealth and pride. Later in the chapter that great ship sinks, and so its fall is announced.

Whatever beautiful things we have, whether money, talents or success, can make us feel secure without God. Today we can give thanks for what He has given us, use it with humility, and remember that our true security is in God, not in what we boast of.
exp.36:13:
God promises to put his Spirit in his people to give them new life. When this is fulfilled, they will know that God has spoken and also acted, because his word is not left as empty promises.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. This statement closes the vision of the dry bones, which represent Israel without hope. God promises to restore his people, and interpreters see here both the return from exile and, for many Christians, an image of the spiritual renewal that God gives.

Today we can remember that God gives life where there seems to be no way out. If you feel exhausted or without hope, ask him to renew you by his Spirit, and trust that he does what he says.
exp.12:11:
It says that when the wall falls, people will mock those who covered it with mud and will ask them: "Where is the coat of plaster you put on it?" The "daubing" is the layer of mud or plaster, and "daubed" means to cover it with that layer. It was a show of appearance, with no strength.
