God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The false prophets said "peace" when there was no peace, and they encouraged the people with pleasant messages. They were like someone who builds a weak wall and only covers it with paint. God announces that his judgment, like a storm, would expose the falsehood.

For today: let us not build our lives, our families, or our faith on appearances or on words that only sound good. Let us seek God's truth, even when it corrects us, because only it can stand the storms.
exp.21:22:
This verse is an introductory phrase. "And the word of the Lord came unto me" means: "God spoke to me." With these words, Ezekiel makes clear that what follows does not come from his own opinion, but from God.

Ezekiel is a prophet who lives among the exiles of Judah, in Babylon. Earlier, God had announced that Jerusalem would be like a furnace where silver is melted. Now a new message begins, which explains why that judgment is coming: the injustice of the leaders, the prophets, and the people. In other words, God does not punish without reason, but first states clearly what is going wrong.

Today we can learn to hear the word of God with seriousness, without softening it. Before we set ourselves to judge others, it is good to ask God: "Is there anything in me that needs to be corrected?"
exp.32:12:
God says that if he promises life to a person who is righteous, and that person trusts in their good works and then does evil, their good deeds of the past will not be remembered. Here "righteousness" means an upright life, and "wickedness" is evil. Because of the evil he has done, he will die.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom He set as a watchman over Israel. The exiled people were saying that God was unjust, and God answers them that He takes no pleasure in anyone's death. He warns them that neither a reputation for goodness nor a past record protects someone who rebels, and that the one who repents always has a door open.

For today: do not live off your past merits, nor settle into thinking you are already good enough. Walk each day with humility, depending on God, and if you fail, return to Him soon, because He wants you to live.
exp.28:11:
God says he will leave the land of Egypt desolate, just like other lands that have been ruined. Its cities will remain in ruins for forty years. He also says he will scatter the Egyptians among the nations.

Speaking through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon, God addresses Egypt. Egypt considered itself powerful and had been a deceptive support for Israel. God judges it for its pride. The forty years can be understood literally or as a symbolic period of punishment; scholars interpret them in different ways, and there is no certainty about how this was fulfilled historically.

For today: let us not place our final trust in human powers, whether money, fame, or governments. Only God is secure. And even in judgment, the following text shows that he leaves a door open to restoration.
exp.15:3:
This verse describes a newborn whom no one cared for. Her navel cord was not cut, she was not washed with water to clean her, she was not rubbed with salt (an ancient custom for caring for a baby), and she was not wrapped in swaddling cloths to keep her warm.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl to represent Jerusalem. Her origins, the Amorite and the Hittite, show that she had nothing that made her special. God wants the people to remember that everything they came to have was by his grace, not by their own merit.

For today: when you are tempted to feel proud or self-sufficient, remember that everything good in your life is a gift from God. That leads us to live with gratitude and humility, and also to care for those who today are alone and helpless.
exp.47:20:
It says the land that is left over on each side of the holy portion and of the city belongs to the prince. That land stretches toward the east and toward the west, alongside the twenty-five thousand (reeds, a unit of length). Even so, the sanctuary stands in the center of the holy portion.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, and in the final vision of the book he divides the land for the exiled people. The sanctuary is placed at the center, and the prince has his own share set apart. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic or related to the future.

For today: although the prince had his own land, God remained at the center. Put God at the center of your plans and your possessions, and let him order everything else.
exp.36:19:
It says that the two sticks on which Ezekiel wrote, one for Judah and one for Joseph (Ephraim), were to be held in his hand, in plain sight of everyone. "Sticks" are pieces of wood, like rods. "Writest" means "write." In this way the people would see the symbolic act with their own eyes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile. For centuries the people had been divided into two kingdoms, and now they were scattered. God asks him to join the two sticks together in his hand as a sign that one day he will gather Israel into one nation, under one king. The people would ask what it meant, and so Ezekiel could explain the promise to them.

For today: God can heal divisions that seem impossible. We can pray and seek reconciliation in the family or in the church, trusting that He is the one who unites.
exp.39:24:
It says that this gate had windows and arches all around, similar to those of the other gates that had already been measured. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The word "arches" probably refers to porches or entry halls of the gateway.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him, in which a guide takes him through a new temple and measures everything carefully. The Jewish people were exiled in Babylon and the temple had been destroyed. These exact measurements showed them that God had an orderly plan. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God is a God of order and of care for details. If today you find yourself in a time of ruin or waiting, trust that he has not forgotten his people and continues building with purpose.
exp.22:23:
This verse describes a great army that comes to attack Aholibah. They arrive with war chariots, carts, wheels, and many peoples. The shields are large, and the helmets are head coverings. They surround the city fully armed. God says he will set judgment before them, and they will judge her according to their own laws.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter, Aholibah represents Jerusalem, which turned away from God and sought alliances with Assyria and Babylon instead of trusting him. God uses those same nations as an instrument of judgment. Scholars understand this as a strong and poetic image of unfaithfulness.

For today: when we place our trust in things that are not God, sooner or later they fail us and hurt us. Today is a good day to return to him with sincerity.
exp.15:28:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to an unfaithful woman, kept increasing her unfaithfulness toward God. Now she did this also with the land of Canaan and with the Chaldeans (Babylon). "Adultery" here means idolatry and alliances with other nations, not only sexual sin. "Being satisfied" means being content. Despite all her searching outside of God, she never became content.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells the story of Jerusalem as a girl whom He rescued, cared for, and adorned. She, however, turned to idols and to neighboring nations. God shows her her sin in order to call her to acknowledge it. Some understand the references to Canaan and Chaldea as religious and political influences; the text uses them as a strong image.

For today: when we look for satisfaction in things that are not God, such as money, success, or approval, it is never enough. Today you can ask yourself what you are pursuing to fill your emptiness, and bring it to God in prayer.
exp.13:17:
It says that even if three very righteous men lived in a sinful land (in context, Noah, Daniel and Job), they would not be able to save even their own sons and daughters. Only they themselves would be saved.

The words "deliver" and "men" in the quoted phrase are not translated here, so the explanation of the older wording is omitted.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, swearing "as I live." Some elders of Israel had idols in their hearts, and God warns that a people who turn away from him will face judgment. God shows that the righteousness of others does not cover the guilt of someone who persists in sin. Scholars disagree about how this relates to intercession, but the central point is personal responsibility.

Today: faith is not inherited or borrowed. Pray for your family, but seek God yourself with sincerity and return to him each day.
exp.45:18:
It says that the angelic guide brought Ezekiel, in the vision, through an entry beside the gate into the holy rooms of the priests. Those rooms faced north, and behind them, toward the west, there was a separate space. The guide "brought me through" is the meaning of the verse, and the rooms are chambers, or halls.

Ezekiel receives a vision of a new temple, and a guide shows him each place in turn. What follows explains that this place was used for cooking the sacred offerings, so the priests did not have to carry them out into the outer court where the people were. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares about order and reverence in what is holy. We can set apart a time and a quiet place to be with Him, taking care that what is sacred is not mixed up with the hurry of each day.
exp.35:14:
God promises the land of Israel, speaking to it as if it were a person, that it will no longer have to hear insults from other nations or bear their mockery. The word for insults is rendered here as words of contempt and disgrace. He also says that he will no longer let the people of the land be bereaved of their children, meaning that the land will no longer be a place of loss and misfortune.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel at a time when the people were living in exile. The neighboring nations mocked Israel, saying that its land devoured its inhabitants. God answers by promising to restore the land and its honor. The verse that follows reminds the people that they themselves had defiled the land with their sin.

For today: if you carry shame over mistakes from the past or over what others say about you, remember that God is able to restore. Bring your story to him honestly and trust that he can give back your dignity and hope.
exp.47:16:
It describes an open space around the city, called the "common land," meaning free and shared ground with no buildings. This space would measure 250 measuring rods on each side: north, south, east, and west. A measuring rod was a unit of length; in Ezekiel it is usually understood to be about three meters, although scholars do not fully agree.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. In this final vision, a land is described as divided in an orderly way, with a holy place and a city at the center. Some believe it is a symbolic picture of God's restoration; others think of something literal and future. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: God values order and shared space. We can leave "open spaces" in our lives: time to rest, pray, and care for others, without filling every corner with activities.
exp.21:26:
The explanation says that the leaders of Jerusalem, described here as "princes," were like wolves catching their prey. By shedding blood and destroying lives, they were seeking only to enrich themselves. The word "prey" in the verse is what their ambition fed on. "Souls" here refers to people, to human lives.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God denounces the sins of Jerusalem: prophets, priests, princes, and people had failed. Those who were meant to care for and guide others were taking advantage of them. For that reason, judgment was coming upon the city.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, ask yourself whether you are using it to serve or to profit. God expects those who lead to care for people, not to use them. Ask Him for a just and generous heart.
exp.33:2:
The explanation says that Israel's shepherds took advantage of the flock: they took the milk, dressed themselves in the wool, and killed the best-fed sheep, but they did not care for the sheep. Feeding and caring for the flock is what the shepherds were supposed to do. To kill is to slaughter an animal.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The "shepherds" were the leaders of Israel, especially the kings and rulers. God rebukes them because they used their position for their own benefit and not to serve the people, who were left wounded and scattered. Then God promises to care for His flock Himself.

Anyone who has some responsibility over others, whether in the church, at work, or in the family, should ask themselves: am I serving, or am I being served? Caring for others with humility and attention is the true way to lead.
exp.30:17:
God asks Pharaoh: who is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? And He answers that you will be brought down along with them, down to the underworld, the place of the dead. You will lie among the uncircumcised, that is, pagan peoples, and among those who died by the sword. All of this refers to Pharaoh and his people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter He compares Egypt to a huge cedar, like those of Assyria, which filled itself with pride and fell. The "trees of Eden" are images of powerful nations. It is poetic language, and scholars debate the details of this picture of the place of the dead.

For today: power, success, and fame do not make us invincible. God opposes the proud, so it is wise to be thankful for what we have and to live with humility, remembering that everything comes from Him.
exp.46:2:
The man who was guiding Ezekiel went out toward the east with a measuring line in his hand. He measured a thousand cubits (about 500 meters, since a cubit is roughly half a meter) and led him through the water, which reached only to the ankles.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile, about a restored temple. From the temple flows a river that grows deeper with every thousand cubits measured. Many understand it as an image of the life and blessing that come from God's presence. Some see it as a promise for Israel, and others relate it to Christ and the Spirit. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: life with God can begin with little, like water up to the ankles. Take one more step, pray, read, obey, and let Him lead you deeper.
exp.16:20:
God says that all who flee from the king, together with his troops, will fall by the sword, and that the survivors will be scattered in every direction. The words "fugitives" and "bands" are the ones translated in the verse as those who escape and his troops; "by the sword" means by the sword; and "toward all winds" means toward all sides. In the end, everyone will recognize that God kept his word.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. King Zedekiah of Judah had made an oath of loyalty to Babylon in God's name and then broke it, seeking help from Egypt. God regards that oath as his own. Later in the same chapter, God promises to plant a tender shoot that will become a great cedar. Many Christians see this pointing to the Messiah, although it is interpreted in different ways.

Today: God takes our promises seriously. Keeping the word we have given, even when it costs us, is a way of honoring him, and trusting in him is safer than seeking ways out on our own.
exp.40:13:
This verse gives one more measurement of the temple that Ezekiel sees in his vision: the front of the house, together with the open space that lay to the east, measured one hundred cubits in width. A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The word "separate place" does not mean a department, but an area set apart or reserved beside the temple. Its exact use is not known with certainty.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives this vision from God. A guide leads him, measuring every part of the temple. Chapters 40 to 48 show a temple that is orderly and symmetrical. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares about order and about details. We can devote the small things of daily life to him with care, because he dwells among his people.
exp.11:21:
God speaks to Ezekiel and asks him about a popular saying that was going around in Israel. The people were saying, "The days pass and no vision will be fulfilled." A saying is a common expression, and a vision refers to the messages God gave through his prophets. It was a way of mocking the warnings.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people saw that the judgment announced was taking a long time, and they concluded it would never come. With that excuse, they ignored the call to turn back to God. That is why the Lord says he will put an end to that saying, because his word will indeed be fulfilled.

For today: when God's response seems slow, do not mistake his patience for absence or indifference. His word still stands. Use the time to listen to him, correct your path, and trust that what he says is true.
exp.29:15:
God says he will send fire, that is, destruction, upon Egypt. Sin (probably a fortified city in the northeast) will suffer great pain. No (the city of Thebes) will be invaded, and Memphis will live under constant distress. The phrase about the city not being torn apart is hard to translate, and other versions render it as being broken open through breaches.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around the time when Babylon dominated the region. Egypt was a power in which Judah had placed its trust. God announces that this human security will fall, and that he is Lord over all nations.

For today: examine where you are placing your security, whether in money, work, influence, or your own strength. All of these can fail. Rest first in God, who does not change, and ask him for wisdom to use well what you have.
exp.39:8:
It says the guide measured the porch, or inner entrance, of the gateway: it was eight cubits deep, and its posts or pillars measured two cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm (about 45 to 50 cm). The posts are the pillars on either side of the entrance. The final phrase indicates that the gate faced toward the side of the temple.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a temple. A man with a measuring reed guides him and shows him every detail. This takes place in a time of great discouragement for Israel. Scholars interpret the vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of God's presence, or as a spiritual image.

For today: God is concerned with order and with details. We can approach Him with reverence and trust that, even in difficult times, He continues to build and has not forgotten us.
exp.20:3:
He says that God will draw out his sword, that is, his judgment, and that it will reach everyone in the land: the righteous and the wicked. "Cut down" means to cut off or strike down, "north" is the direction the sword points, and "all flesh" refers to every person. From south to north, no one would be left out.

The LORD speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their persistent sin. That the righteous would also fall is hard to understand. Some think the righteous would share in the consequences of a national calamity; others think the text speaks in general terms. The passage does not fully explain it.

For today: let us take God's warning seriously and not grow comfortable with the sin around us. Let us ask him to give us a humble heart, and trust in his justice and mercy even when we do not understand everything.
exp.22:32:
It says that Jerusalem will be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, like someone who drinks a bitter cup. "Cup" here is a cup that stands for God's punishment. The cup of astonishment and desolation means being left alone, empty and destroyed. It is the same cup that her sister Samaria drank.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells a story about two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, who represent the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Both turned away from God and sought help from other nations and their idols. Since Samaria had already been destroyed, God warns that Jerusalem will meet the same end if she follows the same path.

For today: learn from the mistakes of others. If we see that turning away from God brings ruin to other people, we can return to Him in time, before suffering the same consequences.
exp.39:40:
There were eight tables in total beside the gate of the temple: four on one side and four on the other. On them the animals were slaughtered, that is, they were killed and prepared for the sacrifice. It was an orderly place, arranged with care for that work.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple, and a guide with a measuring reed shows him every detail. Scholars disagree about its meaning: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence restored among his people. For a discouraged people, it was a promise that God would once again dwell with them.

For today: God cares about order and reverence when we draw near to Him. We can prepare our hearts before we pray or worship, without haste or carelessness, remembering that Christ has already made the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.40:3:
Here the guide measures the innermost part of the temple. He measures twenty cubits in length and twenty in width, that is, a perfect square. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. Then the guide says to Ezekiel: "This is the most holy place," the most sacred room, where the presence of God was symbolized.

Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple, and a man shows him each measurement. It is Ezekiel who tells what he sees. Interpreters do not agree on its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, others of a spiritual picture of God's hope to be with his people. For the exiles, it was a promise that God had not forgotten them.

Today we can remember that God is holy, but he also wants to be close to his people. Set aside a quiet moment each day to pray, with reverence and trust.
exp.28:4:
God tells Pharaoh that he will be left thrown out in the wilderness, along with all the fish of his rivers. He will fall on the open field, and no one will gather him up or bury him. He will be food for the wild animals and the birds of the sky. The phrase "the open field" refers to the surface of the field, and the word "gathered" means brought together for burial.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Pharaoh is called the great dragon of the rivers, a picture of the power of Egypt and the Nile. He had thought himself the owner of everything and said: "My river is mine, and I made it for myself." Moreover, Egypt had been a fragile reed on which Israel leaned, and it failed.

For today: everything we have, such as health, work, or achievements, is a gift from God. Trusting in our own power or in human supports ends up failing. We can thank God every day and rest in him.
exp.23:5:
God declares a "woe" against Jerusalem, called the "bloody city," meaning a city full of violence and death. He compares it to a dirty pot whose scum was never removed. God commands that the meat be taken out "piece by piece," without casting lots, that is, without choosing who is saved and who is not: judgment will reach everyone.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel, while Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, around 588 BC. The pot is a parable: the city and its inhabitants will be put into the fire. Their sin was not hidden; the blood spilled was in plain sight, like blood on bare rock.

For today: let us not minimize or hide our faults. Let us ask God to cleanse us, and seek justice and compassion toward others.
exp.38:5:
God says he will send fire on Magog, which is the land or people of the leader called Gog, and also on those who live at ease in the coastlands, or distant lands. The phrase about living at ease means that they live with confidence, without fear. The result will be that everyone will recognize that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he announces judgment on Gog and his allies, who attack Israel. Interpreters disagree: some see a historical event, others a future event, others a symbol of evil defeated by God. God wants to protect his people and show that he is holy.

For today: let us not trust in a false sense of security that ignores God. We can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his own and has the final word over all injustice.
exp.19:46:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the forest of the south, that is, to the south. God says he will kindle a fire that will burn every tree, both the green and the dry, and that no one will be able to put it out. The phrase about faces refers to the surface, or to everything there is, from the south to the north.

God speaks, and Ezekiel is his messenger. Many understand that the forest is an image of Jerusalem and Judah, and the fire is God's judgment for their disobedience. The idea of green and dry trees suggests that the judgment would reach everyone. Then Ezekiel says that the people take him for someone who speaks in riddles, and so they do not understand the warning.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly or think they are simply stories. If something in your life needs to change, respond soon and with humility, because God corrects us to invite us to return to him.
exp.22:16:
The explanation says that the Babylonians came to Aholibah, the woman in the story, into her bed of love, and they stained her with their unfaithfulness. She too was defiled by them, but then she grew weary and sick of them. "Fornication" here speaks of unlawful sexual relations, and also of spiritual unfaithfulness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), to show how his people abandoned God and sought alliances with foreign nations. Aholibah fell in love with Babylon and pursued her, but that alliance ended in disappointment and judgment.

For today: what seduces us away from God promises much, but leaves emptiness. Before you chase after something, ask yourself whether it draws you closer to Him or farther away, and return to God when you notice you are drifting away.
exp.15:8:
He says that God washed the young woman with water and removed the blood that was on her. Then he anointed her with oil. The word "blood" here refers to the filth of her birth described earlier in the chapter. The verb used in the original, which means to anoint or to perfume, was a way of caring for someone and honoring them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl whom He rescues, cares for, and takes as a wife. That girl represents Jerusalem and the people of Israel. God reminds them how much He loved them and how greatly He favored them, to show how serious their unfaithfulness is, which is denounced later on.

For today: nothing good we have came from ourselves. God cleansed us and cared for us when we could not do it alone. Today you can thank Him for one specific way He has cared for you, and respond to Him with faithfulness and gratitude.
exp.31:22:
It says that the graves of Assyria lie in the deepest parts of the pit, and that its people are buried around its tomb. All of them died by the sword, though earlier they spread fear among the living. "Pit" is the place of the dead; "by the sword" is the same as "by the sword"; "uncircumcised," here, describes foreign peoples, without a covenant with God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who laments over Egypt. He shows Egypt in the realm of the dead, alongside mighty nations such as Assyria and Elam, which have already fallen. The message is that no empire, however fearsome, escapes God's judgment. The details of that world of the dead are poetic images, and scholars interpret them in various ways.

Today: do not let yourself be intimidated by human power or envy it. What is held up by fear and pride does not last; trust in God, who rules over all.
exp.33:23:
It says that God himself will be the God of his people, and that "my servant David" will be a prince among them. "Prince" here means ruler or leader. It ends with "I the Lord have spoken it," which works like a seal: what has been said is firm and sure.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile. Earlier he had condemned the unfaithful shepherds who mistreated the sheep. Now he promises to rescue them. David died centuries before, so "David" is understood as a future king of his line. Christians see in this Jesus, the Good Shepherd, though others read it differently.

For today: when leaders fail you or you feel lost, remember that God remains your Shepherd. Trust his guidance and seek to follow Jesus, who cares for his people faithfully.
exp.16:5:
It says that the seed that was planted grew and became a leafy vine, but a low one, not a tall one. Its branches leaned toward the eagle that had planted it, and its roots stayed beneath it. The new shoots of the vine are the tender growths that spring from it, and the branches that take root and produce new plants are the ones that spread its life further.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who presents a parable about two eagles and a vine. Almost everyone understands that the first eagle represents Babylon, and that the vine is Judah under the king whom Babylon placed on the throne. Its growth was humble and dependent. God uses this image to show the need to remain faithful to a covenant, and the foolishness of Judah in seeking help from Egypt.

Today we can ask ourselves on whom we truly depend. Growing under God's blessing is good, but seeking security in human powers, instead of trusting in Him and keeping what has been promised, leaves us fragile.
exp.42:8:
God says that Israel must put away from him their "whoredom," which here means idolatry and spiritual unfaithfulness, and also "the carcases of their kings." If they do this, he promises to dwell in the midst of them forever.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. Earlier, the people and their kings had defiled his name with idols, and it seems they also had tombs or funeral monuments near the temple, separated by only a wall. Some understand the "carcases" as lifeless idols; others understand them as royal tombs. It is uncertain which meaning predominates.

For today: God desires to be near us, but he asks for a heart with no rivals. We can ask ourselves what thing has taken God's place in our lives, and with his help put it away so that he may be the center.
exp.23:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel on an exact date: the ninth year, the tenth month, the tenth day. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" is an older way of saying "I received a message from the Lord". Jehovah is the name of God.

The one speaking is God, and the message comes to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The following verses explain that on that same day the king of Babylon began to besiege Jerusalem. Many understand the date to correspond to January 588 B.C., though the exact calculation may vary. God wanted his people to understand that what was happening was not chance.

God acts in real history, on specific days and in specific places. Even when everything seems to be falling apart, he continues to speak and remains in control. Today we can approach his Word with humility, especially in difficult times, trusting that God is not absent.
exp.43:9:
It says that the Levites who turned away from God when Israel went after its idols will have to bear the consequences of their sin. "They shall bear their iniquity" means they will answer for their guilt.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision about the new temple. God rebukes Israel for having brought foreigners with no commitment to him to serve in his sanctuary. The Levites who failed are not destroyed, but they lose their closest service: they remain as gatekeepers and assistants. Some interpreters see here discipline mixed with mercy, since they continue to serve.

Today: whoever leads or serves others carries greater responsibility. If we have gone astray, God invites us to acknowledge it and return, even though at times the consequences remain while we continue serving with humility.
exp.16:11:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the rebellious people of Judah. He asks them whether they do not understand the meaning of the parable of the eagles and the vine that Ezekiel has just told. Then he gives them the explanation: the king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar) came to Jerusalem, took its king and its princes, and led them away as captives to Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The people did not want to accept that their situation was the consequence of their disobedience, and God explains clearly what had happened and why. This took place when King Jehoiachin was taken captive, around 597 B.C.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us plainly, and we do not want to understand. We can ask him for humility to recognize our mistakes, to listen to his correction, and to trust him again, instead of hardening our hearts.
exp.35:12:
This verse says that God speaks to the mountains of Israel, which stand for the land itself. The neighboring nations said of the land, "Thou land devourest up men," meaning a land that consumes its own people, and "hast bereaved thy nations," meaning that it makes its own inhabitants die out.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The land had been left empty by war and punishment, and the enemy peoples mocked it. God promises to bring Israel back, to make the land bear fruit again, and to take away that shame. Some understand the promise as fulfilled in part by the return from exile, while others also see a future fulfillment.

Today, when someone puts a humiliating label on you because of your failures, remember that God does not define you by that. He knows how to restore and to give a new beginning. Bring your shame to Him in prayer.
exp.34:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," an expression that stresses that he is a simple human being. He is told to set his face toward Mount Seir, that is, to look straight at that region with determination, and to announce a message of judgment against it.

The Lord, the God of Israel, is speaking. Seir was the mountainous region of Edom, a neighboring people descended from Esau. Ezekiel was prophesying during the exile in Babylon, and the next chapter shows that Edom took advantage of Israel's fall and kept up an old hostility. God presents himself here as the defender of his wounded people.

For today: God sees injustice and is not indifferent to those who rejoice in the suffering of others. We can trust that he will act justly, so there is no need for us to take revenge. And we should examine whether we ourselves take delight in the downfall of others.
exp.19:47:
It says that all people will see that God himself kindled this fire, and that no one will be able to put it out. The phrase "all flesh" means every human being. "Jehovah" is the name of the God of Israel.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to prophesy against "the south forest." Many understand this as a picture of the judgment that would come upon Judah and Jerusalem because of their disobedience. The fire consumes green trees as well as dry ones, meaning no one escapes. Afterward Ezekiel complains that the people do not take him seriously and see him as someone who speaks in riddles. Some believe the fire represents the invasion of Babylon, but the text uses symbolic language.

Today we can remember that God speaks in earnest and that his word is not a mere story. Instead of hardening our hearts or mocking his warnings, we can stop, examine our lives, and turn back to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.32:26:
Here the explanation says that God, with an oath ("As I live"), announces a certain punishment. Those who live among the ruins will die by the sword. Those who are out in the open field will be given to wild beasts to be devoured. Those who hide in strongholds and caves will die of plague. No one will escape, wherever they are.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Jews who remained in the land after the fall of Jerusalem. They believed God would give them the land, as he had given it to Abraham. But they lived with violence, idolatry, and immorality. God answers them that they cannot claim his promises while they despise his way.

For today: it is not enough to say "I belong to God" while we live as we please. Ask the Lord to show you something you should change, and obey him today with humility.
exp.38:8:
It says that, after the army of Gog is defeated, the people of Israel will go out to gather the enemy's weapons and use them as fuel for seven years. The shields in the verse, the large ones, and the clubs, the hand weapons, are the things it describes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He tells the Israelites that he himself will defend them and show his holiness before the nations. Christians understand this scene in different ways: as a historical event, as something still to come, or as a symbolic picture. The number seven may indicate something complete, but there is no certainty about that detail.

For today: trust that God is greater than any threat. He can turn into peace what others used to harm, so hand him your fears and let him be your defender.
exp.22:11:
She says that Oholibah, the younger sister, fell in love with the Assyrians, her neighbors: captains and princes dressed in fine clothes, horsemen on horses, all of them very attractive young men. The second part of that description means young men worth desiring, and the phrase about their clothing refers to uniforms or very fine clothes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria, the northern kingdom) and Oholibah (Jerusalem, Judah). With this picture of marital unfaithfulness, God denounces that his people sought political and religious alliances with foreign powers instead of trusting in him. Samaria had already been destroyed, and Jerusalem did not learn the lesson.

For today: examine what things dazzle you and where you place your security: money, power, fame, or influential people. What shines on the outside can draw you away from God, so ask him to keep you faithful.
exp.35:1:
This verse begins a message from God. He says that the enemy mocked Israel and cried out, "Aha!", an expression of scorn and triumph. The enemy claimed that the ancient high places, that is, the old mountains of the land, now belonged to them as their inheritance. Because means "because" in the sense of "for the reason that," so the sentence simply gives the cause of what follows.

Ezekiel speaks to the mountains of Israel on God's behalf. The people were in exile and the land had been left in ruins. The neighboring peoples, and the text names Edom in particular, took advantage and boasted. God answers because the land and his people matter to him.

For today: when others mock your situation or write off your life, remember that God sees and hears. You can bring him your pain with confidence, because the last word belongs to him, not to the one who mocks.
exp.45:16:
This verse says that if the prince gives part of his land to one of his servants, that gift belongs to that servant only until the "year of liberty," and then it returns to the prince. But what the prince gives to his sons remains theirs as an inheritance.

God speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and of the life of the restored people. Many understand the "year of liberty" to refer to the Jubilee year, according to the law in Leviticus 25, although some interpret it in other ways. The rule aims to protect the people's lands from being taken away by the prince.

For today: God cares about justice and does not want those who have power to abuse what belongs to others. If you have any authority, in your home, work, or church, use it with honesty and respect what belongs to other people.
exp.42:2:
Ezekiel says that this vision of God's glory looked like the two he had already seen: the one of Jerusalem's destruction and the one by the river Chebar. When he saw it, he fell facedown on the ground.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here as a priest exiled in Babylon. Earlier he saw God's glory leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now, in a vision, he sees that glory returning through the east gate. It is a message of hope: God does not abandon his people forever. Some believe it refers to a restoration that was near, others to something still in the future.

For today: when God draws near, the natural response is humility. You can begin your prayer today with reverence, remembering who God is, before asking him for anything.
exp.29:8:
God says that he will send messengers in ships to frighten Ethiopia, a nation that lived at ease and felt secure. That country will tremble with fear, as happened when Egypt fell. The word "frighten" here means to cause great fear, and the word "secure" refers to a sense of being safe and free from worry. What he announces is about to arrive.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Egypt trusted in its power and its allies, among them Ethiopia, which would be shaken by Egypt's fall. According to the context, God would use Nebuchadnezzar as an instrument of judgment. The details of these "messengers in ships" are understood in different ways.

For today: check where you rest your confidence too firmly, such as money, work, or influence. All of these can fail; only God is a firm trust. Bring it to him in prayer today.
exp.20:18:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to draw two roads along which the sword of the king of Babylon can advance. The two roads start from the same country and are drawn where the way toward the city begins. The phrase about casting lots seems to refer to the king deciding his route by means of chance or divination.

The Lord speaks, and He does so through a symbolic action that Ezekiel is to act out. According to the following text, one road led to Rabbah of the Ammonites and the other to Jerusalem. The king of Babylon consulted idols and the livers of animals, but the passage presents God as the one who directs the outcome and announces judgment on Judah.

For today: even though we sometimes feel that our lives depend on luck or on the decisions of powerful people, we can trust that God still governs. Today you can bring your decisions to Him in prayer.
exp.44:16:
This verse says that the prince will be responsible for providing the animals and offerings for Israel's festivals: the burnt offerings (offerings burned completely), the sin offerings, the drink offerings (wine poured out), and the peace offerings (offerings of fellowship). The "festivals" are the appointed feasts, and the "new moons" are the beginning of each month. "To make atonement" means to cover sin in order to restore the relationship with God.

The Lord GOD speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the order of worship. The people contribute the offerings, and the prince presents them on behalf of everyone. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as literal and future, others as symbolic, and others connect it with Christ.

For today: those in leadership should serve responsibly, helping the people worship God with order and sincerity. And all of us can give with joy.
exp.39:18:
He says the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the distance from the lower gate, the outer one, to the front of the inner court. It was one hundred cubits, and the measurement was taken toward the east and toward the north. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so we are talking about about fifty meters. The word "forefront" means front, and the court is an open courtyard of the temple.

Ezekiel tells of a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple in full detail. Interpreters do not agree: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his people.

For today: God cares about details and desires order and reverence when we approach him. We can come near with calm and respect, knowing that he dwells with his people.
exp.44:17:
Thus says the Lord God. In the first month, on the first day of the month, God commanded that a young bull without defect be taken from the herd to cleanse the sanctuary. To cleanse means to take away guilt or cover it through a sacrifice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a restored temple and worship (chapters 40–48). After the exile, the people needed to see that the presence of God requires purity. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture. There is no complete agreement on this.

For today: God cares for the holiness of his house and of his people. We can begin each year or each new stage with humility, asking for forgiveness. Christians believe that Christ is the perfect sacrifice who cleanses us completely.
exp.15:10:
It says that God adorned the woman of the story with jewelry: he put ornaments on her, bracelets on her arms, and a chain on her neck. The explanation of "adorned" and "bracelets" has been left out, since those words appear in the verse as the King James Version gives it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl, whom he took in, cared for, and enriched. She represents Jerusalem and the people of Israel. God reminds them of how much he gave them, because later they forgot his kindness and were unfaithful to him. This image is a comparison, not a literal story.

For today: Everything good we have comes from God's grace, not from our own merit. Today you can pause and thank him for three concrete blessings, so that the heart does not become proud or forgetful.
exp.32:29:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel that his people talk about him at the corners and in the doorways of the houses. They gather with their relatives and invite one another: "Come, let's hear what message he brings now from the LORD." The word that is rendered here as "talking against" can be understood as talking about him with curiosity or with mockery; scholars read it in different ways.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was already among the exiles in Babylon. He had announced the fall of Jerusalem and the desolation of the land, and those words had come true. Even so, the people saw his preaching as an interesting show, not as a serious call.

Today we can hear sermons, read the Bible, or listen to Christian songs only for enjoyment or out of habit. Let us ask God for a willing heart, and let us choose today one teaching that we can put into practice.
exp.36:5:
God tells Ezekiel to announce to the dry bones what He will do. He will put sinews (tendons) on them to join the bones, make flesh grow, and cover them with skin. Then He will give them spirit, which can also be understood as breath or the breath of life. With that they will live, and they will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the middle of the exile in Babylon. The bones represent Israel, which felt it had no hope. The same chapter explains it this way: it is a promise of the people's restoration. Some also see in it an image of resurrection, but the text emphasizes the renewal of Israel.

For today: when you feel that something in your life is dry or has no way out, do not depend only on what you see. Pray, trust in God's Word, and wait for Him to be able to restore life and hope.
exp.13:8:
It says that if a prophet is deceived and speaks a false word, God himself intervenes: "I the Lord have deceived that prophet." Then he will stretch out his hand against him and "destroy him," that is, remove him completely from the midst of his people.

God speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders of Israel had idols in their hearts and yet still sought a word from God. God says he will answer according to the condition of that heart. Interpreters explain "deceived" in various ways: as a judgment in which God allows the deception to take effect, or as strong language about his sovereignty. The text does not say that God is a liar. Both the one who asks and the prophet bear their guilt.

For today: before seeking direction from God, examine what occupies your heart. Ask him to remove whatever competes with him, and test every teaching by Scripture.
exp.14:3:
It says that a vine branch which has already been thrown into the fire, burned at both of its ends and also in the middle, is no longer good for making anything. The "ends" are the two extremes of the branch, and "devoured" means that the fire destroyed it. The final question calls for a clear answer: no, it is no longer fit for any work.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to the wood of the vine, which is useful for bearing fruit but not for building. Because Jerusalem was not faithful to him, God announces that he will give her over to the fire, that is, to judgment through her enemies.

For today: our worth does not lie in how we appear, but in remaining joined to God and bearing fruit for him. Let us ask him to keep us faithful and humble, and to lead us back to him in time.
exp.37:4:
This verse names other peoples who will join Gog in the attack: Persia, Ethiopia, and Libya. All of them go armed with shields and helmets. They are well-equipped soldiers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that Gog, a leader from distant lands, will gather a great alliance against Israel. But the text makes clear that it is God who puts hooks in his jaws, that is, who leads and controls him. Scholars understand in different ways who Gog is and when this prophecy will be fulfilled.

For today: although the powers of the world may seem enormous and well armed, God still governs history. We can trust in Him when we feel fear before problems that are bigger than we are.
exp.19:7:
They say that the people of Israel, while still in Egypt, rebelled against God. They did not want to obey his call to put away the "abominations of their eyes," that is, the images and detestable things they worshiped. Nor did they give up the idols of Egypt. For this reason God said he would pour out his wrath upon them; the phrase about accomplishing his anger means letting his anger run its full course.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. The elders of Israel came to consult him, and God reminds them that their disobedience goes back a long way. This account does not appear in the same way in Exodus, and some scholars think Ezekiel summarizes the history with his own emphasis. The verse that follows shows that God acted for the sake of his name.

For today: the heart easily grows accustomed to what it sees. Ask God to show you which thing around you has taken his place, and dare to let it go with confidence in his mercy.
exp.43:11:
God speaks with seriousness against certain Levites. They helped the people worship idols, and so they became a stumbling block, meaning a cause through which others trip and fall into sin. Their conduct led others into wrongdoing. God declares that they "shall bear their iniquity": they will carry the consequences of their guilt.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of the new temple. Some Levites had turned away and had served before the idols. For this reason they lose the privilege of being priests, although God still allows them to serve in tasks of care and support. Both his justice and his mercy are shown. Interpreters explain this vision in different ways.

Those who serve God carry a greater responsibility, because their example influences others. We can ask him to help us live in such a way that our lives bring others closer to him, and not cause them to stumble.
exp.40:16:
It says the guide also measured the upper part above the door, and the whole inside and outside of the temple, going around the walls on every side. The phrase "above the door" is an old way of saying the top part of the door. "Round about" means all the way around.

Ezekiel speaks of a vision God gave him. A man who looked like bronze guides him and measures every part of a new temple. The Jewish people were in exile, and this vision showed them that God had not forgotten them and that his presence matters. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: God cares about details, and nothing in his house is careless. We can draw near to him with order, reverence, and attention, and trust that he also cares about the details of our lives.
exp.26:33:
It says that Tyre, the great seafaring city, will be broken by the seas, in the depths of the waters. Its trade will also fall there, along with all the people who worked with it. "Lamentations" are sad funeral songs, and "company" here means the crowd that went with her: sailors, merchants and partners.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is in exile in Babylon. This chapter is a poetic lament over Tyre, famous for its wealth and its trade. With the image of a sunken ship, it announces that her pride and her power will not save her. Many understand the sinking as a picture of total collapse; the exact way it happened is interpreted in different ways.

For today: wealth and success can disappear quickly. It is worth asking ourselves where we are placing our security. We can work with effort and honesty, but trusting God, not in what we have.
exp.38:9:
It says that Israel will not need to cut firewood or go into the forest, because it will have more than enough weapons to use as fuel. The weapons of the defeated enemy will be burned in the fire. "They shall spoil those that spoiled them, and rob those that robbed them" means that those who were once plundered will now gather what their attackers left behind. The large shields are the big shields carried in battle.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel 38 and 39 announce the defeat of Gog, an enemy leader who attacks Israel. Some believe this is a prophecy about a future event, while others see it as symbolic language of God's final victory. What is clear is that God defends his people and changes history.

For today: trust that God can turn your struggles into provision. When you face injustice or fear, hand it over to him and wait for his justice, without taking revenge on your own.
exp.14:5:
God says that Jerusalem will be like a branch of a vine that has already been thrown into the fire. The inhabitants are the people who live there, and the unfaithfulness of the people is their betrayal of God. Just as that wood burns, God will allow the inhabitants of Jerusalem to suffer judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. In the Bible, the vine often represents Israel. But here the wood of the vine is not useful for building anything; it has value only for its fruit. Because the people were not faithful, they became worthless for God's purpose. Scholars understand in different ways how this connects with the fall of Jerusalem, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: our life bears fruit only when we remain united with God. Jesus said, "Apart from me you can do nothing." Let us ask him for faithfulness and a sincere heart.
exp.32:21:
He says that God's hand was upon Ezekiel in the evening, before the survivor from Jerusalem arrived. Also, God opened his mouth before the man appeared in the morning. From then on, Ezekiel no longer stayed silent. Someone who fled and was saved is one who got away. The hand of the Lord expresses the power of God acting upon the prophet.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet exiled in Babylon. Earlier, God had told him he would be unable to speak until the news of Jerusalem's fall arrived (Ezekiel 3:26; 24:27). Now that news has come, in the twelfth year of the exile, and God restores his speech. Many interpret the muteness as a limit on speaking freely, and not everyone understands it the same way.

God knows how to prepare us before difficult news. When an unexpected blow comes, we can trust that he has already gone ahead of us. We can also ask him for wise words to comfort others and to speak the truth to them.
exp.41:14:
This verse says that, when the man had finished measuring the temple on the inside, he led Ezekiel out through the gate that faces east and began to measure the area all around. The phrase "house within" refers to the temple building and its inner courts. The explanation of the old wording has been left out, since the reader's verse reads "he brought me forth," "measured it," and "round about," and these are plain enough as they are.

Ezekiel describes what he sees in a vision. A guide with a measuring reed shows him the temple in full detail. He has just spoken of the holy chambers of the priests, where the separation between the holy and the common is stressed. The measurements that follow, five hundred reeds on each side, show an orderly enclosure. Interpreters differ on whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness, and he cares about details. We can approach him with reverence and put our lives in order, so that there is room for his presence.
exp.23:1:
God asks Ezekiel to write down the exact date of that day. "Son of man" is the way God addresses the prophet. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "set himself against" means that Babylon began to besiege it, that is, to surround it with its army.

God is speaking, and Ezekiel is in exile in Babylon. The exiles believed that Jerusalem would never fall. That is why God marks the exact day the siege began: on that very day, far away, the announced judgment was being fulfilled. In this way it became clear that God had spoken and that his words were true. Many understand that this day corresponds to January of 588 B.C., although the exact calculation is debated.

God does what he says, both his warnings and his promises. Today we can listen to him with humility and not put it off, trusting that his word is firm.
exp.19:38:
God tells the people of Israel: "Go on serving your idols, since you will not obey me." But he asks them not to dishonor his holy name any longer by mixing their offerings with that idolatry. The words "go" and "serve" in the verse mean what they say, and "pollute" means to dishonor or treat as something common.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of the people, who were in exile. Many wanted to worship God and at the same time keep other gods. Many read these words as a severe irony: God rejects divided faith. Then he promises to purify the people and restore them, so that they may truly serve him on his holy mountain.

For today: God is not satisfied with a half-hearted faith. Examine whether something in your life occupies the place that belongs to him, and give it up to him with sincerity.
exp.17:10:
This verse continues to describe the son of a righteous man who does not follow his father's example. The phrase "and does not do any of those duties" means that he fails to keep the good commands his father kept. The verse also says "even hath eaten upon the mountains," which refers to eating at places of idol worship, and "defiled his neighbour's wife," which means committing adultery with another man's wife.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is accountable for their own choices, and that a father's faith does not automatically save his son.

For today: let us not live on inherited faith or excuse ourselves with the mistakes of our family. Today you can choose to be faithful to God in your home, your work, and your relationships, with humility and sincerity.
exp.46:15:
This verse lists places that mark the northern border of the land God promises to Israel: Hamath, Berothah and Sibraim, between the territory of Damascus and the territory of Hamath, and also Hazar-hatticon, next to the region of Hauran.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He tells them to divide the land among all the tribes, and recalls that he swore to give it to their fathers. Today it is not known exactly where some of these places were, and there are different interpretations about whether this vision speaks of something literal or symbolic.

For today: God keeps what he promises and cares even for the details. We can trust that his faithfulness does not stay at the level of general ideas, but also reaches the concrete details of our lives.
exp.23:3:
God tells Ezekiel to fill the pot with the best parts of the sheep: the leg, the shoulder, and choice bones. The word "fill" here means "fill it." The "pieces" are the chunks of meat. Everything that goes into the pot is the best.

God speaks through Ezekiel to a rebellious people, on the day Babylon began to besiege Jerusalem. The pot is a parable of the city: the people of Jerusalem believed they were safe, but the fire of judgment was already lit. The best cuts may represent its important inhabitants, though scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: let us not trust in our position, our strength, or our good appearances to feel secure. When God calls us to turn back to Him, it is best to respond quickly, with humility and repentance.
exp.32:28:
God says that when the land is left as a desolate, empty ruin, the people will come to know who he is. The cause is their "abominations," meaning the detestable things they did, such as idolatry, violence, and injustice. The word "most desolate" in the verse refers to a place left empty and abandoned.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel after Jerusalem had already fallen (Ezekiel 33:21). Those who remained in the ruins of Judah were still confident and had not repented. God tells them that his judgment is real and that his words will come true.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only hear the Word of God with pleasure or whether we truly obey it. Right now you can choose one concrete action that God is asking of you and put it into practice with humility.
exp.33:25:
God promises to bless his people and the places around his hill, that is, the mountain where he makes his presence known, probably Zion or Jerusalem. He says he will send the rain in its season, that is, at exactly the right time. And he calls it showers of blessing.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel's leaders had mistreated the people, who were like a flock left without a shepherd. So God promises to be the shepherd who cares for them. He offers them a covenant of peace, safety, and good harvests. Many Christians see in the promise about "my servant David" a sign of Jesus, the good shepherd, though some understand it in other ways.

For today: God cares for his people and gives what is needed in its time. We can trust him when waiting becomes long, and thank him for the simple blessings of each day.
exp.22:25:
This verse says that the enemies will strip Jerusalem of her clothing and take away her valuable possessions. The fair jewels are the ornaments and beautiful goods that she took pride in. In other words, she will lose her honor and her wealth.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 23 he tells the story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. They gave themselves to other nations, looking for security in alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting in God. Now he allows those same allies to punish them.

For today: what we rely on to feel secure or important, such as money, reputation, or human support, can disappear. Let us put our trust in God, who does not fail us, and ask him to free us from depending on other things.
exp.31:21:
This verse says that Assyria, with all its army and its people, is already in the place of the dead. Its graves are all around it, and every one of them was killed by the sword. The word "knife" here means sword, and "people" refers to its soldiers and its nation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a funeral song against Egypt. Assyria was an empire feared for its violence, and here it appears as an example of a great power that fell. The message is that Egypt, with all its pride, will meet the same end. The language is poetic and describes the grave as a place of shadows, without teaching details about the afterlife.

For today: the power, success, or fear that we cause in others does not protect us before God. It is better to live with humility and justice, knowing that only He endures.
exp.41:18:
It says that the guide, a man whom Ezekiel sees in a vision, turned toward the west side of the temple grounds and measured five hundred units with the measuring rod. "Turned about" means he walked around. The "reed" was a long measuring rod. Here the measurement of all four sides is completed, and all of them come out equal.

Ezekiel speaks of a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. The guide measures the whole enclosure carefully. The next verse explains the purpose: to separate the holy from the common. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness. We can ask what healthy boundaries we need to care for our spiritual life, such as times of prayer and decisions that honor God.
exp.43:7:
It says that the people did not take proper care of the holy things that God had entrusted to them. Instead of serving faithfully themselves, they placed other people in charge of the service in the temple. The phrase about the "instructions concerning what is holy" refers to the rules about what is sacred, and "keepers" refers to those appointed to watch over and attend to the sanctuary.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. He rebukes Israel because they let in foreigners without wholehearted commitment to serve in the sanctuary, and in this way their house was dishonored. Some scholars see here a call to purity in worship; others debate how this vision of the temple will be fulfilled.

For today: God asks us to care sincerely for what He has entrusted to us, without leaving it all in the hands of others. Ask yourself what spiritual responsibility you need to take on personally.
exp.13:20:
It says that God will send against Jerusalem his four severe judgments: war (the sword), famine, wild animals (the evil beast), and disease (the plague). "To cut down" means to cut off or destroy, and "judgments" are just punishments. If earlier he had spoken of a single judgment upon any land, now the question is: how much more upon Jerusalem, if he sends them all together?

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. The people believed Jerusalem would not fall, and some thought the righteousness of a few would save it. God answers that the wickedness was great and the punishment was not without cause. Even so, he shows that a remnant would remain.

For today: we cannot rely on the faith of others or on our religiosity. Each person needs to turn to God sincerely and trust in his mercy, which is also shown in the remnant.
exp.19:5:
He says that God, on the day he lifted up his hand, made a solemn oath: he would bring Israel out of Egypt and into a land that he himself had prepared. Lifting up the hand was a gesture of firm promise. The phrase about flowing with milk and honey describes a fertile and abundant land. The phrase about the glory of all lands shows God's affection for his gift. The word "espied" means prepared or sought out in advance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is with the elders of Israel in exile. God reminds them of their history: from Egypt he was faithful, but the people fell into idolatry. With this he shows them that their present situation is not due to any lack of goodness on God's part.

For today: God keeps what he promises and prepares what is best for us. Trust in his goodness, and do not let any modern idolatry take the place that belongs to him.
exp.23:18:
The people ask Ezekiel what his actions mean. He is acting in a very strange way: his wife has just died, and he does not carry out the customary mourning. The old words are explained this way: the first is a turban or headdress, the second is a cloak that covered the face, and the third was the food that friends brought to those who were grieving.

The speakers are the people of Israel, who are in exile in Babylon. God had commanded Ezekiel not to weep openly for his wife, so that he would be a living sign. His silence showed what the grief of Israel would be like when Jerusalem and the temple fell: a blow so great that there would not even be strength for weeping.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us through difficult situations. When something puzzles us, we can humbly ask what it teaches us, and listen to his Word sincerely before the pain arrives.
exp.15:26:
God says that he stretched out his hand against Jerusalem and took away part of what she needed each day. He handed her over to the daughters of the Philistines, who despised her. Even they were ashamed of her conduct. The phrase about her daily provision means her food and her daily sustenance. The way of her shameful living is a disgraceful life.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who went after other peoples and their idols. It is strong language, used as an image of idolatry and of alliances with pagan nations. God corrects his people because he loves them and wants them to return.

For today: when we look for security or satisfaction in things that are not God, they never fill us. If we feel that something is missing, we can ask ourselves what we have clung to and return to God with humility.
exp.16:8:
God tells Ezekiel to ask whether the vine will prosper. The answer is no: its roots will be pulled up, its fruit cut off, and all its fresh leaves will wither. Without great power or many people, it will be plucked up by the roots.

God speaks through Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon, using a parable. The vine represents King Zedekiah of Judah, who broke his covenant with Babylon and sought help from Egypt, the other great eagle. Many interpreters see in this a judgment for that disloyalty.

For today: trusting in allies, money, or human plans rather than in God may seem safe, but it does not give lasting life. Ask yourself today where you are resting your roots, and bring it to God in prayer.
exp.22:35:
God tells Ezekiel to act as a judge. The question "Will you not judge?" means: "Do it now." He is to accuse Aholah and Aholibah and make them face their sins openly, declaring their detestable practices to them.

The Lord speaks to the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Aholah and Aholibah are two sisters who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. God uses this vivid picture to show that his people were unfaithful to him, chasing idols and alliances instead of trusting him.

God does not stay silent in the face of sin, but he exposes it in truth to call his people back to himself. Today we can ask him to show us the areas where we have turned our backs on him, and respond with humility and repentance, without excuses.
exp.31:23:
Elam was an ancient and powerful people, and the passage says that Elam, with all its army, is now in the world of the dead, lying around its own grave. All of them died in battle, killed by the sword. The phrase about being uncircumcised points to people who did not carry the mark of Israel's covenant. They spread terror among the living, but they ended in shame, along with the others who go down to the grave.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This is a lament over Egypt, which is going to be brought down to the world of the dead. God shows him that other proud and violent nations, such as Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal, already met that same end. Scholars understand the scene as a poetic image, not as a literal map of the afterlife.

For today: power used to frighten and dominate does not last. You can ask yourself whether you use your influence to serve or to intimidate, and ask God to make you humble and just.
exp.47:0:
This verse begins to divide the land among the tribes of Israel. Dan receives a strip at the far north, near Hethlon, Hamath, Hazar-enan and the border of Damascus. "Border" means the edge or boundary line. The "sides" are the two edges of the strip, running from east to west. The "sea" refers to the Mediterranean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the last vision of the book. After the destruction of Jerusalem, the people live in exile. God shows them a restored land, with a temple and an orderly division of the territory. Scholars disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to the final restoration that God promises.

For today: God cares for every detail and forgets no one. Even when you feel that your life is out of place, you can trust that he has prepared a place for you and keeps his promises.
exp.36:16:
God tells Ezekiel to join the two sticks, one with the name of Judah and the other with the name of Joseph or Ephraim, until they become one. The verse's instruction "join them" means to bring them together as one. The phrase "in thine hand" means that, when he holds them, they will look like a single stick.

Ezekiel speaks to a people in exile and divided. For centuries, the northern kingdom (Israel or Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah) had been separated. God uses this action as a sign to prompt people to ask questions, so that he can explain his promise: one day he will gather them and they will be one people under his hand.

For today: if God promises to join what was broken, we too can seek reconciliation. Think of a divided relationship, in your family or in your church, and take a humble step toward peace today, trusting that God knows how to heal what seems impossible.
exp.38:4:
It says that Gog, the enemy leader, will fall dead "upon the open field," that is, on the surface of the ground, out in the open. No one will bury him right away, since his body will be food for the birds and the wild animals. The phrase "for I have spoken it" shows that God presents this as certain, a word that will come to pass.

God himself, "the Lord God," speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that a powerful enemy, called Gog of the land of Magog, will attack Israel, but God will defeat him. The purpose is that the nations and his people will know that he is the Holy One. Scholars interpret in different ways who or what Gog represents: a historical event, a future event, or a symbol of evil.

For today: we can rest in the knowledge that no power, however great it may seem, stands above God. When you feel fear before threats or injustice, remember that his word is fulfilled and that he cares for his own.
exp.15:18:
God reminds Jerusalem that He gave her the finest food: the best flour, oil and honey. But she took it and set it before idols as an offering of a pleasing aroma, that is, as incense pleasing to them. The phrase "and thus it was" means: this really happened.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter He describes Jerusalem as a woman whom He cared for and clothed, but who turned away from Him. The unfaithfulness described here is a picture of idolatry: breaking faith with the covenant with God.

For today: everything good we have comes from God. We may ask ourselves whether we are using His gifts to honor Him, or whether we are putting them to the service of things that take His place, such as money, success or comfort.
exp.43:17:
God says that the priests will wear linen turbans on their heads and linen undergarments around their waists and thighs. The first word refers to turbans or caps, and the second refers to linen garments that cover from the waist down. The phrase about not girding themselves to sweat means they will not wear clothing that makes them perspire, nor belts that weigh them down.

God speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. He is referring to the priests descended from Zadok, who would serve closely before Him. Linen, unlike wool, was light and clean. Many understand that sweat suggests human effort or impurity, but interpreters explain it in several ways, and they also debate how this vision is fulfilled.

For today: serve God with reverence, but without anxiety or strain. Your service rests on His grace, not on your exhausting effort.
exp.43:18:
Ezekiel 44:19 says that when the priests went out from the inner court to the outer court, where the people were, they had to take off the garments they had ministered in. They would leave them stored in the holy chambers of the sanctuary and put on other clothes. The phrase about them not sanctifying the people with their garments means that, by touching what was holy in those vestments, the people would be set apart or affected in a way that did not fit them.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the future temple, and gives him rules for the priests. Interpreters disagree about whether that vision will be fulfilled literally or whether it has a symbolic meaning. Either way, the message is that what is holy must be treated with reverence and order.

For today: serving God is a serious matter, but it should not become a spectacle. We can serve with reverence and humility, without presumption or displaying the spiritual to impress others.
exp.35:0:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel, as if they could hear him. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, reminding him that he is an ordinary human being. The word "hear" in the verse is the command to listen, and "the Lord" is the name of the God of Israel.
