God speaks, and Ezekiel is his messenger. The mountains represent the land of Israel, which had been left desolate and mocked by the neighboring nations. The verses that follow explain that God responds to those taunts. After chapters of judgment, here begins a message of hope and restoration. Some see in this promises for the Israel of Ezekiel's time, and others also see a foreshadowing of things to come.

For today: when you feel that your life lies in ruins or that others mock you, remember that God still speaks and cares about what seems abandoned. Listen to him with hope.
exp.22:24:
God says he will set his jealousy against Jerusalem, meaning the anger of a wounded husband. Her former lovers will attack her with fury. The verse says they will take away her nose and ears, a cruel punishment of ancient warfare. Whoever survives will fall by the sword, they will take her sons and daughters, and what remains will be consumed by fire.

God speaks through Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), to describe the people's unfaithfulness, which sought alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting in him. Babylon, once admired, becomes the instrument of judgment. The language is strong and symbolic, but it reflects God's grief over betrayal.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust apart from God. What now seduces you may wound you later. Return to him sincerely; his discipline seeks to restore us.
exp.26:11:
It says that Tarshish traded with Tyre. Because of the great abundance of riches that Tyre had, Tarshish brought it silver, iron, tin and lead to sell in its fairs, that is, in its markets. The word "merchant" means a trader or dealer. Tarshish was a distant place; no one knows for certain where it was, though many think it lay in the western Mediterranean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a seafaring city that was very rich and proud. He compares it to a beautiful ship loaded with goods from many nations. This list of trading partners shows its enormous wealth, but it also prepares the announcement of its fall.

For today: riches and success are not bad in themselves, but they are not a secure foundation. Ask yourself what you are really trusting in, and ask God for a grateful and humble heart that uses what it has to bless others.
exp.30:14:
He says that when this great tree fell and went down to the grave, God caused the whole of creation to mourn for it. The phrase "caused it to mourn" means that God brought about grief. "The deep" refers to the deep waters, and the trees "fainted" means they grew weak, like someone who has lost their strength.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares the Pharaoh of Egypt to a very tall cedar of Lebanon, and he warns him with the example of Assyria, another proud nation that had already fallen. It is poetic language: nature weeps as if it were a funeral. Some read it only as an image of the fall of an empire.

For today: power and success do not make us untouchable. God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Ask him to help you live with humility and not to trust in your own greatness.
exp.29:9:
God announces that he is going to bring to an end the "multitude" of Egypt, that is, its great population, wealth and power. To do this he will use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The phrase in the verse "I will make to cease" means that this power will be brought to a stop.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Egypt was a proud nation that trusted in its own strength and had been a deceptive support for Judah. God shows that he rules over all nations and that he can use even a king who does not know him to carry out his judgment. Scholars recognize this prophecy within the Babylonian campaigns against Egypt, although the historical details are debated.

Today we can remember that no human power is secure: not money, not fame, not allies. It is wise to place our trust in God, who continues to govern history.
exp.44:20:
It says that in the first month, on the fourteenth day, the people will keep the Passover, a feast of seven days in which unleavened bread is eaten. The words "Á" and "comeráse" are rewritten in the verse above as "a" and "shall be eaten," which is the same sense. Unleavened bread is bread made without yeast.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a renewed temple and worship (chapters 40 to 48). Earlier, there is talk of cleansing the house from sin, and afterward the sacrifices of the prince are mentioned. The Passover remembers when God brought Israel out of Egypt. How this vision will be fulfilled, whether literally or symbolically, is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God wants his people to remember their deliverance with gratitude. We can set aside a regular moment to remember what God has done for us and to remove from our lives whatever draws us away from him.
exp.46:4:
He says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured another thousand cubits, and the water was already so deep that it could not be crossed on foot. It had risen so much that one could only pass through it by swimming. "Stream" here is the river, and "swimming" means swimming.

Ezekiel speaks of a vision that God gave him. A guide with a measuring cord takes him along a river that flows out from the temple. At each stretch the water rises: ankles, knees, waist, and now full depth. Many understand this as a picture of the life and blessing that come from God's presence, though it has been interpreted in various ways.

For today: God invites us not to stay on the shore or in the shallows. We can move forward step by step in prayer, in the Word, and in trust in Him, letting go of control and allowing ourselves to be held up by His grace.
exp.36:17:
This verse says that when the people see Ezekiel holding the two sticks joined together, they will ask him what it means. In other words, the sign would arouse curiosity and open the way to explain the message. "The children of your people" are his fellow Israelites, and "what do you mean by this" asks what he is trying to tell us by this.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles. He commands him to perform a symbolic action: to join two sticks, one for Judah and another for Israel (also called Joseph or Ephraim), the northern kingdom. God wanted to show that one day he would gather his divided people into a single nation under his hand.

For today: God can use what we do, and not only what we say, to stir questions in others. Let us live with unity, forgiveness and peace, and be ready to explain with humility why we do so.
exp.43:8:
He says that God will not allow any foreigner who is uncircumcised in heart and in flesh to enter his sanctuary. Being uncircumcised in heart means having a stubborn heart that neither obeys nor loves God. The sanctuary is the holy place of the temple.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the temple. God rebukes Israel because it had let foreigners serve in his house without respecting his rules, and so the place was defiled. Some understand that the emphasis is on the attitude of the heart, not only on the person's background. Unfaithful Levites would also be corrected.

For today: God seeks sincere devotion, not merely religious appearances. Let us examine whether our hearts are truly surrendered to him when we come to worship him.
exp.35:28:
It says that God himself will cleanse his people from their "uncleannesses," that is, from everything that made them unclean before him: sin and idolatry. It also promises that he will "call for the corn," as one who gives a command, so that it will multiply and there will never again be hunger.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had suffered the consequences of their disobedience. God promises to restore them, to give them a new heart and his Spirit, and to bring them back to their land. First comes inner cleansing, and then provision.

For today: God cares for our heart and also for our daily needs. You can ask him to cleanse you from whatever keeps you from him, and trust that he will take care of you, though in his own way and in his own time.
exp.21:9:
The explanation says that serious sexual abuses were committed in Jerusalem within families. "Uncovering the nakedness" is a biblical expression that refers to forbidden sexual relations with a father's wife or with someone in his close family. Forcing a woman during a time that the law of Moses forbade is one form of this sin. The verse describes violence and abuse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is accusing Jerusalem, called the city of blood, for its sins: despising what is holy, violence, idolatry, and abuse. These wrongs show that the people had forgotten God, and for that reason judgment would come.

For today: God cares about protecting the weak, especially within the home. If you know of abuse, do not hide it; seek help and protect the person who has been harmed. A life that honors God cares for and respects others.
exp.28:16:
This verse gives a date and announces that God spoke again to Ezekiel. It says it was "in the seven and twentieth year," on the first day of the first month. "The word of the Lord came unto me" means that God's word came to Ezekiel, that is, God spoke to him.

Ezekiel was a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. This is one of the latest dated messages in the book. It is generally understood that the twenty-seventh year is counted from the exile of King Jehoiachin, which brings us to roughly 571 BC. After this introduction, God speaks about the army of Nebuchadnezzar, which worked hard against Tyre and received almost no pay, and announces that Egypt will be his compensation.

For today: God speaks in his own time and does not forget his promises or his plans. We can approach his Word with patience and confidence, knowing that he is at work even when we do not understand everything right away.
exp.29:25:
God says that he will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and drive them from one country to another, the way someone throws grain into the wind. The verb rendered "scatter" means to spread them out, and the image is of throwing them far away. The final purpose is that they will know that the Lord is God.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Egypt had trusted in its power and in its king, Pharaoh, and God announces judgment against it. In this passage, Babylon appears as the instrument God uses. The Bible presents this as God's judgment on the pride of the nations.

For today: nothing we use to feel secure, whether money, power, or prestige, can stand if God does not hold it up. Today you can ask yourself what you are really trusting in, and turn your trust back to God, who is faithful and above all things.
exp.11:27:
This verse is God's answer to a mocking saying. God tells Ezekiel to tell the people that there will be no more delay: what God has spoken will be fulfilled.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. Some in Israel were saying that the warnings of judgment were for a very distant future, and so they felt at ease and had no need to change. God corrects that idea: his word is not a distant or doubtful matter. Scholars understand this as referring to the judgment on Jerusalem that was drawing near.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are putting off something God has already shown us, such as asking forgiveness, giving up a bad habit, or obeying clear guidance from his Word. Today is a good day to take that step with humility and trust that God does what he says.
exp.35:33:
This verse says that the land that was laid waste and abandoned will be worked again and planted. "Desolate" means left in ruins, emptied and destroyed. "Tilled" means plowed and cultivated. What once was looked upon with pity by everyone who passed by will now be seen full of life and fruit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites, who had suffered exile and the ruin of their land because of their sin. God makes clear that he will restore his people not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his holy name. First he promises to cleanse them from their wickedness, and then to rebuild cities and fields.

For today: if there are areas of your life that look like ruins, they are not lost to God. Come to him with sincerity, ask for his forgiveness, and get to work with hope, trusting that he can make life grow where there was destruction.
exp.42:20:
It says that the bull offered for sin was to be taken and burned whole in an appointed place outside the sanctuary. "Atonement" means covering or removing the guilt of sin. "According to the law of the house" means according to the rules given for the temple.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple. There it is described how the altar would be consecrated so that the people could worship again. The priests descended from Zadok would carry out the service. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's holiness and of restoration.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but He also provides a way of cleansing. We can come to Him with sincerity, and Christians remember that Christ offered the final sacrifice for us (Hebrews 13:11-12).
exp.26:8:
Tyre is compared to a great ship, and it received help from other cities. The elders and wise men of Gebal, a coastal city near modern Byblos, were in Tyre to repair its cracks and leaks, so that no water would get in. Large oared ships came to Tyre with their sailors to trade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a city rich and proud of its trade. The poem describes its beauty and power, but it does so to show how much Tyre trusted in itself before its announced fall.

For today: everything we have, our work, our reputation or our success, depends on the help of many people. Let us thank those who support us and not place our security in what we have achieved, but in God, who is the only one who never wears out.
exp.33:22:
God promises to set over his people one shepherd who will care for them and feed them. "To set up" means to raise up or bring forth, and "to feed" means to lead the flock to eat and to look after it. He calls him "my servant David," and repeats three times that he will be their shepherd.

The passage comes from the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile. Earlier he had condemned the leaders who took advantage of the people, like strong sheep that shove the weak ones aside. David had died centuries before, so many understand this name to point to a future descendant of his. Christians see in it Jesus, the Good Shepherd; others read it as a king who would restore the people.

For today: when you feel lost or mistreated, remember that God provides a Shepherd who cares for you. And if you have any influence over others, care for them tenderly, without pushing the weak aside.
exp.33:26:
This verse promises that the land will once again yield good fruit and that the people will live there without fear. God says he will break the bonds of their yoke, that is, the straps or ties that held the yoke in place, and free them from those who had enslaved them. Then they will know that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile. Earlier, he has criticized the shepherds who mistreated the people. Now he promises to become their shepherd himself and to make a covenant of peace. Many see in this a hope that also points to Christ, the good shepherd, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: if you feel tied down by some burden or by the abuse of others, pray and trust that God can give rest and freedom. Ask him to help you recognize his care and to walk in peace.
exp.15:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Jerusalem. He reminds her that her origin and her lineage come from the land of Canaan, and that her father was an Amorite and her mother a Hittite.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God wants to show the people their abominations. Many understand that this is not speaking of a literal biological inheritance, but that Jerusalem, before belonging to Israel, was a Canaanite city. In this way she is humbled, to remind her that everything she had was a gift from God.

For today: do not boast of what you are or what you have, as if it were your own merit. Remember where God took you from, and live with gratitude and humility.
exp.46:19:
This verse marks the boundary of the west side of the land. The "great sea" is the Mediterranean Sea. The border would follow that coast up to a point opposite Hamath, in the north. "Border" means the limit or boundary line, and "over against" means directly across from that place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile. In a vision, he describes to him how the land would be divided among the tribes of Israel. This gave hope to a people who had lost everything. The boundaries on all four sides show that God cares even about the details. Afterward, the land is also shared with the foreigners who live among them, and they are treated as children of the people. Some understand this literally, others symbolically.

For today: God is a God of order and of promises kept. Trust that he has a place for you, and open your heart and your table to those who come from outside.
exp.24:13:
God says he will punish Edom, and that he will do it through his people Israel. The words "vengeance," "anger," and "fury" speak of a just judgment from God, not of a human outburst. In the end, Edom will know that this punishment comes from God himself. "They shall know" means they will recognize it through the force of what happens.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around the time Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Edom, a neighboring nation descended from Esau, had held a grudge and took revenge on Judah with cruelty in its time of weakness. God responds to that wickedness. Scholars debate how and when this prophecy was exactly fulfilled.

For today: do not take revenge on your own, and do not hold on to old grudges. Leave judgment to God, because he sees every injustice and is the only one who judges with perfect justice. Trust in him and seek peace.
exp.13:12:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him that when a land is unfaithful to him and rebels against him, God will act in judgment. The first quoted word is not in the verse, so I will simply state the idea: the land turns against God by breaking faith and betraying the trust between them. The second quoted phrase means taking away the means of support, the thing people rely on to eat. It speaks of famine and of the loss of people and animals.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. Some of the people's leaders kept blaming others and trusting in idols. God warns that his judgment is not arbitrary but a response to persistent unfaithfulness. His aim, according to the previous verse, is that the people stop straying and return to belonging to him.

For today: let us not take for granted our daily bread or our peace, as if they were secure without God. Let us ask him for a faithful heart, and examine in what things we are placing our trust in place of him.
exp.36:7:
He says that Ezekiel saw the dry bones coming back together: the sinews appeared, the flesh grew, and the skin covered them. But they were still lifeless bodies, because they lacked the breath of life, which here can also be understood as breath or wind. The sinews probably refer to the tendons that join the bones.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of a valley full of bones. They represent Israel, discouraged and in exile, who felt they had no hope. God promises to restore his people, and the restoration happens in stages: first the body and then the life.

For today: sometimes a life can look orderly on the outside and be empty on the inside. We can ask God not only to fix our circumstances but also to give us new life through his Spirit, and to wait on him with confidence.
exp.26:34:
All who live in the islands and along the coasts will be astonished at the fall of Tyre. Even their kings will tremble with fear, and their faces will be troubled, that is, marked with an expression of horror. The phrase "their faces shall be troubled" means that their expression will change at the shock.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a very rich seafaring city, compared to a great ship full of merchandise. Tyre had enriched many nations through its trade, but it became filled with pride. The text announces that its shipwreck will astonish everyone. Scholars agree that it is a judgment against its arrogance, although they debate how and when it was fulfilled in history.

For today: wealth and success are not a secure foundation for life. We can thank God for what He gives us, but it is wise to ask Him for humility and to trust in Him, not in what we have or achieve.
exp.19:43:
God says that his people will come to recognize who he is when he deals with them according to his own name and his mercy, and not according to what Israel deserved because of its wickedness. The explanation of the verse's wording is removed here because the reader's verse does not use those words; the remaining meaning is that God acts for his own name's sake, meaning his reputation and faithfulness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. The chapter reviews the people's constant rebellion since Egypt. Even so, God promises to bring them back to their land. There they will feel shame for their sins and understand that their restoration was an act of grace, not a reward.

For today: when you fail, remember that God treats you according to his faithful character and not according to your mistakes. That grace is not an excuse to sin, but a reason to repent with humility and to give thanks for his goodness.
exp.35:11:
In this verse God promises that his people Israel will once again walk upon the mountains of Israel. The phrase about bringing them back means that he will bring them home to live there. The promise that they will possess the land means the land will belong to them again, and it will be theirs as an inheritance, something received and passed down to their children. God adds that the land will no longer bereave them of their children, meaning it will no longer be a place of loss and death.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the mountains of Israel. The people had been carried into exile and the land lay in ruins. The neighboring nations mocked, and so God promises to restore both the land and his people.

For today: God knows how to rebuild what seems lost. If there are areas of your life or your family that lie in ruins, you can wait on Him with confidence and pray for their restoration.
exp.13:2:
God tells Ezekiel that these men have set up their idols in their heart. Besides that, they keep before their eyes the thing that makes them fall into sin. A stumbling block is a stone over which a person trips and falls. Then God asks whether He should allow Himself to be consulted by them. The question sounds like a refusal: one cannot seek God with a divided heart.

God speaks to Ezekiel, calling him "son of man." Some elders of Israel came to hear him, perhaps looking for a word from the Lord. But God sees that their heart is still attached to their idols. His answer seeks to call them back to Him.

For today: before asking God for direction, we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our heart. If there is something we love more than Him, let us sincerely give it to God, and He receives us.
exp.46:10:
It says that the swampy places and the marshes along the sea, where the river reaches, will not be made healthy. They will remain salty and will serve as salt flats, that is, places where salt is harvested. Here the words for these low, wet areas refer to waters that stand still, without current.

Ezekiel recounts a vision God gave him while the people were in exile. A guide shows him a river flowing out from the temple that brings life to everything it touches. This verse is an exception within that healing. Some think the salt was useful and valuable. Others see a warning: what lies outside the river does not receive its life. The text does not explain this, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: do not remain like stagnant water. Stay close to God through prayer, the Bible, and community, so that his life can flow through you.
exp.35:23:
God promises that he will take his people from among the nations where they had been scattered. He will gather them out of all the countries and bring them back to their own land. The word "heathen" means foreign nations or peoples, and "countries" refers to the land of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote while Israel was in exile because of its disobedience. The people had damaged the good name of God among the nations. God makes clear that he acts for the holiness of his name and out of faithfulness to his promise, not because Israel deserves it. After this promise comes cleansing and a new heart.

For today: if you feel far from God or lost, remember that he takes the initiative to rescue and restore us by pure grace. You can return to him with confidence and ask him for a new heart.
exp.15:12:
God says that he adorned Jerusalem with gold and silver, and with fine clothing of linen, silk, and embroidered work. She ate the best food: finest flour, honey, and oil. She was exceedingly beautiful and became like a queen.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the picture of an abandoned girl whom He took in, cared for, and clothed as a wife. It represents Jerusalem and her history with God. He reminds her of everything He gave her, because she later trusted in her beauty and went after other gods and alliances. The verses that follow say this plainly.

For today: all the good we have, whether talent, success, or blessings, is a gift from God. Remembering this keeps us grateful and humble, and keeps us from trusting in ourselves more than in Him.
exp.45:14:
Every morning, the text says, a lamb was to be offered to God, along with a grain offering of flour and oil.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the restored worship (chapters 40 to 48). There it is described how the people would once again worship in good order. Interpreters differ: some see a literal temple in the future, while others see a symbolic picture of worship and of Christ, the Lamb of God.

For today: God values a daily offering, not only an occasional one. We can begin each morning by offering Him our time, our strength, and our heart, with a simple prayer of thanksgiving and dedication.
exp.31:9:
He says that God will make many peoples astonished at what will happen to Egypt. Its kings will be filled with great fear when God waves his sword before them. The word "astonished" here means very amazed, left without words. "They will be terrified" means they will shake with fear, all the time, on the day Egypt falls.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Pharaoh and Egypt. God announces judgment because of their pride. The verses that follow say that the sword of the king of Babylon would be the instrument. The language of darkness and dimmed stars is poetic and symbolic, and not everyone interprets it the same way.

For today: power and fame do not make us safe. We can ask ourselves where we place our trust, and ask God for a humble heart, one that depends on him and not on what it boasts of having.
exp.41:3:
It says that in front of the chambers of the priests there was a walk ten cubits wide (about five meters) going inward. The doors of the chambers faced north.

Through a vision, God shows Ezekiel a new temple with very exact measurements. Ezekiel writes in exile, and the people had lost the temple. These chambers served for the priests to eat the holy offerings and to dress for service. How this vision should be understood, whether literally or symbolically, is debated among interpreters.

God cares even for the details of how he is worshiped, with order and respect. Today we can ask ourselves what order and reverence we give to our time with God. Perhaps setting aside a fixed moment each day to pray and read his Word.
exp.34:10:
God swears by himself that he will deal with Edom as Edom dealt with Israel. The phrases "according to your anger" and "according to your envy" mean that Edom will receive the same kind of treatment it showed. "Hatreds" refers to the grudges kept in the heart. "I will make myself known among them" means that, in judging them, God will reveal himself as just and present.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against Mount Seir, that is, Edom, a nation neighboring Israel. Edom held an old grudge and wanted to take the lands of Israel and Judah when they were wounded. God heard their words of mockery and scorn, and he answers by defending his people.

Today, this verse reminds us that God hears what we say and sees what we keep in our hearts. If we have been hurt, we can leave justice in his hands. And if we hold on to resentment, it is wise to ask him to remove it before it harms us.
exp.44:18:
This verse says that the priest will take some of the blood of the sin offering and put it in three places: on the posts of the house (the temple), on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the posts of the gate of the inner court. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing sin. A "post" is the frame of a door.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a restored temple. There a cleansing of the sanctuary is described at the beginning of the year. The blood showed that sin is serious and needs to be cleansed. Interpreters differ on whether this vision refers to a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of the renewal of worship.

For today: Christians believe that Christ offered his blood once for all. We can draw near to God with sincerity, confess our faults and receive his forgiveness, without hiding anything or treating sin lightly.
exp.37:19:
It says that when God intervenes against Gog, all of creation will feel his presence: fish, birds, animals, reptiles and people will tremble. There will also be a great earthquake: the mountains will be torn down, the steep places will fall, and every wall will come down to the ground. The phrase about the face of the earth means the surface of the land.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog comes to attack Israel, and God responds with zeal and anger to defend his people and to show who he is. Interpreters differ on whether this refers to a future event, something symbolic, or both, but all recognize that God is sovereign over the nations.

For today: no human force, no wall or power, can compare with God. We can live with reverence toward him and trust that he cares for his own, even when the world seems unstable.
exp.12:4:
The explanation says that the false prophets did not do what was necessary to protect Israel. The "gaps" are the breaches or openings in a fallen wall. "Made up the hedge" means repairing and raising a defense. "The day of the Lord" is the time of judgment, when the battle against the people would come.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who prophesied among the exiles in Babylon. God rebukes the prophets who invented messages of peace from their own ideas. Instead of calling the people to repentance, which would have been like repairing the wall, they left them unprotected before the judgment that was coming.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we speak God's truth even when it is uncomfortable, or only what comforts. Truly loving others includes speaking to them with honesty, with tenderness, and on the basis of the Bible, not on the basis of our own wishes.
exp.15:16:
It says that Jerusalem took the jewels and beautiful objects of gold and silver that God himself had given her, and with them she made figures of men to worship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he presents Jerusalem as an abandoned girl whom he rescued, cared for, and enriched. Then she used those gifts to give herself over to idolatry. God wants the people to see their ingratitude and recognize their sin. Scholars debate exactly what those "images of men" were, but they are clearly idols.

For today: everything we have, such as talents, money, or health, comes from God. Ask yourself whether you use it to honor him or to feed things that take his place in your heart.
exp.37:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "And the word of the Lord came unto me" is the old-style way of saying it. It is not an idea that came from the prophet himself, but a message he receives from God before passing it on.

The one speaking is the Lord, the God of Israel, and the one listening is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. This phrase opens a new message, directed against Gog, of the land of Magog. Scholars disagree about who or what Gog represents: some see a historical enemy, others a future or symbolic one.

For today: before speaking on God's behalf, we must first listen to him. We can set aside time to read the Bible calmly, asking God to speak to us, before we give our opinion or make decisions.
exp.28:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel on an exact date: the tenth year, the tenth month, the twelfth day of the month. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" is the start of a new message.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel is the prophet who receives it. He was among the exiles in Babylon. Many scholars place this date around 587 B.C., when Jerusalem was under siege. Here God begins a series of messages against Egypt, a nation in which Judah had put its trust instead of trusting in Him.

For today: God speaks at concrete moments in history, and He remains Lord over the nations and over our circumstances. We can learn to place our trust in Him and not in human powers, whether money, governments, or influence. Let us listen to His Word carefully and respond with faith.
exp.19:24:
Here God says that, because Israel rejected his good laws, he gave them statutes that were not good, rules that did not give them life. The words that the earlier wording quoted are not in this verse, so the explanation's comment on them is removed here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel, during the exile. He reminds them of their long history of rebellion, going back to the wilderness. The verse is hard, and it is interpreted in several ways: some believe God handed them over to the punishment of following pagan customs, such as sacrificing firstborn children; others think it refers to laws that showed the hardness of their hearts. God does not approve of those practices; the next verse says they were a defilement.

For today: when we turn our backs on what God says, we can end up tied to burdens that do not give life. Let us return to his Word with humility.
exp.35:27:
God promises that his people will live again in the land he gave to their ancestors. He also renews the relationship that has always existed. The explanation of the old wording, "ye shall be my people" and "I will be your God," is that the phrase means "you will be my people" and "I will be your God." Where the source had "Dí," this reflects the verb "gave" in "the land that I gave to your fathers."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote while the people of Israel were in exile, far from their land, because of their disobedience. Before this promise, God announces a new heart and his Spirit within them. First he changes the inside; then the restoration comes. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also see it in the work of the Spirit in the church or in a future complete fulfillment.

Today, God does not only want us to change our behavior; he wants to change our heart and to live in fellowship with us. Today you can pray to him, "Lord, give me a heart that is tender toward you."
exp.13:11:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again.

The one speaking is God, and the prophet Ezekiel receives it. Earlier, God had spoken about false prophets and those who sought answers from idols, and about his desire that the people stop defiling themselves and be his again. Now God begins another teaching, addressed to Ezekiel and to the people exiled in Babylon.

For today: God still speaks, and we need to listen. We can set aside time each day to read the Bible carefully, asking God to speak to us through it.
exp.21:14:
God says that he will scatter Jerusalem among the nations, the way someone winnows grain to separate the chaff from the wheat. The word "consume" means to bring to an end and to destroy completely, and "filthiness" refers to moral impurity. God promises to put an end to the people's wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had accused Jerusalem of violence, injustice, and greed. This announcement of judgment aims to remove the sin of the people. The following verse shows the purpose: that they may know that he is the LORD.

For today: let us not minimize sin or hide it. God wants to cleanse us, and sometimes that involves painful correction. We can humbly ask him to show us what we need to leave behind, and respond with sincere repentance.
exp.40:14:
Here the prophet continues recording the measurements of the temple he sees in the vision. The building was a structure at the side and behind the temple, and the separate area around it was the open space set apart. The side rooms were chambers, and the courtyard was the open court. The whole complex was one hundred cubits (a cubit was roughly half a meter). The inner sanctuary and the porches facing the court are also mentioned.

Ezekiel speaks from exile in Babylon, and a figure with the appearance of a man shows him the temple and measures it. For a people without a temple, this vision was a hope of restoration and of God's presence. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual symbol.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and what He does with His people is not improvised. You can trust that He also cares for the details of your life, and live with the same seriousness and reverence toward what is holy.
exp.15:4:
It says that no one felt pity for this newborn girl. No one did for her the basic care of a baby, such as cutting the cord, washing her, or wrapping her in cloth. They left her lying out in the open field, meaning on the open ground, because her life mattered to no one. The phrase about her life being despised means that they looked down on her and scorned her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. He uses the image of an abandoned girl to show the humble and fragile beginnings of the people. By saying that their roots were Canaanite, He reminds them that they had no merit of their own. Everything they became came from God's mercy, which continues in the verses that follow.

For today: if you have ever felt ignored or worthless, remember that God looks on you with compassion. And if He has lifted you up, respond with gratitude and humility, never forgetting where He brought you from.
exp.16:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man", a way of saying "human being". He asks him to "put forth a riddle", that is, a puzzle, and to "speak a parable", a story with a hidden message, addressed to the people of Israel.

The LORD speaks. Ezekiel is living in exile in Babylon, alongside other Jews taken captive. God will use the story of the eagle, the cedar and the topmost shoot to show what happened to the kings of Judah and the political decisions of the people. Many understand that the eagle represents Babylon, but the following text explains this in more detail.

Today: God sometimes speaks to us in images so that we will think and recognize our mistakes. Let us listen with humility, without becoming defensive, and let his word correct and guide us.
exp.27:20:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to set his face toward Sidon, a city neighboring Tyre, and to speak a message against it. "Set your face" means to direct your attention firmly.

"Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel throughout the book, reminding him that he is an ordinary human being.

The LORD speaks. Earlier he had already announced judgment on the king of Tyre for his pride. Now the message extends to Sidon, another Phoenician city that had also mistreated Israel. The purpose God declares is that they will know that he is the LORD.

For today: God sees all nations and all people, and he does not ignore injustice. We can trust that he is just, and also examine whether our pride is pulling us away from him.
exp.31:17:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to sing a funeral lament over the great multitude of Egypt. A lament is a song of mourning. To "cast down" means to bring them down or throw them downward. Egypt and the cities of other powerful nations are sent down "unto the nether parts of the earth," a poetic image of the place of the dead, together with those who go down to the pit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the twelfth year of the exile, when Judah was already falling before Babylon. Egypt seemed strong and secure, but God announces its fall. Many understand this scene as symbolic and poetic language about God's judgment, not as a literal description of the afterlife.

Today, this text reminds us that no human power, wealth, or fame is eternal. We can trust God, not what seems strong, and live with humility today.
exp.13:15:
Noah, Daniel, and Job are said to be in the midst of a land under judgment, but even if they were there, they would save only their own lives. Neither their sons nor their daughters would be spared, and the land would be left in ruins. "Deliver" means save; "desolate" means destroyed; "men" are people; "as I live" is an oath of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel, who were in exile. Many believed that Jerusalem would be saved because of the righteous people within it. God answers that the judgment for the people's persistent wickedness would be so firm that not even the most righteous could save others by their righteousness. About the details of these three men, the Bible says nothing more here.

For today: do not live confident in the faith of others, such as your parents or your church. Seek God yourself, with repentance and sincere trust, and pray for your own.
exp.37:12:
Ezekiel 38:13 names distant nations, Sheba, Dedan, and Tarshish, along with their young lions (probably strong young leaders or rulers), who put a question to Gog. They ask whether he really comes to take spoil, to carry off silver and gold, livestock and goods. Spoil and prey mean plunder taken by force.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog plans to attack a people who live in peace and without walls. These nations seem to be merchants who neither stop nor defend him; they only question his motives. Interpreters differ: some see a protest, others a mockery or a simple observation. There is also debate about who Gog is and when this happens.

Today we can notice that greed always disguises itself as something else, but God sees the true motive. Let us ask Him to examine our hearts and trust that He cares for His people.
exp.29:22:
The explanation says that God will scatter the Egyptians among the nations. The verse's word "scatter" means to spread or disperse, and the phrase about winnowing means to throw them far away, as grain is tossed so the wind carries off the chaff. "Nations" here means the peoples of the earth, and "countries" means various lands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. Egypt had been a false hope of help for Judah, and God announces its fall. Pharaoh's "broken arm" symbolizes the breaking of his military power. Babylon appears as the instrument of God's judgment. How this scattering was exactly fulfilled is something scholars debate.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in human powers, whether money, governments, or people. Only God is a firm refuge. Ask yourself what you are trusting in more than in Him.
exp.25:8:
He says that the army of Nebuchadnezzar will attack the city of Tyre with battering rams, which were thick tree trunks used to strike and bring down the walls. He will also break down its towers with axes, that is, with iron tools or weapons made for demolition. It is a siege scene: the city that thought itself safe will be torn down piece by piece.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud city, and it rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking it would gain from it (Ezekiel 26:2). God announces that Babylon will come against it. It is known that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for years; the details of how that siege ended are interpreted in various ways.

For today: no human wealth, fame, or strength gives us true security. We are also called not to rejoice in the misfortune of others. Let us place our trust in God, who humbles the proud and cares for the humble.
exp.22:28:
Ezekiel 23:29 says that Aholibah's former lovers will deal with her in hatred, take away everything she worked for, and leave her stripped bare, exposed to shame. The sentence that explains the old wording is rewritten to fit the verse: the words "naked and bare" mean she will be left with nothing and open to shame. Her wrongdoing, both her shameful conduct and her unfaithfulness to God, will be brought fully into the open.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter He uses the picture of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, to show how His people turned away from Him by forming alliances with other nations and by worshiping idols. The allies she trusted will turn against her. This is a judgment, but it is also meant to wake the people up.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether money, approval, or power, eventually fails us. Today you can ask yourself what you trust more than God, and return to Him with humility.
exp.16:15:
God says, with an oath by his own life, that the king of Judah will die in Babylon. There lived the king who had placed him on the throne. This king despised his oath and broke the covenant he had made with him. "Despised" means he took it lightly, without giving it any value.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had placed Zedekiah on the throne, and Zedekiah pledged loyalty before God. Afterward he rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God regards this as a serious offense, because the oath had been made in his name. Scholars often identify the king with Zedekiah.

For today: our word matters to God. Strive to keep your promises, in marriage, work, or agreements, even when it costs you. And when you fail, turn to God with humility instead of looking for ways out on your own.
exp.36:20:
God promises that he will take the children of Israel out from the nations where they were scattered. He will gather them from every place and bring them back to their own land. The word "heathen" here means foreign nations or peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people were discouraged and divided: the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah). With the sign of two sticks that become one, God announces that there will be restoration and unity. Some see a partial fulfillment in the return from exile; others see a future or spiritual fulfillment in Christ.

For today: even if you feel far away, scattered, or broken inside, God is still the one who gathers and restores. Trust that he can heal your relationships and give you hope again.
exp.13:18:
This verse speaks of a third judgment: a plague, or deadly disease, that God would send upon a land. "Pour out my fury upon it in blood" means a punishment that brings death, and "cut off" means to remove or destroy, as one cuts down a tree. It would affect both people and animals.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the exiles of Judah in Babylon. The leaders of the people kept idols in their hearts and yet still sought God. He warns that when a people becomes corrupt, not even the prayers of righteous men like Noah, Daniel, and Job would save others; only they themselves would be saved. Commentators debate why he mentions Daniel, but the central message is clear.

Today: the faith of others, though valuable, does not replace my own relationship with God. Let us examine whether there is anything we love more than Him, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.22:45:
God says that he is going to bring against Aholah and Aholibah a large crowd of enemies. He will hand them over to terror and to plunder, which means violent robbery. It is the announcement of a punishment that has already been decided.

Here God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter, Aholah and Aholibah represent Samaria and Jerusalem, that is, the people of God who were unfaithful to him by seeking alliances and idols from other nations. God uses the image of adultery to show the pain of a betrayed promise, and also the injustice of his people. Scholars agree that this is symbolic language.

For today: God takes the faithfulness of the heart seriously. Examine the things you place your trust in before him, and return to him with sincerity, because his desire is to restore, not only to correct.
exp.11:25:
This verse says that a new word from God came to Ezekiel. The phrase "Again the word of the Lord came to me" marks the point where God begins speaking to him once more.

Ezekiel is the one speaking, writing down what God tells him. He lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. People mocked his warnings, thinking the judgment would take a long time or would never come. This verse introduces God's answer to that mockery, right after saying that there would be no more false visions.

For today: God still speaks through his Word, and obedience should not be put off by thinking "there will be time later." Today you can open the Bible with simple attention, ask God to speak to you, and respond without delay to something specific you already know he is asking of you.
exp.11:22:
God orders Ezekiel to tell the people that He is going to put an end to a popular saying: "The days go on and on, and no vision ever comes true." A saying like this is a phrase everyone repeats. Instead, God announces that the days are now near when every vision He has given will be fulfilled.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Many mocked his warnings and believed the judgment would take a long time or would never come. God answers that attitude of doubt and excuse.

For today: let us not take God's word lightly just because it seems slow to come true. His patience is an opportunity to turn back to Him, not a sign that His words don't matter. Today we can obey what we already know He asks of us.
exp.29:13:
It says that God will punish several important cities of Egypt. The phrase "I will make desolate" means to leave in ruins, and the word "Pathros" names the region of Upper Egypt, "Zoan" was a city in the Nile Delta, and "No" is the city of Thebes. The phrase "execute judgments" means that God will bring his justice upon them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Egypt was a proud power, with idols and princes who felt secure. God announces that no fortress or false god will be able to save them. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment, although the text speaks of "foreigners."

For today: do not put your security in power, money, or prestige, for all of these can fall. Trust in the living God, who governs the nations and is just. Ask him today what you have put in the place of him.
exp.42:25:
It says that during seven days the priests will make atonement for the altar and purify it. To "make atonement" means to cover sin in order to repair the wrong. The phrase "they shall fill their hands" is an old expression. It refers to the consecration of the priests, to whom what was needed for service was placed in their hands. Some understand that it also speaks of dedicating the altar for its use.

God speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. Before the altar is used for regular worship, it must be dedicated with a ceremony lasting seven days. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as literal and others as symbolic.

For today: before serving God, we need to approach him with humility and a clean heart. We can ask him for forgiveness and give him our hands, that is, our time and our strength, to serve him.
exp.11:13:
It says that God will scatter all who surround the prince to protect him: his helpers and his troops. "Scatter toward every wind" means that he will throw them out in all directions. "Draw out the sword after them" means that he will take out the sword to pursue them. "Companies" refers to his guards or armies.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces the punishment that would come upon Jerusalem and its king, generally understood to be Zedekiah. The people had rebelled against God, and the message aimed to make them acknowledge that He is the LORD.

For today: there is no true security in power, money, or the people around us if we live with our backs turned to God. It is worth asking ourselves what we are truly trusting in, and returning with humility to rest in Him.
exp.13:1:
It says that, after some elders of Israel came to visit Ezekiel, God spoke to him. The phrase "the word of the Lord came unto me" in the verse above is the same as saying that God Himself intervened and gave him a message for those men.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here; he was living among the exiles in Babylon. The elders were leaders of the people, and they came, probably, to seek a word from God. But God sees beyond their visit: He notices that their hearts are divided by idols, and so He answers them with a warning.

For today: before seeking an answer from God, it is good to ask ourselves what things hold first place in our hearts. God does not only look at what we do on the outside; He desires a sincere heart that is devoted to Him.
exp.33:21:
He says that God himself will rescue his people, who are compared to sheep. In addition, God will bring order among them, judging between one sheep and another, that is, doing justice between those who abuse and those who suffer.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, while the people were in exile. Israel's leaders, called shepherds, had cared for themselves and not for the flock. Some strong sheep also pushed and scattered the weak ones. God promises to intervene and, later, to send a shepherd called "David." Many Christians see this as a sign pointing to Jesus, although the original text speaks of a future ruler from David's line.

Today, we can trust that God sees injustice. And if we have any kind of influence, we should use it to protect and care for the weakest, not to take advantage of them.
exp.35:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak on his behalf. He says that Israel's enemies tore the land apart and swallowed it up on every side, that is, they conquered it completely, so that they could keep it as their own inheritance. In this way, Israel became a subject of mockery and a cause of shame among the nations.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile. The mountains represent the wounded and humbled land. The neighboring nations, such as Edom, mocked it and wanted to take it for themselves. God shows that He sees this injustice and that He will respond, preparing a promise of restoration.

For today: if you go through shame, mockery, or loss, remember that God sees your pain and does not forget you. You can bring that wound to Him with confidence, trusting that He will be faithful to restore.
exp.38:21:
This verse says that, after what God will do on that day, Israel will know clearly and lastingly that the Lord is their God. "From that day and forward" means that this knowledge would not be passing, but would mark a before and an after.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 describe the defeat of Gog, an enemy who attacks Israel. God delivers his people and shows his glory before the nations. Interpreters disagree about whether this refers to historical events, to a future time, or to symbolic language. What is certain is that the purpose is for Israel and the nations to know God.

For today: do not wait only for difficult moments to recognize God. Today, remember how he has cared for you, and trust that he remains your God.
exp.36:3:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak to some dry bones as if they could hear. "Prophesy" here means to announce what God says. "Hear" means "listen," and "LORD" is the name of God. The command seems absurd, because bones do not hear, but God asks that his word be spoken to them.

God is speaking, showing Ezekiel a vision of a valley full of bones. According to the same chapter, those bones represent Israel, a discouraged people in exile who felt they had lost all hope. God wants to teach that he can give them back their life and restore them.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, whether in your family, your faith, or your spirit, do not just stand there looking at the dryness. Read and declare the word of God with faith, and ask him to do what you cannot do.
exp.12:20:
God says he will tear away the "veletes," which were veils or coverings that those women used in their divination practices. He promises to rescue his people from their hands, so that they will no longer be prey to them, like animals caught in a hunt. In the end, everyone will know that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He was speaking against false prophetesses who deceived the people with lies and magic in exchange for barley and bread. Scholars are not sure exactly what those objects were like, but the meaning is clear: they used deception to dominate people.

For today: God cares for those who are manipulated by false voices. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and if someone has deceived you, remember that God can set you free and give you the truth.
exp.47:1:
It says that the tribe of Asher receives a strip of land, right beside the one belonging to Dan. That strip runs from east to west, from the east side all the way to the sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea. The word "border" means a limit or boundary line.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes from exile. In chapters 40 to 48 he describes a vision of Israel's restoration: a temple, a land, and a people set in order. Here the land is divided into strips of equal size, one for each tribe. Interpreters differ on whether this should be fulfilled literally or whether it is a symbolic picture of future hope.

For today: God does not forget anyone. Even a tribe that is seldom mentioned has its assigned place. You can trust that God has a place and a purpose for you too, and be encouraged to value others in your church.
exp.39:23:
The explanation says that the angel leads Ezekiel toward the south, and there he finds another gate of the temple. The man measures it, and its posts and its arches have the same measurements as those of the east gate.

Ezekiel recounts this vision in the first person, years after Jerusalem fell, when the people were living in exile. God shows him a new temple, measured in detail by a man who guides him. Scholars interpret it in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of God's presence with his people, or as a spiritual image. But all of them note the order and holiness it displays.

For today: God is a God of order and faithfulness. If he took care with every measure of his house, he also cares for your life. Seek him with confidence and order in your daily life.
exp.17:21:
This verse says that God will not keep a record of the wrongs of the one who turns back to Him. "Transgressions" are the times a person rebelled against God, and "they shall not be mentioned unto him" means that God will not hold them up against him. "Shall live" refers to having life before God, not to being punished with death.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. Some were saying that they suffered for the sins of their fathers and that there was no remedy. God answers that each person answers for himself, and that there is always an open door to return to Him. He then clarifies that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but in his turning from his evil way.

For today: if you feel trapped by your past or by your family's history, God invites you to return to Him. With sincere repentance, you can begin again, trusting in His mercy.
exp.19:33:
God promises to bring Israel out from the nations where they are scattered and to gather them together. He will do this "with a mighty hand, and with a stretched out arm," expressions that speak of power, as in the exodus from Egypt. "With fury poured out" means that his discipline will be firm and real. Gathering them is the same as bringing them back together.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of the people exiled in Babylon. They were thinking about becoming like the pagan nations and worshiping idols of wood and stone. God answers that he will not allow this: he will remain their King. The verses that follow show that there will be judgment, as there was in the wilderness with their fathers, before the restoration.

For today: God does not let go of us even when we want to live like everyone else. His correction is not rejection, but love that seeks to bring us back. If you have wandered away, return to him with confidence and humility.
exp.19:27:
He says that God brought them into the land he had promised them with an oath, "lifting up his hand." But as soon as they arrived, they looked for any high hill and leafy tree to worship there. The sacrifices they offered were animals killed on the altar, the drink offerings were liquids poured out as an offering, and the pleasing aroma was the incense or smell of their sacrifices. They offered all of it to other gods.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel during the exile in Babylon. He reviews their history to show that the rebellion was not new: their ancestors were already doing the same thing. With this he asks them whether they are going to follow the same path.

For today: God gives us good gifts, and it is easy to use them to worship other things. Today, ask the Lord which thing is occupying the place that belongs only to him, and surrender it to him.
exp.29:14:
He says that God will pour out his anger on Sin, which was a strong city of Egypt, a kind of defense on its frontier. He also says that he will cut off the multitude of No, that is, that he will destroy it or cut it down, as one cuts down a tree. No was not the ancient city of Thebes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Egypt considered itself secure and had given Israel false hope. God announces judgment on its cities, its idols and its pride. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of that judgment, as the nearby context of the chapter says.

For today: let us not place our security in how strong something seems, such as money, power or fame. Only God is a true fortress. We can ask ourselves what we are trusting in and return to rest in him.
exp.40:19:
The explanation says that the walls of the temple were decorated, from the floor up to above the door, with carved figures of cherubim (angelic beings) and palm trees. This decoration covered the whole wall of the temple.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, describing a vision God gave him, while a guide who looked like a man measured the temple. This takes place when the people were in exile in Babylon. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a symbol of God's presence and restoration. The cherubim and the palm trees recall the tabernacle and Eden.

For today: God cares about details and wants his presence to be honored with beauty and reverence. We can draw near to him with respect and joy, and also bring into our daily lives a sincere care for what we offer him.
exp.26:3:
The explanation says that Tyre, the great city of commerce, was located in the middle of the sea. "Borders" means its limits or boundaries. The word "thy" is an older form of "your." Those who built it left it with a perfect beauty, like a beautiful and well-equipped ship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to make a lament for Tyre. This city was rich and proud, and it boasted of its perfect beauty. The passage describes Tyre as a great ship, but that praise sets up the announcement of its fall. Its beauty was real, but its pride would lead it to ruin.

Everything good we have, such as talent, success, or possessions, comes with help from others and from God. Let us give thanks with humility, without trusting in what we accomplish or boasting about it.
exp.27:8:
It says the king of Tyre thought himself a god, but when his enemy comes, the one who is going to kill him, it will be seen that he is only a man. The question is a mockery: will you still say "I am God" in front of the one who takes your life?

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Tyre, proud of his wisdom and his riches, had set himself in God's place. God announces that he will send foreign peoples, strong and cruel, to humble him. Those who had no covenant with God were a name for the pagan nations, and to die at their hands was a death without honor.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us believe we control everything. Today we can remember that we are creatures, that we depend on God every day, and ask him for humility so that we do not trust only in our talent, money, or success.
exp.29:24:
God says he will strengthen Babylon and its king, and that he will weaken Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. "Arms" represents power and the ability to fight. The "sword" is God's judgment, which he will place in the hand of the Babylonian king so that he attacks Egypt. The final purpose is that they will recognize him: "they shall know that I am the Lord."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. Egypt was a power in which Judah sometimes trusted for protection, and God announces its fall. Babylon appears as an instrument of judgment, not as someone God approves of in every way.

For today: No human power, whether money, position, or influence, is as firm as it seems. Today you can examine what you trust most and place your security again in God, who rules over everything.
exp.27:11:
God tells Ezekiel, who is called "son of man," to raise a funeral song over the king of Tyre. The "lamentations" are cries of grief for someone who has died. The phrase "you set the seal to the proportion" is hard, and it is understood in several ways: as someone who believes he is a model of perfection, or as someone who appears complete and without fault. The king is described as full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around 587 B.C., within a message against Tyre, a rich and proud city. The king considered himself almost a god. Many believers see in the verses that follow only a human king described in poetic language; others also see an echo of the fall of Satan. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: wisdom, talent, and beauty are gifts from God. If they fill us with pride, they will bring us down. Let us receive everything with gratitude and humility.
exp.40:12:
It says that the angel measured the temple's length and gave it a hundred cubits. He also measured the separate area behind the temple, the building on the west side, and its walls, and the total came to a hundred cubits in length. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so we are talking about around fifty meters.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, is in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, orderly and perfect. The measurements remind the people that God still has plans for them and that his presence is holy. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about details and seeks order and reverence. We can ask ourselves what place God has in our routine. Setting aside a fixed time each day to pray and read the Bible is a simple way to give his presence a place.
exp.27:21:
God speaks to Ezekiel and commands him to announce a message against the city of Sidon. He says that he is against her, that he will be glorified in the midst of her, that is, honored and acknowledged as great. When he executes his judgments (his just punishments), Sidon will know that he is the Lord.

"Shall be sanctified" means that he will show his holiness, which is set apart and perfect.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Sidon was a neighboring city of Israel, and the following passage says that it had been a thorn and a terror to Israel, for it had despised them. God promises justice and relief for his people. The text does not detail every historical event, so it is not wise to add more.

For today: God sees unjust treatment and is not indifferent. We can trust him instead of taking revenge, and live in such a way that his holiness is seen in us.
exp.29:3:
It says that a war, "the sword," will come upon Egypt. The wounded will fall in the land, and even Ethiopia (in Hebrew, Cush, south of Egypt) will tremble with fear. The enemy will carry off the wealth and the people, and the foundations, that is, what held the nation up, will be broken down.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. It is a message of judgment against Egypt, called "the day of the LORD." The next chapter indicates that Babylon would be the instrument (30:10). Egypt had been a deceptive support for Judah, and its pride would fall.

For today: no human strength, no money, no power, no alliances, is a secure foundation. Ask yourself what you are leaning your life on, and trust first in God, who is firm when everything else falls.
exp.17:14:
This verse describes the son who decides not to follow his father's bad example. He does not eat "sobre los montes," that is, he does not take part in the meals and offerings at the pagan shrines on the high places. He does not lift his eyes to the idols of Israel, meaning he does not give them his trust or worship. And he does not dishonor his neighbor's wife, that is, he does not commit adultery.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The people in exile were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for their own choices. The righteous son will not be condemned for his father's wickedness, and this shows that there is always room to change.

For today: your family past does not define you. Even if you grew up with bad examples, you can choose faithfulness to God, respect for others, and care for your relationships. Ask God for help to begin a new path.
exp.32:32:
The explanation says that when what God announced comes to pass, the people will recognize that there really was a prophet among them. The word "lo" in the verse is an exclamation that stresses that this fulfillment is certain, and "it" refers to what Ezekiel had prophesied, namely the judgment on Jerusalem.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile in Babylon. The exiles were going to listen to him the way someone attends a good concert, enjoying his words but not obeying them. Their hearts were still set on gain. God assures him that reality will eventually prove his message right.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy a good biblical message or good Christian music. Before life forces us to recognize the truth, let us choose today one teaching we have heard and put it into practice this week.
exp.30:6:
It says this great tree became very beautiful because of its size and its long, spreading branches. The reason is that its roots reached a great deal of water, and this fed it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the Pharaoh of Egypt. He uses the image of an enormous tree, comparing it to Assyria, to warn him that his power will also fall. Many understand that the tree represents Assyria as an example, though some see it as a direct image of Egypt. God makes clear that the tree's greatness was a gift from him.

Everything good we have, such as talents, success, or influence, comes from God. We can thank him for it and use it to bless others, without becoming filled with pride.
exp.33:20:
It says that the strong sheep pushed with their side and shoulder, and struck the weak ones with their horns, until they left them scattered and outside the flock. Pushing hard is the sense of the verb for pushing with the side and shoulder; striking with the horns is the sense of the verb for butting; and the weak ones are the diseased.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel for neglecting the people. Now he also rebukes the powerful within the people, who were abusing the most vulnerable. God promises to judge between sheep and sheep, to save his flock, and to raise up a shepherd, a figure many Christians see as a sign of Christ.

Today this invites us to examine how we use our strength, influence, or position. God cares for the weak; so it is wise to protect, listen to, and welcome those who feel excluded, in the church, the family, or the workplace.
exp.41:19:
The explanation says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured the four sides of the temple area. The wall that surrounded it formed a square, five hundred reeds on each side. A reed was a measuring rod; many scholars calculate it was about three meters, though the exact figure is debated. The wall served to separate the holy from the common, that is, from what was ordinary and not meant for worship.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. In it, a guide with a measuring rod shows him a new temple. This vision gave hope to a discouraged people: God would remain present among them. Interpreters differ on whether it speaks of a literal temple in the future or of a symbolic picture.

For today: God values what is holy. We can set healthy boundaries, such as a daily time of prayer, so that what is ordinary does not crowd out what is sacred.
exp.16:18:
God says, swearing by his own life, that the king of Judah despised the oath made in God's name and broke the covenant. Therefore, God will bring the consequences of that sin down upon the king's own head. The explanation of "despised" as "held in low regard" is omitted here, since that word appears in the verse above as "despised." The word "covenant" in the verse above is itself the word for a pact or agreement, and the phrase about turning the punishment back upon him means that God will repay him with the punishment he deserves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Zedekiah, king of Judah, had sworn loyalty to Babylon before God, but he rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God regards that oath as something serious, even though it was made to a foreign king.

For today: our word matters to God. If we promise something, at work, in the family, or in the church, let us try to keep it with honesty. And if we fail, we can ask him for forgiveness and for help to be faithful.
exp.12:9:
They say that the false prophets deceived God's people by announcing "peace" when there was no peace. He uses an image: someone builds a weak wall, and others, instead of strengthening it, cover it with loose mortar, that is, a thin mixture that only makes it look good.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people live under the threat of judgment from Babylon. The false prophets were saying what the people wanted to hear, without calling them to repentance. That is why God rebukes them and announces that their wall of lies will fall in the storm.

For today: let us not look only for words that comfort us. Let us ask God to speak to us with truth, even when it corrects us, and build our lives on his Word and not on appearances.
exp.15:44:
God tells Jerusalem that she resembles her mother and her sisters. They "rejected" their husbands and their children, that is, they turned them away and abandoned them. The words "Hittite" and "Amorite" name peoples who were pagan inhabitants of Canaan. By this it is said that Jerusalem was acting like the nations that did not know God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is accusing Jerusalem of unfaithfulness, and he uses the image of a wife who betrays her husband. The part about the mother and the father speaks of the Canaanite origin of the city, not of a literal genealogy. Interpreters understand it as a way of showing that her sin was an inheritance from her surroundings.

For today: let us not copy without thought the customs that surround us. Let us ask God to show us where we have drifted away from him, and return with humility.
exp.26:6:
It says that Tyre's ship was of great luxury. Its sail, called here a "sail" in the verse, was of fine linen with embroidered work, brought from Egypt, so that everyone could see it from afar. Its awning over the deck was of blue and purple cloth, and of scarlet, from the isles of Elishah. It is thought that Elishah was in the Mediterranean, but where exactly is not known for certain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a trading city famous for its wealth. He describes it as a beautiful ship, made with materials from many nations. Behind that image there is a warning: such beauty and pride would not save it from the judgment that was coming.

For today: enjoying what God gives us is not wrong, but we can place our trust in success, money or image. Today you might ask yourself: what is my security resting on? Rest in God, who does not sink.
exp.42:7:
God says that the Israelites set their threshold and their doorpost, that is, the entrance and frame of their own buildings, right up against those of his temple, with only a wall between them and God. In this way they defiled his holy name with their detestable practices, a word that refers to idolatrous practices God hates. Therefore, he says, he consumed them in his fury, meaning he judged them severely.

God speaks in a vision the prophet Ezekiel receives after the glory of the Lord returns to the new temple. He is referring to the earlier kings, who built next to the temple and mixed false worship with what was holy. Many scholars think this alludes to nearby royal palaces and tombs, although the details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: God wants to be the only Lord of our lives, not just one more loyalty alongside others. We can ask ourselves what we have set up close beside God, and hand it over to him.
exp.43:28:
It says the priests would eat from the offerings that the people brought to the temple: the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering. Also, "every dedicated thing" would belong to them, that is, whatever was set apart for God in Israel. The sin offering is the offering made to cover guilt.
