God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a restored temple. The Levitical priests, descendants of Zadok, would receive no land, because God himself would be their inheritance. For this reason the people supported them with the offerings. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic.

For today: those who serve God deserve support, and all of us can learn to give with gratitude. In addition, this reminds us that our greatest security lies not in what we possess, but in God himself.
exp.25:18:
This verse says that God will turn the city of Tyre into a destroyed and empty place, like those cities where no one lives anymore. The word for "turn" in the source means to change something into something else, and the word for "ruined" describes a place laid waste. The images of the deep and of the great waters show that the sea will cover the city, as if it were buried beneath it.

God Himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and powerful city that lived from maritime trade. Earlier in this chapter, its pride is described, and how it rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem. Some scholars see the fulfillment across several historical stages, not in a single event.

For today: power and wealth are not a safe refuge. We can ask ourselves where we place our trust, and ask God to give us humility to depend on Him and not on what we have.
exp.34:11:
God says that he heard everything Edom (Mount Seir) spoke against the mountains of Israel. Edom's insults and offenses, and the fact that they said them out loud, are what the verse is about. Edom was rejoicing that Israel lay in ruins and thought they could now take the land for themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, Israel's neighbor, had an old hostility toward that people. When Israel fell to Babylon, Edom rejoiced and wanted to seize its territory. God makes clear that the land was not theirs and that he had heard every word. By speaking against Israel, they also spoke against God.

For today: God hears what we say, including when we rejoice over the downfall of others. We can ask him for help not to mock someone who is suffering, but to pray for them, help them, and trust that God is the just judge.
exp.17:2:
God swears by his own life, something very solemn, and says that the people will no longer use a popular saying: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." Sour grapes are unripe green grapes, and having your teeth set on edge is that unpleasant sensation in the teeth. With that saying they meant that the children paid for their parents' sins.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, when part of the people were living in exile in Babylon. Some used the saying to claim that their suffering was the fault of earlier generations and not their own. God corrects that excuse and teaches that each person answers for their own decisions. The verses that follow make this clear.

For today: do not use your family's past as an excuse for not changing, and do not condemn yourself for other people's mistakes. Recognize your own responsibility, ask God for forgiveness, and walk with Him from today.
exp.25:1:
It says that Tyre, a great trading city, rejoiced when Jerusalem fell. The words "Aha" are an expression of mockery and satisfaction, like saying "how good!" Jerusalem was the gateway of the peoples, that is, a place through which trade and people passed. Tyre thought that, with Jerusalem fallen, she would be enriched: "I shall be replenished," while Jerusalem would be "laid waste."

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, called "son of man." This takes place shortly after Jerusalem's fall before Babylon. God does not overlook the fact that Tyre mocked and sought gain from the pain of others, and for this reason he announces his judgment in the verses that follow.

Today we can examine our hearts: do I rejoice when others are doing badly, or when their fall benefits me? God calls us to compassion, not to the selfish profit of another's suffering.
exp.31:10:
This verse says that God himself, the Lord GOD, announces that the sword of the king of Babylon will come against Egypt. "Thee" refers to the pharaoh, the one to whom the prophecy is addressed. The "sword" stands for the army and for war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. This chapter is a lament over the pharaoh, who was thought to be powerful and proud. God tells him that his fall will be seen by many nations. Here Babylon is presented as an instrument of judgment, not as a power acting on its own. This is understood as part of God's rule over the nations.

For today: let us not place our security in power, wealth, or prestige, because all of these can fall. Better to trust in God and live with humility, knowing that He governs history.
exp.11:8:
God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man", that is, a simple human being. He asks whether the people of Israel, whom he describes as a rebellious house, have asked him what he was doing.

Ezekiel had just acted out, in plain view of everyone, a person going into exile: he carried out his belongings by day, and at night he dug a hole through the wall. The people were curious, and God uses that question to explain the message to them: Jerusalem and its prince would be taken captive. God speaks this way because he wanted them to understand the consequences of their rebellion.

For today: when God shows us something clearly, let us not take it merely as curiosity. Let us ask what he wants to change in us, and respond with humility and obedience.
exp.26:18:
This verse says that people from Dan and Javan came to the markets of Tyre to trade. They sold worked iron, myrrh in liquid form, and aromatic cane, a plant used for perfumes and for worship. Fairs are large markets. The word for "going to and fro" is a difficult one: some believe it describes Javan as a traveler, and others think the text refers to a place with a different name. There is uncertainty here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This is a lament over Tyre, a city very rich from its sea trade. The long list of merchants shows its fame and its pride. Then God announces that this wealth will not save it from its fall.

For today: enjoying work and possessions is not wrong, but we should not place our trust in them. Ask yourself today: "Where do I place my security?" God invites us to trust Him first.
exp.47:23:
This verse says that, next to the territory of Benjamin, the tribe of Simeon is given a strip of land. That strip runs from east to west, from the east all the way to the sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the final vision of the book. There a land is described, divided into equal strips, with the temple and the city in the center. The exiled Jews needed the promise that God would restore them. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is literal, symbolic, or fulfilled in Christ and his people.

For today: God does not forget anyone. Simeon has his assigned place, and so do you. Trust that God cares for you and gives you a place among his people.
exp.30:13:
He says that God allowed the great tree to fall so that no other tree beside the waters would become proud of its height. The word "grave" is an old term for a tomb or burial place, and the thick foliage refers to dense branches. All of them, however great they may seem, end in death, just like any other human being.

God speaks through Ezekiel and addresses the pharaoh of Egypt. He is compared to an enormous cedar, like Assyria, which also fell. Many scholars see here a warning: if an empire so great was brought down, Egypt will not be spared. Some details of the poetic language are interpreted in several ways.

For today: success, a position, or talent does not make us superior or eternal. We can be thankful for what God has given us, and practice humility, remembering that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.15:47:
God swears by his own life, a very solemn oath, and says that Sodom, together with her dependent towns, did not sin as much as Jerusalem and her villages. It is a comparison that surprises and hurts. Here "sister" is used as a figure for cities related through their conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. In this chapter he accuses Jerusalem of unfaithfulness, like a wife who abandons the one who cared for her. The following verses explain Sodom's sin: pride, plenty, comfort, and failing to help the poor. Jerusalem had received more light and yet did worse.

For today: let us not compare ourselves with others to feel righteous. God looks at how much we have received from him and how we respond. Let us ask him for a humble heart and open hands to help the needy.
exp.36:10:
God explains to Ezekiel what the dry bones he saw mean: they are the whole people of Israel. They themselves feel this way and say that their bones are dried up, that their hope is lost, and that they are cut off for their parts, cut off and separated like a felled tree.

The Lord speaks with the prophet Ezekiel. The people were in exile in Babylon, far from their land and their temple, and many thought that God had finished with them. The vision answers that discouragement: God promises to give them life again and bring them back home.

For today: when you feel that everything is over and that there is no hope left, tell God honestly how you feel. He can give life where you see only dryness. Trust in his word and wait for his work, even when it takes time.
exp.43:6:
The explanation says that the people let strangers enter the sanctuary who were uncircumcised, neither in the flesh nor in the heart. The verse's word "pollute" means to defile or profane those things that were holy. The phrase "my bread, the fat, and the blood" refers to the offerings: the bread was the food of the sacrifice, the fat was the animal's fat, and the blood was the blood that was offered. "Broken my covenant" means they violated the agreement with God.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, to rebuke Israel. The priests had neglected the care of the temple and allowed people without commitment to God to serve in holy things. Interpreters explain the temple details in these chapters in different ways, but the rebuke is clear: a faithful heart was lacking.

For today: God looks for a surrendered heart, not merely religious appearances. We can ask ourselves whether our worship and our service come from sincere faith, and take care that what is holy is treated with reverence.
exp.31:29:
The explanation says that the princes of the north and all of Sidon, who once spread terror, now lie dead in the grave. The word for "north" means north. "Uncircumcised" here describes the pagan peoples, and lying down with them was a dishonorable death. "By the sword" means by the sword. Their strength did not save them, and they were put to shame.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against Egypt. He shows Pharaoh that other powerful nations have already fallen: Edom, Sidon, and the peoples of the north. Exactly which group the northern peoples are is not known for certain. The message is clear: no empire escapes God's judgment.

For today: power, money, or fame do not give us true security. If we use our strength to dominate or harm others, it ends in shame. Today you can use what you have to serve, and place your trust in God, who is just.
exp.35:8:
God says to the mountains of Israel: "Look, I am on your side, and I will turn toward you." The words "here I am" mean "I am here." "Plowed" means turned over by a plow, and "sown" means that seed will be scattered on them. In other words, the land will be worked again and will bear fruit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was in exile, and its land had been left in ruins and mocked by the neighboring nations. God promises to restore the land and his people, so that they will live there again and the land will bear fruit once more.

For today: when you feel that your life is like dry or abandoned ground, remember that God can turn toward you. Bring Him your ruins honestly and let Him work them again. Restoration is usually a patient process, like a field being prepared before it bears fruit.
exp.26:31:
This verse says that those who see the fall of Tyre will compose sad songs, lamentations sung for the dead. In the midst of their weeping they will ask, "What city is like Tyrus?" that is, what city could be compared with her? They speak of her as one destroyed in the midst of the sea, because part of the city of Tyre stood on an island.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very wealthy trading power, and the chapter presents her as a great ship that sinks. The sailors and merchants, who had grown rich through her, mourn her ruin. God judges her for her pride, although the lament shows how much others depended on her wealth.

For today: riches and success are not a secure foundation. It is wise to trust in God and not in what can be lost in a single day.
exp.37:9:
He says that, when that day comes, ideas will come into Gog's mind, that is, plans will arise in his thoughts. And those thoughts will be an evil thought: an idea of doing harm. The phrase "you shall conceive" means he will form it and let it grow inside himself.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. He speaks of Gog, a leader who will come against Israel when that nation is living in peace, after being gathered from among the nations. Interpreters differ about when this happens and whether it is literal or symbolic. Here we see that God knows the hidden plans and directs them for his purposes.

For today: evil plans begin as thoughts. Ask God to examine your heart, and reject harmful ideas toward others before they take root. God sees everything.
exp.31:25:
It says Meshech and Tubal, with all their people, are in the place of the dead. Their graves are all around them. They were uncircumcised, that is, people outside Israel's covenant, and they died by the sword. The reason is that they spread terror in the land of the living. The phrase "by the sword" means "by the sword."

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt and its fall. He presents Egypt going down into the grave, where other violent nations already lie, such as Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal. Scholars debate how exactly to understand this scene of the place of the dead, but the message is clear: the power that terrifies others does not escape God's judgment.

For today: do not envy or imitate those who impose themselves through fear and violence. Their strength may seem great, but it comes to an end. Instead, seek to use your influence to protect, serve, and give life to others.
exp.25:11:
This passage describes how the invading army will plunder the city of Tyre. They will carry off its riches and merchandise, break down its walls, and destroy its houses, which were pleasant to look at. Even the stones, the timber, and the dust from the rubble will be thrown into the water, that is, into the sea.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against Tyre, a city rich and proud through its trade, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem. The text names Nebuchadnezzar as the invader (v. 7). Many understand that verse 12 was also fulfilled later, when the rubble of the coastal city was thrown into the sea, although some interpret it only of Nebuchadnezzar and others of several conquerors.

For today: riches and success are not a secure foundation. Let us place our trust in God, and treat those who suffer with humility, without rejoicing in their fall.
exp.41:16:
He measured the north side, five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed round about. This explanation says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured the north side of the temple area, and that it was five hundred reeds. The measuring reed was a rod used for measuring; "round about" means that he measured the whole perimeter. With the other three sides, the enclosure forms a perfect square.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, a guide with the appearance of bronze shows him a new temple and measures it. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence and holiness. The equal measurements suggest order and separation between the holy and the common (v. 20).

For today: God is a God of order and holiness, and He cares how we approach Him. Take some quiet time to prepare your heart before prayer, setting aside distractions, as one who enters a sacred place.
exp.31:15:
It says there will be a funeral song over Egypt. A "lamentation" is a mournful song sung over someone who has died. The "daughters of the nations" are the women of the nations, who will sing this lament for Egypt and all its people. God Himself declares it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt was a proud power, and God announces its fall as judgment. The verses before this one speak of the land laid waste, so that everyone will know that He is the Lord. Afterward, Ezekiel is commanded to chant the lament. This is a prophetic poem, using figurative language.

For today: power, wealth and fame are not secure forever. You can trust in God, who is above every nation, and live with humility, without resting your life on things that pass away.
exp.12:5:
The explanation says that certain prophets saw false things and gave deceptive messages. Their vision was empty and worthless, and what they claimed to be a spiritual message was a false one. They declared that the Lord had said it, but God had not sent them. Even so, the people hoped that what was spoken would come true.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He is rebuking the false prophets of Israel. They did not stand up for the people or call them back to God; instead they soothed them with false words. That is why God says he is against them.

Today we can learn to test what we hear against the Bible, even when it comes with phrases like "God told me." We should also take care that our own words do not put in God's mouth what He has not said.
exp.31:12:
The explanation says that God will destroy all the animals of Egypt that live beside the great waters, that is, the Nile River and its canals. After that, no human foot or animal hoof will stir up those waters again. Stirring up the water means making it dirty or churning it. The animals here may refer to livestock and, figuratively, to people and their power.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces judgment against Egypt and its pharaoh, who thought himself powerful and proud. God would use the sword of Babylon. Some understand the still waters as the end of Egyptian activity and splendor; others see them as an image of desolation. The final purpose is that they will know that God is the Lord.

For today: God humbles human pride, whether in nations or in individuals. Today we can examine what we trust in more than in Him and surrender it to Him with humility.
exp.21:29:
God says that he looked for someone who would build up the wall and stand in the gap. It is the image of a city wall with a break in it: God was looking for a person who would repair the wall and stand in that breach to defend the city. He would do this "before me," that is, to intercede, so that God would not have to destroy the land. But he says: "I found none."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He has just accused the prophets, priests, leaders, and the people of lying, robbery, and oppression of the poor and the foreigners. No one rose up to plead or to correct. Then comes the judgment.

Today we can be someone who "stands in the gap": praying for our family, church, or country, and speaking the truth and defending the weak, without waiting for someone else to do it first.
exp.15:25:
This verse says that Jerusalem, pictured as an unfaithful woman, gave herself to the Egyptians, who were her neighbours. The image of being unfaithful is the picture of her infidelity. The phrase about the Egyptians being large and strong speaks of their physical vigour and abundance, and the wording is an old and very blunt one. The word "provoke" shows that by doing this more and more, she stirred up the anger of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. The whole of chapter 16 is a parable: God cared for Jerusalem from when she was young, but she left him. Here the unfaithfulness stands for the alliances with Egypt and for idolatry, in place of trusting in God.

For today: let us examine where we look for security apart from God, such as money, fame or other people. Let us return to trusting in him, who is faithful and forgives the one who comes back.
exp.33:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "And the word of the Lord came unto me" is an older way of saying that a message from God came to him. It is how the book introduces a new message from God.

Here God is the one speaking, and Ezekiel is the one who receives the message. The prophet lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. The verses that follow show that God is going to speak against the people's leaders, called shepherds, because they looked after themselves and not the flock.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before wanting to lead or teach others, it is good to stop and listen to what he says, and to let it first examine us.
exp.22:6:
It says that Oholah, who represents Samaria (the northern kingdom of Israel), gave herself to the Assyrians, the most select men of that people. The word for her acts here refers to spiritual unfaithfulness, not only sexual sin. The phrases about her being infatuated and about her defiling herself with all their idols show that she sought political alliances and also took on their false gods.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, using an allegory of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah (Samaria and Jerusalem). Israel had made a covenant with God, but sought security in foreign powers and in its idols. Therefore God handed her over into the hands of the very ones she had clung to, and Assyria ended up destroying her.

For today: examine the things in which you seek security or worth apart from God, such as money, prestige, or relationships. Return to trusting Him first, because whatever takes God's place ends up enslaving us.
exp.17:18:
This verse records a question from the people: "Why does the son not pay for the father's sin?" God answers that the son who has practiced "judgment and justice," that is, who has acted uprightly and fairly, and who has kept his ordinances (his commandments), shall surely live. To "bear" means to carry the guilt and its consequences.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were repeating a saying: that children paid for their parents' sins. By this they implied that God was unjust. God makes clear that each person answers for his or her own choices. Interpreters debate how far this touches the social consequences of sin, but the emphasis here is personal responsibility before God.

Today, do not use your family past as an excuse or as a sentence of condemnation. With God's help, you can choose to walk in justice and mercy, and He receives you just as you are.
exp.22:21:
Here God speaks to Aholibah and announces a punishment. He says he will rouse up the very lovers she has grown weary of, and bring them against her from every side. These lovers are the nations she allied herself with in search of security.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Aholibah represents Jerusalem and Judah, described as an unfaithful woman who gave herself to Assyria, Babylon and Egypt instead of trusting God. It is strong, symbolic language, meant to show how serious her idolatry was. The judgment came through Babylon.

For today: whatever we place our trust in instead of God, such as money, reputation or people, can end up hurting us. Today we can return to Him sincerely and rest in His care.
exp.37:11:
He says that Gog, the leader of the attack, has a plan: to plunder and seize goods. He intends to turn his hand against places that were once in ruins and are now inhabited again, and against a people gathered from among the nations, who already have livestock and possessions.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that, in a future time, Gog will form an evil plan when he sees a people living in peace and without walls. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future event, others a symbolic picture of evil against the people of God. God makes it clear that he knows the hidden intentions of the heart.

For today: God sees our thoughts before they become actions. We can ask him to examine our hearts and to reject greed in time. We can also rest, because he cares for his own.
exp.14:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man", that is, a simple human being. He asks him a question: in what way is the wood of the vine better than any other piece of wood? The branch of the vine has no special value for building anything among the trees of the forest.

Here the LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God uses this comparison to speak about Jerusalem and its inhabitants. The vine is good for bearing fruit, not for making furniture or tools. If it does not bear fruit, it is almost worthless. The verses that follow develop this.

For today: our worth before God does not come from our strength or our appearance, but from remaining in him and bearing fruit. We can ask ourselves with humility: am I united to God, and do I live in a way that bears fruit?
exp.33:13:
God promises to care for his people the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. He will lead them to good pasture, and on the high mountains of Israel they will have their fold, which is the pen or resting place where they lie down. There they will lie down in peace, and they will feed in a good pasture, meaning abundant and rich.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel's leaders, called shepherds, had neglected and mistreated the people, and the sheep were scattered into other lands. God promises that he himself will gather them, bring them back, and care for them with justice.

For today: when you feel tired, lost, or abandoned, remember that God wants to care for you personally. Take a moment today to pray and rest in his care, trusting that he knows how to give you what you need.
exp.35:18:
God says that he scattered Israel among the nations. The phrase rendered there as "scattered them" is about God doing the scattering, and the word "dispersed" means they were spread out through the countries. "According to their way" refers to how they lived. God judged them according to what they did, not unfairly or arbitrarily.

The passage is spoken by God through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Before this verse, God explains that the people had defiled the land with idolatry and violence. The exile was the consequence. But the passage continues and shows that God will act afterward for the sake of his holy name.

For today: our choices have consequences, and God invites us to acknowledge them with humility. Even so, his discipline is not the end; he seeks to restore us. We can draw near to him with sincerity, trusting in his mercy.
exp.25:3:
God announces that the enemies of Tyre will tear down its walls and its towers. He says that he will "scrape her dust from her," that is, leave her without rubble or soil, and make her a bare rock, a bare stone where nothing built remains.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre, a trading city by the sea, rejoiced when Jerusalem fell, thinking that now it would grow rich. God answers that he will judge that attitude of mockery and greed. Historians recall that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre and that centuries later Alexander the Great attacked it; not all of them agree on how each event relates to this prophecy.

Today, this verse invites us not to rejoice in the misfortune of others, and not to trust in our wealth or security. We can ask ourselves: do I feel glad when someone else is doing badly? Better to pray for those who suffer and to place our trust in God.
exp.23:12:
God tells Jerusalem that she will suffer for her filthiness, that is, her wickedness and her idolatry. He wanted to cleanse her, but she did not want to be cleansed. Therefore she will not be clean again until the fury of God has come to rest upon her, that is, until the judgment is fully carried out and his anger is satisfied. "Thou shalt not be purged" means "you will not be cleansed."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Jerusalem is compared to a dirty, rusted pot set on the fire. God had given her warnings and opportunities, but the people rejected them. The following verse shows that the judgment is firm and just.

For today: when God corrects us or points something out to us, let us not harden our hearts. His call to change is an offer of cleansing. We can respond to him today with sincerity and repentance.
exp.15:55:
It says that Judah (Jerusalem) did not even mention Sodom, her sister, while she was living in pride. The word "sister" in this sentence means a close relative, and "pride" here means arrogance or self-importance. Jerusalem thought itself better and did not want to speak about Sodom's fall.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful wife who fell into idolatry and wickedness, even more than Sodom and Samaria. God reminds her of her pride so that she will feel shame and repent. Later he promises to restore her, so the message does not end only in judgment.

For today: when you feel that you are better than others, remember that all of us need the mercy of God. Before pointing out the faults of others, examine your own heart and ask God for humility.
exp.12:12:
God says he will send a very strong wind, a flood of rain, and hailstones. These storms represent his anger against something that has been badly built. The verse's wording about the wall being plastered over and the mixture being loose and unable to hold anything is explained by the picture of a wall covered with a thin coat of mud or plaster, and a weak mortar that holds nothing together.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. There were false prophets who announced peace when there was no peace. They were like people who cover a weak wall with paint so that it looks firm. God says that wall will fall, and it will be seen that the foundation was rotten.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are building our lives on the truth of God or only covering up what is wrong. Pretty words do not hold up a house; obedience and truth do. It is worth examining our foundation before the storms arrive.
exp.25:13:
God says that Tyre will become like a bare, smooth rock, where fishermen will only spread their nets out to dry. "Smooth rock" is a rock with no buildings on it, and "a place to spread nets" is a place where fishing nets are dried. God adds that the city will not be rebuilt, and that he says this with his own authority.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a trading city, rich and proud, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking it could profit from it (Ezekiel 26:2). God announces judgment for that pride. Scholars debate how it was fulfilled: some think of Nebuchadnezzar and later Alexander the Great, and others understand it in a broader way.

For today: do not place your security in your riches, and do not rejoice in the misfortune of others. What God affirms remains, and what we build with pride can fall.
exp.15:37:
It says that God himself will be the judge of Jerusalem. She will be judged with the punishment the law gave to women who committed adultery and to those who shed blood. "I will give you in blood of wrath and of jealousy" means that God will give her a violent punishment, born of his anger and his jealousy, that is, of his love wounded by the unfaithfulness of his people. "Lovers" are the nations and the idols to whom she gave herself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile. Throughout this chapter, God compares Jerusalem to a wife he cared for who then betrayed him with other gods and alliances, even sacrificing their children. God announces judgment for that unfaithfulness.

For today: God takes our loyalty seriously. Examine where you place your trust and your heart, and return to God with sincerity, because his judgment seeks to awaken us and his mercy always waits for us.
exp.25:19:
God tells the city of Tyre that he will bring it down into the pit, the place of the dead, along with the peoples of long ago. "People of the ancient times" means people from very ancient times. Tyre will be placed in the lowest parts, like old ruins, and will never again be inhabited. At the end, God says he will set glory in "the land of the living," meaning that his people will be restored.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud trading city, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own gain. God announces his judgment. Scholars understand in different ways how this prophecy was fulfilled in history, and some see in it several stages.

For today: power and wealth are not secure if we forget God. We can ask him for a humble heart, one that does not rejoice in the misfortune of others and that trusts in him, not in what we have.
exp.43:10:
The explanation says that the Levites who turned away from God will not serve as priests, but they will still have service duties in the temple: guarding the gates, slaughtering the animals for the people's sacrifices, and helping the people. The gatekeepers are the ones who watch over the entrances. The burnt offering was the offering that was burned whole, and the sacrifice is the animal that was offered.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of the new temple. The Levites had served before idols and caused Israel to stumble, so God takes away their priesthood, but he does not abandon them altogether. He gives them humble service. Some scholars see discipline combined with mercy here; others debate how this vision of the temple is fulfilled.

For today: our failures have consequences, but God can still use us in humble service. Serve with gratitude wherever he places you, without demanding a place of honor.
exp.33:6:
God calls the shepherds to attention and asks them to listen to what He is about to say. The phrase "Therefore" shows that what follows is a consequence of what came before. The word "hear" is the older way of saying "listen." "Lord" is the name of God.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. In these chapters, the "shepherds" are the leaders of Israel, above all the kings and rulers. The "sheep" are the people. God accuses them of having neglected the people, who were scattered, unprotected, and without anyone to seek them out, while they took care of themselves.

Today, anyone who has some responsibility over others, in the church, the family, or the workplace, can ask: am I serving those I care for, or am I only seeking my own benefit? Before acting, it is wise to first listen to the word of God.
exp.32:4:
It says that if someone hears the sound of the trumpet (a horn that gave warning of danger) and pays it no attention, he himself is responsible for whatever happens to him. "His blood shall be upon him" means that the guilt for his death is his own. But whoever pays attention and takes warning, that is, puts himself on alert and acts, will save his life.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls a watchman of Israel. A watchman warned the city when the enemy was coming. God uses that image to explain that Ezekiel must warn the people, and that each person is accountable for how he receives the warning.

Today, when the Bible, wise counsel, or your conscience warns you of a spiritual danger, do not ignore it. Listen with humility and change in time, because God warns us out of love.
exp.47:11:
It says that the priests descended from Zadok would receive as an inheritance a special portion of land, set apart from the rest of the territory. It calls this portion "most holy," that is, the most sacred, and it would lie beside the land assigned to the Levites. The word "portion" means a share or inheritance, and "border" means a limit or boundary.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He divides the land and places the sanctuary at the center. The priests of Zadok are rewarded because they remained faithful when others turned aside. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as literal and future, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God notices and honors faithfulness, even when many around us turn aside. We can ask him for help to stay firm in the small things of each day, trusting that he sees and cares for his own.
exp.31:18:
The explanation says that Egypt, which thought itself so beautiful and superior to the other nations, will fall just like all of them. The phrase "Whom dost thou pass in beauty?" is ironic: it mocks their pride. "Go down, and be thou laid with the uncircumcised" means that Egypt will be placed among the dead of the pagan nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around 585 B.C., as the text indicates in its dating. It is a lament, that is, a funeral song, over Pharaoh and his multitude. God announces judgment on them for their arrogance. For an Egyptian, being counted among the uncircumcised and among those slain by the sword was a great humiliation. The details about the grave, the realm of the dead, are understood in several ways, and many see them as poetic language.

For today: beauty, power, or success do not protect us from God's judgment. Ask him to give you humility, and trust in his grace, not in your achievements.
exp.47:5:
This verse says that, alongside the territory of Ephraim, another strip of land was set aside for the tribe of Reuben. Each portion stretches from east to west, "from the east side even unto the west side," that is, all the way to the Mediterranean Sea. "Border" means a boundary or edge, and "portion" is the share assigned.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile in Babylon. In this final vision, it describes how the land would be divided among the tribes, with even strips and the sanctuary at the center. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal promise, others as a symbolic picture of God's restoration.

For today: God cares that each person has their place, and that He is at the center. We can ask ourselves whether, in our lives, our families, and our church, we are giving God that central place.
exp.24:6:
God says he will stretch out his hand against Ammon to punish it. He will hand it over to other nations, who will plunder it. He will cut it off from among the peoples and wipe it off the earth. In the end, Ammon will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Ammonites rejoiced and mocked when Jerusalem and the people of Israel suffered. God takes that contempt seriously. This message is part of the oracles against neighboring nations, and it shows that God rules over all peoples.

Today we can learn not to rejoice in the pain of others, even when we have been wronged by them. God sees the heart. If someone is suffering, it is better to pray for that person, help them, and treat them with compassion and humility.
exp.21:6:
It says that in Jerusalem the people dishonored their parents, cheated or abused the foreigner, and took what belonged to the orphan and the widow. "They treated with contempt" means to hold someone in disdain; "slander" here refers to unjust and oppressive treatment; "took by force" means to steal from or take advantage of someone who is defenseless.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He is accusing Jerusalem of its sins: violence, injustice, and idolatry. The leaders and the people had forgotten the law that commanded honoring one's parents and caring for the weakest (Exodus 22:21-22). For God, this was not a minor social matter but part of faithfulness to Him.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat those who cannot defend themselves. Think of a vulnerable person near you, such as an elderly person, an immigrant, a widow, or a child without support, and help them in a concrete way this week.
exp.38:18:
God invites the birds and the wild animals to a great banquet. He says they will eat fat until they are full and drink blood until they are drunk, that is, until they are completely filled. This banquet is called "my sacrifice," but what is offered are the bodies of the fallen enemies. "Fat" means the richest part of the animal.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This follows the defeat of Gog, a powerful enemy who attacks Israel on the mountains of Israel (chapters 38 and 39). The image is very strong and symbolic: it shows that God judges evil and protects his people. Interpreters disagree about whether it will be fulfilled literally or symbolically. Revelation 19:17-18 uses a similar image.

For today: we can rest in the fact that God is just and has the final word over evil. When we see violence or injustice, let us trust in him, pray, and seek peace, without taking revenge.
exp.22:2:
They say that the two sisters, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, fell into unfaithfulness from their youth, while they were in Egypt. "Committed whoredoms" here means giving themselves to others instead of being faithful. "Youth" is their early years. The images of breasts pressed and bruised speak of abuse and of a purity lost early on.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and uses a harsh parable to show the story of Israel. There was one people, divided into two kingdoms. God reminds them that they turned away from him from their beginnings, when they mixed themselves with idolatry and Egyptian alliances. Scholars debate how much historical detail lies behind this image.

For today: it is not enough to say that we belong to God; we must look at the things to which we give our hearts. Today we can ask him to show us the things we trust in more than him, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.43:22:
It says the priests will have the task of teaching the people to distinguish between the holy, that which belongs to God, and the profane, the common or what is not fit for his service. They are also to teach people to recognize the clean and the unclean, according to the law of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 40 to 48 describe a vision of a temple and its service. Here God gives instructions to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, so that they will live with reverence and be guides for the people. Interpreters differ on whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic.

Today, as God's people, we can ask him for wisdom to discern from the Bible what draws us closer to him and what pulls us away. And those who teach or advise others should do so with humility and by their own example.
exp.38:23:
He says that God dealt with Israel according to their defilement and their rebellions. "Uncleanness" speaks of a life stained by sin, above all by idolatry. "Hid my face" means that God withdrew his favor and his protection, and left them to face the consequences of their own choices.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. God explains that the exile was not a defeat of his power, but the result of his people's sin. This verse comes just before a promise: God will bring the captives back and will have mercy on them.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not harden yourself or lose heart. Acknowledge your failure honestly and return to God. His discipline is not the final word; his desire is to restore you.
exp.17:5:
This verse describes a righteous man by what he avoids. He does not eat "over the mountains," that is, he does not take part in pagan worship meals held on the high places. He does not lift his eyes to the idols of Israel, meaning he does not give them his trust or his worship. He does not dishonor his neighbor's wife, and he does not come near a woman during her time of impurity, something the law of Moses forbade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their fathers. God answers that each person answers for himself, and he shows what a righteous life looks like: faithful to God and respectful toward others.

For today: examine where you place your trust and your worship. Ask God to be first in your life, and guard your faithfulness in your relationships.
exp.20:23:
It says that God, the Lord, speaks to Jerusalem. They have made their wickedness be remembered, since their betrayals and sins were revealed in everything they did. Therefore they will be taken by the hand, that is, captured by force. "Betrayals" here refers to rebellions or acts of unfaithfulness against God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Babylon uses divination to decide whether to attack Jerusalem, and the people do not believe it, because they trust in their alliances. But God uses that attack to judge the people's wickedness. The verses that follow announce that the king of Israel will lose his crown.

For today: we cannot hide sin as if God did not see it. It is better to acknowledge it sincerely and ask Him for forgiveness before it brings harsher consequences. God is just, but He also forgives those who turn back to Him.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that God will put an end to the false visions and divinations of certain women who were prophesying lies. "Vanity" means something empty, without worth or truth. "You shall divine divinations" means continuing to practice that false divination. God promises to rescue his people from their hands, and that by this they will know that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He confronts false prophetesses who deceived the people: they discouraged the righteous with lies and encouraged the wicked to continue in their evil ways. The "veils" mentioned earlier are a difficult term; some believe they were bands or cloths used in their practices, although their exact meaning is uncertain.

For today: do not follow someone who tells you only what you want to hear. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and trust that God defends those who are being deceived.
exp.46:16:
This passage sets out the northern boundary of the land that God promises to his people. It begins at the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, passes Hazar-enan, and follows the border of Damascus and Hamath. "Border" means a boundary or limit. The words "the north northward" simply repeat that this is the line on the north side.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of restoration after the exile. God shows how the land will be divided among the tribes. Scholars do not agree on the exact location of some of these places, nor on whether this vision is to be fulfilled literally or spiritually.

For today: God is a God of order and concrete promises. He cares for the details of our lives and keeps what he says. We can trust that he has a place and a purpose for each of us.
exp.16:22:
God says he will plant a tender shoot on the high mountain of Israel. That young branch will grow, put out boughs, bear fruit, and become a magnificent cedar. Birds of every kind will make their home in its shade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, he told a parable about kings and an eagle, and he announced judgment on Judah. Now he offers hope: God himself will raise up something new. Many Christians see here a prophecy of the Messiah, Jesus, and his kingdom that gives shelter to all peoples. Others see it first as a promise of restoration for Israel. Both readings have been held.

When everything seems lost, God can begin something small and make it grow. Trust him, even if today you see only a weak shoot in your life or your family.
exp.28:8:
God says that Egypt will be left desolate and empty. The word for "desolate" here means destroyed, left in ruins. In this way Egypt will know that the Lord is God, because its king used to say, "The river is mine, and I have made it," as if all his power and wealth came from himself alone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing while the people of Judah were exiles in Babylon. Egypt had been to Israel like a fragile reed: when they leaned on it, it broke and wounded them. God judges Egypt for its pride and for the false security it offered. The Nile River was the source of its strength.

Today we can ask ourselves what we lean on. Everything good we have, such as our work, our health, and our accomplishments, comes from God. Living grateful and humble, trusting him and not our own strength, frees us from pride and from leaning on reeds that break.
exp.30:7:
It says that no tree in the garden of God could be compared to this huge tree. The cedars could not hide it, and neither the fir trees nor the chestnut trees had branches like its branches. Some words in the explanation are old-fashioned, and this has been kept in mind for the English version: the names of trees in the original are debated in their exact translation, so the verse above uses the names as they appear. The tree was incomparable in its beauty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the pharaoh of Egypt. He uses the image of a magnificent tree, and the text compares it to Assyria. God shows that all greatness comes from Him, and that pride brings a fall, as the passage goes on to show.

For today: if you have talents, success, or influence, remember that they are a gift from God. Use them to bless others, like that tree that gave shade and shelter, and not to boast. Humility keeps you steady.
exp.31:30:
Ezekiel 32:31 tells us that when Pharaoh arrives in the place of the dead, he will see the other nations that have already fallen, just as he has. Pharaoh will be comforted in the sense that he will find some relief in seeing that he is not the only one. "Slain by the sword" means killed in war. The verse stresses that Pharaoh and all his army will also die in this way.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against Egypt. The whole chapter describes Egypt going down to the grave together with Assyria, Elam, Edom, and Sidon, powerful nations that spread terror. Many read it as a message of judgment against Egypt's pride. Pharaoh's "comfort" is ironic: it is not true hope, only the company of others in ruin.

No power, success, or human fame protects us from God's judgment. Today we can examine where we place our trust: in our own strength or in God? Let us live with humility, using what we have to serve and not to dominate.
exp.25:2:
God says to Tyre, a great trading city by the sea, that he is against her. He announces that he will bring many nations against her, one after another, like the waves of the sea that rise and rise without stopping. Here "nations" means nations or peoples.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the eleventh year of the exile. Tyre had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking she would now have more business, since Jerusalem was a gateway for the nations. God answers that mockery and that greed. Scholars often connect the fulfillment with Babylon and, later, with other armies, although there is debate about how each detail came about.

For today: let us not rejoice in the misfortune of others or seek to gain at the expense of someone else's pain. God sees the heart and calls us to compassion, not pride.
exp.15:34:
This verse is a call to attention. God tells Jerusalem, whom he calls "harlot," to hear his word. The phrase "hear the word of the Lord" marks the point where God moves from describing the fault to announcing the consequences.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout this chapter he presents Jerusalem as a woman whom he cared for and blessed, but who was unfaithful to him. Sexual unfaithfulness is an image of idolatry and of alliances with other nations. God confronts her firmly, because she paid her lovers instead of being faithful to him.

For today: when God corrects us, it is good to listen with humility and not harden our hearts. His correction seeks to bring us back to him, who loves us and waits for our return.
exp.43:1:
God tells Ezekiel that the east gate of the sanctuary must remain shut. No one will be able to open it or pass through it, because the Lord, the God of Israel, entered by that gate. "Then said the Lord unto me" is the opening of the message, and "no man" here means any person at all.

The Lord speaks in a vision of the temple that Ezekiel receives during the exile. In chapter 43 the glory of God returned to the temple through that east gate. The gate remains closed as a sign that the place through which God entered is holy. The text goes on to mention the prince, who will be allowed to eat there before God. Interpreters explain this vision in several ways, and not all of them agree.

For today: let us value what God has set apart. Let us draw near to Him with reverence, remembering that His presence is a holy gift and not something ordinary.
exp.36:2:
God asks Ezekiel whether these dry bones can live again. "Son of man" is a way of addressing the prophet, reminding him that he is simply a human being. Ezekiel does not say yes or no; he answers that only God knows.

God speaks, and Ezekiel responds. The prophet was among the people of Israel exiled in Babylon, and the vision represents a nation that felt its hope was dead. Many interpreters see here a promise of restoration for Israel. Afterward God commands him to prophesy to the bones and promises to give them breath and life.

There are situations that seem finished, such as a broken relationship, a faith that has gone out, or a lost dream. We can imitate Ezekiel's response: not pretending that everything is fine, nor giving up, but humbly saying to God, "You know." Handing over what seems dead opens space for his work.
exp.29:4:
God announces that the fall of Egypt will drag down its allies as well: Ethiopia, Libya, Lydia, the mixed peoples who served it, Chub, and the inhabitants of the land of the alliance, that is, the league. The phrase "by the sword" is the sense of the verse's final words. Some of these places cannot be located with certainty, and "the land that is in league" is interpreted in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at the time of the fall of Jerusalem. Egypt seemed a secure power, and Judah trusted in its help. God warns that this support would fail, because He governs all nations and their alliances.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, connections, or power. All of that can fail. Trust first in God, who sustains your life when everything else collapses.
exp.11:14:
This verse says that God will make the people come to know who he is. This will happen when he scatters them among the nations and spreads them out across different countries. The word "scatter" means to throw or spread out in every direction. Here "spread" means to distribute across the land. The "nations" are the peoples and foreign lands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The message announces judgment on Jerusalem and its king, who would be captured and taken to Babylon. Many understand this to refer to King Zedekiah. The people had lived in rebellion, and God warns that the punishment would make them recognize that he is the Lord. God leaves some survivors so that they can tell what happened.

For today: sometimes we only recognize God when our plans fall apart. We do not need to wait for that moment. We can listen to him today, correct our course with humility, and trust that his discipline seeks to bring us close to him.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that the next morning, God spoke to Ezekiel again. "And in the morning came the word of the Lord unto me" means that God's message came to him. The phrase "in the morning" marks that the night had already passed in which the prophet went out carrying his belongings on his shoulder.

God speaks, and He speaks to Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God had asked him to represent with his own body the flight from Jerusalem, as a sign before a rebellious people. Now God is going to explain the meaning of what he did, since the people were asking him what he was doing.

For today: God does not leave His actions unexplained. If we do not understand something He asks of us, we can come to His Word with patience and listen. Often the light comes "in the morning," after we have obeyed in the dark.
exp.46:9:
When the river's water reaches the sea, there will be fishers along its shore. From En-gedi to En-eglaim the nets will be spread out to dry, and there will be fish of many kinds, as many as in the great sea. The phrase about the net-drying place refers to a spot where the nets are laid out to dry.

An angel guides Ezekiel through a vision of the new temple. From it flows a river that runs eastward toward the Dead Sea, whose waters are salty and lifeless. En-gedi lies on its western shore; the location of En-eglaim is not certain. Many see in this an image of the restoration and life that God gives; others also expect a literal fulfillment in the future.

For today: where God acts, He can bring life to what seemed dead. Bring Him that dry area of your life, your family or your work, and trust that He can renew it with patience and hope.
exp.32:24:
God asks this with irony: how do they expect to keep the land if they eat meat with the blood, worship idols, and shed innocent blood? The phrase "to lift up their eyes to the idols" means to place their trust and desire in them. The question makes clear that the answer is no.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to those who remained among the ruins of Israel after the fall of Jerusalem. They boasted: "Abraham was only one man and he received the land; we are many, so the land is even more rightly ours." God answers them that the land is not secured by numbers, but by living faithfully to Him.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we expect God's blessings while living as we please. His grace invites us to return to Him with sincerity, not to rely on our privileges or inheritance.
exp.36:11:
What it says: God commands Ezekiel to announce a message to his people. God promises to open their graves, to make them come up out of their tombs, and to bring them back to the land of Israel.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Israelites were exiled in Babylon and felt that their nation was dead, like dry bones. Many understand the image to speak of the people's restoration to their land. Some Christians also see in it a sign of the future resurrection, although the text is addressed first to Israel.

For today: When you feel that your hope has dried up, remember that God can give life where there seems to be no way out. Bring Him your weariness honestly and trust His promise.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that the leaders of Israel, the princes, used their power, each one according to his ability and position, to kill and shed innocent blood in Jerusalem. "To their power" means that each one was abusing the strength he had.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He accuses Jerusalem, called a city that sheds blood, of its crimes, its idolatry, and its injustice. The verses that follow show that they mistreated the fathers, the foreigners, the orphans, and the widows. God especially condemns the leaders, who were supposed to protect the people.

For today: if you have any authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it to care for the weak and not to take advantage of them. Ask God to give you a just and humble heart.
exp.12:7:
God says that the prophets of Israel spoke empty things and saw false visions. Empty things means something hollow, without worth or truth. Because they claimed their messages came from God when He had not sent them, God declares: I am against you. It is a firm and direct warning.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. There were false prophets who made up visions and promised peace when there was no peace. In this way they gave false hope, and the people did not turn back. God defends the truth of His word and protects His people from deception.

Today we can examine carefully what we hear in God's name and compare it with the Bible. Also, if we speak of God to others, let us do so with humility and honesty, without saying "God told me" just to give weight to our own ideas.
exp.30:10:
It says that God will hand this great tree over to a mighty one from among the nations. "The mighty one of the heathen" is a foreign king, and the phrase "he shall surely deal with him" means he will treat it as he pleases. God states that he drove it out for its wickedness.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He compares Assyria, or according to others the pharaoh of Egypt, to a very tall and beautiful cedar. It grew proud, and for that reason God brings it low. Scholars disagree about exactly who is meant, but the message is clear: no human power is safe from the judgment of God.

Everything we have, whether beauty, talent, or success, comes from God. If we fill ourselves with pride, we move away from Him. Today we can thank Him with humility for what we have received.
exp.31:2:
It says that God himself will catch the pharaoh of Egypt the way one catches a large animal in the water. The net and the throw-net (a round fishing net thrown by hand) show that he will not be able to escape. God will use many peoples, that is, gathered nations, to drag him up onto the shore.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is to sing a funeral song of lament over the pharaoh. The pharaoh was like a monster that stirred up the waters, and his pride and power harmed others. God announces that his fall will come.

For today: No one is so powerful that God cannot humble him. We can trust that He sees injustice, and we can also examine our own pride before He has to break it.
exp.47:6:
It says that the tribe of Judah receives a strip of land next to that of Reuben. That strip runs from east to west, from the east side to the Mediterranean Sea. The sea is the Mediterranean, and the border is the boundary line.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of the future division of the land, after the exile in Babylon. The tribes appear in parallel strips. Judah lies right beside the holy portion, where the sanctuary will be. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some see it as a literal promise, others as a symbolic picture of restoration and of God's presence.

For today: God cares that each one has their place. We can live with confidence, knowing we have a place among his people, and seek to have God at the center of our lives.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "The word of the Lord came unto me again" is an older way of saying that a message from God came to him. It is an opening phrase that announces that what follows is not the prophet's own ideas, but what God wants to say.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile in Babylon with other Israelites. Many of them believed they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors and not because of their own choices. God gives Ezekiel a message to correct that way of thinking, and in the verses that follow he does so with a popular proverb.

For today: before listening to God, it helps to stop blaming others for our situation. His word invites us to look honestly at our own lives, and to receive his correction with humility and hope.
exp.24:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to turn his face squarely toward the Ammonites, a people neighboring Israel, and to deliver a message from God concerning them. "Son of man" is how God addresses Ezekiel, and it simply means a human being. Setting one's face toward someone means facing them with firm resolve. To prophesy is to speak what God says.

The LORD speaks. Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. The Ammonites had rejoiced when the temple was defiled and Judah was taken captive. For this reason God, who cares for his people, announces judgment against them. This is the beginning of a series of messages against neighboring nations.

For today: rejoicing in another's pain displeases God. When someone suffers, even someone with whom we have differences, God calls us to compassion and not to mockery.
exp.28:3:
God says he will put hooks in the jaws of Pharaoh, as if he were a great monster of the river. The fish of the Nile will stick to his scales, and God will bring him up out of the water with all of them. "Stick" here means to cling fast, and the reed staff is a weak stick that breaks when leaned on.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Pharaoh, compared to a dragon or crocodile, boasted that the river was his and that he himself had made it. Egypt was a great power, but it proved a fragile support for Israel, and God judges it for its pride.

For today: everything we have, such as strength, work, or success, is a gift from God. When we believe we made it all ourselves, we become proud. Today you can give thanks to God and trust in Him, not in your own resources.
exp.27:14:
It says that this figure was created perfect, without fault in his conduct, until wickedness appeared in him. "Created" means made by God. The verse says that wickedness was found in him, meaning it came to light in him. The words do not say that God made the evil, but that the evil arose afterward.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against the king of Tyre, a proud ruler. The language uses images of Eden and of a cherub, and for this reason some believe it also alludes to Satan, while others see it only as a poetic portrait of the king. Christians interpret it in both ways.

For today: what God gives us, such as talents, success, or beauty, can become pride if we are not humble. Let us ask him for a grateful and watchful heart.
exp.32:6:
God tells Ezekiel that he has set him as a watchman, that is, a lookout who keeps guard from a tower and gives warning when danger approaches. Ezekiel must listen to what God says and warn the people, that is, give them a warning on God's behalf.

God speaks to Ezekiel and addresses him as "son of man." The people of Israel were in exile in Babylon. God gives Ezekiel the responsibility of giving warning, but not of forcing anyone: each person answers for what they decide to do with the warning.

For today: if God places us near someone who is turning away from Him, we can speak to them with love, truth and humility. We do not have to force anyone or judge them, but we are called to be faithful in saying what God shows us, and to entrust the outcome to Him.
exp.37:8:
God describes Gog, the leader of a great coalition of nations, advancing against Israel. He says he will come up like a storm and like a cloud that covers the land, with all his troops and many allied peoples. The image shows a huge, noisy, threatening force.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel appears restored and living in security, and God announces that someone will come to attack it. Scholars interpret this in different ways: as a historical event, as a future event, or as a symbol of the final opposition against God's people. There is no full agreement about who Gog is.

For today: even when evil seems like a huge storm, God still reigns and knows every step. We can rest in Him without ignoring the dangers, and pray with confidence when everything seems to darken.
exp.35:26:
God promises to put his Spirit within his people. With that Spirit, they will walk according to his commandments, keep his judgments, and put them into practice, that is, they will truly obey them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon, who had failed to obey him. He promises to restore them, cleanse them, and give them a new heart. This obedience would not come from their own effort, but from God's work in them. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of the work of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament, though it can be debated how this relates exactly to Israel.

For today: do not rely only on your own willpower. Ask God to change you from the inside through his Spirit, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting in his help.
exp.45:5:
This verse says that on the new moon (the first day of each month), the prince was to offer to God a young bull from the herd, six lambs, and a ram. All of them were to be "without blemish," meaning healthy animals with no flaw at all.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of a temple and of a renewed worship. There, rules are given for the prince, who would lead the people in worship. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic, and there is no complete agreement.

For today: God deserves our best, not what is left over. We can give Him the first of our time, affection, and resources, with a sincere heart.
exp.20:22:
The inhabitants of Jerusalem will think that the king of Babylon's divination is false, because they believe they are protected by their oaths and alliances. But "he" reminds them of their wickedness so that they may be taken. The word "taken" means seized or caught. Some think that "he" is the king of Babylon, others that it is God; the following verse points more toward God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Babylon is drawing near to Jerusalem, and God even uses the king's pagan practice to carry out his judgment. The people trusted in human agreements and did not repent. Some believe this refers to the oath of loyalty that Zedekiah made to Babylon and broke.

For today: do not rest on your human securities or on what others promise. Instead, examine your heart honestly and return to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.17:9:
This verse begins a second example. Earlier, a righteous man who lives well was described. Now it says: if that man has a son who is a robber, a shedder of blood (that is, a murderer), or who does any of the wicked things that follow, that son will be judged for his own actions.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were repeating a saying: "the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." With it they claimed they were suffering for their parents' sins. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life.

For today: do not use your family past as an excuse, and do not lean on your parents' faith. Today you can choose to obey God, and He receives you with mercy.
exp.39:10:
This verse continues the measurement of the east gate of the temple. The man measures the width of the entrance, which is ten cubits, and the length of the gateway, which is thirteen cubits. A cubit is an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The gateway is the passage or building at the entrance.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision he received. A guide, who looks like a man, takes him to a new temple and measures each part in great detail. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol, or as a promise of restoration. For a discouraged people, it showed that God was still putting everything in order and wanted to dwell among them.

For today: God cares about order and care. We can draw near to Him with reverence and confidence, and trust that He has a plan, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.31:14:
He says that God will leave Egypt desolate. When God strikes all who live there, they will know that He is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. This word is part of a lament against Pharaoh and Egypt, a proud nation that felt secure. The verses before it use images of waters and rivers, and the text does not make clear every detail of how it would be fulfilled.

For today: nothing we have, not money, strength, or reputation, is a secure foundation for life. It is wise to trust God and not in what can be lost. Today you can hand Him your sense of security and ask Him for humility.
exp.22:14:
He says that the men Oholah saw painted on the wall wore belts of leather around their waists and colorful turbans on their heads. All of them looked like military leaders, dressed like the Babylonians, born in the land of the Chaldeans. "Belts" are straps worn at the waist, and "turbans" are tall caps or headpieces.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells a parable about two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. Here the focus is on Oholibah (Jerusalem), who let herself be impressed by the power and appearance of Babylon instead of trusting God. God uses very strong language to show how painful the unfaithfulness of his people is.

For today: be careful about what dazzles us. Power, image, and success can attract us more than God does. Before you admire something, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to him or pulls you away.
exp.19:21:
God says that he held back his punishment. "I withdrew my hand" means that he pulled back his hand of judgment and did not destroy them. He did this for the honor of his name, so that it would not be dishonored, that is, disgraced or despised, before the nations who saw how he brought them out of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. He reminds the leaders of Israel that their rebellion goes back a long way, all the way to the wilderness. Even so, God did not finish them off, because his reputation was tied to his people. The verses that follow show that discipline came anyway, later on.

For today: our hope does not rest on how good we are, but on God's faithfulness to his own name. His patience with you is not permission to keep doing the same things, but an invitation to return to him and to live in a way that honors him before those who watch you.
exp.36:8:
God tells Ezekiel to prophesy to the "wind", that is, the breath or wind of life. He is to call to it from the four corners of the earth so that it blows on the dead and they live. The explanation of the word itself has been removed, as the verse uses "breath" and "wind" directly.

God speaks, and Ezekiel is his prophet. The people of Israel were in exile, without temple or land, and felt that everything had ended. The dry bones are an image of that despair. The verses that follow explain that they represent the house of Israel, and the vision announces that God will restore them.

For today: when you feel that something in your life is dry or beyond repair, do not stop praying and trusting in God's Word. Only he can give new life, and he invites us to take part by speaking with faith and hope.
exp.42:17:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," and tells him that he is going to give the rules for the altar of the new temple. He speaks of the time when the altar is finished: there the burnt offering will be made, a sacrifice burned completely for God, and blood will be sprinkled on it. "Ordinances" means instructions or rules.

God speaks in a vision that Ezekiel receives of the temple, after the people had been taken into exile. Before the altar is used, God asks that it be set apart and purified. Interpreters differ: some see a real temple that was expected to be rebuilt, others see a symbol of God's presence, and others see a future promise.

For today: before serving God, it is good for us to draw near with reverence and humility. We can begin the day by asking him for forgiveness and cleansing, remembering that Christ opens the way for us to God.
exp.32:27:
God says that he will turn the land into a desolate and empty place. What gave the people pride, their strength and their power, will come to an end. The mountains of Israel will be left in ruins, so badly that no one will want to pass through them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to those who remained in the land of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. They assumed the land belonged to them, even though they continued in violence, idolatry, and immorality. God shows them that they cannot claim his blessing while living in injustice. His judgment aims to make them recognize who he is.

Today, we can examine what we take pride in or feel secure about. If we trust in what we have and do not obey God, that security is false. Today is a good day to return to him with humility.
exp.33:14:
God promises that he himself will care for his people, like a shepherd who feeds his sheep. To "feed" them means to lead them to eat and to look after them. The place where the sheep rest and feel safe is where God says he will cause them to lie down. So God says: I will feed them, and I will give them a place to rest.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The shepherds of Israel, that is, its leaders, had neglected and mistreated the people, and the sheep were scattered. For this reason God decides to act himself, to gather them and bring them back to their land.

For today: when you feel tired, lost, or without direction, remember that God does not leave you alone. Turn to him in prayer and seek his rest, trusting that he himself cares for you and guides you.
exp.22:48:
God says that the consequences of their wickedness will fall on Oholah and Oholibah. Here "lewdness" means their dirty and immoral conduct, especially their unfaithfulness. "You shall bear the sins of your idols" means they will carry the punishment for having worshiped other gods. The final result is that they will know who the Lord is.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Oholah and Oholibah are two symbolic women who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. With this harsh image, God accuses his people of being unfaithful to him by seeking foreign alliances and gods. The chapter shows the judgment on that betrayal. Scholars agree that this is symbolic language, though they debate some details.

Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking God's place in our hearts. Recognizing them with humility and returning to him in time is better than learning through the consequences.
exp.20:19:
God tells Ezekiel to mark out on the ground a road along which the sword of Babylon will come: one branch toward Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and another toward Judah, to attack Jerusalem, the city with strong walls. The word "marcarás," meaning "you will mark out," is the key action here, as Ezekiel is to draw the route clearly.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. With this action, like a drawn map, he announces that the Babylonian king would advance and that Jerusalem would not escape judgment for its sin. The king seeks guidance through divination, but the Bible shows that God directs events.
