For today: although we may sometimes feel secure in what seems strong, only God is our true refuge. We can examine what we trust in and return to him with humility.
exp.41:8:
This verse describes an entrance located below the chambers, on the east side. Through it one passed from the outer court into those rooms. The "chambers" are rooms or halls of the temple, and the "court" is the open yard that surrounded the buildings.

In a vision, God shows Ezekiel a temple with very exact measurements. A guide measures everything for him. According to the chapter, these chambers were for the priests, where they ate the holy offerings and kept their garments. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we draw near to Him. There is a way and an order for entering His presence. Today we can approach Him with reverence and gratitude, trusting that Christ has opened the door for us.
exp.18:8:
They caught this young lion, put him in a cage with chains, and brought him before the king of Babylon. They shut him up in strongholds, that is, in well-guarded places, so that his roar would no longer be heard on the mountains of Israel.

God speaks through Ezekiel and composes a lament about the princes of Israel, using the image of lions. Many understand that it refers to kings of Judah taken captive, such as Jehoahaz, who was taken to Egypt, or Jehoiachin, who was taken to Babylon. Interpreters do not fully agree on which king is described here. The central message is that the pride and violence of the rulers ended in downfall.

For today: power and fame are not secure forever. If you have authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it with humility and justice, and remember that you answer to God.
exp.26:13:
This verse says that the people of Togarmah brought horses, riders, and mules to the market of Tyre to sell them. "Riders" here means men who ride on horseback. The phrase "traded in thy fairs" means that they did business there, handing over their goods in exchange for other goods.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a city made rich by sea trade. The list of nations and products shows how great and prosperous it was. Togarmah was probably in the region of Anatolia, north of Israel, though its exact location is debated. The purpose of the list is to show Tyre's pride before announcing its fall.

For today: wealth and success are not wrong in themselves, but they can make us proud. Thank God for what you have and use it with humility and generosity, remembering that everything comes from Him.
exp.29:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man", that is, a simple human being. He is told to deliver a message: the people must wail, that is, cry out and weep loudly, because a terrible day is coming. "Woe worth the day!" expresses pain and dread at what is approaching.

The Lord is speaking, and the message is directed against Egypt, as the following verses make clear. Ezekiel prophesied during the exile, and this judgment speaks of the sword, fear, and the fall of a powerful nation. Scholars disagree about the exact date of its fulfillment, but the theme is clear: God rules over all nations.

For today: let us not trust in power, money, or fame, for none of these protects us before God. Let us be humble, live with justice, and trust in Him, who offers us mercy while there is still time.
exp.18:6:
This young lion, who represents a king of Judah, became violent. "Destroyed" is the sense of the word, and his roaring is what the text calls the sound of his voice. The phrase about knowing their widows is difficult: some understand that he left many women widowed, while other versions read that he tore down their strongholds. His roar filled the land with terror.

Ezekiel sings this lament over the princes of Israel, using the image of a lioness and her cubs. He is in exile, and he explains why the dynasty of David fell. It is not certain which king this is: many think of Jehoiachin, and others of Zedekiah. What is clear is that he ended up a prisoner in Babylon.

For today: power without justice ends up destroying others and oneself. If you have authority, at home, at work, or in the church, ask God to use it to care for people and not to crush them.
exp.40:2:
He says that the guide of the vision went into the innermost part of the temple, the most holy place, and measured the entrance. The side pieces of the doorway are the frames on each side of the door, and each one measured two cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The door was six cubits, and the opening seven.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, is in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide who looked like a man shows him a new temple and gives him its measurements. This encouraged a discouraged people, because God still intended to dwell among them. Interpreters disagree: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual symbol.

For today: God is orderly and cares about the details of his presence. Draw near to him with respect and reverence, knowing that Christ opened the way to God.
exp.19:48:
Here Ezekiel speaks with God and complains. He says "Ah, Lord GOD!" like someone sighing in worry. He tells that the people mock him and say: "Doth he not speak parables?", that is, with stories and figurative language that are not understood or not taken seriously.

God has just given him a message about a fire that would burn a forest, an image that probably refers to the judgment on Judah and the land of the south. Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, fears that the people will not take him seriously and will dismiss him as a storyteller. In the Hebrew text of the Bible this verse is 21:5, and that is where the clarification in the next chapter comes from.

For today: when people reject or ridicule the truth you share, bring it to God honestly, as Ezekiel did, and stay faithful without depending on their approval.
exp.42:14:
This verse describes the highest part of the altar: a section four cubits high, and on top of it four horns that projected from the corners. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, and here it is the "long cubit," that is, an ordinary cubit plus a handbreadth (the width of the hand).

Ezekiel recounts a vision of a new temple, and a heavenly guide gives him its measurements. This takes place after the exile, when the people had lost the temple. The horns of the altar were a symbol of refuge and atonement. Scholars interpret the temple in various ways: some see it as something literal and future, others as a symbol of God's presence.

For today: God cares about the details of worship and wants us to draw near to Him with reverence. Today we can come with confidence to Christ, our refuge and perfect sacrifice.
exp.37:17:
This verse says that when Gog comes to attack the land of Israel, God will be filled with anger. The phrase about his anger rising up in his face is an old way of saying that his wrath will flare up with great force.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog is a leader who comes with many nations against the people of Israel. God says he allows this attack so that the nations will acknowledge him as holy. Interpreters differ: some see it as a historical event, others as something still to come, and others as a symbol of evil that rises up against God.

For today: we can trust that God is not indifferent to injustice or to those who harm his people. When evil seems strong, we can rest in the knowledge that God has the final word.
exp.32:19:
Here God quotes what the people were saying: "The way of the Lord is not equal," that is, "God's manner of acting is not just." God answers that he will judge each person according to their own ways. The word for "way" means path or manner of conduct, and "judge" here speaks of dealing with each person according to what they have done.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The Israelites accused God of being unjust, because it seemed to them that he was not treating them well. God shows them that he always offers the chance to turn back to him: the wicked can repent and live, and the righteous must persevere. Shortly afterward comes the news that Jerusalem had fallen.

For today: instead of blaming God for what happens to us, we can examine our own path. If we have failed, we can today turn back to him with confidence, for his mercy awaits us.
exp.40:8:
It says that the outer wall of the side chambers of the temple was five cubits thick (roughly two and a half meters). It also mentions an open space left over, that is, a free area between those chambers and other parts of the temple. A cubit was an ancient measure, the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers.

The speaker is the prophet Ezekiel, who recounts what he saw in a vision. A guide showed him a new temple, measuring it carefully. Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell with his people. Interpreters differ on whether it describes a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: God cares about details and values order and boundaries. Just as the temple had well-defined spaces, we can leave room in our lives for his presence.
exp.17:15:
This verse describes a righteous man: he does not oppress anyone, he does not keep the pledge that someone gave him as security for a loan, he does not rob, he gives bread to the hungry and clothes the one who has no clothing. The word "oppress" means to mistreat or abuse; here "withholding the pledge" speaks of unjustly keeping an item that was given as security.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. They were saying that they suffered for the sins of their fathers. God answers that each person is accountable for his or her own choices. The son who sees the wrongdoing of his father and decides not to imitate it will live. This verse is part of a list of behaviors that show a life faithful to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we can help with something concrete: food, clothing, or fair treatment. And if we come from a family with bad examples, God invites us to choose a different path.
exp.27:15:
The explanation says that the king God is speaking to was filled with wickedness and sinned because of his great trade. For that reason God cast him out of the holy mountain and drove him from among the stones of fire. "Trade" means commerce or business. "Covering cherub" describes a being of high rank who protected or guarded the presence of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the king of Tyre, a city rich from its commerce. Many believe the language also alludes to Satan; others think it is simply a poetic image of the king's pride. Christians have understood it in both ways.

For today: riches and success can make us proud and dishonest. Today, ask God whether there is some business, profit, or achievement that is occupying the place that belongs to Him alone.
exp.22:4:
Aholah, who represents Samaria, was unfaithful to God while she still belonged to him. "Fornication" here does not refer only to sexual sin, but to abandoning God to give herself to others. "Was infatuated" means she fell in love passionately. The Assyrians were the powerful neighboring nation, and she sought security and attraction in them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, to show that his people sought political alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting him. It is strong language, meant to shake consciences and reveal the pain of a faithful God before betrayal.

For today: examine the things in which you seek security or worth outside of God, such as money, the approval of others, or success. Return to trusting him first.
exp.30:11:
It says a huge and proud tree will be brought down. Foreigners, "the terrible of the nations," that is, the most powerful and cruel nations, will cut it down and leave it lying there. Its branches will fall on mountains, in valleys, and by all the rivers of the land. The peoples who used to rest in its shadow will leave and abandon it.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, and directs this message to the pharaoh of Egypt. He compares him to a very tall tree, like Assyria. God judges him because his heart was filled with pride. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment.

For today: power, success, and fame are neither secure nor eternal. If I start to trust in what I have and look down on others, it is wise to remember that God opposes the proud. We can ask him for a humble heart and use our influence to serve.
exp.39:11:
The explanation says that in front of the side rooms of the gate there was a small space, a border or barrier, one cubit on each side. And each room measured six cubits by six, that is, it was square. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about half a meter. The side rooms were small guard rooms beside the entrance.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he had during the exile, in which a man with a measuring reed showed him a new temple. This guide measures the east gate with care. Scholars disagree about whether this temple should be taken literally, symbolically, or as something yet to come.

For today: God cares about details and order. If He measures His house with such care, we can trust that nothing in our lives escapes His notice. Today, put a small area of your life in order with attention and faithfulness.
exp.46:11:
It says that on both banks of the river there will grow all kinds of trees that give food. Their leaves will not wither or fall, and their fruit will never run out. They will bear new fruit every month, because the water that feeds them comes from the sanctuary, that is, from the temple. The fruit will serve as food and the leaves as medicine. The phrase "according to his months" means "every month."

God shows the prophet Ezekiel a vision of a river that flows out of the temple and brings life wherever it goes. The people of Israel, who were in exile and needed hope of restoration, receive this. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it as a promise for Israel, others as a spiritual symbol. Revelation 22:2 uses a similar image.

Today we can remember that life and healing come from the presence of God. Set aside time each day for prayer and for the Bible, and ask him to fill you so that you can be food and comfort for others.
exp.30:3:
It says that a great cedar grew very tall thanks to the abundant waters. The deep waters beneath the earth, which fed it, are what the verse calls "the deep." Its channels, which ran around its base, and its streams carried water to all the other trees of the field. In this way, the tree grew and also gave life to others.

God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to speak to the pharaoh of Egypt. To warn him about his pride, He compares Egypt with Assyria, described as an enormous cedar that fell. Some scholars debate the details of this comparison, but the message is clear: no great nation is safe if it exalts itself.

For today: everything we have, our talents, success, or influence, comes from the hand of God. If we receive it with humility, we can bless others instead of becoming proud.
exp.17:30:
God tells the people to cast away all the wrongs they have committed, the ones by which they rebelled against Him. He asks them to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit, that is, a life renewed from the inside. And he ends with a painful question: why will you die, house of Israel?

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Some of the people, in exile, were saying that the way of the Lord was not fair, meaning that God was unjust. He answers that each person will answer for their own actions, and he invites them to turn back to Him. At the end he makes clear that he does not desire the death of anyone.

For today: if there is something in your life that pulls you away from God, do not hide it or excuse it. Acknowledge it, leave it behind, and ask God to renew your heart. He offers this because He wants you to live.
exp.19:26:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak to the people of Israel. The message is that their ancestors dishonored him, that is, they offended and disrespected him by rebelling against him. The phrase "even in this" shows that, beyond what has already been said, there was one more failure: following their own ways instead of God's.

Here God himself speaks, through Ezekiel, to the exiles in Babylon. He reviews their history to show them that their rebellion goes back a long way. The verses just before this one are difficult: they speak of statutes that were not good and of sacrificing children. They are interpreted in several ways; many understand that God gave them over to the consequences of their own idolatry.

For today: let us not minimize our faults or excuse them by pointing to what others did. Let us humbly acknowledge where we have turned away from God and return to him, who is always ready to forgive.
exp.20:9:
The verse speaks of a sword that has been sharpened and polished. "Polished" means burnished, made well smooth, so that it shines. Its purpose is to slaughter, that is, to kill many. The question "should we then make mirth?" sounds like an anguished question. The second part is hard to translate, and scholars interpret it in several ways. It seems to say that this sword despises or surpasses every rod or staff, perhaps even the authority of Judah, the son of God.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces that judgment will come upon his people and their rulers because of their persistent rebellion. The sword, which many connect with Babylon, is ready to act.

Today we can take God's warning seriously, without hardening our hearts. If He corrects us, let us return to Him soon with humility.
exp.17:12:
If someone lends money and charges abusive interest on it, taking advantage of a brother in need, and grows rich from it, he will not live. The "increase" in the verse is the extra gain taken above what was lent. The "abominations" are the things God detests, like those in the earlier verses: idolatry, theft, adultery, and oppressing the poor. The words "his blood shall be upon him" mean that he himself is responsible for his punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were saying that they were suffering because of their parents' sins. God answers that each person answers for his own actions. Here he describes a son who repeats the sins of a righteous father.

For today: examine whether your profits and your dealings with others, especially with the most needy, are just. Do not use other people's hardships to enrich yourself. God invites each one to live with integrity, without making excuses based on what others did.
exp.39:3:
A man whose appearance was bright, like bronze, speaks to Ezekiel. He asks him for three things: to look closely, to listen carefully, and to set his heart on what is shown to him. "Man" means a human being, and "son of man" is the way God usually addresses Ezekiel. At the end, he is told to tell everything to the house of Israel.

Ezekiel was in exile in Babylon. Around 573 BC, in a vision from God, he was taken to a high mountain in Israel. There this guide begins to measure a building, which many understand to be a temple. Scholars debate whether it is literal, symbolic, or about the future. The purpose is for Ezekiel to see and then report to a discouraged people.

When God teaches us something, a quick glance is not enough. Take time to read the Bible with attention, listen to it with humility, and keep what you have learned in your heart. Then share it with others simply.
exp.43:13:
He says that God will appoint these Levites as keepers of the house, that is, the temple. They will take charge of all its service and of everything that needs to be done there.

The phrase "keepers of the charge" means watchmen, or those in charge of the duties of guarding and work. "I will make them" is the same as "I will appoint them."

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. These Levites had ministered before the idols and caused Israel to stumble, so God removes them from the priesthood. They will not be able to come near the most holy things, but they are not left without a place: they will have lesser tasks of service. The sons of Zadok, who were faithful, will serve as priests. In this way God's justice and mercy are shown together.

God can restore someone who has failed, even though there are consequences. If we have failed, we can serve with humility wherever He opens the door for us, without bitterness.
exp.22:18:
It says that Oholibah (Jerusalem, the younger sister) did not stop, but sinned even more. The word "whoredoms" here means spiritual unfaithfulness, and "youth" refers to the days of her early years. She kept recalling her youthful days in Egypt, and those memories pushed her to keep seeking other lovers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Judah), to show how his people abandoned God and gave themselves to alliances and gods of other nations, such as Egypt and Babylon. The language is harsh because it is meant to show God's grief over betrayal and to lead the people to see their sin.

For today: let us be careful about what we bring to mind. Remembering with desire a past that drew us away from God can lead us to repeat it. Better to remember his faithfulness and return to him.
exp.15:7:
God says that he passed by Jerusalem, whom he describes as a young girl, and looked upon her when it was the time of love, that is, the age for marriage. He spread his cloak over her and covered her nakedness, a gesture of protection and of marriage commitment. He gave her his oath, and entered into a covenant with her. In the end he says: "you became mine."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile. He uses a parable: Jerusalem is an abandoned girl whom God rescues and with whom he joins himself in a covenant. He does this to remind her of his grace before rebuking her unfaithfulness, which comes later in the chapter.

For today: God loved us and cared for us when we had nothing to offer. Remembering that grace helps us live with gratitude and faithfulness, not out of obligation, but because we are loved.
exp.28:14:
This verse says that Egypt will be a lowly kingdom, smaller than the others. It will never rise again above the nations, because God himself will make it smaller. The quoted phrase about ruling is an old word meaning to dominate or give orders over others, so the sentence means God wants Egypt to no longer be able to govern the peoples. (Rewritten: the phrase means to rule over others, and God wants Egypt no longer able to hold rule over the peoples.)

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile in Babylon. Egypt had been proud and was also a false source of security for Israel, which sought its help instead of trusting God. God promises to restore Egypt after forty years, but without its former greatness. Scholars debate exactly how and when this was fulfilled.

For today: trusting in power, money or prestige is always fragile. God brings down the proud, but he also offers restoration. Today we can place our security in him and not in things that pass away.
exp.14:4:
It says that the wood of the vine is good for nothing when making anything, not even when it is whole. How much less, then, if the fire has already burned it at both ends and in the middle, will it be good for anything. The sentence that explains the old word that the verse does not use is removed here.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to a vine whose wood is useless. In the Bible, the vine represents God's people, and its value lies in bearing fruit. Jerusalem was not bearing the fruit of faithfulness, and for that reason judgment would come upon it.

For today: our worth does not lie in how we appear, but in remaining joined to God and bearing the fruit of obedience and love. We can ask ourselves with humility: in what area do I need to return to God before I harden myself further?
exp.38:24:
God announces that he will now bring back the captives of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. He will have mercy on the whole house of Israel and will guard his holy name with zeal. "Bringing back the captivity" means bringing the exiled home again and restoring their situation. Here, "being jealous" means protecting with fervent love what belongs to him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Shortly before, he explained that Israel was taken captive because of their sin and rebellion. Now he promises to restore them. God acts not only out of compassion for them, but also so that his name will be honored among the nations.

For today: although our failures have real consequences, God does not tire of offering restoration. If you have drifted away, you can return with confidence, acknowledging your mistake honestly and knowing that his mercy is greater than your past.
exp.11:18:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to "the people of the land," that is, to the Jews who were with him. The message is that the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Israel will eat their bread with fear and drink their water with dismay. Desolate means ruined and laid waste. The phrase about their multitude is understood to mean that the land will be left empty of everything in it. The cause is the wickedness, or violence, of those who live there.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Earlier, God asked him to eat with trembling as a visible sign. Through this he announced that Jerusalem would be besieged and destroyed because of its sin. The word aimed to awaken the people, who did not believe that judgment would come.

For today: let us not ignore God's warnings by thinking that everything will simply stay the same. Today we can examine our hearts, confess what is wrong, and return to Him with confidence, for His correction seeks that we know Him.
exp.15:39:
This verse says that God will bring against Jerusalem a multitude of people. They will stone her and pierce her with swords. The phrase "a company" in the verse means a crowd or assembly. These were punishments that the law of Moses applied to adulterers and murderers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter he describes Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who abandoned God for idols and alliances with other nations. These words announce judgment upon her. It is often linked to the invasion of Babylon, although interpreters explain it in different ways. At the end, the text speaks of God's anger coming to rest.

Today it reminds us that God takes faithfulness seriously. We can ask ourselves what things occupy the place that belongs to Him, and turn back to Him sincerely, trusting in His mercy.
exp.31:7:
It says that God will make all the bright lights of the sky grow dark because of the pharaoh. The lights are the sun, the moon, and the stars. He will also bring darkness over his land.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over the pharaoh of Egypt, who was thought to be powerful like a monster of the river. The darkening of the heavenly lights is poetic language: it shows that the fall of a great king shakes the whole world. Some see it only as a picture; others remember the plague of darkness in Egypt. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: no human power is above God. If something intimidates you or impresses you too much, remember that God governs even the great. Trust in Him and live with humility.
exp.40:21:
Ezekiel describes a wooden altar, three cubits high (about a meter and a half) and two cubits long. All of it, its corners, its top surface and its sides, is made of wood. A guide says to him: "This is the table that is before the Lord." Here "table" and "altar" are used as one and the same thing. Some think it recalls the table of the bread of the presence or an altar of incense; this is not entirely certain.

Context: Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple. A man shows him and measures each part. The people were wounded by the destruction of the temple, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again be near them. Interpreters disagree about whether it is a literal or a symbolic temple.

For today: God wants to be close to his people and to have fellowship with them. Set aside a moment each day to come before his table: pray, read his Word, and thank him calmly.
exp.27:22:
God says that he will send deadly disease (pestilence) upon Sidon, and violence in its streets. There will be dead people inside the city, and the sword will surround it on every side. The final result is that they will know that he is the LORD, the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Sidon was a neighboring city of Israel, and the passage mentions it among the nations that looked down on Israel. God announces judgment on it to show his holiness and his justice. Then he promises that Israel will no longer have anything that pierces and hurts them, and that it will be gathered back into its land. The passage does not say here how or exactly when the judgment on Sidon happened.

For today: God sees injustice and is not indifferent. You can trust that he cares for his people and will have the final word, so do not seek revenge; give your pain to him in prayer.
exp.25:7:
It says that the army of Babylon will kill with the sword the towns of Tyre that were on the mainland, called the city's "daughters." Then it will surround the city with siege engines (war machines), build a siege ramp or tower, and raise a shield wall to protect the attackers as they assault the walls.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a proud city, rich from trade, and it rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own profit. God announces judgment and uses Nebuchadnezzar as his instrument. Historians debate how exactly this prophecy was fulfilled: Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city for years, and other parts were fulfilled later.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success, or human defenses. Whoever rejoices in another's misfortune and trusts only in themselves falls easily. Better to live with humility and compassion, trusting in God.
exp.39:25:
The explanation says that the gate on the south side of the temple had a staircase of seven steps. In front of those steps stood a porch or entryway, which in this older translation is called "arches." On the posts of the entrance there were carved palm trees, one on each side. The "cubits" were an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of a forearm.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, recounting a vision God gave him. A guide leads him through and carefully measures the temple. The people were exiled in Babylon, and this vision showed an orderly place where God would dwell. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture.

For today: drawing near to God is not something disorderly or rushed. The steps invite us to come with respect and reverence, and the palm trees remind us that before Him there is life and joy. Today, before you pray or read the Bible, pause to calm your heart.
exp.42:15:
This verse says that the top of the altar, where the offerings were burned, measured twelve cubits long by twelve wide, that is, a perfect square. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The phrase "in the four squares thereof" simply means that all four sides were equal.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, receives in vision a new temple. God himself shows him the measurements and gives him the ordinances of the altar. The people were in exile, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell with them. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic image.

For today: God cares about order and reverence when we draw near to him. We can set aside fixed, attentive times for prayer and for his Word, without doing it in a hurried or careless way.
exp.24:11:
This verse says that God holds Edom accountable for having taken vengeance on Judah. Edom acted out of spite and hostility, and in doing so committed a serious wrong. The phrase that describes them as having greatly offended means that they sinned very grievously. The words "revenged himself upon them" show that Edom sought to get even with God's people.

The one speaking is God himself, through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and, according to the Bible, had a long-standing enmity with that people. Here God announces that he will judge the nations that rejoiced in or took advantage of Judah's fall. The verses that follow explain the punishment that would come upon Edom.

For today: let us not take vengeance into our own hands. If someone has wounded us, we can hand the matter over to God, who judges with justice, and ask him for a heart free of resentment.
exp.43:29:
This verse says that the best and first of everything the people produce belongs to the priests. The "firstfruits" are the first produce of the harvest. The "dough" refers to the first batch of flour kneaded into bread dough. If the people give this to the priest, God promises that his blessing will rest on every household.

God speaks through Ezekiel in the vision of the new temple. The Levite priests received no land as an inheritance, so they lived from the offerings. God himself was their inheritance. Interpreters understand in different ways how this vision is fulfilled.

For today: offer God the first, not what is left over. When you receive your wages or income, set aside a portion first for God and for supporting those who serve, trusting that he cares for your home.
exp.41:15:
He says that the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the east side of the temple grounds with a measuring rod. It came to five hundred rods, and the same is repeated for the other sides. A "rod" is a long measuring stick; the word for "around" in the verse simply refers to measuring all the way round.

Ezekiel recounts a vision God gave him, in which a guide carefully measures the temple and its grounds. It was a message for the people in exile. The space formed a large square, and the wall separated the holy from the common. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness, and He cares how we draw near to Him. Set aside a defined time today to pray and read His Word, and take care that what is holy does not get mixed up with the rush of everyday life.
exp.22:33:
It says that Jerusalem (Aholibah) will drink the cup of punishment to the very end, just as her sister Samaria did. The cup stands for God's judgment: she will drink all of it, and she will even break the pieces of the jar. "You will tear out your breasts" is a very strong image of pain and despair. "To mock" means to make fun of someone with contempt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter, Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two sisters who were unfaithful to God, seeking alliances and foreign gods. Judgment comes because they forgot Him and turned their backs on Him.

For today: God warns us out of love before the consequences arrive. If today we notice that we have set Him aside, we can return to Him with humility, for He forgives those who repent.
exp.43:19:
It says that the priests must not shave their heads completely, nor let their hair grow long, but must trim it with scissors to keep it short and neat. "Cutting with scissors" means cutting the hair with shears, and keeping it even is what the verse calls for by "poll their heads."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the vision of the new temple (chapters 40 to 48). There he gives rules for the priests descended from Zadok, who would serve with reverence. These rules aimed to make their appearance show order and respect for what is holy. Some understand that both the mourning customs of the pagans and carelessness were being avoided. About how this vision will be fulfilled, there are several interpretations.

For today: serving God with order and reverence, without excess or carelessness. We can ask ourselves whether our way of living and of presenting ourselves shows respect for God and cares for our witness before others.
exp.40:10:
Each side room of the temple had a door that opened onto the "space that was left," that is, an open strip around the building. There was one door toward the north and another toward the south. That open space was five cubits wide all the way around. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers.

Here the prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision he received while in exile. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple in great detail. Interpreters do not agree: some see a literal temple in the future, while others see a symbol of God's presence with his people. The measurements speak of order and care.

For today: God cares even for the small details. Leave room in your life too, orderly and open spaces to draw near to him, such as a daily time of prayer.
exp.45:23:
He says the guide shows Ezekiel the kitchens of the temple, the places where the ones who serve the house cooked the meat of the sacrifices the people brought. The guide tells Ezekiel these are the places of them that boil, where the ministers of the house shall boil the sacrifice of the people.

The one speaking is the man who, in the vision, guides Ezekiel through the future temple and explains each part to him. This vision is found in chapters 40 to 48. The verses before describe four courts in the corners, with places for cooking. How this temple should be understood is something scholars interpret in different ways: literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: God cares even about simple services, such as cooking and feeding others. What you do in everyday life, such as preparing a meal for your family or for someone in need, can be a worthy service done with love for God.
exp.28:20:
He says that God will cause the horn of Israel to bud forth again. In the Bible, the horn is a symbol of strength and power; to bud forth again means to sprout anew, like a plant coming back to life. He also promises Ezekiel that he will be given an opening of the mouth: that he will be able to speak with confidence among them. In the end, everyone will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, he announced that Egypt would be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar. This is the only message of hope in the chapter: while Egypt falls, Israel will receive renewal. Many believe that "that day" points to a future restoration of Israel, though it is not known with precision what moment is meant.

For today: when you feel your strength has dried up, remember that God can make new life spring up. Trust that he keeps his promises, and when the moment comes, speak of his faithfulness with courage.
exp.19:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the leaders of Israel. They had come to inquire of the Lord, that is, to ask for a word or direction from him. But God answers with a pointed question: "Are ye come to enquire of me?" He swears by his own life that he will not give them an answer.

Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. Some of the elders sat down in front of him, waiting for a word from God. But God knew their hearts: his people had lived in rebellion and idolatry. So before answering them, he confronts them with their history of unfaithfulness, as the following context shows.

For today: we cannot come to God only to ask for help while we keep unconfessed sins. Before asking for guidance, it is good to examine the heart and return to him with sincerity. He receives with grace those who truly repent.
exp.44:3:
This verse says that a portion of the land set apart for God will belong to the priests who serve in the sanctuary, those who draw near to minister to the Lord. There they will have room for their houses, and also a holy place where the temple will stand.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the future temple and of the land divided among his people. The Israelites were in exile, and this vision gave them hope of restoration and order in worship. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it literally, others as a spiritual symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and he also wants what is holy to hold a central place. Let us set apart time and space in our lives for him, and support with gratitude those who serve in the church.
exp.45:9:
He says that the prince does not enter the temple separately or as someone above the others, but goes in together with the people when they come to worship, and goes out when they go out. The two words in the explanation that are old forms of "enter" and "go out" in its wording are not used here, so the sentence is simply translated as its meaning: here the prince mixes with the people during the festivals.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the vision of a new temple (chapters 40 to 48). He gives instructions about the order of worship. It is not known with certainty who "the prince" is: some think of a future leader, others of a symbolic figure, and others connect him with the Messiah. What is clear is that he too worships and submits to God's order.

For today: no leader stands above worship. We can remember that, whatever our role or position, we come to God alongside others, with humility and unity.
exp.39:34:
In this verse, a guide takes Ezekiel to the north gate of the temple and measures it using the same measurements as the earlier gates. The phrase "then he brought me" means the guide took him there. The phrase "he measured it according to these measures" means that this gate had the same size and design as the others.

Ezekiel records a vision he received while Israel was in exile. A man with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, step by step. Some believe it is a literal future temple, while others see it as a symbol of God's presence and holiness. The Bible does not fully explain it, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and He leaves nothing to chance. If He is concerned with every detail of His house, He is also concerned with the details of your life. You can trust that His plan is orderly and faithful, even when you cannot see the whole of it.
exp.40:23:
It says that each entrance to the temple had two doors, and that these doors "turned," meaning they were leaves that swung or folded on their hinges. Each doorway, both the one to the temple and the one to the inner sanctuary, had two leaves.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision that God gave him. A guide who looks like a man shows him and measures a new temple, with many details. Scholars disagree about its meaning: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we draw near to him. The doors speak of orderly and respectful access. We can approach God with reverence but without fear, remembering that in Christ we have open access to his presence.
exp.18:10:
It says the vine, which represents the mother of the prince, grew with strength. It had firm branches, so good that they were used to make scepters, that is, staffs of authority for rulers. It rose very high among the foliage and could be seen from afar, with many branches. The long shoots of the vine are the tendrils that spread out from its stem.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over the princes of Israel. The vine probably represents Judah or its royal dynasty, and its branches are the kings. Some think of specific kings, but the text does not make this entirely clear. The following verses show that this greatness ended in judgment and exile.

For today: blessings, success, and influence are no guarantee of security if we forget God. Let us be thankful for what he gives us, use what we have with humility, and remember that our strength comes from remaining in him.
exp.17:3:
God says that all people belong to him, both the father and the son. And that whoever sins is the one who will die. "Soul" here means the whole person, their life.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. They kept repeating a saying: the parents ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge, meaning the children pay for their parents' sins. With this they seemed to excuse themselves, as if they were not to blame. God rejects that saying and affirms that each person answers for himself before him. Some understand that "will die" refers mainly to the present consequences of sin, and others also to spiritual death.

Today we cannot blame our family or our past for our mistakes. Even if we inherit wounds, God invites us to repent and to begin again, with the assurance that we belong to him.
exp.21:2:
This verse is a message from God against a city, which from the context is Jerusalem. It accuses her of two serious sins: shedding innocent blood and making idols. The phrase "that her time may come" means that judgment is already drawing near. "Defile herself" means becoming impure before God.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," and charges him to declare the city's sins publicly. This happens during the time of the exile, when the people still remained in rebellion. God does not act on a whim: first he makes the guilt clear, and then he announces the consequences.

For today: a person cannot worship God and at the same time harm others. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts and whether our treatment of others reflects justice and compassion. God invites us to repent before the harm grows.
exp.43:16:
The explanation says that the priests, when they entered the inner court of the temple to serve, were to wear linen clothing and not wool. The phrase "will rest upon them" means "will be put on them" or "will be upon them." "Minister" means serving in the sacred duties of worship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a future temple. He first praises the priests who descended from Zadok, who remained faithful when Israel turned away from Him. Now He gives them rules for serving with order and reverence. Interpreters differ on whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic. The following text explains that the linen prevented sweating, meaning the service was to be done with calm and purity.

For today: serving God deserves care and respect. Whether you help in your church or at home, do it with a clean heart, without anxiety or pride, and with gratitude for the privilege of drawing near to Him.
exp.42:10:
God tells Ezekiel that if the people feel shame for their sins, he should show them the plan of the temple: its form, its entrances and exits, its measurements, and its rules. The word "plan" here means a design or blueprint. The word "layout" refers to how everything in it is arranged. Ezekiel must draw it before their eyes so that the people will carry it out faithfully.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. God promises to dwell among his people again, but first he wants a repentant heart. The vision of the temple shows the holiness of God. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future temple, and others as a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: sincere shame over sin is not the end, but the beginning of drawing near to God. If you recognize a failing, bring it before him and ask him for help to live according to his Word.
exp.17:6:
The righteous man, it says, does not abuse anyone or take advantage of the weak. If someone gave him something as security for a debt, he returns it. He does not steal, he shares his bread with the one who is hungry, and he gives clothing to the one who has none. The quoted word for "abuse" is rendered here as "oppress," meaning to treat harshly or take advantage of others; the word "pledge" refers to an item left as security for a loan, which the verse calls the debtor's pledge.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they suffered for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is responsible for his own life, and he describes how someone who is righteous lives. This verse is part of that list: righteousness includes honest and compassionate treatment of others.

For today: look this week at whom you can help in a concrete way, with food, clothing, or time. And check whether you should return something or pay what you owe. Obeying God also shows in how we treat those in need.
exp.31:6:
It says that when God brings an end to the pharaoh of Egypt, the heavens will grow dark: the stars will lose their brightness, the sun will be covered by clouds, and the moon will not give its light. The phrase "I shall put you out" means "I will finish with you," and "to darken" means to make dim. A thick cloud is what is meant by the word cloud.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the pharaoh, who was regarded as a powerful monster in the Nile. The darkness is poetic language, used in the Bible to speak of divine judgment. Many read it as imagery rather than a literal event; others also see an echo of the plagues of Egypt.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, stands above God. We can trust that He does justice, and we should avoid placing our security in money, prestige, or power.
exp.37:16:
God asks Gog, "Art thou he of whom I have spoken in old time by my servants the prophets of Israel?" He says that they prophesied that one day He would bring Gog against his people.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel. Gog is a leader from the north who will attack Israel in the latter days. God shows that this is neither a surprise nor a loss of control: He had already announced it. Scholars disagree about whether Gog is a historical figure, a future one, or a symbol of the evil that rises up against God. What is clear is that God rules and will be glorified.

For today: when the world seems chaotic and threatening, we can rest in the knowledge that God knows the future and remains in control. Trust his Word, pray calmly, and do not live ruled by fear.

sum.0: Ezekiel, a priest exiled by the Kebar River, sees the heavens opened and a great storm with fire. In it appear four living beings with several faces and wings, wheels full of eyes, and, above all, a throne of sapphire. There he sees a figure with the appearance of a man, surrounded by radiance, which is the glory of Jehovah, and he falls face down to the ground.
sum.6: In Ezekiel 7, God announces that the end has come for Israel because of its wickedness, its violence, and its idolatry. Neither gold nor silver will save them, and war, famine, and plague will come. No one will find peace or counsel, and so they will know that he is the LORD.
sum.10: In a vision, God shows Ezekiel the leaders of Jerusalem who give bad advice and fill the city with the dead, and He announces judgment on them. Then Pelatiah dies. God promises to gather the scattered people, give them a new heart, and be their God. After that, His glory leaves the city, and Ezekiel tells the exiles everything.
sum.11: God tells Ezekiel to act out the part of someone going into exile: he is to bring out his belongings by day, dig a hole through the wall, and leave at night with his face covered. This is a sign that the prince of Jerusalem and the people will be taken away as captives. God also says that he will not delay any longer in fulfilling his word.
sum.9: Ezekiel sees the cherubim and the wheels full of eyes again, with a sapphire throne above them. God commands the man dressed in linen to take burning coals and scatter them over the city. The glory of the LORD moves away from the threshold of the temple and stops at the east gate, showing that God is withdrawing from Jerusalem.
sum.2: God gives Ezekiel a scroll to eat, sweet as honey, and sends him to speak to a stubborn people. He gives him a hardened resolve so that he will not be afraid. He appoints him as a watchman, responsible for warning both the wicked and the righteous. Then he tells him that he will be shut in and unable to speak until God opens his mouth again.
sum.7: In a vision, God takes the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem and shows him the idolatry the people are practicing, even inside the temple: images, elders secretly burning incense, women weeping for Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun. Because of this, God announces that he will act in anger and will show no pity.
sum.5: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people were worshiping idols. He announces judgment by sword, famine, and plague, with their altars destroyed and their cities left desolate. But he promises that some will survive. Among the nations they will remember God, they will feel ashamed of their unfaithfulness, and they will know that he is the LORD.
sum.3: God tells Ezekiel to act out a sign showing the siege of Jerusalem: he draws the city on a clay tablet, lies on one side for many days bearing the wickedness of Israel and Judah, and eats only a small ration of bread and water. In this way he announces that the people will suffer hunger and distress because of their sin.
sum.8: God summons six executioners and a man dressed in linen to judge Jerusalem for its wickedness and violence. First, he marks the foreheads of those who grieve over all the detestable things being done, and they are protected, while the judgment begins at the sanctuary. Ezekiel pleads in distress, and the man in linen reports that he has carried out the command.
sum.1: God raises Ezekiel to his feet, gives him his Spirit, and sends him to speak to the Israelites, a rebellious and stubborn people, whether they listen or not. He tells him not to be afraid and not to rebel as they do, but to open his mouth and take in what God gives him. Then he sees a scroll written on both sides with laments and woes.
sum.4: God tells Ezekiel to shave off his hair and beard and divide it into three parts. This is a sign of what will happen to Jerusalem: some will die by fire, some will die by the sword, and others will be scattered. Jerusalem was placed at the center of the nations, but she rebelled and behaved worse than they did. Because of this, God will judge her with famine, disease, and war, so that they will know that he has spoken.
sum.32: God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman to warn Israel, and he tells him that He does not want the wicked to die, but to turn from their ways and live. Each person will be judged according to their own way, yet the people still refuse to obey. When the news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen, God announces judgment on the land and declares that they will know a prophet had been among them.
sum.19: Some elders of Israel come to consult God, but he refuses to answer them and reviews the history of their rebellion. From Egypt, through the wilderness and into the promised land, Israel kept following idols, and God acted for the sake of his name. He promises to judge them, gather them, and restore them. The passage ends with a prophecy of fire against the forest of the south.
sum.43: Ezekiel sees the east gate of the sanctuary shut, because the Lord entered through it, and only the prince may sit there to eat bread before God. Then God rebukes Israel for letting in foreigners who were not committed to him, and he assigns the unfaithful Levites to lesser tasks. The priests who were descendants of Zadok, who remained faithful, will serve close to God under rules of holiness.
sum.39: In a vision, fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem, God takes Ezekiel to a very high mountain in Israel, where a man with a measuring reed shows him a temple. The man measures in detail the gates, the courtyards, the tables for the sacrifices, and the chambers for the priests and singers, and he tells Ezekiel to report everything to Israel.
sum.21: God sends Ezekiel to denounce Jerusalem for its violence, its idolatry, and its injustice against the weak. Just as dross is melted down in a furnace, so the people will be gathered and purified under the fire of his anger. The leaders, prophets, and priests have failed, and God found no one who would stand in the gap.
sum.36: God takes Ezekiel to a valley full of dry bones, and as he prophesies, the bones come back to life and form a great army. This is a sign that God will restore Israel, which had lost hope and been scattered. Then, using two sticks joined together, God promises to gather Judah and Israel into one nation, cleanse them, give them a shepherd named David, and live among them in an everlasting covenant of peace.
sum.35: God promises to restore the mountains of Israel, which had been humiliated by the nations, and to fill the land again with people, crops, and cities. Israel had defiled the land and God's name with its sin and idolatry, and that is why it was scattered. But God will act for the sake of his holy name: he will gather his people, cleanse them, and give them a new heart and his Spirit.
sum.18: Ezekiel chants a lament over the princes of Israel. He compares their mother to a lioness whose two cubs, now grown into lions, were captured: one was taken to Egypt and the other to Babylon. He then compares her to a strong vine that was uprooted and planted in the wilderness, and fire consumed its branches. It is a funeral song mourning the fall of the kings.
sum.25: God announces judgment against Tyre, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem because it expected to profit from it. He will send Nebuchadnezzar and many nations to destroy her walls and riches, and the city will be left like a bare, smooth rock. The islands will tremble at her fall, and everyone will know that God is the Lord.
sum.16: God tells a parable about eagles and a vine. Babylon carried off the king of Judah, but that king broke his oath and sought help from Egypt, so he will not escape judgment. In the end, God promises to plant a shoot on the high mountain of Israel, and it will become a magnificent cedar where everyone will find shelter.
sum.37: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, a leader from the north who will gather many nations to attack Israel, a people living in confidence and without walls. God Himself will bring him in and destroy him with earthquake, sword, plague and fire. In this way the nations will know that He is the LORD, holy and great.
sum.13: Some elders of Israel came to consult Ezekiel, but God said they had idols in their hearts and called them to turn away from those idols. He then explained that even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in the land, they would only save their own lives, not the lives of their sons and daughters, when the four judgments came upon Jerusalem. Even so, a remnant would be left behind to bring comfort to the people.
sum.40: In this vision, a guide takes Ezekiel through the temple, measuring the entrance, the Holy Place, the Most Holy Place, and the chambers that surround the building. The walls were carved with cherubim and palm trees, and there was a wooden altar called "the table before the LORD." Everything shows order, holiness, and the presence of God.
sum.28: God announces judgment against Pharaoh, who thought he owned the Nile, and Egypt will be left desolate for about forty years because it was a "broken reed" to Israel. Afterward God will restore it, but as a humble kingdom. He also gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment, and promises to strengthen Israel.
sum.33: God rebukes the shepherds of Israel, who looked after themselves and mistreated the sheep, and promises to take the flock away from them. He himself will search for his people, rescue them, and care for them. He will judge between the strong sheep and the weak ones, and he will set his servant David over them as shepherd. He will give them peace, blessing, and safety.
sum.42: The glory of God returns from the east and fills the temple. God promises to live with Israel forever, if they give up their sins and idolatry. Ezekiel is to show the plan of the temple to the people, and the measurements of the altar and the offerings to purify it over seven days are given.
sum.31: God asks Ezekiel to sing a lament over Pharaoh, whom he compares to a river monster that will be caught, and he announces that Babylon's sword will destroy Egypt. Then Egypt is sent down to the place of the dead, along with other nations that spread terror. In this way God shows that no proud power escapes his judgment.
sum.14: God asks Ezekiel what good the wood of a vine is. It is useless for making anything, and even less so after it has been burned. The people of Jerusalem will be the same: God will turn against them, fire will consume them, and the land will be left desolate because of their unfaithfulness.
sum.29: Through Ezekiel, God announces that a day of judgment is coming upon Egypt and its allies. Babylon, under King Nebuchadnezzar, will be the sword that destroys its cities, its idols, and its power. God will break the arm of Pharaoh, and in this way the Egyptians will know that Jehovah is the Lord.
sum.30: God tells Pharaoh to compare himself with Assyria, a huge and beautiful cedar that gave shade to many nations. But Assyria's heart grew proud, so God handed it over to a powerful nation, which cut it down. The same fate awaits Pharaoh: pride ends in downfall and death.
sum.27: God condemns the prince of Tyre for thinking himself a god because of his wisdom and wealth, and announces that foreigners will bring him down. Then he laments over the king of Tyre, whose beauty and pride led him to sin and fall. Finally, he judges Sidon and promises Israel that they will return to their land and live in safety.
sum.41: In this vision, a guide leads Ezekiel through the outer courtyard and shows him chambers on several levels, to the north and south of the temple. He explains that they are holy: there the priests eat the offerings and change their clothes before going out to the people. Then the whole enclosure is measured, and its wall separates what is holy from what is common.
sum.17: God corrects the saying that children pay for their parents' sins: each person answers for their own life. The righteous person who turns away from God will die, and the wicked person who repents will live. God does not desire the death of anyone, and he calls Israel to turn back to him and receive a new heart.
sum.15: God shows Jerusalem as an abandoned infant girl whom He rescued, cared for, and adorned. But she trusted in her own beauty, gave herself to idols and to alliances with foreign nations, and even sacrificed her children. Because of this, she will be judged and shamed, worse than Sodom and Samaria. Even so, God promises to remember His covenant and restore her with mercy.
sum.44: God commands that a holy portion of the land be set apart for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, the city, and the prince. He tells the princes to stop using violence and to use honest weights and measures. He also sets out offerings and festivals, including the Passover, to make atonement for the people's sins.
sum.20: God tells Ezekiel that his sword of judgment will fall on Jerusalem and the whole land of Israel, without distinguishing between the righteous and the wicked, and the prophet must groan as a sign of anguish. The king of Babylon consults his divinations and decides to attack Jerusalem. God removes the crown from the wicked prince, and he will also judge Ammon.
sum.22: God uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), to show how his people were unfaithful to him with Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and with their idols. Samaria was handed over to her Assyrian lovers, and Jerusalem, who did not learn from her sister, would receive the same punishment. In this way God intends to put an end to that wickedness, so that they will know that he is the Lord.
sum.45: In this vision from Ezekiel, God gives rules for worship in the temple: when the eastern gate is opened, what offerings the prince presents, and the daily sacrifice of a lamb each morning. He also commands that the prince must not take land away from the people, and the places where the sacrifices are cooked are shown.
sum.47: Ezekiel describes how the land will be divided among the tribes of Israel, in strips running from east to west. In the center there is a holy portion set apart for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, the city, and the prince. The city will have twelve gates bearing the names of the tribes, and it will be called "The LORD Is There."
sum.38: God promises to destroy Gog and his armies on the mountains of Israel. Israel will burn their weapons and bury the bodies to cleanse the land. In this way the nations will know that God is holy and just. Then God will bring his people back, have mercy on them, and pour out his Spirit upon them.
sum.23: God shows Ezekiel the parable of a pot set over a fire. It stands for Jerusalem, a city full of blood and filth that will be burned in judgment. Then his wife dies suddenly, and God forbids him to mourn. This is meant as a sign that Israel will lose the temple and its sons and daughters and will be left without comfort. When the news arrives, Ezekiel will speak again.
sum.24: In Ezekiel 25, God announces judgment against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines, because they mocked Judah and Israel in their disaster, or took revenge against them. In this way it teaches that God sees pride and cruelty, and that he acts so that everyone will know that he is the LORD.
sum.26: God told Ezekiel to sing a lament over Tyre, the seafaring city that boasted of its perfect beauty. Tyre is described as a great ship, built with fine materials and made rich through its trade with many peoples. But a storm will sink it, and everyone will mourn its fall.
sum.34: God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir, that is, Edom, because it held an ancient hatred against Israel, handed Israel over to the sword in its time of distress, and wanted to take over its land. God heard their mockery and promises to leave it desolate. In this way it teaches that God sees wickedness and defends his people.
sum.12: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the prophets and prophetesses of Israel who were making up messages from their own hearts and saying "God says this" when God had not spoken. They were offering false peace, like a badly plastered wall that will collapse when the storm hits. God promises to judge them and to rescue his people from their deceptions.
sum.46: In a vision, Ezekiel sees a river flowing out from the temple, and the farther it goes, the deeper it becomes. Wherever it reaches, it brings life and healing, and trees grow along its banks with fruit and leaves used for medicine. Then God marks out the boundaries of the land and commands that it be divided among the tribes, including the foreigners who live among them.
